subject: ANTHRO
title: Landscapes of Health: Spaces, Species, and Social Worlds
description:
Epidemics, toxic exposures, natural disasters, and war increasingly show that health is not only a human issue. These processes involve multiple species and unfold in specific environments. Even when they become global, they take place somewhere. Space matters. 

This course examines health, space, things, and beings—human or otherwise—through an anthropological lens. It engages critically recent frameworks in the natural and medical sciences that seek to integrate humans, animals, and environments into health as a shared field of concern. In dialogue with approaches such as One Health and Planetary Health, the course asks what they make visible and what they leave out, emphasizing the social, political, historical, and spatial conditions through which health and illness are produced. 

Through readings in anthropology, geography, history, science and technology studies, as well as films and literature, students will analyze landscapes as sites of health. A hands-on component develops skills in observation, ethnographically focused spatial research, and analytical writing, enabling students to produce grounded accounts of how humans and other species inhabit and produce shared and at times contested environments.

course.subject: ANTHRO
course.title: Reading and Composition in Anthropology
course.description: Reading and composition courses based on the anthropological literature. These courses provide an introduction to issues distinctive of anthropological texts and introduce students to distinctive forms of anthropological writing, such as ethnography and anthropological prehistory. Readings will be chosen from a variety of texts by authors whose works span the discipline, from bioanthropology to archaeology and sociocultural anthropology. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.

subject: ANTHRO
title: The politics of infrastructure
description: Infrastructures are presently in a state of disarray. An international war has taken shipping infrastructures as its primary tactical object, greatly straining global energy systems; water reclamation projects in the U.S. southwest require bureaucratic and technological overhaul to withstand enduring drought; flood control mechanisms in the U.S. Gulf South face an existential fork, as their design, role, and sufficiency are (yet again) brought into question; the threat of energy-intensive data centers has provoked political disquiet throughout the U.S., as homeowners and tenants struggle to provision their homes — and on and on. This class takes up the question of infrastructures from an anthropological perspective, asking after their social and political content. Together we will consider early debates on the (contested) place and meaning of 'infrastructure' within anthropology, technopolitics and the relationship between infrastructure and the state, ecologies and/as infrastructure, infrastructure’s intimacies (how does infrastructure bear on one’s interiority, relationships, or sensory experiences?), and a contemporary (emergent?) politics of infrastructure. Through this R&C course, students will develop their skills in close reading, synthesis of complex texts, seminar discussion, and writing composition.

subject: ANTHRO
title: Zora Neale Hurston’s Spyglass: Writing the self
description: Historically anthropology has been a handmaid of colonial and imperial expansion; however, its method of ethnography has also been a powerful tool for challenging systems of power.  This course explores the formation of autoethnography and how writing the “self” into research becomes a powerful tool to challenge relations of power and deconstruct fixed ideas of race, gender, and place. Foregrounding the praxis of Black feminist anthropology and theory we will ask: What counts as autoethnography and how does one do it? What different forms can autoethnography take beyond the academy (text, art, media etc.)? From close readings of Barracoon by Zora Neale Hurston to Persepolis by the late Marjane Satrapi we will examine how anthropologists, literary scholars and artists use the “I” as a lens to critically analyze the social worlds around them. As part of the R5B series, this seminar emphasizes best practices for close reading and analytical writing. Students will gain writing skills such as finding and forming a research question, creating an outline, revising, and peer reviewing. Additionally, students will build research skills through engaging in community, keeping fieldnotes, and transcribing and coding data. At the end of the semester students will have a finalized autoethnographic research paper.

subject: ANTHRO
title: What is Science: An Anthropological Approach
description:
What is science? The different ideologies, disciplines, technologies, and media through which we respond to this question, oftentimes without a singular, satisfying answer, expose the messy web that science weaves in our modern life. In this course, we will engage with materials that attempt to untangle the web by answering a further set of questions: How science is made; What science is doing to our lives; and essentially, What is and/or is not science. 
 
We will start with historical accounts, ethnographies, and social studies that highlight the presumably null background of science-making; the institutionalization of labs, the politics of the clinics, and the particularity of histories and cultures. We will also engage in debates on the conditions of living in the world of science, whereas the dubious reality of "science" juggles between the altitude of technological optimism on one end, and a complete AI takeover on the other. At the end of the course, we will return to the question itself by either giving it a constructive answer, or diving deeper into the dark side to face science's many opponents: magic, pseudo-science, conspiracy theories, fiction, or even … collective consciousness.
 
This course encourages students to engage with the course materials not only as different versions of answers to "what is science" but also as a roadmap for formulating their own line of questioning, and further developing it through writing. How does a question come to be? What are the methods for answering and/or complicating them? And most significantly, why question at all? With these reflections, students will draft a research paper based on their own questions throughout the semester.
 
The workload of this course is organized primarily through reading and writing. Students are expected to show up in class having read the course materials. The assignments are designed for students to complete a research paper at the end of the semester, with each stage drafting specific sections or paragraphs. Students are expected to discuss their thoughts on the writing and receive feedback from the instructor at each stage.

subject: ANTHRO
title: A Survey of the Anthropology of Bears
description:
Oski and Ursa Major, Paddington and jukumari, the teddy bear and berserkir. Throughout time, special relationships and entanglements between humans and bears have been ubiquitous in places where they share space and resources. 



This course takes human-bear relationships across cultures as case studies in ideas relevant to anthropological research. Themes to be discussed include: the wielding of bears and bear imagery to channel physical, political, and spiritual power, the anthropomorphization of bears and its role in cultural perception, the association of bears and the wilderness concept in Western ontology, and the development of conservation as a cultural perspective. Students in this course will read broadly from ethnographic accounts, Indigenous science and philosophy, folklore, archaeological and historical analyses, and perspectives in conservation to grapple with human-bear relationships throughout time and space. They will investigate the various cultural perspectives that influence how humans understand bears, their relationship with them, and moreover, with the environment writ large. Assigned readings will expose students to the aforementioned variety of texts and develop their abilities in analysis, summary, and critique. Class meetings will center around textual analysis in a seminar format as well as workshops in research, outlining, drafting, and revision. Through a series of papers, students will progress their skills in research, argumentation, and analysis, culminating in the finalization of a research paper.

course.subject: ARABIC

course.description: Intensive reading and analysis of texts of different genres. Guest lectures, films, documentaries, oral presentations, research papers. Formal and informal styles of writing and correspondence. Extensive vocabulary building.
course.requirements: ARABIC 20B or ARABIC 30 with a minimum grade of C- or with the consent of the instructor.

subject: ARABIC
title: The Arab Renaissance: History, Literature, and Culture
description:
What was the Arab Renaissance(Nahda)? Was it a revival of a past that had never truly passed, or an “enlightenment” moment catalyzed by the Arabs’ encounter with European civilization in the early 19th century under colonial institutions? How did Arab thinkers and writers perceive their historical reality at the time? In what ways did they wrestle with their anxieties, aspirations, and ambitions—socially, politically, and culturally? And how were these concerns expressed through literary texts and cultural practices, and to what end? Was Arabic literary modernity born out of cultural and political submission to European hegemony; did it emerge as a reaction to Ottoman imperial rule; or was it a creative reconfiguration of Arab literary heritage aimed at keeping pace with the rapid transformations of the modern age?

In this advanced Arabic seminar, we closely examine the Arab Nahḍah by engaging with texts that vary in literary form, rhetorical strategy, and epistemic intent, authored by pioneering men and women. We explore how Arab intellectuals and writers imagined their civilizational condition during the 19th and early 20th centuries, responded to the cultural, social, and political questions of global modernity, defined a modern identity, and articulated their place among world nations.

subject: ARCH
title: Staging Replicas
description:
Replicas, copies, editions, duplicates, and substitutes abound in architectural work(s). Historically, reconstruction has been reserved for pre-modern buildings — acts of preservation that aspire to fix form and meaning in time. However, through contemporary art practices such as Thomas Demand’s photo–model–photo process, the logic of replication acknowledges how images circulate, how absence and mediation construct history, and how making itself becomes a mode of inquiry. This seminar examines the replica not as a fixed 1:1 copy but as an instrument that moves between model, drawing, photograph, and text, by approaching the CED archive as a staging site—a place where architectural and institutional knowledge is produced through acts of replication, reconstruction, and re-presentation. Between the archive and its supporting structures is a field of architectural work(s): logistics of display, material thresholds, labor, specifications, and systems of notation. By engaging archival models through drawings, notes, and specifications, students will reinterpret, restage, and reconstruct them not as faithful replicas but as critical re-presentations.

Through readings, discussion, and hands-on research, the course will examine conceptual frameworks for understanding archives and replicas, applying these schemas to develop design methodologies for the re-production of a model from the CED archive. Working in groups, students will be asked to translate archival material between formats, scales, and media, to develop productive frictions between representational and material conventions.

The seminar assumes enrolled students have a working knowledge of architectural drawings and model-making, and proficiency in Rhino and Illustrator. Shop access and training are required, specifically with the Zund.

course.description: This class introduces students to the history and practice of design theory from the late 19th century to the present, with emphasis on developments of the last four decades. Readings and lectures explore specific constellations of theory and practice in relation to changing social and historical conditions. The course follows the rise of modernist design thinking, with particular emphasis on the growing influence of technical rationality across multiple fields in the post World War II period. Systematic approaches based in cybernetics and operations research (amongst others) are examined in the context of wider attempts to develop a science of design. Challenges to modernist design thinking, through advocacy planning and community-based design, the influence of social movements and countercultures, and parallel developments in postmodernism within and beyond architecture, provide the critical background for consideration of recent approaches to design theory, including those informed by developments in digital media and technology, environmental and ecological concerns, questions surrounding the globalization of architectural production, and the development of new materials.

subject: ARCH
title: Spaces of Queer Theory
description:
This seminar examines the relationship between space, power and identity through the critical and creative frameworks of queer theory. Over the last two decades, queer theory has undergone a series of shifts and transformations, as its central concerns with challenging heteronormativity and institutional productions of gendered and sexed identities have been both broadened and decentered by intersecting forces of transgender, class, race, nationhood, and ecology amongst others. The result is a composite field in which queer theory operates in collaboration with an increasingly diverse array of conditions, spaces and identities. 

This course will move across spatialized contexts of power and difference while engaging with critical themes that include rethinking queer theory through intersectionality; crip theory, queer disability studies and the built environment; transgender and unbuilding; and urban space and queer black studies. The final segment of the class will focus on queer ecological imaginations, indigeneity and climate crisis. Course requirements include weekly reading responses, class presentations, and a final creative project related to one or more of the course themes. Spaces of Queer Theory is open to upper division undergraduates and graduate students from all disciplines within the CED and across the Berkeley campus.

subject: ARCH
title: Prepared Mass: Drawing Heat and Its Environments
description:
Buildings and their mechanical systems rely on energy to condition the environments we inhabit. In contemporary practice, the techniques of architecture that manage these conditions are typically defined through two primary systems: first, a membrane or enclosure that delineates favorable interior environments from exterior climates, and second, mechanical technologies that regulate the atmosphere within.

As global temperatures continue to rise due to climate change, conditions of heat are becoming increasingly central to architectural thinking. Regions historically characterized by temperate climates are experiencing longer and more intense heat events, while already hot regions face even more extreme environmental conditions. At the same time, equitably sourced material and energy resources are becoming more limited. In this context, architects must better understand the reciprocal relationship between matter and energy. Forward-looking environmentalisms cannot focus exclusively on mechanical systems or material systems alone, but must instead reconsider how the materials with which we build participate in conditioning interior environments—storing, releasing, and redistributing heat and air while demanding more or less energy to make buildings habitable.

Through the lens of thermal mass in hot and hot-arid climates, this seminar investigates how thermally massive buildings—and the architects who design them—can “prepare mass” that enables human inhabitation in environments defined by heat. The course focuses on experimental drawing as a method for visualizing environmental phenomena that are often invisible in architectural representation, including heat transfer, air movement, and thermal storage.

Students will study thermally massive case studies across hot climates through images, drawings, and model analysis while engaging weekly readings, responses, and collective discussions. Through iterative drawing exercises, students will develop techniques for representing thermal environments and atmospheric processes within architecture.

This is a conceptually focused course on architectural representation, emphasizing drawing as a tool for thinking about environmental forces. The seminar does not focus on quantitative performance metrics or the use of environmental simulation software; instead, students will explore how architects can visualize and reason about heat and atmosphere through drawings and physical models.

The seminar culminates in the construction of a chunk model, in which students build a fragment of a thermally massive assembly to understand  how material mass, geometry, and environmental forces interact to produce conditions of comfort.

Technical Expectations 
This course assumes prior proficiency in Rhino 3D modeling, architectural drawing, Adobe Illustrator/Photoshop. Students without advanced proficiency in these skills may find it difficult to keep up with the pace and expectations of the seminar. 

Making Expectations 
This course assumes prior proficiency in making and craft. Access and training in the CED Digital and Fabrication shops is required. Students should expect to expect to incur costs for model-making materials.

subject: ARCH
title: Modernity and Materiality
description:
Embodied within materials are multiple agencies, ‘natural’ behaviors, skills, systems of labor, modes of production, processes of extraction, laboratory science, cultural practices, symbolic meanings, formal suggestions, geopolitical relationships, human and geological histories. In short, materials operate on a far richer territory than the one starkly divided by claims of material ‘truth’ or authenticity invoked by modernist architects. This course aims to re-place architectural materials within this thick and historically layered territory. We begin with deceptively simple questions. Namely, “What is a material?” How do we begin to describe the complexity of a material? How are architectural materials connected to historical materialism and other approaches to understanding the world through its "material" conditions? 

This course focuses on three historical pivot points. We begin with an examination of the industrial revolution (and the introduction of industrially produced materials into architecture); followed by the synthetics revolution (when petroleum products made their way into the building materials industry). The final pivot point will examine a turn towards "sustainable materials". All three “pivot points” will be considered with respect to the new geological periodization of the Anthropocene.

subject: ARCH
title: Histories of Architectural Representation
description:
As a rule, architects do not build. They draw, write, annotate, diagram, model, map, sketch, photograph, animate, and otherwise visualize objects, spaces, and territories; they make visual and verbal presentations; they compile visual and written analyses and reports; and they issue visual and written instructions.

This lecture course traces these activities between the 15th c. (with Brunelleschi's 're-discovery of optical perspective) and the present, introducing key episodes in the history of architectural visualization across a variety of geographic and cultural contexts. The approach is thematic and follows a loose chronology built around concepts, problems, and practices associated with the long development of the architectural profession both within and outside of academia. In and through these, we will observe architectural knowledge being constructed, drawings and buildings interacting, and ideas, techniques, and imagery circulating.

Each lecture considers a specific set of cultural techniques within the history and theory of modern and contemporary architecture, the history of technology, and theories and practices of visualization. A limited number of drawings, models, photographs, films, and other visual artifacts will be analyzed in depth. Some readings situate these examples historically, while others offer conceptual orientation. Though formally a history and theory lecture, the course brings together concerns shared among different aspects of the CED architecture curriculum.

Material covered includes classical and modernist diagramming, travel sketches, orthographic projection, axonometry, representations of movement, perspective, construction drawings, urban cartography, architectural and aerial photography, atmospheric rendering, and stages of digitalization.

subject: ARCH
title: Urbanism
description:
What is Urbanism, and why does it seem to matter so much these days? Where do cities come from, is it possible to understand the forces that produce their streets, buildings, neighborhoods, regions, and the shape that they take? How can an operational understanding of Urbanism profoundly inform an Architect’s, Landscape Architect’s, or City Planner’s design practice? These are the questions this Seminar will interrogate through a series of Lectures, the analysis of canonical texts on the subject, and several brief exercises workshopped in class together. An interdisciplinary approach in the course will not seek
to produce a singular, shared answer to this inquiry, but rather, support each student to develop and define their own.

course.description: This course in particular focuses on the principles of architectural drawing and three-dimensional modeling, emphasizing precision in projection-based representation and digital modeling workflows. Students develop fluency in constructing and editing spatial representations through technical drawing, surface modeling, and volumetric exploration using professional tools (e.g., Rhino, Illustrator). Through structured exercises, students refine their ability to generate clear, communicative drawings and models that serve as foundational design representations.

Students engage with methods for simulating material properties, lighting conditions, and atmospheric effects to produce compelling visualizations that support design narratives. Emphasizing both technical precision and aesthetic considerations, the course equips students with the skills necessary to develop evocative architectural imagery for design presentation and critique.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: The Dialectic of Poetics and Technology
course.description: This seminar examines the relationship between technology and design philosophy in the work of architects through analysis of individual buildings within the context of the complete oeuvre and an examination of the architect's writings and lectures. The seminar poses questions such as: What is the role of technology in the design philosophy of the architect and how is this theoretical position established in the architect's writings, lectures, and interviews? A series of lectures explores these questions in relation to the architect and a set of required readings introduces the work of the architect and explores the relationship between technology and design philosophy.

subject: ARCH
title: Spaces of Queer Theory
description:
This seminar examines the relationship between space, power and identity through the critical and creative frameworks of queer theory. Over the last two decades, queer theory has undergone a series of shifts and transformations, as its central concerns with challenging heteronormativity and institutional productions of gendered and sexed identities have been both broadened and decentered by intersecting forces of transgender, class, race, nationhood, and ecology amongst others. The result is a composite field in which queer theory operates in collaboration with an increasingly diverse array of conditions, spaces and identities. 

This course will move across spatialized contexts of power and difference while engaging with critical themes that include rethinking queer theory through intersectionality; crip theory, queer disability studies and the built environment; transgender and unbuilding; and urban space and queer black studies. The final segment of the class will focus on queer ecological imaginations, indigeneity and climate crisis. Course requirements include weekly reading responses, class presentations, and a final creative project related to one or more of the course themes. Spaces of Queer Theory is open to upper division undergraduates and graduate students from all disciplines within the CED and across the Berkeley campus.

subject: ARCH
description:
This interactive class provides training in research skills and critical thinking in the field of Architecture, Building Science, Engineering with a focus on energy use, indoor environmental quality, and human well-being, comfort, and productivity. Readings will cover both building science theory and research methods, and classes will be organized around a series of individual and group homework. Topics will include literature review, design of both lab-based and field experiments, physical measurements, post-occupancy evaluation, statistical analysis and interpretation of data, data visualization, and methods of enhancing the spread and impact of scientific results (Wikipedia editing and public presentations). Throughout, we will discuss ways in which research can influence the design and operation of buildings, including building standards and codes.  Depending on the status of students’ thesis work or research interest, there will be opportunities to develop your research plans. All graduate students with learning how to do research are warmly welcomed.
The main aim of this course is to provide students with knowledge and abilities to 1) plan, develop, execute, interpret, and spread research in the architecture/building science/engineering and 2) develop fact/data-based answers to design questions concerning the impact of the built environment on humans, energy consumption, and sustainability.

Teaching philosophy: You can learn how to research by doing it. In this course, we will practice the research methods used in architecture and engineering. Many design choices can’t be verified. This course will teach how to find, interpret, manage, and use research data that feed an informed design approach.  A vital aspect of this class is flexibility. It is understood that students are all in different places regarding their experience (i.e., diverse academic backgrounds, humanities vs. science training, professional work experience, etc.) and thesis or dissertation progress. All assignments are intended to be flexible and can be modified to meet students’ particular needs and interests.
The class is conducted as a seminar and will mix presentations by the instructor with discussion, student presentations, class demonstrations, project reviews, and guest speakers. We will use hand-held instrumentation and introduce the laboratory facilities. The class is shaped around five mandatory, and one optional assignment developed to fulfill the learning objectives described above.

Topics will include literature review, design of experiments/simulations, physical measurements, post-occupancy evaluation, statistical analysis, data visualization, and spreading of scientific results.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Natural Cooling: Sustainable Design for a Warming Planet
course.description: Climate-responsive, person-centered design can reduce energy use, create experiential delight and connection to nature, and be more sustainable. This course covers design and operational strategies, low-and high-tech solutions, material choices, dynamic high-performance facades, natural ventilation, and a range of other integrated climate-control strategies most relevant to warm climates. Students will use interactive and experiential exercises, simulation tools, case studies, design exercises. Depending on the semester offered, students may also use the Building Science Wind Tunnel to test design solutions for natural ventilation.
course.requirements: ARCH 140 or 240 or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Mechanical Systems Design for Sustainable Buildings
course.description: This class will focus on how to design integrated mechanical systems for sustainable buildings. The building sector plays an important role in global warming, and it is critically important to reduce building energy use in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Roughly one-third of the primary energy consumed in buildings is used for controlling the indoor environment through Heating, Ventilating and Air Conditioning (HVAC) and lighting systems. Achieving net-zero or positive energy or carbon buildings demands the integration of architecture, structure, and building systems to optimize both passive and active systems.
course.requirements: Arch 140 or Arch 240 or consent of the instructor

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Daylighting in Architecture
course.description: Daylighting is a cornerstone of architecture design, a fundamental aspect of space making. The course focuses on design approaches to natural light, resorting to the study of precedents in modern and contemporary architecture, daylighting vocabularies and grammars, rules of thumb, field measurements, quantitative studies and computer simulations. Other topics include health and comfort, energy conservation, metrics and standards. Weekly sessions comprise both lectures and labs. Final projects are developed in groups and use both qualitative and quantitative methods to assess design solutions.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Building Energy Simulations
course.description: Energy saving in buildings is among the most cost-effective and environmentally sustainable measures to reduce greenhouse gasses emissions and energy consumption. 40% of the primary energy use and 75% of total U.S. electricity consumption is used in buildings. Computer-based energy analysis tools are important for architects, building designers, engineers, and sustainability consultants to use for evidence-based design, sustainability ratings, energy code compliance, building control and optimization, policy development, and assessment.
course.requirements: Arch 140 or Arch 240 or consent of the instructor

subject: ARCH
title: Sensory Spaces
description: This 10-week class is about how to create rich multisensory experiences in buildings, connecting people to nature, and embracing the value of environmental variability and delight. It advocates for design to embrace a broader view of experiential aesthetics, choreographing visual, thermal, acoustic and olfactory elements of the sensescape to contribute to the beauty and memorability of space. Students will learn about the science of sensory experience, and how this can be the basis for experiential design—a people-based approach where subtle variations alleviate experiential monotony and bring inhabitants’ back to the center of design intentions, all in support of simultaneously minimizing energy use, enhancing occupant well-being and supporting environmental stewardship. We will utilize observational exercises and case studies in support of simple design exercises. There will be a combination of individual and group assignments.

description: This 1-unit course focuses on what architects need to know about acoustics. The first part deals with the fundamentals of acoustics, including how sound levels are described and measured, and human response to sound. subject: ARCH
title: Prepared Mass: Drawing Heat and Its Environments
description:
"Buildings and their mechanical systems rely on energy to condition the environments we inhabit. In contemporary practice, the techniques of architecture that manage these conditions are typically defined through two primary systems: first, a membrane or enclosure that delineates favorable interior environments from exterior climates, and second, mechanical technologies that regulate the atmosphere within.

As global temperatures continue to rise due to climate change, conditions of heat are becoming increasingly central to architectural thinking. Regions historically characterized by temperate climates are experiencing longer and more intense heat events, while already hot regions face even more extreme environmental conditions. At the same time, equitably sourced material and energy resources are becoming more limited. In this context, architects must better understand the reciprocal relationship between matter and energy. Forward-looking environmentalisms cannot focus exclusively on mechanical systems or material systems alone, but must instead reconsider how the materials with which we build participate in conditioning interior environments—storing, releasing, and redistributing heat and air while demanding more or less energy to make buildings habitable.

Through the lens of thermal mass in hot and hot-arid climates, this seminar investigates how thermally massive buildings—and the architects who design them—can “prepare mass” that enables human inhabitation in environments defined by heat. The course focuses on experimental drawing as a method for visualizing environmental phenomena that are often invisible in architectural representation, including heat transfer, air movement, and thermal storage.

Students will study thermally massive case studies across hot climates through images, drawings, and model analysis while engaging weekly readings, responses, and collective discussions. Through iterative drawing exercises, students will develop techniques for representing thermal environments and atmospheric processes within architecture.

This is a conceptually focused course on architectural representation, emphasizing drawing as a tool for thinking about environmental forces. The seminar does not focus on quantitative performance metrics or the use of environmental simulation software; instead, students will explore how architects can visualize and reason about heat and atmosphere through drawings and physical models.

The seminar culminates in the construction of a chunk model, in which students build a fragment of a thermally massive assembly to understand  how material mass, geometry, and environmental forces interact to produce conditions of comfort.

Technical Expectations 
This course assumes prior proficiency in Rhino 3D modeling, architectural drawing, Adobe Illustrator/Photoshop. Students without advanced proficiency in these skills may find it difficult to keep up with the pace and expectations of the seminar. 

Making Expectations 
This course assumes prior proficiency in making and craft. Access and training in the CED Digital and Fabrication shops is required. Students should expect to expect to incur costs for model-making materials.

subject: ARCH
description: This course is the advanced structural design course at CED and is offered each year to a combined group of design, architecture and engineering students to explore new avenues of interdisciplinary collaboration. The course delves into the intricate relationship between geometry and structural behavior across various systems, categorized by their load-bearing mechanisms. In an era dominated by generative AI programs like Midjourney, which can produce visually stunning designs without considering physical constraints, this course addresses the growing gap between form generation and structural feasibility. Students will critically examine this disparity, focusing on vector-, form-, and surface-active structures, including wide-spanning space frames, cable nets, membranes, gridshells, and continuous shells. The curriculum begins with comprehensive lectures providing a holistic overview of these structural systems, coupled with discussions on both ancient and modern form-finding and analysis methods. Through a blend of playful physical and digital experiments, students will explore how different structural states influence a structure's shape and how this interplay can creatively drive the design process. The course incorporates software tutorials and targeted assignments to deepen understanding of cutting-edge numerical form-finding methods, utilizing advanced digital modeling and simulation tools. Students will gain insight into the mathematical foundations of these methods, enabling them to critically evaluate their applicability and limitations. Practical applications of modern form-finding techniques will allow simultaneous investigation and manipulation of form and structural states. Open discussions will focus on the detailing and realization of the designed systems. The course culminates in a final project where interdisciplinary teams apply their newly acquired skills to design a small architectural concept, installation, prototype, or mock-up. This course is tailored for students who have completed Arch 150, Arch 250, or an equivalent introductory structures course, with strong recommendations for prior knowledge of software programs such as Rhinoceros and Grasshopper.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Form and Structure
course.description: The class investigates the interplay between geometry and structural behavior of different structural systems categorized with respect to their load-bearing mechanism. Special focus is placed on form-active and surface-active structures like cable nets, membranes, gridshells, and continuous shells. The class will begin by providing a holistic overview of ancient and cutting-edge form-finding approaches and analysis methods. Using playful physical experiments, students will gain a hands-on understanding of how different structural states can affect the shape of a structure and how this interrelation could be used creatively to drive the design process.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Introduction to Construction, Graduate Level
course.description: This course addresses the methods and materials of construction. While students will not be experts at the end of the semester, the course should give students the confidence to feel comfortable on a construction site or when designing a small building for a studio. The course will focus on four major territories: structural materials, building envelope, built elements such as stairs and cabinets, and costs, labor conditions, conventional practices, and the regulatory environments that control design.

course.subject: ARCH
course.title: Off-Site Fabrication: Opportunities and Evils
course.description: This seminar looks at the implications of off-site fabrication in architecture: consistent, protected environments; worker efficiency and safety; coordination of trades; cheaper, semi-skilled labor; construction periods shortened; and completion dates more predictable. Off-site fabrication can allow for increased refinement and trial assemblies. However, it may also create monotonous sameness when the processes and results are not considered with care.
course.requirements: 160, 260 or consent of instructor.

subject: ARCH
title: Cheapskates: Experiments in Economy
description: How do we do more with less? Today, architecture is so expensive that very few can afford it, all in the face of a gaping housing shortage and a dearth of public amenities. We will investigate the design approaches of a series of ‘cheapskate’ architectures – termed as such for their emphasis on economy – to find opportunities for new forms of generosity and delight in architecture. A particular emphasis will be on the problems and opportunities unique to contemporary American construction. Through a series of readings, case studies, and speculative design rooted in architectural economy and standard construction methods, we will explore both the origins and contemporary reformulations of economy in architecture.

Drawing on a wide range of examples from architectural, design and art practice students will explore the technical and aesthetic dimensions of the material and speculate on its applications for the future.

subject: ARCH
title: Modernity and Materiality
description:
Embodied within materials are multiple agencies, ‘natural’ behaviors, skills, systems of labor, modes of production, processes of extraction, laboratory science, cultural practices, symbolic meanings, formal suggestions, geopolitical relationships, human and geological histories. In short, materials operate on a far richer territory than the one starkly divided by claims of material ‘truth’ or authenticity invoked by modernist architects. This course aims to re-place architectural materials within this thick and historically layered territory. We begin with deceptively simple questions. Namely, “What is a material?” How do we begin to describe the complexity of a material? How are architectural materials connected to historical materialism and other approaches to understanding the world through its "material" conditions? 

This course focuses on three historical pivot points. We begin with an examination of the industrial revolution (and the introduction of industrially produced materials into architecture); followed by the synthetics revolution (when petroleum products made their way into the building materials industry). The final pivot point will examine a turn towards "sustainable materials". All three “pivot points” will be considered with respect to the new geological periodization of the Anthropocene.

subject: ARCH
title: Histories of Architectural Representation
description:
As a rule, architects do not build. They draw, write, annotate, diagram, model, map, sketch, photograph, animate, and otherwise visualize objects, spaces, and territories; they make visual and verbal presentations; they compile visual and written analyses and reports; and they issue visual and written instructions.

This lecture course traces these activities between the 15th c. (with Brunelleschi's 're-discovery of optical perspective) and the present, introducing key episodes in the history of architectural visualization across a variety of geographic and cultural contexts. The approach is thematic and follows a loose chronology built around concepts, problems, and practices associated with the long development of the architectural profession both within and outside of academia. In and through these, we will observe architectural knowledge being constructed, drawings and buildings interacting, and ideas, techniques, and imagery circulating.

Each lecture considers a specific set of cultural techniques within the history and theory of modern and contemporary architecture, the history of technology, and theories and practices of visualization. A limited number of drawings, models, photographs, films, and other visual artifacts will be analyzed in depth. Some readings situate these examples historically, while others offer conceptual orientation. Though formally a history and theory lecture, the course brings together concerns shared among different aspects of the CED architecture curriculum.

Material covered includes classical and modernist diagramming, travel sketches, orthographic projection, axonometry, representations of movement, perspective, construction drawings, urban cartography, architectural and aerial photography, atmospheric rendering, and stages of digitalization.

title: What is to be done? The Crises of Design
description: This reading group will offer a collaborative framework for exploring readings and discussions related to the multilayered planetary crises that is shaping all aspects of our lives today. The readings for the class will be selected by those who participate. Four interrelated crisis conditions of democracy, ecology, economy and embodiment, will be examined as starting pointing for discussion of alternative futures. Upper Division Undergraduates and Graduate Students from across the campus are welcome to attend.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Production, Industrial Organization, and Regulation in Agriculture
course.description: Basic concepts of micro and welfare economics: partial and general equilibrium. Industrial organization: monopolistic competition, vertical integration, price discrimination, and economics of information with applications to food retailing, cooperatives, fishing, and energy.
course.requirements: Economics 201A or equivalent or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Probability and Statistics
course.description: This is an introduction to probability theory and statistical inference. It is primarily intended to prepare students for the graduate econometrics courses 212 and 213. The emphasis of the course is on the principles of statistical reasoning. Probability theory will be discussed mainly as a background for statistical theory and specific models will, for the most part, be considered only to illustrate the general statistical theory as it is developed.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Applied Econometrics
course.description: Standard and advanced econometric techniques are applied to topics in agriculture and resource economics. Techniques include limited dependent variables, time series analysis, and nonparametric analysis. Students will use computers to conduct statistical analyses.
course.requirements: 211 and 212 or equivalent or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Econometric Project Workshop
course.description: Techniques for preparing econometric studies, including finding data sources, the reporting of results, and standards for placing research questions with existent literature. With faculty guidance, students prepare approved econometric projects, present projects to the class, provide comments on other student projects, and revise projects in response to faculty and student comments.
course.requirements: 210, 211, and 212 or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Economics and Policy of Production, Technology and Risk in Agricultural and Natural Resources
course.description: This course covers alternative models of production, resource and environmental risk management; family production function; adoption and diffusion; innovation and intellectual property rights; agricultural and environmental policies and their impact on production and the environment; water resources; pest control; biotechnology; and optimal control over space and time.
course.requirements: 201 and 202, or Economics 201A-201B, or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Agricultural, Food, and Resource Policy Workshop
course.description: Presentation and criticism of ongoing research by faculty, staff and students. Not necessarily offered every semester.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Rural Economic Development Workshop
course.description: Presentation and criticism of ongoing research by faculty, staff and students. Not necessarily offered every semester.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Environmental and Resource Economics
course.description: Theory of renewable and nonrenewable natural resource use, with applications to forests, fisheries, energy, and climate change. Resources, growth, and sustainability. Economic theory of environmental policy. Externality; the Coasian critique; tax incidence and anomalies; indirect taxes; the double dividend; environmental standards; environmental regulation; impact of uncertainty on taxes and standards; mechanism design; monitoring, penalties, and regulatory strategy; emissions markets.
course.requirements: Ph.D.-level economic theory or consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Natural Resource Economics Workshop
course.description: Presentation and criticism of ongoing research by faculty, staff, and students. Not necessarily offered every semester.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

course.subject: ARESEC
course.title: Microeconomics of Development
course.description: Theoretical and empirical analyses of poverty and inequality, household and community behavior, and contract and institutions in the context of developing countries.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

subject: ARMENI
description:
THE 101A-101B COURSE SEQUENCE BEGINS IN THE FALL TERM ONLY.

Armenian 101A is designed for students with a diverse range of language proficiencies, from second-year language learners to heritage speakers to those formally educated in the language. The course emphasizes reading and analyzing literature (fictional prose, drama, and poetry) and film as a means of language acquisition. Students will hone their language skills through discussions, written assignments, and a variety of creative group activities. While students choose whether they wish to write and speak in Eastern or Western Armenian, they also learn to navigate both literary standards with greater ease.

Course may be repeated for credit.

Texts: All readings will be made available on bCourses. Selections will be determined based on student proficiency.

Prerequisites: Armenian 1A-1B or consent of instructor.

Requirements: weekly homework (reading, annotation, viewing, and writing assignments); performative reading of a play; journaling; class participation; weekly reading aloud recordings; presentation; and take-home final exam.

course.subject: ARMENI
course.title: Continuing Armenian
course.description: The purpose of this course is to further develop students' Armenian proficiency in all four language skills, using discussion, oral presentations, written assignments, and a variety of readings (literature, non-fiction, folklore, newspaper articles, etc.) chosen partly for their cultural significance and partly based on student needs and interests. Emphasis on particular skills (e.g. reading) depending on student needs and interests.
course.requirements: 1A-1B or consent of instructor.

subject: ARMENI
description:
THE 1A-1B COURSE SEQUENCE BEGINS IN THE FALL TERM ONLY.

Armenian 1A is for students with no or almost no knowledge of Armenian. It begins by covering the alphabet, after which it emphasizes basic reading, writing, speaking, listening, and translating skills. The two literary standards of modern Armenian, Eastern and Western, are taught through parallel lessons. Students will gain an understanding of the commonalities and differences between the two standards, while choosing the one they wish to study.

Required Text: Practical Textbook of Western Armenian by Haroutiun Kurkjian (any edition), available online at Abrilbooks.com and Amazon, ASIN: B003IGI1P4.

Prerequisite: None.

Requirements: weekly homework (textbook exercises); five quizzes; reading aloud assignments; class participation; and take-home final exam.

course.subject: ARMENI
course.title: Introductory Armenian
course.description: An introduction to Armenian language and culture, aiming to give students basic competence in all four skills and an introduction to traditional and contemporary Armenian culture.
course.requirements: 1A: None. 1B: 1A or equivalent; consent of instructor.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Painting: Research and Methods
course.description: This studio course for Art Practice majors involves practical and experimental research into the varied processes, skills, materials, and methods of historical and contemporary painting. Emphasis on creating unconventional drawing/painting tools, making pigments for painting, and examining unofficial and official archives as source materials will be an integral part of the course. Students will expand their technical, conceptual, and professional skills, and will develop self-generated projects and critical engagement through critiques and open discussion. Students will attend library tours and field trips, and explore mediums and concepts to generate research for long-term investigation. Prerequisites: ART 8 and ART 13 or equivalents
course.requirements: ART 8 and ART 13 or equivalents.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Painting: Reconsidering the Portrait & Figure
course.description:
This studio course investigates histories of portraiture, including how dominant signifiers of race, gender, class, religion, and their various intersections determine which and how individuals are depicted. The course includes working from live models, creating self-portraits that challenge conventional expectations, lectures, student lead discussions, in-class prompts, field trips, and visiting artists. The course will examine the politics of representation through different collusions of art and history. We will reconsider how conventional portraiture has impacted relationships within the past and present, and consider future possibilities.

Prerequisites: ART 13 Painting: Foundations or by permission of instructor.
course.requirements: ART 13 Painting: Foundations or by permission of instructor.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Ancient Pigments & Contemporary Drawing Practices
course.description: This is an advanced studio drawing course that compares and contrasts traditional Asian and European pigments, surfaces, and images with contemporary strategies, sources, and methods.  Students will use various traditional hand-made pigments, binders, papers, and drawing materials to explore cultural developments and representations of space, time, and objects. A major course outcome is to create hybrid, diverse content that combines contemporary images and narratives with traditional historic sources. The course provides lectures, demonstrations and studio research methodologies.
course.requirements: ART 8 and ART12 or equivalent

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Drawing: Remixing the Figure
course.description:
This studio course investigates representations of the human body across different periods and locations to explore what it means to depict the body in the 21st Century. How do dominant signifiers and various intersections of race, gender, class, religion, sexuality, and disability influence the rendering and image reception of human bodies? The studio component of the course will work from live models as well as creating full body self-portraits that challenge the parameters of the canon and conventional expectations. We will explore drawing across all mediums through art history lectures, student-led discussions, in-class prompts, field trips, and visiting artists. 

Prerequisites: ART 12 or by permission of instructor.
course.requirements: ART 12 or equivalent

course.subject: ART
course.title: Global Perspectives in Contemporary Art
course.description: What is the contemporary art world? Where is its center? And, what is on the periphery? This seminar course will examine contemporary art production and place it within the larger framework of a global culture. The discussions, readings, presentations, and assignments will address themes of imperialism, the diaspora, migration, otherness, technology, materiality, and the environment. We will pay close attention to writings by artists in articulating the aspirations and values of art in the present. In addition, we will examine centers of cultural influence including museums, galleries, and the increasing range of biennials—from Karachi to Senegal to Sao Paulo. This course is a requirement for the Art Practice major.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Drawing: Foundations
course.description: This course will explore a wide range of approaches to mark making, composition and materials for building a drawing practice. Students will engage with drawing from life as well as conceptual and abstract compositions. This course will feature lectures, field trips, visiting artists and demonstrations in order to expose students to a variety of applications, methods and techniques within the field of drawing. This course is a recommended prerequisite for upper division Drawing classes.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Printmaking: Screen Print
course.description: This class teaches the fundamentals of screen printing, which requires images to be converted into stencils and secured to a matrix through which ink can be transferred. Hand drawn, photographic and digitally manipulated images are explored. Image content and development is examined through primary research drawings and studies. Screen printing requires the use of specialized tools and equipment; students will therefore learn and adhere to proper safety and shop procedures. Students’ progress is assessed by individual and group critiques.
course.requirements: Open to upper division art majors or by consent of instructor.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Painting: Foundations
course.description: This course will introduce students to a broad scope of painting practices. Students will learn about and challenge conventions as well as experiment with modes of viewing, producing and engaging with painting within historical and contemporary contexts. This course will feature lectures, field trips, visiting artists and demonstrations in order to expose students to a variety of painting applications, methods and techniques. This course is a recommended prerequisite for upper division Painting classes.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Ceramics: Research and Methods
course.description:
This course builds on the foundations of ART 15 to introduce students to more advanced techniques, concepts, and technologies. From traditional forms to experimental structures, students will connect ceramic processes to larger fields of contemporary art. This course encourages interdisciplinary thinking and pushes students to think of material as metaphor. Methods may include: casting and mold-making, wheel throwing, handbuilding, mixed media assemblage, collaboration, ceramic 3-D printing/modeling. Field trips, artist lectures, and readings/discussion will accompany studio time.

Priority enrollment for Art Practice majors and intended Art Practice majors. 
Prerequisites: ART 15 Ceramics: Foundations or by permission of instructor.
course.requirements: ART 15 or equivalent

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Sculpture: Meaning in Material
course.description:
This advanced studio class will investigate the physical and conceptual potential of materiality in sculpture, while exploring what methods and materials may be considered non-traditional. Combining hands-on demonstrations with group critiques and studio practice, students will focus on building a strong conceptual foundation while developing and expanding practical studio skills. Students will explore topics through self-generated projects, lectures, readings, and field trips.

Priority enrollment for Art Practice majors and intended Art Practice majors. 
Prerequisites: ART 14 Sculpture: Foundations or by permission of instructor.
Prerequisites: ART 14 Sculpture: Foundations or by permission of instructor.
course.requirements: Art 14 or equivalent

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Sculpture: Radical Wearables
course.description:
How have contemporary artists used textiles, garments, and "fashion- like"
sculptures to create artworks that challenge issues of gender, identity, and
use? Far from being neutral territory, artist-produced props and wearables
often incorporate aesthetic experimentation in order to critique existing
power structures and highlight alternatives. This hands-on studio course will
focus on the production of experimental costumes, garments, and fashion
in the context of contemporary art and critical ideas.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Sculpture: Foundations
course.description: This course is the study of the interaction between physical form and space. We will focus on building a strong conceptual foundation while developing the practical studio skills needed to translate your ideas into three dimensions. Shop practices will include hand, machine, and computer-aided fabrications. Field trips and illustrated talks will help acquaint students with the ideas sculptors have explored through history and in contemporary sculptural practices. This course is a recommended prerequisite for upper division Sculpture classes.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Ceramics: Foundations
course.description: This course will prepare students to use ceramics to explore and understand three-dimensional space. We will develop a practical understanding of how clay and glaze behave, while building a conceptual framework through which to apply this knowledge. Studio practice includes hand building, modeling, carving, and glazing as possibilities for turning ideas into three dimensional propositions. Assignments, critiques and class discussions will help acquaint students with the ideas artists have explored through history and in contemporary sculptural practices. This course is a recommended prerequisite for upper division Ceramics classes.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Printmaking (Relief & Intaglio): Foundations
course.description: The process and techniques of traditional relief and intaglio printing are explored in this fine art printmaking course. Lectures and demonstrations introduce students to two of the historically oldest and most continuous of print processes. Unique drawing skills are demonstrated for students to render images onto linoleum and metal plates to produce small editions of relief and intaglio prints. This course is a recommended prerequisite for upper division Printmaking classes. Additional fees required.

subject: ART
title: Relief through Text, Texture and Technique
description: This course explores relief printmaking through various times, forms and materials. Our work will span ancient technology, textiles, democratization of text, consumer goods, decorative craft, and contemporary art. Relief is the oldest form of printmaking, which stems from the human desire to spread text, images and ideas to one another. Today, relief printmaking can be a generative way to explore repetition, layering, materials, pattern, attention, labor, and printed multiples. Topics in this class range from technical and traditional to experimental and modern, as we survey this fundamental practice which has roots across the globe. Students will advance techniques in woodcut, color reduction and registration but will also explore conceptual and contemporary approaches in social practice, post-digital-print and DIY culture. Alongside intensive art projects, the course will consist of experiments, research, discussions, field trips, readings, critiques and presentations. Through process-oriented work, students will gain true comprehension of their craft while navigating a collaborative printshop environment. Students will be encouraged to explore their personal research, interests, and goals in art practice and printmaking, culminating in an ambitious final project.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Special Topics in Visual Studies
course.description: Special Topics courses offer students opportunities for more concentrated focus beyond general curriculum offerings. Courses may align with an instructor’s own research, they may propose topics responding to contemporary events and issues, or they may offer a specialized skill. Primarily intended for advanced undergraduates and graduates in Art Practice but open to others.

subject: ART
title: Artificial Art
description:
Artificial intelligence is often framed as a frictionless technology of the future, but its systems are built on vast material infrastructures. This studio course takes a critical look at AI through artistic practice. Students will experiment with generative tools while exploring how artists are engaging machine learning and other algorithmic systems in their work.Through hands-on projects and discussion, the class considers questions of authorship and what it means to make art with — and about — computational systems.

At the same time, the course investigates the ecological and material realities behind AI. We will look at the energy demands of data centers, the extraction of minerals used in computing hardware, the environmental costs of large-scale computation, and the global labor networks that sustain AI technologies. Students will develop projects that engage these hidden infrastructures, using artistic practice to question how technological “progress” shapes the environment and our collective future.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Art, Medicine, and Disabilities
course.description: This interdisciplinary studio course explores how contemporary art and disability studies intersect. Through lectures and readings, students engage with the history of disability justice and activism, depictions of disabilities in art, disability art theory, and the work of historical and contemporary artists with disabilities, chronic illnesses, and cognitive differences. The course considers intersectional representations of bodies, disability as identity, accessibility, interdependence, care work, medicine, and healing as a socio-political, cultural, and collective practice. Students connect critical theories with personal creative practice to develop self-directed projects grounded in lived experience, communal care, and solidarity.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Printmaking Foundations: Screenprint
course.description: This class teaches the fundamentals of screen printing, which requires images to be converted into stencils and secured to a screen through which ink can be transferred. Lectures and demonstrations introduce students to current procedures and historical practices. Students will develop hand-drawn, photographic, and digitally manipulated images, and will learn print workflow procedures and safety procedures to create limited-edition prints. These will be assessed through individual and group critiques.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Video Projects
course.description:
This course develops more advanced technical and conceptual skills in video art, with focused attention on the pre- and post-production practices of writing and production design as well as image and sound editing. Class meetings include technical workshops, studio work, individual and class critique, and discussion of readings and screened course materials. Course projects vary in focus depending upon instructor; areas of emphasis may include: video in performance practices; video for sculptural installation; and social activist video.

Priority enrollment for Art Practice majors and intended Art Practice majors.
course.requirements: 8, 12, and 26; or equivalents.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Digital Media: Computer Graphics Studio
course.description:
Computer Graphics constitute a default method of image synthesis, from fine art to game design, cinema, and advertising. This production-intensive studio course introduces students to professional CG tools (Blender, Python) as well as an overview of CG aesthetics. Weekly project assignments based on tutorials cover modeling, texturing, lighting, animation, rendering, physics simulations and data-driven image synthesis. Final projects focus on portfolio work with scenes and characters to be exported into VR, AR, and game design. Current laptop or desktop with good graphics performance required.

Priority enrollment for Art Practice majors and intended Art Practice majors.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Electro-Crafting
course.description:
This studio class aims to provide students with the digital tools for expanding and augmenting their work in traditional media such as photography and sculpture, and also to encourage the exploration of new hybrid forms of art-making. If you are interested in exploring sound, sensors, immersive experience, interactivity, bots, wearable computing, gamification, AI, feedback systems, process-oriented artwork or data-driven artworks in any media--then this may be the class for you. Students will learn to use basic software and hardware for the manipulation of sound, image and video that were designed by artists for artists, like: pf5.js, sonic pi, makey-make, arduino and others.

Priority enrollment for declared or intended Art Practice Majors

course.subject: ART
course.title: Advanced Digital Photography
course.description: This course will cover a range of digital media and practices, with a view towards exploring current and future possibilities for photography. Inclusive of multiple approaches to scale, execution, and technique, the course enables students to examine and push the limits of photographic practices. This course will help students advance their digital shooting and Photoshop skills from a beginning to a more advanced level, and will cover the workflow of digital photography: camera usage, scanning, image editing, management, and printing. Priority enrollment for Art Practice majors and intended Art Practice majors. Prerequisites: ART 21 Digital Photography: Foundations or by permission of instructor.
course.requirements: ART 21 or equivalent

course.subject: ART
course.title: Junior Seminar: Meaning and Making
course.description: This immersive studio/seminar class for Art Practice majors and intended Art Practice majors focuses on contemporary models of art making, exposing students to current issues in the art world, and fostering interdisciplinary models of thinking and making. Through field trips to museums, galleries, and alternative art spaces, as well as studio visits with local contemporary artists, students will be able to situate their own projects within the larger sphere of contemporary art. Language and writing skills around artist statements, critical readings, and the critique process will be emphasized to understand how research methods give meaning in a studio practice. Includes presentation of a final studio project.
course.requirements: Junior level students, with the permission of the instructor.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Senior Projects/Professional Practices
course.description: This course helps students understand their work within critical and professional cross-disciplinary contexts, and prepares students for graduate school and life beyond. Through class and individual critiques, readings, guest artists, and field trips, students explore practical and conceptual components of their own media and practice within broader discussions of artistic production. The class will help develop tools for supporting one's work within a community of artists, arts professionals, and arts organizations, including developing an online presence, producing and sustaining exhibition-ready work, completed portfolios, documentation, presentation, written artist statements, etc.
course.requirements: Senior level students only.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Digital Photography: Foundations
course.description: This course introduces students to technical skills including manual functions of digital cameras, image creation and capture, file management and workflow, image adjustment and digital printing. Assignments will use primary Adobe software tools to test creative possibilities of both the camera and the computer. The course will introduce students to photography history and theory, and a range of contemporary practices. Group critiques and individual tutorials will help develop ideas and technical skills. By the end of the course, students should feel comfortable shooting digitally, editing and producing final images for print or the web. This course is a recommended prerequisite for upper division Photography classes.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Seminar: Theory and Criticism
course.description: Weekly meetings will provide a forum for the discussion of issues related to assigned readings in the fields of esthetics, theory and art criticism.
course.requirements: Graduate standing and consent of instructor.

course.subject: ART
course.title: DIGITAL MEDIA: FOUNDATIONS
course.description: Data and logic form core interfaces for information technology. New media art requires understanding their key dynamics. Students gain experience with data generation, visualization, and their impact on real persons, environments and situations. Can we measure, count and weigh everything? Is data fair? What is the role of privacy? How do digital conditions affect human conditions? From memes to machine learning, students participate in emerging data cultures including sampling, visualization, animation, video, interactive design, and music. Assignments follow readings on media and design theory, abstraction, interactivity, archives, performance, identity, privacy, automation, aggregation, networking, diffusion, diffraction and subversion.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Graphic Novel: Foundations
course.description: Using the format of the graphic novel as a site of investigation, this studio production class will explore graphic novels as dynamic political, societal, historical, and cultural vehicles. Using creative research methods of analysis, fabrication, and collaboration, students will create their own graphic novel elements as artistic responses to their diverse life experiences. Production assignments will inform students about possible relations between text and image, frame and page, page and narrative arc, imagination and reality, and finally book and audience. Guest lecturers will share different writing styles, drawing and coloring techniques including digital painting, and storytelling methods.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Moving Image: Foundations
course.description: A practical and critical introduction to moving image media, focusing primarily on independent and experimental film and video art. Students learn video production and post-production and are introduced to key moments and concepts in moving image history and criticism. Course instruction includes basic camera operations, sound recording, and lighting, as well as basic editing, compression, and dissemination formats. Solo and group assignments are completed, and group critiques of class projects train students to recognize and discuss the formal, technical, critical and historical dimensions of their works. Weekly readings in philosophy, critical theory, artist statements and literature are assigned.

course.subject: ART
course.title: Art, Water and California
course.description: Water is one of the most precarious resources in California, yet many people believe the water supply to be unlimited. The arts and visual cultures contribute to such popular misconceptions of natural resources, but media art can also help people develop more accurate and relevant conceptions of natural resources. The course introduces students to interdisciplinary creative research and media art production with the end goal of advancing popular conceptions about water. Students study water cultures in California from the 1750's onwards and experience a wide range of watercourses and waterworks  to inspire new art. Art projects include data visualization, short fiction, billboard designs, and interactive gallery displays.

course.subject: ART
course.title: The Teaching of Art: Practice
course.description: MFA course utilizing aspects of pedagogical and andragogical teaching, the interactive lecture, collaborative learning, simulations, and brainstorming-freewriting, this semester-long seminar will focus on these various intergrative teaching approaches, to facilitate communication in the diverse and wide-ranging arena which is fine arts today. Discussion of course aims, instructional methods, grading standards, and special problems in the teaching of art practice.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

course.title: Introduction to Visual Thinking
course.description: A first course in the language, processes, and media of visual art. Course work will be organized around weekly lectures and studio problems that will introduce students to the nature of art making and visual thinking. This course is a prerequisite for applying to the Art Practice major.
