course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Environmental Fluid Mechanics I
course.description: Fundamental fluid mechanics with application to the environment. Analytical solutions and numerical modeling of advection-diffusion and Navier-Stokes equations, with a focus on understanding both the numerical techniques needed to predict environmental flow and transport and the underlying physical processes described by the mathematical equations. Fluid kinematics, scalar transport, numerical error and stability analysis, scaling analysis, channel flows, Stokes flows, and introduction to turbulence.
course.requirements: Undergraduate fluid mechanics, basic computer programming or permission of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Water Quality Engineering
course.description: The fundamental concepts of physical, chemical, and microbiological processes that affect water quality in natural and engineered environmental systems. Focus is on developing a qualitative understanding of mechanisms as well as quantitative tools to describe, predict, and control the processes that effect water quality. The class consists of three main parts: (1) Physical Processes: mass balance, chemical kinetics, reactor hydraulics, reactor models; (2) Biological processes: microbiological principles, pathogens, and microbial transformations; (3) Chemical contaminants: properties, partitioning and reactivity.
course.requirements: CE 111 (Introduction to Environmental Engineering), CE 115 (Water Chemistry)

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Air Quality Engineering
course.description: Quantitative overview of the characterization and control of air pollution problems. Summary of fundamental chemical and physical processes governing pollutant behavior. Analysis of key elements of the air pollution system: sources and control techniques, atmospheric transformation, atmospheric transport, modeling, and air quality management.
course.requirements: Graduate standing in engineering or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Structural Analysis Theory and Applications
course.description: Theory and applications of modern structural analysis. Direct stiffness method. Matrix formulations. Virtual work principles. Numerical solution methods. Modeling and practical analysis of large frame structures. Elastoplastic analysis of frames. P-delta effects.
course.requirements: 121 or equivalent.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Dynamics of Structures
course.description: Evaluation of deformations and forces in structures, idealized as single-degree of freedom or discrete-parameter multi-degree of freedom systems, due to dynamic forces. Evaluation of earthquake-induced deformations and forces in structures by linear response history analysis; estimation of maximum response by response spectrum analysis; effects of inelastic behavior. Laboratory demonstrations.
course.requirements: 220 (may be taken concurrently) or equivalent.

subject: CIVENG
title: Waves --- ideal, real, and in between
description: Waves are everywhere, including biology, ecology, sociology and physics. We will examine many types of waves, with a particular emphasis on the water waves encountered in oceanography and environmental engineering. We will focus less on the wave dynamics as taught in physics classes and more on how many of the wave types observed in nature do not fit into this rather narrow mathematical description. For each wave type we explore, we will examine some of the creative ways that applied mathematicians have tried to capture essential features of the wave. We will then explore the limits of these approximate models, and discuss the practical implications of making engineering decisions based on idealized models. The class will read chapters from popular-science books on waves, with supplementary material presented in class to motivate and support group discussions.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Freshman Seminars
course.description: The Berkeley Seminar Program has been designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small-seminar setting. Berkeley seminars are offered in all campus departments, and topics vary from department to department and semester to semester.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Concrete Technology
course.description: Properties of fresh and hardened concrete; strength, elastic behavior, creep, shrinkage, and durability to chemical and physical attacks. New concrete-making materials. Recent advancements in concrete technology: high-strength, high-workability, and high-performance concrete; fiber-reinforced concrete, and roller-compacted concrete.
course.requirements: 165 or equivalent.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Reinforced Concrete Structures
course.description: Analysis and design of reinforced concrete elements and systems that are common in building and bridge structures, with an emphasis on seismic response and design; structural design methods; reinforced concrete materials; confined concrete; line elements under axial, flexural, and shear loadings; bond, anchorage, and development; seismic design principles; earthquake-resistant building frames, walls, diaphragms, and foundations; earthquake-resistant bridges.
course.requirements: Civil and Environmental Engineering 123.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Operation of Transportation Facilities
course.description: The management of vehicle flows and fleets. Traffic stream properties and their measurement. Theories of traffic flow. Capacity analysis and queueing. Flow control and fleet scheduling.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Systems Analysis in Transportation
course.description: The systems approach and its application to transportation planning and engineering. Prediction of flows and level of service. Production functions and cost minimization. Utility theory and demand modeling. Transportation network analysis and equilibrium assignment. Decision analysis and evaluation of transportation projects.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Global Metropolitan Studies: Introduction to Theories, Histories & Methods
course.description: Implications of increasing urbanization are widespread: from environmental challenges, to segregation, to new political and social movements. This course provides an overview of different disciplinary approaches to understanding urban systems, drawing on engineering, the social sciences, urban planning, and the natural sciences. Students will learn from other disciplines to enrich the study of cities within their own field and be better prepared for interdisciplinary collaborations.
course.requirements: PhD standing (any discipline)

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Transportation Sustainability
course.description: This multi-disciplinary course is intended to introduce students to the fundamentals of sustainable transportation, with an emphasis on: 1) current trends, climate and energy science, and the policy context; 2) methodological and analysis techniques; 3) vehicle technology, fuels, and intelligent transportation systems (ITS) solutions (supply side); and 4) land use, public transportation, and demand management.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Analysis of Transportation Data
course.description: Probabilistic models in transportation. The use of field data. Data gathering techniques, sources of errors, considerations of sample size. Experiment design for demand forecasting and transportation operations analysis. Analysis techniques.
course.requirements: College calculus or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Lean Construction Concepts and Methods
course.description: Inspired by the Lean revolution in manufacturing, production management principles and methods are presented in the context of Lean project delivery. Key concepts include transformation, flow, value, variability, and waste. Key methods include production system design, work structuring, value stream mapping, Last Planner® System and takt planning, tolerance management, design of construction operations, mistakeproofing, Visual Management, and collaborative decisionmaking using Choosing by Advantages. Students learn concepts, principles, and methods by participating in in-class simulations, reading, doing homework, and studying real project management processes and construction operations. The course includes two fabrication shop visits.
course.requirements: Graduate standing in Civil and Environmental Engineering

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Environmental Life-Cycle Assessment
course.description: Methods and tools of environmental life-cycle assessment (LCA, an international standard), especially as applied to infrastructure, but also applicable to other products, processes, services, and systems. Focus on design, management, and supply chains of the entire life cycle: manufacturing, construction, transportation, operation and maintenance, and end of life. Economic life-cycle cost analysis. Models and tools for life-cycle environmental inventory, impact, and improvement analysis.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Advanced Project Planning and Control
course.description: Cost and time estimating and controlling techniques for projects. Evaluation of labor, material, equipment, and subcontract resources, scheduling techniques, earned value concepts. Measuring project percent complete. Contractual risk allocation. Project investment analysis techniques.
course.requirements: CIVENG 167

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Advanced Geomechanics
course.description: Advanced treatment of topics in soil mechanics, including state of stress, consolidation and settlement analysis, shear strength of cohesionless and cohesive soils, and slope stability analysis.
course.requirements: CIV ENG 175

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Geotechnical Earthquake Engineering
course.description: Seismicity, influence of soil conditions on site response, seismic site response analysis, evaluation and modelling of dynamic soil properties, analysis of seismic soil-structure interaction, evaluation and mitigation of soil liquefaction and its consequences, seismic code provisions and practice, seismic earth pressures, seismic slope stability and deformation analysis, seismic safety of dams and embankments, seismic performance of pile foundations, and additional current topics.
course.requirements: 175 or equivalent, or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Infrastructure Sensing and Modeling
course.description: The future of infrastructure relies on smarter information; the rich information obtained from embedded sensors within infrastructure and large-scale computer simulations will act as catalysts for new design, construction, operation and maintenance processes for integrated infrastructure systems linked directly with user behavior patterns. This course will teach the fundamentals of various sensing and modeling tools used for infrastructure engineering and present case studies. The trend in entrepreneurship for emerging technologies in infrastructure and smart cities industry will be discussed.
course.requirements: ENGIN 7, CIVENG C30, and CIVENG 93.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Engineering Geology
course.description: Influence of geologic origin and history on the engineering characteristics of soils and rocks. Application of geology in exploration, design, and construction of engineering works.
course.requirements: A course in physical geology.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Inclusive Infrastructures for Civil and Environmental Engineers
course.description: Placement and design of civil infrastructure, redlining, and other structural biases have built a legacy of neighborhoods and districts that require environmental and social justice, and with whom we can learn how to design and build more inclusive infrastructures. Given the importance of space and place in building personal relationships, and understanding the culture, history, and infrastructures of a neighborhood/district, the goal of this course would be to critically address how infrastructure projects can be conceived and designed to make societies more just, sustainable and equitable.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Civil Systems: Control and Information Management
course.description: Mathematical methods and information technologies for controlling CEE systems. Emphasizes designing component organizations that interact with the world in real-time to control a large system. Methods applied to transportation operations, supply chains, and structures. Management of design complexity by hierarchical specification, systematic use of simulation and verification tools, semantics, polymorphism,information management services, and compilation from high-level design languages.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Data-driven Control Methods for Civil Engineering
course.description:
Introduction to current areas of research at the intersection of machine learning and control with application to civil systems. Investigations of 
machine learning and data-driven algorithms that interact with the physical world. Topics of study will include learning models of dynamical systems, using these models to represent civil systems, and machine learning techniques to manage and control civil applications spanning from energy systems to water networks, to transportation and supply chains. The course will introduce students to methods to either infer dynamics from data with the goal of using classical control algorithms or develop model-free control strategies starting from data.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Climate Resilient Infrastructure Design Studio
course.description: In this course, students develop real-world engineering and design skills to address the effects of climate change. The semester teaches design solutions based on planned and implemented projects to address sea level rise, extreme flooding and other climate risks. Students will explore applications to real-world sites in a project-based format. Topics include engineering tools, high performance landscapes, sustainable infrastructure, urban design, equity and social justice, and resilience of critically impacted built and natural infrastructure systems.
course.requirements: Graduate Standing or Permission of the Instructor

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Probability and Risk Analysis for Civil Engineers
course.description:
Modern civil and environmental engineers must make predictions and design decisions under uncertainty,
whether analyzing structural safety, estimating environmental risks, or modeling the reliability of engineered
systems. This course establishes the probabilistic and inferential foundations underlying infrastructure
reliability, performance-based engineering, and risk analysis.

Students learn how to represent, propagate, and update uncertainty in engineering systems, connecting
classical probability theory with modern computational and AI-based modeling. While examples emphasize
infrastructure resilience, the underlying principles are broadly applicable across engineering domains.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Field Studies in Civil and Environmental Engineering
course.description: Supervised experience in off-campus companies relevant to specific aspects and applications of civil and environmental engineering. Written report required at the end of the semester. Course does not satisfy unit or residence requirements for a master's or doctoral degree.
course.requirements: Graduate standing.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Workshop for Future Civil and Environmental Engineering Teachers
course.description: The course will include supervised teaching of laboratory sections of civil engineering courses, group analysis of videotapes, reciprocal classroom visitations, and an individual project.
course.requirements: Teaching assistant or graduate student status.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Structure and Properties of Civil Engineering Materials
course.description: Introduction to structure and properties of civil engineering materials such as asphalt, cements, concrete, geological materials (e.g. soil and rocks), steel, polymers, and wood. The properties range from elastic, plastic and fracture properties to porosity and thermal and environmental responses. Laboratory tests include evaluation of behavior of these materials under a wide range of conditions.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Individual Study for Master's Students
course.description: Individual study for the comprehensive or language requirements in consultation with the major field adviser. Units may not be used to meet either unit or residence requirements.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Individual Study for Doctoral Students
course.description: Individual study in consultation with the major field adviser, intended to provide an opportunity for qualified students to prepare for the various examinations required of candidates for doctoral degrees. May not be used for unit or residence requirements.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Engineering Geology
course.description: Principles of physical and structural geology; the influence of geological factors on engineering works and the environment. Field trip.
course.requirements: CHEM 1A (may be taken concurrently).

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Engineering Data Analysis
course.description: Application of the concepts and methods of probability theory and statistical inference to CEE problems and data; graphical data analysis and sampling; elements of set theory; elements of probability theory; random variables and expectation; simulation; statistical inference. Use of computer programming languages for analysis of CEE-related data and problems. The course also introduces the student to various domains of uncertainty analysis in CEE.
course.requirements: ENGIN 7 or COMPSCI C8 / INFO C8 / STAT C8.  Student should consult instructor prior to enrolling.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Supervised Independent Study and Research
course.description: Supervised independent study by lower division students.
course.requirements: Freshman or sophomore standing and consent of instructor. Minimum grade point average of 3.3 required.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Supervised Independent Study and Research
course.description: Supervised independent study by lower division students.
course.requirements: Freshman or sophomore standing and consent of instructor. Minimum grade point average of 3.3 required.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Terrestrial Hydrology
course.description: A quantitative introduction to the hydrology of the terrestrial environment including lower atmosphere, watersheds, lakes, and streams. All aspects of the hydrologic cycle, including precipitation, infiltration, evapotranspiration, overland flow, streamflow, and groundwater flow. Chemistry and dating of groundwater and surface water. Development of quantitative insights through problem solving and use of simple models. This course requires one field experiment and several group computer lab assignments.
course.requirements: CHEM 1A, MATH 51, MATH 52, and PHYSICS 7A; or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Remote Sensing of the Environment
course.description: The course will introduce junior/senior undergraduate students to the basic physical concepts of remote sensing as they relate to different earth surface processes. It will introduce students to a variety of recently developed ground, airborne, and satellite instruments and their applications to monitor and analyze environmental processes. These include active (e.g., Lidar), and passive (radiometers) sensors, optical (e.g., Landsat, MODIS), microwave (e.g., SMAP), and gravitational (e.g., GRACE) satellites.

course.subject: MATSCI
course.title: Mechanics of Solids
course.description: Mechanical response of materials: Simple tension in elastic, plastic and viscoelastic members. Continuum mechanics: The stress and strain tensors, equilibrium, compatibility. Three-dimensional elastic, plastic and viscoelastic problems. Thermal, transformation, and dealloying stresses. Applications: Plane problems, stress concentrations at defects, metal forming problems.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Human Mobility and Network Science
course.description: Techniques for analyzing individual daily activities and travels both at urban and at global scale. The course is designed for graduate students interested in methods to analyze human dynamics, and their interactions with the built and the natural environment. Course covers five units each of which is centered in a seminal research paper. Students learn to reproduce the results of the selected paper in the classroom via computer labs, and through a related data analysis and modeling assignments.
course.requirements: An undergraduate-level understanding of probability, statistics, algorithms, and linear algebra is required.

course.subject: CYPLAN
course.title: Transportation and Land Use Planning
course.description: Examination of the interactions between transportation and land use systems; historical perspectives on transportation; characteristics of travel and demand estimation; evaluation of system performance; location theory; models of transportation and urban structure; empirical evidence of transportation-land use impacts; case study examinations.

course.subject: MECENG
course.title: Introduction to Solid Mechanics
course.description: A review of equilibrium for particles and rigid bodies. Application to truss structures. The concepts of deformation, strain, and stress. Equilibrium equations for a continuum. Elements of the theory of linear elasticity. The states of plane stress and plane strain. Solution of elementary elasticity problems (beam bending, torsion of circular bars). Euler buckling in elastic beams.
course.requirements: Mathematics 53 and 54 (may be taken concurrently); Physics 7A.

course.subject: MECENG
course.title: Introduction to Solid Mechanics
course.description: A review of equilibrium for particles and rigid bodies. Application to truss structures. The concepts of deformation, strain, and stress. Equilibrium equations for a continuum. Elements of the theory of linear elasticity. The states of plane stress and plane strain. Solution of elementary elasticity problems (beam bending, torsion of circular bars). Euler buckling in elastic beams.
course.requirements: Mathematics 53 and 54 (may be taken concurrently); Physics 7A.

subject: CLASSIC
description: This course is an introduction (or a re-introduction) to some of the principal surviving authors of the Roman republic, from the traceable origins of literary endeavor at Rome in the third century to the 30s BCE. We will read about 30 OCT pages of Latin prose or 1,000 lines of poetry a week, and the great majority of readings will be drawn from the Latin Phd reading list; exceptions towards the start of the semester are designed to provide basic orientation to issues surrounding the emergence of literary practice at Rome and to some critical early practitioners. A major objective of the course is to increase graduate students’ ability in reading Latin, both in mechanical terms and in terms of responsiveness to the uses and effects of language in different authors’ hands; it also aims to establish understanding of interrelationships among republican authors’ diverse enterprises and to contextualize these against historical and social developments at Rome. Guidance on scholarly approaches to the texts will be offered throughout, but the primary focus in class will be on reading and analyzing Latin and on exploring the detail of developing literary practice at Rome.

course.subject: CLASSIC
course.title: Survey of Latin Literature
course.description: A sequence of readings and lectures on Latin literature.

course.subject: CLASSIC
course.title: Latin Poetry of the Republic and Early Empire
course.description: <Formerly 230A-G>. Study of Lucretius, Vergil, Horace, Ovid, or other topics in Latin poetry from Ennius to Juvenal.

subject: CLASSIC
title: Manichaeism: A World Religion?
description: This seminar will introduce the history of Manichaeism in late antiquity. The seminar will focus on a remarkable set of textual sources that attest to Manichaean ideas, practices and communities stretching across North Africa, Egypt and the Near East, Iran, to Central Asia and western China from the 3rd c. CE to the early 11th c. CE. We will also devote attention to the archaeology available from Kellis (Egypt) and Turfan (China), the sites of two particularly well-documented Manichaean communities, and to the materiality of the extant Manichaean texts. Our inquiry will center on the value of the categories of “religion” and “world religion” as tools for interpreting the history of Manichaeism and for understanding it in the context of early Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and other religions. For interested students, the instructors will support advanced readings for students working in Iranian languages, Greek, and Latin; there will also be opportunities to read Coptic texts.

course.subject: CLASSIC
course.title: Topics in Greek or Roman Literature, History, and Culture
course.description: Select issues in ancient Greek and/or Roman literature or history or culture.

subject: CLASSIC
title: "Craft Production and Industry in the Roman World"
description: This course will explore theoretical and methodological approaches to craft production and industry across the Roman Mediterranean, including potting and glassmaking, textile production, quarrying and stonework, and mining and metallurgy, among other crafts. It will proceed thematically covering both foundational readings and novel approaches, including such topics as scales of production, urban and rural production settings, the chaîne opératoire, communities of practice, cross-craft production, skill and specialization, and labor and identity. The course will also explore methods for understanding and reconstructing production practices, including experimental archaeology, ethnography, the archaeological sciences, and art historical and textual analyses. Our goal will be to better understand the organization of production and the lived experiences of those engaged in extracting raw materials and making Roman objects and architecture. By the end of this course, students will be familiar with the diverse archaeological evidence for production in the Roman world as well as the methods and theoretical approaches to understanding this evidence that are applicable to other times and places.

course.title: Seminar in Classical Archaeology
course.description: Advanced study of ancient Greek art objects and sites.

subject: CLASSIC
description: This course focuses on pedagogy for the teaching of Classics and the pre-modern world more broadly. The course will balance practical help for your first semester teaching with consideration on the larger questions raised by teaching antiquity. The emphasis will be on becoming self-reflective teachers, both as GSIs at Berkeley and in future academic and non-academic careers (which often, explicitly or not, often involve teaching). This course satisfies the requirement that all first-time GSIs complete a course in pedagogy. We will devote time to both the teaching of ancient literature and culture in English and the pedagogy of ancient languages. Issues of equity and inclusion will be continuing themes in all our meetings.

course.title: Teaching of Classics: Methods and Problems
course.description: Seminar in problems of teaching. Required for all new graduate student instructors.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or GSI status.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Human Genome, Environment and Public Health
course.description: This introductory course will cover basic principles of human/population genetics and molecular biology relevant to molecular and genetic epidemiology. The latest methods for genome-wide association studies and other approaches to identify genetic variants and environmental risk factors important to disease and health will be presented. The application of biomarkers to define exposures and outcomes will be explored. Recent developments in genomics, epigenomics and other ‘omics’ will be included. Computer and wet laboratory work will provide hands-on experience.
course.requirements: Introductory level biology/genetics course, or consent of instructor. Introductory biostatistics and epidemiology courses strongly recommended.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Introduction to Computational Biology and Precision Medicine
course.description: Computational biology is an interdisciplinary field that develops and/or applies computational methods including bioinformatics to analyze large collections of biological data such as genomic data with a goal of making new predictions or discoveries. Precision medicine is an emerging approach for human disease treatment and prevention that takes into account individual variability in genes, environment, and lifestyle for each person. Computational biology and bioinformatics tools are critical for advancing precision medicine. This survey course introduces computational tools for the analysis of genomic data and approaches to understanding and advancing precision medicine.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Berkeley Connect in Computational Biology
course.description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate. Course may be repeated.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Classics in Computational Biology
course.description: Research project and approaches in computational biology. An introducton to the diverse ways biological problems are investigated computationally through critical evaluation of the classics and recent peer-reviewed literature. This is the core course required of all Computational Biology graduate students.
course.requirements: Acceptance in the Computational Biology Phd program; consent of instructor.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Computational Biology Seminar/Journal Club
course.description: This seminar course will cover a wide range of topics in the field of computational biology.  The main goals of the course are to expose students to cutting edge research in the field and to prepare students for engaging in academic discourse with seminar speakers - who are often leaders in their fields.  A selected number of class meetings will be devoted to the review of scientific papers published by upcoming seminar speakers and the other class meetings will be devoted to discussing other related articles in the field.  The seminar will expose students to both the breadth and highest standards of current computational biology research.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Algorithms for Computational Biology
course.description: This course will provide familiarity with algorithms and probabilistic models that arise in various computational biology applications, such as suffix trees, suffix arrays, pattern matching, repeat finding, sequence alignment, phylogenetics, hidden Markov models, gene finding, motif finding, linear/logistic regression, random forests, convolutional neural networks, genome-wide association studies, pathogenicity prediction, and sequence-to-epigenome prediction.
course.requirements: CompSci 70 AND CompSci 170, MATH 54 OR ELENG 66 OR an equivalent linear algebra course

subject: CMPBIO
title: Single-cell immunology: from statistical machine learning to biomedical discovery
description:
Advances in single-cell technologies have transformed modern immunology, enabling major discoveries in cancer, autoimmunity, and other diseases. However, the scale and complexity of the resulting datasets necessitate specialized machine learning expertise to fully realize their potential. This course examines the computational challenges posed by emerging biotechnology platforms and how addressing them can advance molecular medicine, with a particular emphasis on cancer immunotherapies.
This is an experimental class designed to mirror the interdisciplinary and collaborative nature of modern biomedical research in industry and academia. Students are expected to have a prior exposure to EITHER the computational or the immunological aspects, but not necessarily both. From the computational side, we will cover statistical inference from atlas-scale omics data, drawing heavily on high-dimensional statistics and variational inference. From the immunology side, we will introduce some of the latest technological developments in single-cell genomics, including spatial transcriptomics and massively parallel pooled CRISPR screens, and survey their applications in molecular medicine. Our guiding focus will be the characterization of molecular states of immune cells in solid tumors (or: "why does the immune system fail to kill the tumor and what can we do to help it").

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Special Topics - Computational Biology
course.description: This graduate-level course will cover various special topics in computational biology and the theme will vary from semester to semester.  The course will focus on computational methodology, but also cover relevant biological applications.  This course will be offered according to student demand and faculty availability.
course.requirements: Graduate standing in EECS, MCB, Computational Biology or related fields; or consent of the instructor

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Doctoral Seminar in Computational Biology
course.description: This interactive seminar builds skills, knowledge and community in computational biology for first year PhD and second year Designated Emphasis students. Topics covered include concepts in human genetics/genomics, microbiome data analysis, laboratory methodologies and data sources for computational biology, workshops/instruction on use of various bioinformatics tools, critical review of current research studies and computational methods, preparation for success in the PhD program and career development. Faculty members of the graduate program in computational biology and scientists from other institutions will participate. Topics will vary each semester.

course.title: Introduction to Research in Computational Biology
course.description: Closely supervised experimental or computational work under the direction of an individual faculty member; an introduction to methods and research approaches in particular areas of computational biology.

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Introduction to Programming for Bioinformatics Bootcamp
course.description: The goals of this course are to introduce students to Python, a simple and powerful programming language that is used for many applications, and to expose them to the practical bioinformatic utility of Python and programming in general. The course will allow students to apply programming to the problems that they face in the lab and to leave this course with a sufficiently generalized knowledge of programming (and the confidence to read the manuals) that they will be able to apply their skills to whatever projects they happen to be working on.

course.title: Introduction to Computational Molecular and Cell Biology
course.description: This class teaches basic bioinformatics and computational biology, with an emphasis on alignment, phylogeny, and ontologies. Supporting foundational topics are also reviewed with an emphasis on bioinformatics topics, including basic molecular biology, probability theory, and information theory.
course.requirements: BioE 11 or Bio 1A (may be taken concurrently), plus a programming course (ENGIN 7 or CS 61A).

course.subject: CMPBIO
course.title: Computational Functional Genomics
course.description: This course provides a survey of the computational analysis of genomic data, introducing the material through lectures on biological concepts and computational methods, presentations of primary literature, and practical bioinformatics exercises. The emphasis is on measuring the output of the genome and its regulation. Topics include modern computational and statistical methods for analyzing data from genomics experiments: high-throughput RNA sequencing data, single-cell data, and other genome-scale measurements of biological processes. Students will perform original analyses with Python and command-line tools.
course.requirements: MATH 54 or ELENG 64/ELENG 66; COMPSCI 61A or equivalent Python course; BIOENG 11 or BIOLOGY 1A; and BIOENG 131. Introductory statistics or data science is recommended.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Introduction to Cognitive Science
course.description: This course introduces the interdisciplinary field of cognitive science. Lectures and readings will survey research from artificial intelligence, psychology, linguistics, philosophy, and neuroscience, and will cover topics such as the nature of knowledge, thinking, remembering, vision, imagery, language, and consciousness. Sections will demonstrate some of the major methodologies.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Neuropsychology of Happiness
course.description: This course will explore cognitive and affective components of happiness and distress, including pleasure, meaning, and well-being, sadness, fear, and anger. Also, negative thought patterns associated with various psychological disorders, including mood disorders, anxiety disorders, and PTSD, and their neurological underpinnings. Then we will turn to the new field of self-directed neuroplasticity to explore evidence-based psychotherapeutic techniques for transforming negative thoughts and cultivating positive ones, including mindfulness, gratitude, and CBT-based techniques. We will compare these to psychoactive drugs and brain stimulation used to treat such disorders. We will also look at recent developments in neuroimaging data.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Computational Models of Cognition
course.description: This course will provide advanced students in cognitive science and computer science with the skills to develop computational models of human cognition, giving insight into how people solve challenging computational problems, as well as how to bring computers closer to human performance. The course will explore three ways in which researchers have attempted to formalize cognition -- symbolic approaches, neural networks, and probability and statistics -- considering the strengths and weaknesses of each.

The course will explore three ways in which researchers have attempted to formalize cognition -- symbolic approaches, neural networks, and probability and statistics -- considering the strengths and weaknesses of each.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Rhythms of the Brain: from Neuronal Communication to Function
course.description: This course provides advanced students in cognitive science, psychology, computer science, and biology with the skills to develop numerical methods used in the study of neuroscience and cognition. We will study several main areas in neuroscience and cognition: memory and the underlying communication between hippocampus and cortical areas; movement control through the study of the cortico-basal-thalamic loops. Modulation of mesolimbic and nigrostriatal pathways by dopamine. Modulation of cortico-hippocampal circuits by acetylcholine and the role of these circuits in the onset of Alzheimer disease. We will study the coherence of electrical oscillations in different parts of the brain and how that coherence can be disturbed in disease.
course.requirements: Prerequisites are a basic familiarity with programming (as might be obtained from COMPSCI 61A or ENG 7), exposure to cognitive science (e.g., CogSci 1/N1/1B), comfort with basic calculus (e.g. Math 51, Math 10A, or Math 16A), and discrete math (e.g. Math 55).

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Music, Language, and Cognition
course.description: Humans across all time periods and cultures have engaged in musical and linguistic activity, but why do all humans engage in these two peculiar kinds of complex behaviors? The purpose of this course is to introduce students to embodied, cognitive perspectives on music and language through the study of a range of topics about music and language including jazz improvisation, the evolution of rhythm processing, and birdsong, to name a few. By completing this course students will gain insight into one of the most fascinating areas of research in cognitive science today and build an understanding of the central roles that music and language play in our mental and social life.
course.requirements: Recommended: CogSci 1, 1B, or N1.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Models of Decision-Making from Brain to Behavior
course.description: This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of how decisions are made by individuals and organizations. We will explore theories and models from psychology, neuroscience, economics, and their applications to fields such as medicine, business, public policy, and technology. You will learn about the cognitive biases, societal factors, and neural mechanisms which shape our decision making processes, and how computational models can be designed to explain and inform decision making in different aspects of life. The course will focus on the concepts underlying computational models and will not cover fitting models to data, but will develop your ability to interpret graphs, understand computational models, and assess statistical results.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Mind, Machine, and Meaning: Living Intentionally in the Digital Age
course.description: This course starts with a hard look at data on screen time and social media use. We examine the science of digital addiction and the impact of overuse on life quality, cognitive function, social connection, and mental health. We then explore The Attention Economy—tech giants' business models and their cultural impacts. The course defines a path to living more intentionally with technology. We review strategies to enhance focus, optimize consumption, boost creativity, improve sleep, and calibrate identity amid online comparisons. We conclude by critically addressing the AI revolution. Students will learn how to remain competitive and leverage AI to be more productive and also focus on preserving your agency and judgment.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Mind, Brain, and Identity
course.description: Do you have a self or are you one?  How is the self related to brain structure and function?  Is the self, for example, identical to some part of the brain or part of the brain’s function?  Can you damage the self by damaging the brain?  In this course we will look at these questions from conceptual, psychological, and neuroscientific perspectives.  We will study both normal and injured brains to help shed light on what is a deeply philosophical and personal issue: What is the human the self.  We will read various papers pertaining to these issues as well as the books listed under required reading.

We will do this through a series of engaging sessions featuring industry professionals, researchers, and alumni from different industries, combined with exploratory and developmental lessons and exercises designed to build career readiness skills in each student. This course is for Cognitive Science however, this course is especially well-suited for Cognitive Science majors in the early phases of their academic path, with a focus on exploration and skill-building.

course.subject: PSYCH
course.title: Basic Issues in Cognition
course.description: Theoretical foundations and current controversies in cognitive science will be discussed. Basic issues in cognition--including perception, imagery, memory, categorization, thinking, judgment, and development--will be considered from the perspectives of philosophy, psychology, computer science, and physiology. Particular emphasis will be placed on the nature, implications, and limitations of the computational model of mind.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Perception
course.description: An introduction to principal theoretical constructs and experimental procedures in visual and auditory perception. Topics will include psychophysics; perception of color, space, shape, and motion; pattern recognition and perceptual attention.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor. 101 recommended.

course.subject: PSYCH
course.title: Cognitive Neuroscience
course.description: This course will examine research investigating the neurological basis of cognition. Material covered will include the study of brain-injured patients, neurophysiological research in animals, and the study of normal cognitive processes in humans with non-invasive behavioral and physiological techniques such as functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Topics to be covered include perception, attention, memory, language, motor control, executive control, and emotion.
course.requirements:
Psych/MCB C61 OR Psych 110, or Psych C120/Cog Sci C100, and relevant prerequisites. Courses may be taken simultaneously with Psych C127.
Enrollment limited to students who are declared Psych, CogSci, MCB, or IB majors, or by permission of the instructor if the student has declared another major.

course.subject: PSYCH
course.title: Computational Models of Cognition
course.description: This course will provide advanced students in cognitive science and computer science with the skills to develop computational models of human cognition, giving insight into how people solve challenging computational problems, as well as how to bring computers closer to human performance. The course will explore three ways in which researchers have attempted to formalize cognition -- symbolic approaches, neural networks, and probability and statistics -- considering the strengths and weaknesses of each.
course.requirements: Calculus, discrete mathematics, CogSci 1/1b/N1,  Computer Science 61A, or equivalents.

course.subject: COGSCI
course.title: Quantitative Methods in Linguistics
course.description: An introduction to quantitative methods for linguistic analysis and applications. Students will be introduced to statistical modeling techniques for linguistic datasets, as well as models that have applications in natural language processing. The class will make use of programming languages (R and/or Python) as necessary—e.g., for data visualization and modeling.
course.requirements: 100 or graduate student standing.

course.subject: LINGUIS
course.title: Language and Thought
course.description: This class explores the relation of language and thought. Is language uniquely human, and if so, what does this reveal about the human mind? Does the particular language you speak affect the way you think, or do human languages reflect a universal conceptual repertoire? The goal of this class is to familiarize you with a set of classic arguments on these themes, together with research that evaluates these arguments, through weekly readings, lecture, and discussion.

subject: COLWRIT
description: This introductory course is designed to improve your public speaking skills and make you more comfortable speaking in front of an audience. Students will learn the fundamentals of public speaking and gain confidence in their oral communication (and listening) skills by delivering speeches and presentations for different occasions and audiences in a supportive classroom environment. Students will not only study and analyze effective speaking strategies but also deliver four speeches of their own (storytelling, persuasive, informative, group) on topics they select. Welcome!

course.subject: COLWRIT
course.title: Introduction to Public Speaking
course.description: This is a strictly introductory course. It presumes no formal training of any kind on the part of the students. Emphasis will be on organization and delivery with goals of improving control over speaking habits and enunciation. Part of the intent of the course is to introduce students to the rudiments of the rhetorical theory which lies behind the practice of public speaking.

course.subject: COLWRIT
course.title: Berkeley Changemaker: Public Speaking
course.description: Emphasizing the Berkeley Changemaker pillars of critical thinking and communication, this variable unit (1 or 2) practicum is designed to help students refine their academic speaking skills. Students will learn the techniques of effective public speaking, practice their skills, and develop confidence in oral communication. Online, asynchronous class sessions will be complemented by “live” opportunities that enable students to practice course content in front of an instructor and audience and receive feedback.

course.subject: COLWRIT
course.title: Introduction to the Craft of Creative Writing
course.description: This course in creative writing focuses on three genres: the personal essay, the short story, and the one-act play. The course emphasizes an introduction to craft--how these types of writing are generated, what their elements are, and how the finished pieces work--which students will explore through careful study of models by published writers and through writing and revising their own short pieces.
course.requirements: Completion of Reading and Composition sequence (1A/1B).

subject: COLWRIT
description:
Personal essays. Biographies. Culture writing. Political analysis. Science explainers. Podcasts. Sports narratives. Food writing. Long form investigations. These are all forms of creative nonfiction writing. In this class, we will explore what nonfiction writing is, where it comes from, and how it both shapes and reflects the times we live in today. You’ll read classic essays alongside contemporary ones and write three nonfiction pieces on topics of your choice. We’ll also discuss pitching editors, starting newsletters and leveraging social media as part of a writing practice. This class fulfills the creative writing minor but students from all majors and levels of experience are welcome.

Tentative texts (check back in August for a final list):

Storycraft, Jack Hart

The Fire Next Time, James Baldwin

Crying in H Mart, Michelle Zauner

Women and Power, Mary Beard

Various essays, online at Bcouses

course.subject: COLWRIT
course.title: Introduction to the Craft of Creative Nonfiction
course.description: This course in creative writing focuses on the craft of reading and writing creative nonfiction.  The course provides an introduction to craft: how creative nonfiction is generated, what its elements are, and how finished pieces work.  Students will explore these aspects of craft through careful study of models by published writers, and through writing and revising their own short pieces.

Sentence structures, summarizing, paraphrasing, correct use of citations, and editing skills will also be addressed.

course.subject: COLWRIT
course.title: Writing in the Biological Sciences
course.description: Intended for both Biology majors and non-majors, College Writing 161 provides students with a rhetorical framework for understanding the conventions of writing within the Biological Science to help them write more effectively for readers in Biology, as well as for readers outside the field. Exploring ideas of audience, genre, style, and authorship, students will read a wide variety of texts, including critical texts from Rhetoric and Composition that analyze writing in Biology, as well as genres specific to Biology and genres intended for wider audiences (e.g., editorials, grant application letters, explanatory articles). Students will also write a variety of these genres.

course.description: This class will examine some of the very best sports journalism with a critical lens, looking at intersections of business, race, culture, disability, gender, performance, technology, politics, social justice, and above all else attention to inquiry through thoughtful writing. At the same time, students will write in a variety of creative nonfiction genres on multimedia platforms, including the writing of a sustained final project on a topic of their own choosing.

title: Access and Diversity in US Public Schools

subject: COLWRIT
title: Conformity Sucks
description: Throughout the history of drama, poetry, fiction, and nonfiction – not to mention real life – rebellion rules. From the subversive characters of Sophocles, Shakespeare, Joseph Heller, and Toni Morrison in drama/poetry/fiction to bigger-than-life iconoclasts like Hatshepsut, Li Qingzhou, John Locke, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Martin Luther King in nonfiction, the rebellious force those in power to bend the knee. This class will take a hard look at the effects that iconoclasts, both real and imagined, good and bad, have had on real life events, particularly as they pertain to natural rights. Any meaningful change in the world was brought about by the most determined protesters, the utmost civilly disobedient, the hardest questioners of authority, and nowhere is this more obvious than in their writing. In short, conformists dot the i’s and cross the t’s of history. Iconoclasts write it.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Human Machines
description:
From self-driving cars, to automated facial recognition software, to chatbots that have literally been trained to mimic us, technological change is reshaping our lives more than ever, raising urgent questions about what it means to be human in an age defined by our connection to machines. In this course, we will examine our evolving and increasingly fraught relationship with technology, artificial intelligence, and the digital lives we live through science fiction and speculative literature, nonfiction, and visual media. Students will develop critical thinking, reading, and writing skills around topics such as automation and surveillance, cybernetic assimilation and transhumanism, and the ethical dilemmas posed by unchecked technological advancement. Through close readings, classroom discussions, and writing essays, we will explore how stories of imagined futures can help us understand–and respond to–the concerns of the present.

Required Texts:

M.T. Anderson, Feed

Unmasking AI, Joy Buolamwini.

Jia Tolentino, Trick Mirror

Pluto: Urasawa X Tezuka Volume 1 by Naoki Urasawa

subject: COLWRIT
title: Is Gen Z's new literature really Literature?
description: The great Italian novelist Italo Calvino claimed in his 1985 lectures that his "faith in the future of literature rests on the knowledge that there are things that only literature, with its particular capacities, can give us". The operative phrase there is "give us", and by future he meant now, this century. And by literature he meant just that, black characters on a white page/screen. Writing. Calvino didn't live into the 21st c. to see if his prognostications were to come true, but, well, did they? Is Gen Z, or any other generation, reading great literature on its own as other generations did? If not, why not? It's no secret that film, music, videos, social media reels, etc, and screens in general appear to have taken the place of those black characters on a page in order to "give" us something. What is it that it gives you? That's your job: to write about that. We'll explore some of these, and in turn you will write both with sustained attention to sources (yes, Literature), but also offer your own views and opinions on the matter to argue various points and see if you can show how this new literature can "give" you something vs. a piece of literature.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Movies, Music, Murals,and more: How does art relate to oppression?
description:
How can a song imitating police brutality empower its victims? How can a groundbreaking hero perpetuate unsettling stereotypes? In this sustained exploration of how we use, and are sometimes used by, art and other products of contemporary culture, you will analyze a diverse array of texts and other media (ranging from music, to film, to graffiti, to paintings and sculpture) toward the mastery of various academic techniques and approaches toward refining your powers as a critical reader, writer and reviser for a variety of academic contexts and beyond.


Book list:

Wannabe: Reckonings with the Pop Culture That Shapes Me by Aisha Harris 

Going All City: Struggle and Survival in LA’s Graffiti Subculture by Stefano Bloch 

Art of Engagement: Visual Politics in California and Beyond by Peter Selz

The Well-Crafted Sentence: A Writer’s Guide to Style by Nora Bacon

subject: COLWRIT
title: Relationships to Power & the Power of Relationships
description: This interactive experiential course focuses on Relationships to Power & the Power of Relationships. We’ll read about immigration, language, culture, and community, as we commemorate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.  You will engage in discussions of politics, land, law, belonging, activism, media, education, and democracy.  As a member of a community of writers, you will have the opportunity to write from different angles–interpreting what interests you most in each text we read as you craft and draft a meaningful analytic argument.   Ultimately, you will revise selected pieces to design and publish a reflective portfolio online showcasing your best work of the course.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Borderlands
description:
A “borderland” is a space between territories where boundaries blur and definitions become less certain. In this course, we will explore three borderland spaces:

AI-Human: As AI becomes increasingly integrated with writing, how do we navigate this new territory? What do we gain, and what is lost, when we utilize generative AI as part of our writing process? 

Linguistic: Languages have fluid boundaries; we use our linguistic resources to communicate ideas – but also to construct our identities. What happens when the norms of linguistic diversity confront the societal demand of conformity to a  “standard”? What is the impact on those who do not conform?

Democratic: Rather than a strict binary, modern political systems occupy a spectrum defined by varying degrees of openness. What role do citizens play in determining whether a society drifts toward autocracy or advances toward a more robust democracy?

Drawing on scholarly texts, journalism, literature, film, and other media, this course emphasizes critical reading, discussion, and analytical writing as tools for understanding these complex spaces.


Required reading includes Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI (2024) by Ethan Mollick and On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century (2017) by Timothy Snyder.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Belonging & Uprooting
description:
What does it mean to belong somewhere — to a society or culture, a community or subculture, or to a small classroom community like this one? R1A: Belonging & Uprooting is meant to be an engaging exploration of different possible answers to these questions, both personal and theoretical. We'll use cultural theory, nonfiction, a novel, and the occasional poem or short film to examine how one's sense of belonging is shaped, looking at its intersections with individual and communal identity, geography, and ancestry.

We'll examine how belonging is constructed through abstract "imagined communities" (in the words of Benedict Anderson, writing about the concept of the modern nation-state); or the ways it reinvents itself out of the ashes of its own absence in diaspora (using the lens of Svetlana Boym's typology of nostalgia, the "longing for a home that no longer exists or has never existed," which she breaks down into reflective and restorative modes), then will apply that lens to Exit West, a lyrical love story turned refugee novel by Pakistani author (and Berkeley alum!) Mohsin Hamid. We'll also read A Map of Future Ruins: On Borders & Belonging by Oakland immigration journalist Lauren Markham, braiding her investigative reporting on the 2020 fire that burned the largest refugee camp in Europe, Markham's own Greek ancestry and their migration story, and the mythmaking that underpins the West's long-held narrative of Greece as the cradle of Western culture.

We’ll explore the opposite of belonging, reading arguments against assimilation and in praise of outsidership and working-class, first-gen identities via the feminist theorist bell hooks (who uses her own experience as a working-class Black woman in academia as a lens to discuss & refute assimilation), the short film Hey Man (which follows an early-transition rideshare driver as they navigate the public/private presentations of self) and multilingual poems excerpted from Tripas, the Pulitzer-winning collection by Brandon Som about Chinese-Chicano belonging, we'll learn new strategies for close reading and analysis of literary texts.

We'll write four mostly-academic essays in conversation with these texts, examine several other modes of personal and analytical writing, and (if there's time!) conduct a handful of exploratory experiments in creative research via micro-interviews, long walks, mapmaking aided by Rebecca Solnit's anthology of artist-made maps of San Francisco, and DIY fieldwork. This class — like all R1A classes — will demand a level of attention to text through close reading, re-reading, and rigorous analysis that many students haven't encountered in high school (so if you've found yourself frustrated with the artificial limitations the five-paragraph essay structure places on your intellectual capacity, you'll get to leave it behind and instantly do far more sophisticated work). We'll also focus heavily on the revision process itself, which is to say that we'll spend the semester immersed in iterative rewriting and revision, making significant changes to each draft in order to break out of old intellectual and writerly habits — and to develop new ones that help us all shine as an increasingly rigorous analytical writers and narrative storytellers. This class might best be described as relaxed yet demanding: not easy (it's six credits, after all), but rewarding and surprisingly relevant, no matter your major or field of study. Expect to put in some hard work and get a lot of writing done, but also to have fun when the stars align.

Books & Materials:  

One or two full-length books: the novel Exit West, and probably also A Map of Future Ruins by Lauren Markham (which I may only excerpt portions of). Together these two will cost around $35, maybe a little less depending on where you get them.

We'll also use a writing handbook — probably the excellent They Say/I Say, which will run you another $20ish. (If cost is an issue for these texts, just let me know.)

We'll read numerous shorter texts (mostly personal essays and beginner-friendly theory), including work by preeminent Black scholar and feminist theorist bell hooks, theorist Benedict Anderson, prolific author and public intellectual Rebecca Solnit, the film Hey Man (dir. Kai Tillman), and others. In addition, we'll read and discuss short essays on the practice and philosophy of writing and revision just about every week. All will be provided in .pdf form or as print-outs.

You'll also need to bring a laptop, tablet, or paper notebook to class every day. Some students opt to purchase annotation software/apps like GoodNotes, Notability, or Kami to use for ongoing annotation assignments I'll assign beginning early in the semester. There's no need to buy these in advance (or at all — you may find free resources that work for you, or opt to print out your .pdfs and annotate by hand), but if you're already exploring digital tools to help make your academic life easier, keep your eyes out for things that allow you to take margin notes or mark up texts easily in order to integrate active reading into your workflow for all your classes, not just one-off R1A assignments.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Fandom
description:
It’s okay if you don't belong to any fan community. You’re probably better off that way; you get to focus more on your work and loved ones. But it’s also okay if you identify as a diehard fan: “There’s nothing in the world quite like being part of a fandom. Never let anyone shame you for it…. Do what makes you happy,” as J.M Darhower maintains in Ghosted. Fans tend to invest emotions, time, money, and confidence in celebrities, TV shows, characters, or sports— sometimes to perplexing degrees that call into question good judgment. Our R1A section focuses on ardency, affinity, and glee as well as frustration in fandoms. We will explore fan behaviors and celebrity reactions, as we delve into how and whom fans interact with— particularly on social media. We will read, write, and talk about related texts, including Eric Smith’s novel, Don't Read the Comments, and Henry Jenkins’ collection of essays, Fans, Bloggers, and Gamers, together with documentaries, short stories, and essays. 

Jenkins, Henry. Fans, Bloggers, and Gamers, New York U P, 2006. 

Smith, Eric. Don't Read the Comments, Inkyard, 2020.

title: Writings of the African Diaspora
description: This course addresses the writings of the African diaspora in a broader definition of the term. It touches on specific themes and ideas from pre-colonial Nigeria to  the “neo-colonial” New World. The course seeks to define the above terms as concepts and attitudes as exemplified in literature and films. This course focuses primarily on developing your critical thinking, reading and writing skills. The course seeks to hone your techniques of expository writing. Basic rhetorical tools such as description, analysis, explanation, narration, speculation and argument are discussed enabling you to share your experiences, information and views with others.  The emphasis all along is on provocative theses, strategies of argument and competent analysis of evidence.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Nature
description:
Nature. The word shows up all around us: on a trail sign, on a label in the grocery store, in our social media feeds, and in the way we might talk about needing to return to some ideal state or to clear our heads. In this class, we’ll read fiction and nonfiction texts that consider our natural world and what we even mean by ‘natural’. Through our readings, we’ll move through forests, mountain ranges, oceans, cities, backyards- and even grocery store aisles. As we do, we’ll pay attention to how those places are described, understood, remembered, argued over, and lived in. Along the way, you’ll engage in conversations through short, low-stakes writing that asks you to go somewhere, look closely, and make connections between your experiences and the texts you read.

The theme of nature gives us a focus for our reading and discussion, but the core work of the class is writing. You will write and revise regularly, building toward a final portfolio that shows your growth as a writer across the semester. That means learning how to sustain analysis of a passage, how to quote and work with texts, how to move from examples to claims, and how to consider rhetorical elements as you write. We’ll practice different kinds of writing, always with the expectation that you engage closely with what you read, with your own writing as a process, and with our class as a community of writers and thinkers.

subject: COLWRIT
title: HOW TO BE MORTAL
description: Death is universal. For as long as human beings have been self-aware, we have faced the challenge of living with the knowledge that we will one day die. The subject of death can be heavy, but this class posits that reflecting on our shared mortality can be empowering, uplifting, and generative. We will analyze a number of works—fiction, drama, poetry, nonfiction, and film—that grapple with the relationship between death and living a meaningful life. We will examine attitudes toward death across cultures, the psychology behind how death has been personified in film and media, critiques of the American funeral industry, and speculations about whether new technologies can extend life or even abolish death altogether. In the process, we will learn to craft essays that analyze, inform, and persuade, with an emphasis on creativity, clarity, rigor, and organization.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Recon, Rove, Reveal, Riot
description:
In Recon, Rove, Reveal, Riot, we’ll examine turbulent phenomena and situations— the explosive rise of A.I.s in our lives, shifting landscapes in elite sports— things that are actively evolving, actively in flux. We’ll use distinct aspects of intelligence to drive these investigations: 


I. Tech & INTEL   INTEL: Data gathered for decision-making > What do you need to know?  After exploring the tech podcast Hard Fork together as a class, each of you will decide on a precise AI-related tech phenomenon you want to look into. What is the intel that you need to understand this thing, so that you might … use it? modify it? resist it? leverage it?  reinvent it?  Once you’ve gained further understanding through credible texts from the popular media (other podcasts, news articles, websites, TED Talks, videos, etc.), you’ll articulate in an expository piece why this emergent tech matters. Why is having this intel important right now? What are the stakes?      


II.  Heroism, Moral Dilemma & EQ   EQ: Emotional Intelligence > psychological capacity and emotional intelligence, including self-awareness and the ability to evolve   In the speculative fiction novel Migrations, where Earth is on the edge of environmental collapse, the hero Franny engages in complicated behaviors on her simultaneous quests. One quest is physical: she stows aboard the fishing vessel The Saghani  to track and save the last surviving flock of Arctic terns. Another is emotional: Franny is trying, paradoxically, to learn how to be still, to allow herself to attach to people and places. As she journeys, what are Franny’s arcs of self-awareness and emotional intelligence? 


III. Elite Athletes, Vulnerability & CQ   CQ: Cultural Intelligence > the ability to understand, respect, and effectively navigate diverse cultural contexts, including actively adapting your own behaviors, and leveraging cultural cues to influence or change cultural environments   In elite sports–think semi-pro, pro, Olympics– a cultural shift is occurring right now: one towards more openness and vulnerability around mental and emotional health. We’ll dive into the journalism on this shift, some of it written by the athletes themselves.  What’s driving this shift? What does it look and sound like, including its meta-narrative (what are people saying about what the athletes are saying?) Is this shift affected by resistance and blowback? 


IV. Endurance, Resistance, Apocalypse & AQ    AQ: Adaptive Intelligence  >  awareness of one’s environment, and how to live in it and alter or shape it when needed   Tochi Onyebuchi’s speculative fiction novella Riot Baby begins in the realism of South Central Los Angeles and the 1992 Rodney King Riots, and travels forward in time and space to Harlem, Rikers Island, Watts, and the present & future. Onyebuchi layers in “speculative” elements, including psychic powers, telepathy, and a police state whose “augments” – officers with augmented reality wired into their bodies– surveil the public just by walking through it.  How does Onyebuchi build explosive impact through writerly ("rhetorical") choices? And what does Riot Baby suggest about adaptation to inequity through endurance? … resistance?  …apocalypse?



COURSE TEXTS TO PURCHASE, IN PRINT (hardcopy)*

Migrations  Charlotte McConaghy

Riot Baby  Tochi Onyebuchi

      *except for students with an access accommodation, of course

subject: COLWRIT
title: "I eat, therefore I am."
description:
Wendell Berry, farmer, poet, and activist articulates a simple yet apparently difficult truth about the relationship between our everyday act of eating and the character and quality of our lives: 

“There is, then, a politics of food that, like any politics, involves our freedom. We still (sometimes) remember that we cannot be free if our minds and voices are controlled by someone else. But we have neglected to understand that we cannot be free if our food and its sources are controlled by someone else. The condition of the passive consumer of food is not a democratic condition. One reason to eat responsibly is to live free.” 

As the world around us seems to spin faster and faster out of our control, one ever-present and unavoidable activity in our daily lives offers us a chance to regain some of that control – the act of eating. In this course, we will practice the art and science of reading and writing by examining the many ways food intersects with our personal lives, our communities, and the planet. We will be reading at least two books, articles about reading, writing, and food, and maybe even a cereal box or two, watching videos, doing some research in the field and in our minds as we learn how to observe and become more aware of our behavior around food, both conscious and unconscious, in order to save the world. Well, maybe not save the world, but at least make a difference in our own lives and the lives of those around us. 

Though the theme of this class is the many facets of food, the main aim of CWR1A is to help you develop your critical reading and writing skills. Over the course of the semester, you will be expected to produce at least forty pages of writing including summaries, reflections, personal narratives, and analyses. A central requirement in this class is that you demonstrate engagement in the writing process, and so you will be writing multiple drafts for each essay. 

Required texts: 

Fast Food Nation by Eric Schlosser

My Year of Meats by Ruth Ozeki  

Also, a course reader at Copy Central

subject: COLWRIT
description: "Place is security, space is freedom: we are attached to the one and long for the other" (Tuan). Freedom and security, however, are vulnerable to being compromised by fear, misconceptions, power, and privilege. We will explore these conflicts by looking at the use of public and private spaces, proximity to others, and proximity to truth. Students will examine a variety of sources; writing assignments will include a text analysis, synthesis, and an autoethnographic essay.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Borderlands
description:
A “borderland” is a space between territories where boundaries blur and definitions become less certain. In this course, we will explore three borderland spaces:

AI-Human: As AI becomes increasingly integrated with writing, how do we navigate this new territory? What do we gain, and what is lost, when we utilize generative AI as part of our writing process? 

Linguistic: Languages have fluid boundaries; we use our linguistic resources to communicate ideas – but also to construct our identities. What happens when the norms of linguistic diversity confront the societal demand of conformity to a  “standard”? What is the impact on those who do not conform?

Democratic: Rather than a strict binary, modern political systems occupy a spectrum defined by varying degrees of openness. What role do citizens play in determining whether a society drifts toward autocracy or advances toward a more robust democracy?

Drawing on scholarly texts, journalism, literature, film, and other media, this course emphasizes critical reading, discussion, and analytical writing as tools for understanding these complex spaces.

Required reading includes Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI (2024) by Ethan Mollick and On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century (2017) by Timothy Snyder.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Writing at the End of the World
description:
Whether it is the threat of nuclear warfare, impending climate disaster, or the apocalyptic prophecies of various religious traditions, anticipating the imminent end of the world is a mode of thinking that is seeded deep within the collective consciousness of many civilizations. For thousands of years, the apocalypse has supposed to have been right around the corner, and anxieties surrounding its approach have manifested in fiction, film, poetry, politics and, more recently, computer science. Will nuclear weapons or climate upheavals render the world into a Mad Max-like hellscape? Will ChatGPT attain consciousness and wipe out humanity in order to protect its own existence? More importantly, what do these questions and depictions tell us about the cultures that are asking them?  

In this course you will learn to read and write as a way of participating in an intellectual community, both at Cal and beyond. You will learn to use writing as a way of thinking. Rather than approaching writing as some mystical, innate affinity with words, this course approaches writing as a craft that can be learned and developed.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Movies, Music, Murals,and more: How does art relate to oppression?
description:
How can a song imitating police brutality empower its victims? How can a groundbreaking hero perpetuate unsettling stereotypes? In this sustained exploration of how we use, and are sometimes used by, art and other products of contemporary culture, you will analyze a diverse array of texts and other media (ranging from music, to film, to graffiti, to paintings and sculpture) toward the mastery of various academic techniques and approaches toward refining your powers as a critical reader, writer and reviser for a variety of academic contexts and beyond.


Book list:

Wannabe: Reckonings with the Pop Culture That Shapes Me by Aisha Harris 

Going All City: Struggle and Survival in LA’s Graffiti Subculture by Stefano Bloch 

Art of Engagement: Visual Politics in California and Beyond by Peter Selz

The Well-Crafted Sentence: A Writer’s Guide to Style by Nora Bacon
