subject: COLWRIT
title: Belonging & Uprooting
description:
What does it mean to belong somewhere — to a society or culture, a community or subculture, or to a small classroom community like this one? R1A: Belonging & Uprooting is meant to be an engaging exploration of different possible answers to these questions, both personal and theoretical. We'll use cultural theory, nonfiction, a novel, and the occasional poem or short film to examine how one's sense of belonging is shaped, looking at its intersections with individual and communal identity, geography, and ancestry.

We'll examine how belonging is constructed through abstract "imagined communities" (in the words of Benedict Anderson, writing about the concept of the modern nation-state); or the ways it reinvents itself out of the ashes of its own absence in diaspora (using the lens of Svetlana Boym's typology of nostalgia, the "longing for a home that no longer exists or has never existed," which she breaks down into reflective and restorative modes), then will apply that lens to Exit West, a lyrical love story turned refugee novel by Pakistani author (and Berkeley alum!) Mohsin Hamid. We'll also read A Map of Future Ruins: On Borders & Belonging by Oakland immigration journalist Lauren Markham, braiding her investigative reporting on the 2020 fire that burned the largest refugee camp in Europe, Markham's own Greek ancestry and their migration story, and the mythmaking that underpins the West's long-held narrative of Greece as the cradle of Western culture.

We’ll explore the opposite of belonging, reading arguments against assimilation and in praise of outsidership and working-class, first-gen identities via the feminist theorist bell hooks (who uses her own experience as a working-class Black woman in academia as a lens to discuss & refute assimilation), the short film Hey Man (which follows an early-transition rideshare driver as they navigate the public/private presentations of self) and multilingual poems excerpted from Tripas, the Pulitzer-winning collection by Brandon Som about Chinese-Chicano belonging, we'll learn new strategies for close reading and analysis of literary texts.

We'll write four mostly-academic essays in conversation with these texts, examine several other modes of personal and analytical writing, and (if there's time!) conduct a handful of exploratory experiments in creative research via micro-interviews, long walks, mapmaking aided by Rebecca Solnit's anthology of artist-made maps of San Francisco, and DIY fieldwork. This class — like all R1A classes — will demand a level of attention to text through close reading, re-reading, and rigorous analysis that many students haven't encountered in high school (so if you've found yourself frustrated with the artificial limitations the five-paragraph essay structure places on your intellectual capacity, you'll get to leave it behind and instantly do far more sophisticated work). We'll also focus heavily on the revision process itself, which is to say that we'll spend the semester immersed in iterative rewriting and revision, making significant changes to each draft in order to break out of old intellectual and writerly habits — and to develop new ones that help us all shine as an increasingly rigorous analytical writers and narrative storytellers. This class might best be described as relaxed yet demanding: not easy (it's six credits, after all), but rewarding and surprisingly relevant, no matter your major or field of study. Expect to put in some hard work and get a lot of writing done, but also to have fun when the stars align.

Books & Materials:  

One or two full-length books: the novel Exit West, and probably also A Map of Future Ruins by Lauren Markham (which I may only excerpt portions of). Together these two will cost around $35, maybe a little less depending on where you get them.
We'll also use a writing handbook — probably the excellent They Say/I Say, which will run you another $20ish. (If cost is an issue for these texts, just let me know.)

We'll read numerous shorter texts (mostly personal essays and beginner-friendly theory), including work by preeminent Black scholar and feminist theorist bell hooks, theorist Benedict Anderson, prolific author and public intellectual Rebecca Solnit, the film Hey Man (dir. Kai Tillman), and others. In addition, we'll read and discuss short essays on the practice and philosophy of writing and revision just about every week. All will be provided in .pdf form or as print-outs.

You'll also need to bring a laptop, tablet, or paper notebook to class every day. Some students opt to purchase annotation software/apps like GoodNotes, Notability, or Kami to use for ongoing annotation assignments I'll assign beginning early in the semester. There's no need to buy these in advance (or at all — you may find free resources that work for you, or opt to print out your .pdfs and annotate by hand), but if you're already exploring digital tools to help make your academic life easier, keep your eyes out for things that allow you to take margin notes or mark up texts easily in order to integrate active reading into your workflow for all your classes, not just one-off R1A assignments.

subject: COLWRIT
title: The Rhetoric of Resistance: Utopian Thought as Process
description: In an interview, historian and scholar Howard Zinn was asked if there have been any moments in world history that he would choose to emulate in thinking about the future of global society. His answer discusses only two examples. The Paris Commune of 1871 and revolutionary Catalonia at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War. In this course, Zinn’s response will serve as a jumping off point to explore literature and writing that engages, simultaneously, with histories of subjugation and more equitable futures. The course will move beyond the examples cited to explore what is at the root of thinking through utopias as a process rather than an end. Course readings may include: The Left Hand of Darkness by Ursula Le Guin, Exit West by Mohsin Hamid, Rebel Cities by David Harvey, and Just Kids by Patti Smith. Course readings are subject to change.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Conformity Sucks
description: Throughout the history of drama, poetry, fiction, and nonfiction – not to mention real life – rebellion rules. From the subversive characters of Sophocles, Shakespeare, Joseph Heller, and Toni Morrison in drama/poetry/fiction to bigger-than-life iconoclasts like Hatshepsut, Li Qingzhou, John Locke, Mary Wollstonecraft, and Martin Luther King in nonfiction, the rebellious force those in power to bend the knee. This class will take a hard look at the effects that iconoclasts, both real and imagined, good and bad, have had on real life events, particularly as they pertain to natural rights. Any meaningful change in the world was brought about by the most determined protesters, the utmost civilly disobedient, the hardest questioners of authority, and nowhere is this more obvious than in their writing. In short, conformists dot the i’s and cross the t’s of history. Iconoclasts write it.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Fandom
description:
It’s okay if you don't belong to any fan community. You’re probably better off that way; you get to focus more on your work and loved ones. But it’s also okay if you identify as a diehard fan: “There’s nothing in the world quite like being part of a fandom. Never let anyone shame you for it…. Do what makes you happy,” as J.M Darhower maintains in Ghosted. Fans tend to invest emotions, time, money, and confidence in celebrities, TV shows, characters, or sports— sometimes to perplexing degrees that call into question good judgment. Our R1A section focuses on ardency, affinity, and glee as well as frustration in fandoms. We will explore fan behaviors and celebrity reactions, as we delve into how and whom fans interact with— particularly on social media. We will read, write, and talk about related texts, including Eric Smith’s novel, Don't Read the Comments, and Henry Jenkins’ collection of essays, Fans, Bloggers, and Gamers, together with documentaries, short stories, and essays. 

Jenkins, Henry. Fans, Bloggers, and Gamers, New York U P, 2006. 

Smith, Eric. Don't Read the Comments, Inkyard, 2020.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Magnificent Diversity: Eco-Thinking in the Age of Climate Change
description: A hallmark of humanity is our extraordinary creativity, born and nurtured within the natural world. Yet human industry and development have caused the alarming loss of nature and climate change. What obligations do we have to other species, ecosystems, each other, and coming generations? How can wild nature be conserved and restored? What can we learn from cultures, past and present, whose vision and values have embraced earth’s wonders? These are some of the questions we will pursue through reading a variety of texts by scholars, scientists, activists, journalists, poets, and others, and through films and art. During the term, you will have the opportunity to share your perspectives in lively discussion and to develop your own unique voice as a writer. This section is reserved for multilingual speakers.

subject: COLWRIT
description: "Place is security, space is freedom: we are attached to the one and long for the other" (Tuan). Freedom and security, however, are vulnerable to being compromised by fear, misconceptions, power, and privilege. We will explore these conflicts by looking at the use of public and private spaces, proximity to others, and proximity to truth. Students will examine a variety of sources; writing assignments will include a text analysis, synthesis, and an autoethnographic essay.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Open to students who have not fulfilled the entry level writing requirement.
description: In an interview, historian and scholar Howard Zinn was asked if there have been any moments in world history that he would choose to emulate in thinking about the future of global society. His answer discusses only two examples. The Paris Commune of 1871 and revolutionary Catalonia at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War. In this course, Zinn’s response will serve as a jumping off point to explore literature and writing that engages, simultaneously, with histories of subjugation and more equitable futures. The course will move beyond the examples cited to explore what is at the root of thinking through utopias as a process rather than an end. Course readings may include: The Left Hand of Darkness by Ursula Le Guin, Exit West by Mohsin Hamid, Rebel Cities by David Harvey, and Just Kids by Patti Smith. Course readings are subject to change.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Navigating Our Differences with Empathy and Humility
description:
Differences, disagreements, and conflicts are inevitable in daily life. Though often stressful, these disagreements can also provide opportunity for reflection and growth, especially when they are relatively minor.  But, what happens when our differences get politicized and we no longer see the humanity in our fellow citizens?  In this course, we’ll consider some reasons for the increasing hostility in our political/civic discourse, analyze what unites and what divides us as a society, and examine strategies for bridging the divide.  In particular, we’ll consider how inequality and rapid (unprecedented) technological and cultural changes have contributed to increasing polarization and examine various strategies that might help us find common ground.

Difficult Conversations:How to Discuss What Matters Most (Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton, and Sheila Heen)

Strangers in their own Land: Anger and Mourning on the American Right (Arlie Russell Hochschild)

title: Writing in the Age of ChatGPT

subject: COLWRIT
title: Recon, Rove, Reveal, Riot
description:
In Recon, Rove, Reveal, Riot, we’ll examine turbulent phenomena and situations— the explosive rise of A.I.s in our lives, shifting landscapes in elite sports— things that are actively evolving, actively in flux. We’ll use distinct aspects of intelligence to drive these investigations: 

I. Tech & INTEL   INTEL: Data gathered for decision-making > What do you need to know?  After exploring the tech podcast Hard Fork together as a class, each of you will decide on a precise AI-related tech phenomenon you want to look into. What is the intel that you need to understand this thing, so that you might … use it? modify it? resist it? leverage it?  reinvent it?  Once you’ve gained further understanding through credible texts from the popular media (other podcasts, news articles, websites, TED Talks, videos, etc.), you’ll articulate in an expository piece why this emergent tech matters. Why is having this intel important right now? What are the stakes?      


II.  Heroism, Moral Dilemma & EQ   EQ: Emotional Intelligence > psychological capacity and emotional intelligence, including self-awareness and the ability to evolve   In the speculative fiction novel Migrations, where Earth is on the edge of environmental collapse, the hero Franny engages in complicated behaviors on her simultaneous quests. One quest is physical: she stows aboard the fishing vessel The Saghani  to track and save the last surviving flock of Arctic terns. Another is emotional: Franny is trying, paradoxically, to learn how to be still, to allow herself to attach to people and places. As she journeys, what are Franny’s arcs of self-awareness and emotional intelligence? 

III. Elite Athletes, Vulnerability & CQ   CQ: Cultural Intelligence > the ability to understand, respect, and effectively navigate diverse cultural contexts, including actively adapting your own behaviors, and leveraging cultural cues to influence or change cultural environments   In elite sports–think semi-pro, pro, Olympics– a cultural shift is occurring right now: one towards more openness and vulnerability around mental and emotional health. We’ll dive into the journalism on this shift, some of it written by the athletes themselves.  What’s driving this shift? What does it look and sound like, including its meta-narrative (what are people saying about what the athletes are saying?) Is this shift affected by resistance and blowback? 

IV. Endurance, Resistance, Apocalypse & AQ    AQ: Adaptive Intelligence  >  awareness of one’s environment, and how to live in it and alter or shape it when needed   Tochi Onyebuchi’s speculative fiction novella Riot Baby begins in the realism of South Central Los Angeles and the 1992 Rodney King Riots, and travels forward in time and space to Harlem, Rikers Island, Watts, and the present & future. Onyebuchi layers in “speculative” elements, including psychic powers, telepathy, and a police state whose “augments” – officers with augmented reality wired into their bodies– surveil the public just by walking through it.  How does Onyebuchi build explosive impact through writerly ("rhetorical") choices? And what does Riot Baby suggest about adaptation to inequity through endurance? … resistance?  …apocalypse?



COURSE TEXTS TO PURCHASE, IN PRINT (hardcopy)*

Migrations  Charlotte McConaghy

Riot Baby  Tochi Onyebuchi

      *except for students with an access accommodation, of course

title: What's love got to do with It?
description: As we read bell hooks' All About Love, Thi Bui's The Best We Could Do, and several short works, we will enter into an academic conversation about love. Through close reading, interactive discussion, and critical reflection, we will create a series of writing projects, both formal and informal, which will help us develop and clarify our writing voices.

subject: COLWRIT
title: The 1619 Project
description: This course covers concepts and skills in critical reading and writing, practicing on the New York Times Magazine's 1619 Project, which offers a new perspective on the United States' history. By considering our nation's birth year not as 1776 but rather when enslaved Africans were first brought to North America, the project offers various written and visual texts that "place the consequences of slavery and the contributions of black Americans at the very center of the story we tell ourselves about who we are as a country." We will read, discuss, and write about essays, books, and films that focus on individual stories, fear and incarceration, segregation in real estate and lending practices, medicine, cultural production, and our sense and experiences of racial identity.

course.title: Reading and Composition
course.description: This writing seminar satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement. The course is designed to offer students structured, sustained, and highly articulated practice in the recursive processes entailed in reading, critical analysis, and composing. Students will read five thematically related book-length texts, or the equivalent, drawn from a range of genres, in addition to various non-print sources. In response to these materials, they will craft several short pieces leading up to three longer essays--works of exposition and argumentation.
course.requirements: Enrollment is limited to students who have satisfied the UC Entry Level Writing Requirement.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Nature
description:
Nature. The word shows up all around us: on a trail sign, on a label in the grocery store, in our social media feeds, and in the way we might talk about needing to return to some ideal state or to clear our heads. In this class, we’ll read fiction and nonfiction texts that consider our natural world and what we even mean by ‘natural’. Through our readings, we’ll move through forests, mountain ranges, oceans, cities, backyards- and even grocery store aisles. As we do, we’ll pay attention to how those places are described, understood, remembered, argued over, and lived in. Along the way, you’ll engage in conversations through short, low-stakes writing that asks you to go somewhere, look closely, and make connections between your experiences and the texts you read.

The theme of nature gives us a focus for our reading and discussion, but the core work of the class is writing. You will write and revise regularly, building toward a final portfolio that shows your growth as a writer across the semester. That means learning how to sustain analysis of a passage, how to quote and work with texts, how to move from examples to claims, and how to consider rhetorical elements as you write. We’ll practice different kinds of writing, always with the expectation that you engage closely with what you read, with your own writing as a process, and with our class as a community of writers and thinkers.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Cults in Literature and Film
description:
What constitutes a cult? Is there such a thing as a good cult? Or all cults fundamentally evil? And, finally, why do people join cults in the first place?

In this course, we will investigate these questions and more, through our encounters with a diverse set of materials, including books, articles, and film.

At the same time, this course will ask you to embrace writing as a process and practice writing as a form of critical thinking. You will also create different types of writing, from your standard academic essay to more multi-modal works. 

Required texts (tentative list):

Cultish: The Language of Fanaticism by Amanda Montell 

The Girls by Emma Cline

Parable of the Sower by Octavia Butler

Other readings will be made available in a course reader. 

Any films we watch will be streamable for free, via our campus library.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Health Justice
description: In this section, you will practice reading and writing every week. In your essays, you will analyze the formal, rhetorical, and thematic aspects of texts, develop original interpretations, and build compelling arguments. Our section will focus on “Health Justice.” Health justice is rooted in Indigenous knowledges, women of color feminisms, disability and LGBTQ+ activism, the natural and social sciences, and more. To develop our understanding of health justice, we will study movements for environmental sustainability, community clinics, harm reduction and mutual aid, reproductive justice, and prison abolition.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Language/Revolution
description: In this class we’ll examine the relationship between language and revolution in three different historical moments. First, we will look at writing and other primary source material from the second half of the 18th century, including the American Declaration of Independence as part of the Berkeley On The Same Page Initiative and in observance of the American semiquincentennial. Then we will turn to the Bay Area in the 1950s and 60s, when students and writers alike were working to redefine the relationship between language and freedom. Finally, we will closely consider developments in the realm of language today, with an emphasis on questions raised by the prospect of an AI driven future. Much of this class will run like a language lab, predicated on the idea that scholars work to investigate, understand, and form opinions on difficult problems through experimentation, observation, and recording findings. We'll do this through close examination of texts and contexts, which will become the basis for guided practice in making arguments. Working in and with a variety of genres, modes, and styles, we will read and think deeply and carefully, asking questions and developing answers while practicing both formal and informal writing through sustained engagement with the revision process.

subject: COLWRIT
title: The Lie You Tell Yourself: Grifters, Magicians, Neuroscience & the Complexities of Belief
description:
Course Overview:

Nothing fools you better than the lie you tell yourself -- Teller

Come behind the curtain. We'll examine why we’re drawn to the unexplainable and why we often create patterns where none exist; weigh how modern illusionists and con men fool their willing audiences, often with an understanding of neuroscience and psychology; explore the relationship between hype, echo chambers, magical thinking and belief in internet culture; and experience the complexity of deception when we start to believe our own lies.

We’ll leverage a rich variety of evidence, including books, academic articles, journalism, podcasts, documentaries and primary source materials, from historical images and artifacts to contemporary Reddit screengrabs and social media posts. And we'll push our ability, through expository essays, multimodal fieldwork narratives, argument essays and more, to critically examine the world around us.


Required Texts:

(purchasing used or digital copies will be fine, as well as library copies)

Kuhn, Experiencing the Impossible: the Science of Magic (MIT Press, 2019)
Graff & Birkenstein, They Say / I Say: the Moves that Matter in Academic Writing (Norton, 2024; 6th ed.)
Course Reader [free articles on bCourses]

Documentaries & Films:

Measom, An Honest Liar (Filmhub Inc, 2014); [streamed for free via Kanopy]

Texts should be available at Cal Student Store, but if you find used or digital versions, please feel free to get those! Where possible, our reading will often feature free, smaller, digital excerpts and articles collected by me in the Digital Course

subject: COLWRIT
title: Reading and Writing the Memoir
description: In memoir, a writer shares a meaningful and “true” narrative about their life. This entails, or can entail: making sense of what happened; selecting and shaping facts and memories; sharing a vision or furthering a cause; promoting values (or sometimes promoting yourself); building community; building bridges; providing a historical perspective, and more. In any case, the “truth” of the story is arrived at and constructed, versus simply transcribed. In this class, we’ll stand on this premise to analyze memoir from various critical perspectives. Over the course of the semester, you’ll further your analytical reading skills and undertake the hard and stimulating work of close reading, brainstorming, note-taking, critiquing, discussing, and revising (there will be a lot of revising), to produce writing you can be proud of. In and through this work you will also develop a critical awareness about writing for different audiences and in different genres.

course.description: This writing seminar satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement. The course is designed to offer students structured, sustained, and highly articulated practice in the recursive processes entailed in reading, critical analysis, and composing. Students will read five thematically related book-length texts, or the equivalent, drawn from a range of genres, in addition to various non-print sources. In response to these materials, they will craft several short pieces leading up to three longer essays--works of exposition and argumentation.
course.requirements: Enrollment is limited to students who have satisfied the UC Entry Level Writing Requirement.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Reading and Writing the Memoir
description: In memoir, a writer shares a meaningful and “true” narrative about their life. This entails, or can entail: making sense of what happened; selecting and shaping facts and memories; sharing a vision or furthering a cause; promoting values (or sometimes promoting yourself); building community; building bridges; providing a historical perspective, and more. In any case, the “truth” of the story is arrived at and constructed, versus simply transcribed. In this class, we’ll stand on this premise to analyze memoir from various critical perspectives. Over the course of the semester, you’ll further your analytical reading skills and undertake the hard and stimulating work of close reading, brainstorming, note-taking, critiquing, discussing, and revising (there will be a lot of revising), to produce writing you can be proud of. In and through this work you will also develop a critical awareness about writing for different audiences and in different genres.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Hi, AI: The Case for Human Intelligence
description:
With the rapid advance of large language models and other forms of artificial intelligence, AI has very much entered the broader public consciousness of late, with all sorts of attendant excitement and anxiety. We wonder how AI might affect our lives: will it be a welcome tool, a fascinating but over-hyped evolution of technology, a threat to our livelihoods, a redefining moment in the history of humanity? Or perhaps all of the above and more? What is the place of human intelligence and agency in the face of the proliferation of AI? Or, put another way, what will life be like for human beings—for us—in a world of AI, and what should we be doing about it?

In this class, we will examine more specific versions of these questions, through a series of shared reading, writing, and research assignments, and then you will each choose a specific topic and question within this broad field of artificial intelligence and its effects on human life this is both important to you and worthy of study for a final research project and paper.


Unmasking AI: My Mission to Protect What is Human in a World of Machines, by Joy Buolamwini

The AI Mirror: How to Reclaim Our Humanity in an Age of Machine Thinking, Shannon Vallor

The Craft of Research, 4th Edition, Booth, et al., editors

course.subject: COLWRIT
course.title: Reading, Composition, and Research
course.description: A seminar satisfying the second half of the Reading & Composition requirement, R4B offers structured and sustained practice in the processes used in reading, critical analysis, and writing. Students engage with thematically-related materials from a range of genres and media. In response, they craft short pieces leading to longer expository and/or argumentative essays. Students develop a research question, draft a research essay, gather, evaluate, and synthesize information from various sources. Elements of the research process--a proposal, an annotated bibliography, an abstract, a works cited list, etc.--are submitted with the final report in a research portfolio. Students write a minimum of 32 pages of prose.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Monsters and Modernity
description:
Monsters used to represent fear of the unknown: unmapped regions in the medieval period were marked by dragons; imperialists in the 19th century bringing the "light" of civilization into the dark continent of Africa feared cannibals. Given the scientific basis of the modern period, would it not be accurate to say that we no longer believe in monsters, that they survive in the modern period if only so that they can serve as the very sign of an unenlightened, and superstitious past? No. Monsters have not been banished to the regions of superstition; they have not been relegated entirely to the past. Once we get over the fear that they might pop out from under our beds, we run to the cinema to delight in observing their contemporary manifestations: as mad scientists, bestial men and women, re-animated corpses, and cyborgs. In the modern period, monsters remain as figures not simply of fear and fascination but of real use. Monsters persist as an emblem of anxiety about a past that is too rapidly disintegrating so as to compromise the very structures of society; or alternatively as a mode of protest against the modernity of the modern period with its new forms of regulation and social control; or then again as the sign of a compromised future wherein the representation of the monster serves to question the "progress of progress," and direct suspicion onto the modern projects of science, industry, and technology. Two analytical papers; one research paper. Literature and film focus.

Book List:

Handmaid's Tale (Margaret Atwood), Dracula (Bram Stoker), Craft of Research (Wayne Booth). 

Film: Alien (Ridley Scott). Video: Dexter season 1

subject: COLWRIT
title: Berkeley Interventions
description: UC Berkeley is known around the world because of the ideas generated by our faculty and students. This online course investigates a selection of influential books written by Berkeley faculty. These books have made significant interventions in their field of research. We will study these books to better understand how influential ideas are developed and communicated. By design, this seminar course explores a variety of disciplines and topics. The final research project enables students to focus on an influential Berkeley text of their own choosing.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Not Knowing, Unlearning, Wonder, and Awe
description: So often knowledge and learning are presented as something to be tested on, something to be “acquired,” or something others know that you don’t yet. Such learning is usually the basis of a lot of classes, both K-12 and in college. Of course, this knowledge is vitally important to having a strong foundation in any field, and there’s a comfort in being able to get the answers “right.” However, the most inventive research happens when we wander into the unknown, when we are inspired by wonder and awe. Getting into that “unknown,” though, is tricky. It’s often uncomfortable because we’ve been taught to memorize and only show what we know. But many of our most famous thinkers are not only comfortable with the “unknown,” they thrive on it. For example, physicist Richard Feynman kept notebooks called “Things I Don’t Know.” It’s in the unknown that we can find mystery and wonder. For this class, we’ll focus on how to get more comfortable with exploring the unknown, sometimes even “unlearning” what things we think we do know, and exploring the things we find awesome, in the real sense of that word. While we’ll approach the unknown in many fields, this class is particularly well suited for those in the sciences. We’ll start with common readings by writers such as Robin Wall Kimmerer (botany), Ed Yong (animal biology), Siddartha Mukherjee (human biology), and Ed Frankel (math), among others. For the second half of the class, you’ll develop your own research projects, ideally projects that both add to established knowledge and point in directions for more research into what we don’t know, at least not yet.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Contemporary Cults
description:
Cults have enthralled the popular imagination for a very long time. We wonder: What makes people join a cult? What makes a cult so powerful that people would kill for a cult leader (Charles Manson) or die for one (Jim Jones)? Are there specific historical, political, even geographical conditions that enable cults and cultish behavior to thrive? Are we in one of those periods now? 

In this course, these questions and more will kickstart your independent research project on the topic of cults. Berkeley and the larger Bay Area will become a particularly rich site for our investigations because of this area’s long history with cults (most infamously, the Jim Jones-led People’s Temple, which resulted in the 1978 Jonestown Massacre in Guyana). 

Since this is a research-oriented course, you will become familiar with our various campus libraries, archives, and databases. You can also expect a highly collaborative classroom because writing and thinking don’t need to (and shouldn’t) be isolating activities. Moreover, you will write a series of different assignments, from smaller, synthesis-driven essays to an annotated bibliography, that will prime you for your final multi-modal, research project. 

Required texts (tentative list): 

Cultish: The Language of Fanaticism by Amanda Montell

Terror, Love, and Brainwashing: Attachment in Cults and Totalitarian Systems by Alexandra Stein

There will also be a course reader that includes readings focused, not just on cults, but on the research and writing process as well.

Depending on their availability, we may also engage with films and podcasts (for example: The Sunshine Place) that deepen our inquiry into cults.

subject: COLWRIT
title: 'For Neighbor and for the Earth'
description: How might we work to heal social fissures and restore our damaged planet in this time of possibility, with so much at stake? Bill McKibben speaks of "people around the world filled with love for neighbor and for the earth who are resisting, remaking, restoring, renewing, revitalizing.” This course explores the intersection between social justice and earth justice as we address the grand challenge of creating a healthier world for all living things in particular, precious places. Among our sources will be thoughtful scholars, scientists, activists, artists and others who will help us consider the roots of current crises, perspectives from people often unheard, and solutions toward healing. You will have the opportunity to discover and share your perspectives in lively discussion and in notebook entries, essays, and a research project, all while developing your own unique voice.

subject: COLWRIT
title: How Experts Communicate:  Preparing for Writing in Your Major and Career
description:
Every academic discipline, profession, and industry has its own ways of asking questions, evaluating evidence, and communicating ideas. Yet these practices are rarely taught explicitly. Instead, students are often expected to figure them out only after they reach upper-division courses, internships, research labs, or the workplace. This course pulls back the curtain on those expectations. 

Working with authentic academic and industry documents, students investigate how experts organize information, construct arguments, present evidence, and communicate with particular audiences and purposes. Rather than simply asking what these documents say, we examine how they accomplish their work and what aspiring practitioners can learn from them.

Throughout the course, students apply these insights in their own reading, writing, and research. With guided practice, they develop strategies for analyzing complex texts, making purposeful communication decisions, and producing documents that reflect the expectations of their intended communities. The course culminates with a research project connected to each student's academic or professional interests, preparing them to participate more confidently in the conversations—and communities—they hope to join.

subject: COLWRIT
title: How Experts Communicate: Preparing for Writing in Your Major and Career
description:
Every academic discipline, profession, and industry has its own ways of asking questions, evaluating evidence, and communicating ideas. Yet these practices are rarely taught explicitly. Instead, students are often expected to figure them out only after they reach upper-division courses, internships, research labs, or the workplace. This course pulls back the curtain on those expectations. 

Working with authentic academic and industry documents, students investigate how experts organize information, construct arguments, present evidence, and communicate with particular audiences and purposes. Rather than simply asking what these documents say, we examine how they accomplish their work and what aspiring practitioners can learn from them.

Throughout the course, students apply these insights in their own reading, writing, and research. With guided practice, they develop strategies for analyzing complex texts, making purposeful communication decisions, and producing documents that reflect the expectations of their intended communities. The course culminates with a research project connected to each student's academic or professional interests, preparing them to participate more confidently in the conversations—and communities—they hope to join.

subject: COLWRIT
title: The Meme & the Human (& AI): Digital Literacies
description:
Together we reflect on and discuss technological change, including AI. We also consider the existential devastation of our sacred earth, and other worldwide crises. With all of these paradigm shifts in mind, we ask, What does it mean to be human? We also analyze motivations for communicating in memes, their links to human identity, and their polysemous nature inviting diverse audiences to interpret them differently. Becoming more savvy digital citizens, we look at memes’ techno-social features, genres, (unwritten) rules of meme-related conduct, and whether the connections memes create are more important than their content. We explore best research practices and the myriad ways that Berkeley’s libraries and librarians empower these. 

You focus on a key issue, topic, or question of your choice and engage in process-based research to build an articulate, sound digital portfolio of inquiry that includes a proposal, abstract, research essay, works cited, annotated bibliography, and research presentation with slide deck, plus other assignments. We have many in-class discussions that springboard off student-suggested topics. Writing well matters, for your professional development and quality of life. Writing is revising for us all. You are invited to invest in writing as a way of honoring your own voice and contributing to the Greater Good too. You are in CWR4B because you have passed a course or a test that said you have the necessary reading & writing skills, and our coursework builds on those prerequisites. You build real-world skills and confidence in CWR4B.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Modern Love, Ancient Brains
description: This course focuses on the burgeoning field of evolutionary psychology, which argues that humans vary little across time and space, and that our behavior is rooted in the choices of our ancestors. These arguments are compelling but also ripe with controversy. We will analyze these arguments from various perspectives – sociology, economics, politics, computer science, and more – and hopefully become better readers, writers, and researchers as we do. Here are some questions you will explore in this class: Is beauty truly in the eye of the beholder? Why are we drawn to certain types of food, people, landscapes, and art? Are people really that different from one culture or era to the next? How much free will do we really have? How are recent technological and economic developments impacting impulses that developed over millions of years? Is society to blame for gender differences, or are these differences a natural part of life?

subject: COLWRIT
title: Gangsters, Gold-diggers & Glamour Girls: The Dialectic of Film and Culture
description:
"Two cliches make us laugh. A hundred cliches move us. For we sense dimly that the cliches are talking among themselves, and celebrating a reunion."

--Umberto Eco


The audience that flocked to theaters in 1959 to see Billy Wilder’s blockbuster film Some Like it Hot delighted in a host of stereotypes of the Roaring 20's—the gangster with his immaculate spats, the buxom song-and-dance starlet, and the dashing leading man. They came expecting to see a portrait of the pre-Depression age of innocence cast as comedy. More than that, though, they came to see the star, Marilyn Monroe, the iconic figure of their own time whose very way of walking and talking expressed the desires of all who had purchased their tickets and consented to sit shoulder-to-shoulder in that dark room. The event of the film itself, its projection in thousands of theaters, amounts to more of a statement about American contemporary culture of the late 50s than about the slice of history it parodies.

In many cases, artistic choices that go into the making of popular films take on unforeseen meanings that influence the fabric of public truth. How did the quirky alt-protagonist of Juno come to be adopted against creator Diablo Cody’s will as the poster child for religious conservatives? How can the artistic dispute between the writer and the director of The Social Network conceal an impassioned public debate over the issue of privacy on the internet? How did the psychological clichés of horror provide Jordan Peele’s low budget Get Out with the recipe for deconstructing racism to a mass mainstream audience?

In this course, you will explore the conversation between Hollywood and American culture. You will start by learning how to analyze the style of the conventional Hollywood film, with help from B.F. Dick’s Anatomy of Film and McKee’s Story. Texts like Lunsford's Everything's an Argument will help you to become conscious of the rhetorical events that underpin written and visual media. The class will culminate in a research-based essay in which you will assess a wide variety of nonfiction sources—essays, histories, blogs, documentaries, interviews, advertising, reviews, tattlers—that enter into the discourse on the formation of American taste in film and TV.

subject: COLWRIT
title: Gangsters, Gold-diggers & Glamour Girls: The Dialectic of Film and Culture
description:
"Two cliches make us laugh. A hundred cliches move us. For we sense dimly that the cliches are talking among themselves, and celebrating a reunion."

--Umberto Eco


The audience that flocked to theaters in 1959 to see Billy Wilder’s blockbuster film Some Like it Hot delighted in a host of stereotypes of the Roaring 20's—the gangster with his immaculate spats, the buxom song-and-dance starlet, and the dashing leading man. They came expecting to see a portrait of the pre-Depression age of innocence cast as comedy. More than that, though, they came to see the star, Marilyn Monroe, the iconic figure of their own time whose very way of walking and talking expressed the desires of all who had purchased their tickets and consented to sit shoulder-to-shoulder in that dark room. The event of the film itself, its projection in thousands of theaters, amounts to more of a statement about American contemporary culture of the late 50s than about the slice of history it parodies.

In many cases, artistic choices that go into the making of popular films take on unforeseen meanings that influence the fabric of public truth. How did the quirky alt-protagonist of Juno come to be adopted against creator Diablo Cody’s will as the poster child for religious conservatives? How can the artistic dispute between the writer and the director of The Social Network conceal an impassioned public debate over the issue of privacy on the internet? How did the psychological clichés of horror provide Jordan Peele’s low budget Get Out with the recipe for deconstructing racism to a mass mainstream audience?

In this course, you will explore the conversation between Hollywood and American culture. You will start by learning how to analyze the style of the conventional Hollywood film, with help from B.F. Dick’s Anatomy of Film and McKee’s Story. Texts like Lunsford's Everything's an Argument will help you to become conscious of the rhetorical events that underpin written and visual media. The class will culminate in a research-based essay in which you will assess a wide variety of nonfiction sources—essays, histories, blogs, documentaries, interviews, advertising, reviews, tattlers—that enter into the discourse on the formation of American taste in film and TV.

subject: COLWRIT
title: The Meme & the Human (& AI): Digital Literacies
description:
Together we reflect on and discuss technological change, including AI. We also consider the existential devastation of our sacred earth, and other worldwide crises. With all of these paradigm shifts in mind, we ask, What does it mean to be human? We also analyze motivations for communicating in memes, their links to human identity, and their polysemous nature inviting diverse audiences to interpret them differently. Becoming more savvy digital citizens, we look at memes’ techno-social features, genres, (unwritten) rules of meme-related conduct, and whether the connections memes create are more important than their content. We explore best research practices and the myriad ways that Berkeley’s libraries and librarians empower these. 

You focus on a key issue, topic, or question of your choice and engage in process-based research to build an articulate, sound digital portfolio of inquiry that includes a proposal, abstract, research essay, works cited, annotated bibliography, and research presentation with slide deck, plus other assignments. We have many in-class discussions that springboard off student-suggested topics. Writing well matters, for your professional development and quality of life. Writing is revising for us all. You are invited to invest in writing as a way of honoring your own voice and contributing to the Greater Good too. You are in CWR4B because you have passed a course or a test that said you have the necessary reading & writing skills, and our coursework builds on those prerequisites. You build real-world skills and confidence in CWR4B.

subject: COMLIT
title: Nuance
description:
“Now, there is a teacher of nuance, literature.” The literary critic Roland Barthes makes this claim in a defense of nuance that will provide us with a point of departure. In this introduction to comparative reading, we will begin with the dual premise that an appreciation for nuance can be taught, and that the study of literature can sharpen our perception and understanding of nuance.

But what is nuance? How can we learn to read with an eye for poetic subtlety, to listen for slight shifts in a narrator’s tone, or to draw out a critical argument’s implications? What’s the difference between close reading, on the one hand, and overinterpretation, on the other? These questions will guide us as we study some frameworks, including Marxist and psychoanalytic frameworks, for comparative reading. These will then let us consider several other related questions: Does reading across languages and cultures mean sacrificing nuance, or can this kind of reading heighten our awareness of minimal but meaningful differences and changing tonalities? What does it mean to attend to nuance and complexity in a digital age that stifles both? How should we understand appeals to “nuance” that are used to mystify, to prevent us from asking politically fraught questions or making certain kinds of political claims? What about appeals to nuance that serve to shore up social distinctions or to police divisions between “high” and “low” literary forms?

We will study poems, pop songs, films, critical essays, and short stories and novels. Assigned texts and films will model various ways of paying attention (or not) and will include works by Samuel Beckett, Samuel Delany, Michelangelo Frammartino, Renee Gladman, Kazuo Ishiguro, Clarice Lispector, Lucrecia Martel, Juan José Saer, and Virginia Woolf, among others. Students will also experiment with a range of approaches to nuance in their own writing.

subject: COMLIT
title: Contemporary Hybrid Forms
description:
This introduction to the discipline of comparative literature focuses on contemporary hybrid texts that work with and between literary genres and forms. While conventions of genre—such as those that define the novel, memoir, or lyric poetry—organize readerly expectation, hybrid texts deliberately push and unsettle generic boundaries. They often include an investment in poetics, autobiographic accounts, procedural narratives, and their own process of research in order to render new approaches to their concerns and objects of study. In concert with formal resourcefulness, the hybrid text requires recourse to a wide range of source materials—images, maps, ephemeral documents, historical and archival records—to animate poetic accounts and multi-perspective narratives.

As students of the hybrid form, we will analyze its exploratory disposition toward writing and formal invention while developing a robust critical language to describe these works and their social, political, and ethical implications. We will investigate how certain kinds of historical conditions and subject positions precipitate the creation of inventive formal approaches to materials and experiences, ones often not included in traditional literary productions. How has the hybrid text been a crucial resource for thinking for scholars and creative writers? What particular capacities do hybrid forms bring to questions of identity, race, class, gender, sexuality? To address these investigative questions, this course considers the hybrid text in relation to historical archives (such as the archive of the trans-Atlantic slave trade) and in conversation with a variety of theoretical modalities (such as gender and feminist studies, postcolonial approaches, psychoanalysis). Our study of this shape-shifting form will focus on works by 20th and 21st century writers, including by the following: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Alexis Pauline Gumbs, Saidiya Hartman, Claudia Rankine, Edward W. Said, Layli Long Soldier, Solmaz Sharif among others.

subject: COMLIT
title: Crises of Patrilinearity and the Generation of Narrative
description: Comp. Lit. 100 is designed to present students with texts from various genres and historicial periods, to introduce them to the methods of comparative study. The thematic focus of this course will be crises of patrilinearity—family romances gone sour. More specifically, we will be looking at how such family crises enable and generate narratives, but also perturb them; how subjects are constituted and deconstructed through descent groups; how the crisis of patrilinearity can become an emblem in literary texts for other cultural crises; and how this theme intersects with issues of gender, sexuality, and race.

subject: COMLIT
title: Sleep With Me: Literature, Rest, and the Politics of Wakefulness
description:
What does it mean to remain awake? In an age marked by burnout, digital overstimulation, political crisis, anxiety, and the increasing demand for perpetual productivity, questions of rest and sleeplessness have become newly urgent. This course explores these questions through a wide range of literary, philosophical, and psychoanalytic texts, with particular attention to Hebrew and Jewish literary traditions (in translation - no language skills needed), which have long been intensely preoccupied with the tensions between wakefulness and sleep. Moving between biblical scenes of dreaming and revelation, modern Jewish political movements organized around the rhetoric of “national awakening,” and modern Hebrew literature, we will examine how writers have imagined sleep, fatigue, and reverie as sites of imaginative and relational possibility.

Our readings will include, among others, texts by Virginia Woolf, Clarice Lispector, Ronit Matalon, Amalia Kahana-Carmon, and Dahlia Ravikovitch, alongside thinkers such as Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Sigmund Freud, Wilfred Bion, Jonathan Crary, and scholars associated with Critical Rest Studies, we will ask why literature persistently returns to states of sleep and withdrawal, and what forms of knowledge might emerge from them. While dreams have occupied a central place in philosophy and psychoanalysis, sleep itself has often remained in the background. We will ask, then, what might emerge if we take sleep seriously not merely as the container of dreams, but as a mode of being, relation, and thought. Along the way, we will consider whether literature itself produces altered states of attention that unsettle the opposition between wakefulness and sleep, and whether reading may at times resemble forms of drifting and surrender.

subject: COMLIT
title: Keats, Shelley--& Modern Poetry, Poetics, Aesthetics, Critique
description:
"Canonical" British Romantic poetry--those famous experiments in form and content that highlight (among other things) nature and subjectivity; sensuousness, imagination, intellection; romance, love, sexuality; longing, melancholy, and their siblings in the realms of feeling; modes of questioning at once urgent and reflective concerning what doesn't or does, what might or should define community, society, and politics; first and finally, the art of poetry itself--as critical, progressive, radical, emancipatory?

It's been decades since that view has been commonly encountered, much less taken for granted. How about judgments going one step further? Here's W.E.B Du Bois, writing in 1954 (in the daily NATIONAL GUARDIAN) about three celebrated ""second generation"" British Romantic poets: 

""Bryon, Shelley and Keats, lord, gentleman and cockney, all were social revolutionists.""

Du Bois doesn't offer that assessment (which echoes and intensifies his many earlier evocations of Romanticism) in a vacuum. He makes it at the height of the McCarthy period, not long after having himself been indicted at the age of 83 by the U.S. government, for what amounted to charges that his political engagements constituted activity on behalf of a foreign power and that it justified his conviction and potential imprisonment. Du Bois' above-quoted words come too after several recent additions to his lifelong string of groundbreaking publications--among them, THE WORLD AND AFRICA (1947) and IN BATTLE FOR PEACE (1952).

Du Bois in his pithy phrasing happens also to join a host of poets, novelists, painters and sculptors, composers, philosophers, and critics who from the nineteenth through the twenty-first century have discerned a particular, strikingly modern dynamic at play in--and between--the work of two of those three named poets: John Keats (1795-1821) and Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792-1822). The dynamic in question concerns how the two poets view artistic form's ways of generating our aesthetic experience, and the critical reflection and agency they think is thereby engendered. The views at issue center around an apparent paradox that Keats and Shelley believe art--and our aesthetic experience of it, our engagement with it--involves. Briefly stated, that apparent paradox is that the the seemingly individual ""autonomy"" of modern art and aesthetic experience--their freedom from being determined by, their  being in excess of, existing CONCEPTS--is what's able to stimulate our aesthetic sensing of a critical capacity and agency that's not only individual in orientation but likewise somehow collective.

Keats and Shelley thus continually stress the role of artistic/aesthetic form in generating and nurturing critical subjectivity and agency. Keats leans more to the side of form, on the view that such intensity of emphasis on ""the formal itself""allows the poem to reach and transform the materials of subjective experience without falling into individualist subjectivity (i.e., placing the subject over or against the collecitve).  Nonetheless, Keasts still cares deeply about form's relation to existential-personal, sociopolitical, and historical materials and to aesthetic form's ability to transform them into content/meaning (with some key instances being aesthetic/artistic form's transformations of feelings, language, ideas, and other materials taken from reality past and present). Shelley for his part, while likewise passionate and even obsessive about form, tends to make poems that voice ethical and sociopolitical concerns a good deal more explicitly than Keats' poetry does, on the assumption that without such voicing form is arrested rather than activated. The two poets continually test and experiment with the relations among materials, form, and content/meaning within their own work; and they simultaneously test the results of their individual approaches vis-à-vis those of the fellow poet with whom history seems, at least in this regard, to have paired them. 

Most of our time in this course will be spent reading, discussing, and writing about Keats and Shelley's poetry and their literary and social criticism, all of it ""on its own terms"" and also in light of the question of form's relations to materials, content/meaning, and critical agency. But throughout the semester we'll also read across a range of later poets, along with other artists, critics, and philosophers.  They all take up the ways that Keats and Shelley's experiments and debates--each of the two romantic poets within their own work, and especially in their ways of posing that individual work in relation to that of their counterpart--have consequences for modern, modernist, and avant-gardist art, as well as for modern and contemporary aesthetics, criticism, and critical theory.

In addition to Du Bois, we'll consider responses to this Keats-Shelley matrix by (time permitting): Marx and Engels, Eleanor Marx Aveling, Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Mohandas K. (""Mahātmā"") Gandhi, T.S. Eliot, Jorge Luis Borges, Bertolt Brecht, Alfred Wolfenstein, Walter Haenisch, Walter Benjamin, Theodor W. Adorno, Jürgen Habermas, Hart Crane, James Joyce, Samuel Beckett, Wallace Stevens, H.D., Muriel Rukeyser, Ella Reeve Bloor (aka ""Mother Bloor""), Jean-Paul Sartre, Octavio Paz, Julio Cortázar, Amiri Baraka, Adrienne Rich, Barbara Guest, John Ashbery, Pier Paolo Pasolini, Michael Palmer, Rosario Castellanos, Mick Jagger, Derek Jarman, Fred Moten, Roberto Bolaño, Jane Campion, and others.

Much of the poetry—as well as the philosophy, criticism, and related materials—that we'll read and write about in this course have a deserved reputation for being challenging, intricate, difficult; and, simultaneously, for being powerful, captivating, exciting, attractive, pleasurable. Our course materials will, in other words, catch currents from at least one significant stream flowing into, and helping in its movements to make, modern poetry, poetics, aesthetics, and critique: into what they've been and what they're still in the process of becoming.

subject: COMLIT
title: On the Move: Modern Yiddish Literatures in Global Migration
description:
Diaspora, migration, displacement, globalization, and translation – in recent years these phenomena have become the prime focus of studies across the humanities. Modern Yiddish literature, a literature in constant global movement, opens up the opportunity to investigate these themes across a diverse range of historical and geographical contexts. In this course we will learn about the culture and history of Yiddish-speaking, Eastern European Jews through works of literature and art that focus on movement. We will follow a far-reaching global itinerary – from the Russian Empire’s Pale of Jewish Settlement to New York City’s Lower East Side, and from remote colonies in the Soviet Far East to Western European capitals, to Palestine, Latin America, the US South, South Africa, and beyond – to see what the world looks like from the Yiddish perspective. Reading across the Yiddish literary canon (as well as some less well-known works), we will be particularly interested in the following questions: How do works of literature make sense of the world, nation-state, collective, assimilation, belonging and estrangement? How do they make sense of different experiences of movement – displacement, domestic migration, back-and-forth diasporic movement, or a hopeful immigration to a promised land? How are gender and race transformed in global migration, in the encounter with new cultures? And how is a loss of languages, or acquiring of new languages, affect literary production?
Readings will be provided in the original and in English translation.

subject: COMLIT
title: How to Be Happy: Philosophy, Art, and Politics of Joy
description:
Year after year, the Scandinavian countries top global rankings of the happiest people in the
world. But what does it actually mean to be happy? And what does it take to foster joyful
citizens? In this class, we explore such questions through philosophy, literature, film, art, and
political thought. We will read reflections on happiness from Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas to
Simone de Beauvoir and Sara Ahmed; watch the aristocratic comedies of Ingmar Bergman;
encounter the deceitful happiness in Henrik Ibsen’s plays; scrutinize the idyllic imagery of
Scandinavian National Romanticism; ponder the “Swedish theory of love”; hear from a professor
of “wellbeing, welfare, and happiness”; examine the use of humor in healthcare; and debate
treatises arguing that individuals have a duty to be happy. Through these engagements, we will
consider the philosophical, artistic, and political stakes of happiness and joy in Scandinavia and
beyond.

The course has no prerequisites, and all readings and discussions will be in English. Smiling is
optional.

subject: COMLIT
title: Men, Masculinity, and Violence in Greek Literature and Film
description: Masculinity is an unstable category. What does it mean to be a man? How do forms of masculinity respond to changing historical circumstances? We will delve deeply into films, novels, and poems to understand how they reflect on the shifting conditions of masculinity during the tumultuous twentieth- and twenty-first centuries in Greece. From the heroic masculinity achieved in war to men on the social margins of Greece, there is a struggle to articulate selfhood in relation to a larger social category. To disentangle frameworks of masculinity, we must understand how they emerge. Turning to ethnographic, feminist, historical, and psychoanalytic theories, we will grapple with the competing meanings of masculinity. The novels, poems, and films that we will engage all reflect on historical violence in Greece throughout the twentieth- and twenty-first centuries, including the Balkan Wars, World War I, the Greco-Turkish War, the Population Exchange, the lasting effects of the National Schism, the Occupation of Greece during WWII, the Greek Civil War, and dictatorship. What is the relationship between masculinity and various forms of violence, including violence against women, the violence involved in nation-building, and the violence of borders, migration, economic crisis, and sexuality? If masculinity has been defined as a social performance, how do literature and film explore alternative possibilities for masculinity that are not mere reproductions of violence? We will read recent criticism on masculinity to consider what is at stake in asking this question now. In this class we will try to understand how masculinity generates questions and anxieties that we can neither answer nor turn away from.

subject: COMLIT
title: Lost and Found: Translation in Theory and Practice
description:
Consider these clichés: Poetry is what gets lost in translation. Reading literature in translation is like kissing your mother through a veil. Translation is the art of failure. The dangers of translation lie on both sides of a tightrope: literal fidelity and creative betrayal. 
Discussions about translation often use these and similar binaries and metaphors to depict translation as derivative. In this seminar we will integrate theory and practice to develop a renewed appreciation for the complicated task of the translator. We will read theoretical texts that have offered different answers to difficult questions about translation, from 19th century Romantic discourse on translation and nationalism, theological debates, structuralist and post-structuralist analyses, the ‘cultural turn’ in translation studies, as well as postcolonial and feminist critique. In addition, students will develop their own translation practice through workshops, peer editing, and group feedback. In doing so, this seminar is designed to have students gain a deeper understanding of important discussions in the field of translation studies, hone their skills as translators themselves, and reflect on the relationship between theory and praxis.

subject: COMLIT
title: Difficult Modern Poetry, Difficult Modern History . . .
description:
"Modern art--and maybe modern poetry especially—is DIFFICULT."

That's not the only judgment out there, but it's a familiar one. It often dovetails with the sense that poetry itself is inherently difficult; indeed, too difficult. Why should it be so hard to figure out what a poem feels like, means, gives us, asks of us: what a poem is or does?

There's plenty of poetry, and other kinds of modern art, that doesn't emphasize difficulty or complexity. But this senior seminar will focus on prominent currents in modern poetic art that generally DO assume that complexities of form and content (and both our pleasures and challenges in engaging them) are of decisive importance. Though the poets we'll read don't share any single aesthetic or political stance, their mostly common point of departure involves a view that modern art—and modern lyric poetry in its intense focus on the experience of how kinds of musicality in language can regenerate our sense of capacity for expanded comprehension, meaning-making, and critical agency—has among its central reasons for being the effort to help us ""get"" not only the specific, substantive difficulties of modern sociopolitical and ethical life, but also to get why our FORMAL experiences of modernity itself (our very ability to process, reflect on, and address it) can be so fraught.


Most of the poetry we'll read emerges from (or locates itself in subsequent, ongoing dialogues with) artistic modernism: essentially, experimentalism in the arts from the early twentieth century onward. We'll spend approximately the first half of the semester considering the unprecedented body of poetry—radically innovative in form and content, and with great international resonance—by Paul Celan, often deemed the most groundbreaking and challenging European poet since 1945. He happens also to be the poet whose work is most crucial to the “after Auschwitz” debates that shadow countless other artists, critics, and philosophers. While reading Celan's poetry and materials contextualizing it, we'll look at other European poets in dialogue with him (e.g., Ingeborg Bachmann, Bertolt Brecht, Jean Daive).

We'll then turn the focus around by way of the late Palestinian poet Mahmoud Darwish, looking at some key moments of his poetry on its own terms and also in its urgent conversations with Celan. This will likewise become a turn in hemispheres: some of the Darwish translations (into English) that we'll be reading from will be by the Palestinian-American poet Fady Joudah, whose own poetry and criticism we'll likewise delve into. That relay to the Western Hemisphere will then bring us round to the poetry of the great Martinican poet, critic, and activist Aimé Césaire, whose work has often been brought together with Celan's (not least, for what's frequently seen as the two poets' shared propensity for a challenging artistic experimentalism that proves both irresistible and devastating).

Time permitting, we'll then try to read from as many as possible among a group of poets (and some other artists) across the Americas who've located their work—at least in part—in related matrices (including Hansberry, Vallejo, D.S. Marriott, PIzarnik, Glissant, Monchoachi, Palmer, Brossard, Levertov, Duncan, Rankine, Tejada, Zurita, Whitney, Salcedo).

Besides reading criticism by (and interviews with) the poets themselves, we'll also read some philosophy and critical theory (most likely including Du Bois, Benjamin, Adorno, Arendt, and Rogers).

The seminar's poetry—as well the philosophy, criticism, and related materials presented—will have a deserved reputation for being, in a word, DIFFICULT; and, simultaneously, for being powerful, captivating, pleasurable, crucial.

subject: COMLIT
title: Arts of the Cure: Film, Literature, and History
description: From cutting-edge medical research to the promises of social media influencers, the cure is everywhere. The desire to be relieved of suffering seems as endless as there are remedies. What is it about the potential of the cure that captures our attention? What is it about the possibility of perfect health that captivates us? What are we seeking when we ask to be cured? This class invites students who are ready to think critically about an idea that seems so ordinary that we rarely pause to consider it deeply, and who are willing to think imaginatively about the cure beyond the absence of symptoms. We will delve deeply into various case studies of the cure, including ancient Greek tragedy and ritual practices, ethnographic accounts of shamanistic cures, the “talking cure” of psychoanalysis, experimental cinema and dreams, and the striving for immortality in literature and beyond. To disentangle frameworks of the cure, we must understand how they emerge. Turning to philosophical, psychological, and theological theories, we will grapple with what the cure consists of. If the cure has been defined as a treatment of a disease and the restoration of health, what does healing look like when there is no proven remedy? When mental pain and physical symptoms resist medical intervention, can aesthetic experiences and artistic practice offer relief? In this class we will try to understand what the search for a cure reveals about the struggle to live life fully.

subject: COMLIT
title: Points of View and/on Sound in Novels
description: We’ll use two novels by Henry James to review discussions of the importance of point of view in the construction both of modernist novels (What Maisie Knew and The Golden Bowl) and of certain models of the social world. Then we will read large sections from a couple of volumes of Proust’s In Search of Lost Time, where the question of what it means to have a point of view on sound (to hear from a certain location; to notice that differently located and constructed ears hear differently) is treated in some detail. We’ll use James Baldwin’s final novel, Just Above My Head, to pursue that question and also to follow out a line of thought about the different reasons why certain novelists become particularly interested in mapping a soundscape in their novels, or in turning their novels in to a kind of sound archive that is also somehow a critical tool for understanding histories of struggles against domination. Along with the novels, there will be ample further readings from literary criticism, sound studies, and sociologies of sound, culture, and literature.

subject: COMLIT
title: Studies in the Nineteenth-Century: Romantic-Period Plant Cultures
description:
CL223 Studies in the Nineteenth-Century: Romantic-Period Plant Cultures 

Under the rubric of “Green Romanticism,” this comparative seminar hones in on Romantic-period plant writing and related theorizations of plant ontologies and plant temporalities. Rather than separating philosophical inquiry into the ways of being in the world and the modes of time-keeping specific to the vegetal from the sociohistorical question of the uses that plants and people make of one another, the seminar’s working title “Plant Cultures” encompasses Romantic-period writings about plants and plant-like writing as well as plants as sites, objects and agents of multi-species tending and cultivation. 

One axis, then, will be the question of “plant writing”—taking writing in the widest possible sense to include inscription, drawing, and the making and unmaking of traces and understanding the phrase to be inclusive both of writing about plants and something performed by plants themselves as figures of recursiveness, re-iteration, dissemination, and time-keeping. 

Another axis will be the question of Romanticism as a response to a particular crisis (in a long series of such crises) of enclosure, primitive accumulation, land theft, dispossession and forced migration, as recently articulated, for example, in Lenora Hanson’s The Romantic Rhetoric of Accumulation (2022). We will take our cue here from Sonya Posmentier’s Cultivation and Catastrophe and its thought that in the context of eighteenth and nineteenth-century plantation economies based on chattel slavery, “‘cultivation’ and ‘catastrophe,’ do not oppose one another but intersect: in the United States and the Caribbean, cultivation in the form of enforced agricultural labor has been a social catastrophe in and of itself; environmental catastrophes in turn have yielded rich traditions of art, music, and poetry. (3).  

This axis will open out onto recent interest in the question of the role played by certain kinds of agriculture (the planting of annual grains) in the accumulation of power necessary to the formation of states and in the origins of what is now called the “Anthropocene” and planetary ecocide.  How do these recent works which entail sweeping accounts of human (pre-)histories—James C. Scott, David Graeber and David Wengrow—help make legible a certain strain of anarchism, subsistence, anti-enclosure writing specific to certain Romantic-period authors (Rousseau, Wordsworth, Clare)?  

Readings by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Erasmus Darwin, J.W. Goethe, William Wordsworth, Dorothy Wordsworth, John Clare, Rober Wedderburn, Mary Prince

To borrow from Mike Hoerger, founding director of Louisiana’s HealthPsych PhD program, I would like to make this class a “COVID Sanctuary” and create a compassionate, inclusive, equitable environment that follows evidence-based COVID precautions and respects the needs of the most vulnerable among us. It is my sincere wish and hope that we will agree to wear masks as a class and that everyone who is able to do so comfortably and without risk will wear a well-fitting, high quality mask (KN94, KN95, N95 or better) at all times. Masks will be provided!

subject: COMLIT
title: Imagination, Fantasy, 'Einbildungskraft'
description: In literary and philosophical traditions, the imagination has been understood in a wide range of ways: as the space where sense impressions take on a shape and an affective charge; as the interface between material forms and psychic life; as a conduit between the human and the divine; as the organ of prophecy and dreams; as the faculty that is at the core of innovation and the creation of fictional worlds. In this seminar we will discuss the significance of notions and practices of the imagination in philosophical and literary traditions, as well as the potential to think with the imagination in current contexts. We will start with a discussion of texts by Plato and Aristotle; move on to the treatment of the imagination in classical rhetoric and in the medieval Arabic tradition; and focus on four key areas where imagination, fantasy, and 'Einbildungskraft' play a significant role: the so-called mystical tradition up to Jacob Böhme; Baroque cultures of the imagination; poetic imagination in the 18th and 19th centuries; and 20th century philosophical approaches up to new materialism. Based on the interests of the participants, a final syllabus will be established at the beginning of the semester.

subject: COMLIT
title: What the Self: Psychoanalysis, Autotheory, and Jewish Modernity
description:
How does one write the self? Every act of self-narration, whether organized chronologically or fragmentarily, written in the first person or displaced onto others, presupposes a theory of subjectivity: an understanding of what a self is, how it is formed, and whether it can ever become fully knowable to itself. From its inception, psychoanalysis was deeply invested not only in theorizing the structure of subjectivity, but also in developing narrative forms capable of representing lived experience.


This seminar traces the long encounter between psychoanalysis and self-writing from Sigmund Freud through object relations theorists such as Wilfred Bion, Marion Milner, and Masud Khan, and into contemporary experiments in autotheory by Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, Alison Bechdel, and Maggie Nelson, all deeply invested in psychoanalytic thought. At the same time, the course will explore the often uneasy relation between psychoanalysis and Jewish modernity. Emerging within the intellectual and historical conditions of modern Jewish life in Europe, psychoanalysis remained deeply entangled with questions of interpretation, textuality, exile, assimilation, otherness, and secularization. By placing psychoanalytic and literary texts in dialogue with Jewish intellectual traditions and modern Jewish writing, we will ask how the problem of writing down the self becomes intertwined with broader questions of historical rupture, cultural identity, and relational existence.
