subject: COMLIT
title: Growing Up Ethnic
description:
Originating in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, the bildungsroman, or the novel of formation, is one of the central genres of the Western novel. These coming-of-age stories follow a protagonist as they grow up, undergo an education, pass from innocence to experience, and reconcile their individual desires with their place in society. In the United States, the experience of coming of age is often accompanied by developing awareness of one’s racial or ethnic identity, including what that means to others. Our course will study a variety of 20th and 21st century novels of formation by writers who are, in various ways, “ethnic.” Although in one sense the term “ethnic” refers simply to a national or cultural origin or tradition, in another sense it also signals otherness, a deviation from the dominant culture or the norm, e.g. when we describe certain cuisines as “ethnic food.” If the traditional bildungsroman ends with the successful integration of an individual into society, how do ethnic writers deploy, negotiate, and remake this genre? Our concerns in the class will include: subject formation, the relationship of the individual to both their own ethnic community and to dominant society, immigration, diaspora and assimilation, citizenship and belonging. 
Possible texts include: James Weldon Johnson, Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man, Jessie Fauset, Plum Bun, D’arcy McNickle, The Surrounded, Ania Yezierska, Bread Givers, Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God, N. Scott Momaday, House Made of Dawn, Toni Morrison, The Bluest Eye, Maxine Hong Kingston, The Woman Warrior, Sandra Cisneros, The House on Mango Street, Junot Diaz, The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao, Faye Myenne Ng, Bone.

subject: COMLIT
title: Berkeley Connect in Comparative Literature
description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program that helps students build intellectual community. The 98 section in Comparative Literature introduces first and second year students to the techniques of reading taught in Comparative Literature and introduce students to the wider campus. We talk about such concerns as when to attend office hours or how to write to faculty about getting off the wait list for courses. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to Cal Performances and the Berkeley Art Museum. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

subject: COMLIT
title: Learning about Translation through Fiction
description:
Imagine that you are reading a story and suddenly you are told that what you are reading is actually a translation. Apparently, the book was first written in an ancient language by an author from a faraway land. How would this affect your relationship with the text? Would you now consider it more interesting and valuable? Or would you start to suspect that the translator may have made changes and additions? Would you be worried—or perhaps excited—about the possibility that there could be different versions of the story? This is a game some Renaissance writers started to play with their readers. They pretended that the story, or part of it, was a translation of an older work. They imitated what real translators did at the time, ridiculing their work and the confusion that translations could create for a reader. 

In this course, we will read fictional works from different periods and literary traditions that imitate translation in this way, and we will identify some of the things that their authors and readers may have found ridiculous or challenging about translation at the time. Our discussions will help us develop hypotheses about how translation was viewed at the time each of these texts was written—and about how we see translation today.

The course satisfies the first half of UC Berkeley’s Reading and Composition requirement. Students will use their comparative interpretations of the assigned texts as the basis for their writing exercises. They will have the opportunity to develop their critical thinking and composition skills as they gain practice in the different stages of the academic writing process. Starting with in-class writing exercises, drafts, and revisions, they will gradually work toward the completion of two short argumentative essays.

subject: COMLIT
title: The Literary Essay in the English and Spanish Traditions
description:
Academic writing norms and expectations vary among cultures. For instance, Spanish writers may be surprised to learn that their thoughtful attempt to emphasize an idea can be seen by English readers as unnecessary repetition, or that a general reflection intended to highlight the argument’s value may be considered a digression. Conversely, the concise style of English writers may seem naïve to Spanish readers. Some of them may also see witticisms as a sign of levity. They may even wonder if it is worthwhile to read a whole essay when the author has already announced all the results at the beginning. And why do sentences in English need to be so short and paragraphs so long? And when did using the passive voice become an unforgivable sin?

In our discussions, we will ask these and similar questions, and we will use them to explore academic-writing conventions. After analyzing an essay by French Renaissance writer Michel de Montaigne, who is considered the father of the genre, we will read a series of texts by representative essayists from the English and Spanish traditions. This comparative historical overview will help us see that writing conventions are not universally valid principles. Instead, we examine the particular historical and social conditions in which they took shape. Then, in our writing exercises, we will treat writing requirements as strategies that we can learn to use in order to convey and test our ideas in specific contexts.

The course satisfies the first half of UC Berkeley’s Reading and Composition requirement. Students will use their comparative interpretations of the assigned texts as the basis for their writing exercises. They will have the opportunity to develop their critical thinking and composition skills as they gain practice in the different stages of the academic writing process. Starting with in-class writing exercises, drafts, and revisions, they will gradually work toward the completion of two short argumentative essays.

subject: COMLIT
title: Rethinking the Americas. Towards an Indigenous archive of critique
description:
In this course, we will dialogue with Indigenous contributions to sociopolitical critiques and movements across Turtle Island/ Abya Yala (the Americas). Through engaging different cultural productions, we will come to understand the role Indigenous thinkers and practitioners have played in working through questions of land, time, space, and sovereignty. The course is guided by questions, such as: what is the role of the Indigenous author/artist in the Americas? How do Indigenous authors and artists challenge the idea of the nation-state? How do Indigenous communities engage national discourses differently in the English-speaking world versus the Spanish-speaking world? In other words, how do Indigenous peoples from the South dialogue with Natives from the North? Alongside these political concerns, we will interrogate whether generic conventions (i.e. novel vs. poetry) or the varied media (i.e. film vs tv show vs writing) used affect how we perceive political critique.

We will work across media to answer the questions posed. From television and film to traditional forms of literature, some of the works we will study include: Smoke signals, Carmín tropical, El retorno de los mayas, poetry by Negma Coy, poetry by Danilo Vásquez, Red weather, Rezervation dogs, El tiempo principia en Xibalbá, Dark winds.

subject: COMLIT
title: Complicated Love
description: What is love? How do a variety of literary traditions and genres define and depict love? What makes love complicated? How does literature function as a privileged site to interrogate the question of love,  whether fraught and anguishing or excessive, transgressive, or non-normative in a given context? We will read a wide array of literature (including novels, short stories, and poetry), religious writings, and philosophical texts. From Plato’s Symposium and selections from Dante and Mechthild of Magdeburg, we will trace a conception of love coming out of the Platonist tradition, and then follow this up by reading stories or novels by a range of authors, with a particular emphasis on 20th-century fiction, to ‘complicate’ our thinking about love. As a class that counts towards R&C requirements, this is a writing-intensive course. Writing workshops will be integrated into class sessions to practice close reading, structuring arguments, and other key skills for effective college-level writing. All readings will be available in English.

subject: COMLIT
title: Black Surrealism
description:
What is surrealism? A dream? An aesthetic? A rupture with reality? In this course, we will explore Black surrealism as a mode of thought and expression that uses the irrational, the fantastic, and the dreamlike to confront the experience of race and racism. Moving across literature, film, and visual art, we will consider how Black writers and artists transform surrealism into a method for reimagining the self and the conditions of possibility for Black life. 

As part of the University’s R&C requirement, this course aims to give you conceptual tools to refine your critical reading and writing skills. Together, we will examine how arguments are made and how we can insert ourselves into the conversation: how to ask meaningful questions about the texts we encounter, craft an arguable thesis, and support claims through close reading. Most importantly, you will learn to engage primary and secondary sources and organize your thoughts into structured, persuasive, and elegantly composed texts. By the semester’s end, these skills will provide a foundation for your continued growth as critical writers, readers, and thinkers.

subject: COMLIT
title: Excavation of Memory
description:
How do we remember what we remember? How do we represent what we remember? These two questions seem similar, but this course emerges out of the nuanced differences between the two. Through a wide array of literature and film from around the world, we will think about how technologies of recording and storage transform our capacity to remember and to reflect on memory and its relationship to the self, to our political formations, to the historical past, and to the future. We will begin the course by examining how writing (and print), photography, and film revolutionized how we document and narrate the present. With the affordances of each medium in mind, we will consider the formally experimental ways that literature and film attempt to relay experiences of historical trauma, exploring the political stakes of representing the past in Japan, South Korea, Cuba, and Palestine. Lastly, we will confront the irruption of nostalgia and memory culture in the late 20th century, with particular attention to Hong Kong, the People’s Republic of China, and Russia. Throughout the semester, we will read and respond to important theoretical writers on these topics, such as Ong, Barthes, Freud, Doane, Nora, Solanas, and Getino. 

Through frequent in-class writing activities and lively discussion, students will hone their ability to read critically and analytically, pose interesting questions, and construct convincing arguments based on visual analysis. By the end of the course, students will write a 7-8 pg. final research paper on a topic drawn from our class discussions. A passing grade in this class satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition (R&C) university requirement.

subject: COMLIT
title: Strange Bodies Adrift in Time: Queer East Asian Fiction and Film
description:
"What does it mean to fall in love, grow up, or age when you identify as “queer”? In this class, we will delve into how queerness can challenge traditional perceptions of time, space, and the body through novels by East Asian writers including Yoko Tawada, Qiu Miaojin, Pai Hsien-yung, Li Kotomi, and filmmakers Toshio Matsumoto and Tsai Ming-liang. We will examine how confronting the taboo of homosexuality can both force and allow creative leaps in fiction—whether through content, as with the post-apocalyptic transgender shapeshifters of The Last Children of Tokyo (2014), or formal technique, as with the jump-cutting and montage in Notes of a Crocodile(1994). To expand our perspective beyond Western conceptions of queerness, we will also read two short texts from premodern China—a story by Pu Songling and an autobiographical piece by Shen Fu—to examine their portrayal of sexuality and gender, as well as pay attention to how transnational and colonial dynamics inflect queer sociality in Japan and postcolonial Taiwan. 

By exploring queerness as a strategy of reading, writing, and textual belonging, this writing-intensive seminar asks how writing can be a mode of ethically engaging with narratives and experiences drawn from communities, regions, historical periods, and languages that are not our own. Through weekly practices of close reading, analytical writing, revising, and the drafting of research outlines and annotated bibliographies, we will help each other go through the various stages of writing that lead to a research paper of 8–10 pages. We will reflect on the difficulties as well as creative possibilities of translation and translingual expression, using queerness as a figure of resilience created in moments of writing and being together."

subject: COMLIT
title: Forms of Knowing
description: What are the necessary and sufficient conditions of knowledge? What are its sources? What is its structure, and what are its limits? Is objective knowledge possible or is knowledge inherently social? To what extent is knowledge in the "body" rather than the "mind"? How do we come to understand others, ourselves, our situations, and what it is we should do? How do we accept anything as a "fact" or as "true"? In this course, we will explore such questions in our reading, our writing, and our researching.

subject: COMLIT
title: The Terror and the Pity: Tragic Form in History
description:
The classic Athenian tragedies confronted their audiences with an uncompromising pessimism seen in the crushing of heroes by gods, the implosion of societies, and the inexorability of the most horrible. Throughout history, the dramatic genre of tragedy has been both vilified as a numbing excess of violent spectacle or esteemed for its serious recognition of human suffering. What is certain is that these plays of “terror and pity” have set our standards for judging intense effect and compelling composition in works of media as different as sculpture, painting, novels, photography, and film. 

This course will pursue two questions on tragedy, the one historical and the other philosophical. We will read the classics of tragedy from antiquity to the 17th century (Sophocles, Shakespeare, Racine) along with modern works aspiring to the genre (Lessing, Wagner, Mishima, Weiss) to ask, first: how has tragedy as a genre shaped and been shaped by a sense of the tragic across time and cultures? The techniques of this “shaping” constitute our second question: what formal solutions do tragedians, whether working in images or works, find to strike a balance between visible spectacle and invisible logic of violence? Here we will look at debates in painting (Caravaggio vs Poussin), film adaptations (Kurosawa’s Shakespeare), and ways of watching the news (Berger, Sontag).

Students will cultivate analytical skills in reading tragic works across a range of genres and media and develop argumentative writing as a mode of investigation and reflection possible only by means of the written word. We will break down the process of researching and composing an interpretive essay into its component steps and work our way up to a university research paper. This course satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.

subject: COMLIT
title: Time Travel Literature
description:
Can we travel in time? What happens when time travel is no longer a speculative thought experiment, but a vivid “reality” made possible through wild literary imaginations? This course examines a wide range of works across historical periods and cultural contexts that mobilize time travel as a central narrative mystique. From premodern China to fin-de-siècle Europe to postwar America, we trace how authors imagine time travel to interrogate historical violence, modernity’s ruptures, political catastrophe, and irredeemable loss – while illuminating the worlds that produced them.

In this class, we will explore time travel as a tracking device for racial and gendered violence of slavery, a fantastic escape from unbearable realities, a laboratory for counterfactual histories, and a stage on which the paradoxes of time and human existence are laid bare. We will follow different groups of time-travelers: figures forced into violent histories or bewildering futures; travelers fleeing catastrophic timelines through fantastic voyages; anachronistic wanderers out of sync with the world; and melancholic ghosts from the past who refuse to settle. Together, we explore how time-travel narratives grapple with human desire, trauma, nostalgia, horror, and hope – and how our imaginations of past and future remain inevitably embedded in the thickness of the historical present.

Over the course of the semester, we will read H. G. Wells’s The Time Machine, Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five, and Octavia Butler’s Kindred; short stories such as Washington Irving’s “Rip Van Winkle” and its Chinese counterparts, stories by Xu Xu, Amiri Baraka, and Ted Chiang; and two films, Chris Marker’s La Jetée and Stanley Kwan’s Rouge. As a writing-intensive seminar, this course will build toward the writing of analytical and research papers through close reading, outlining, drafting, feedback, and revision. We will develop not only the technical skills of crafting arguments and composing essays, but also modes of ethical engagement with the lives of others that extend beyond our immediate horizons of understanding. The ultimate aim is to cultivate more attentive, rigorous, and reflective readers, writers, and thinkers – attentive to time and to its distant echoes.

subject: COMLIT
title: Heroism and Militarism: Necessary and Unnecessary Violence in Literature and Film
description:
This is a course about how literature and film represent violence, and the people who commit it. We will read texts – many of them classical and medieval – that ask us to think about some of the following questions: When is or isn’t it necessary to cause pain or destruction? When is or isn’t it necessary to represent violence and suffering in media? When can or should those depictions be explicit? And what does it mean to be the sort of person who carries out acts of violence? How might the people who do relate to society writ large? 

Our readings this semester will build on each other in grappling with these issues, but as an R&C course the main purpose of the class is to foster sustained critical engagement with the process of writing. We will work together to form an understanding of the partnership between careful reading and analytical writing, as well as dedicating deliberate time and attention to questions of organization, stylistics, and grammar. As we turn to the research-focused portion of our course, we will learn how to position our thoughts about course materials among other writers’ interpretations of those materials. This course will culminate in the production of an 8-10 page research paper, but we will build up to it through a series of smaller assignments targeting different dimensions of the writing and research process.

subject: COMLIT
title: Writing the Disaster | Lyric Interrogations of Formal Collapse
description:
How does representation respond to historical and present sites of violence? What is at stake in what we might consider to be “unrepresentable?” With an eye on the contemporary disasters of genocide, fascism, pandemic, and ecological collapse, we will work towards an understanding of how aesthetic form “informs” anti-imperial resistance- and/or the politics of what resists representation. We will work with varied texts in translation (from Spanish, Arabic, and French literary contexts) to collectively develop a repertoire of writing and critical skills with which to conceptualize the chronic disasters of our own present.

With emphasis on lyric form, we will be in constant conversation with a wide range of other aesthetic modes and critical frameworks, including perspectives from historical materialism, disability studies, and Black studies. Course readings will also include selections from artists and thinkers such as Etel Adnan, Solmaz Sharif, Saidiya Hartman, Christina Sharpe, Adania Shibli, and M. NourbeSe Philip to better think through what might the aesthetic affordances be of the formal ruptures that constitute collapse.

subject: COMLIT
title: Anarchy of the Self
description:
What is a “self”? This course approaches that question through literature, treating selfhood as a historical and cultural formation. Rather than assuming that the self is given, we will ask how it is produced, how it becomes legible, and how it is tested when the norms that sustain it are strained. Our readings will therefore attend to those moments in which the self becomes most visible at its point of instability: when moral boundaries are crossed, when inherited identities no longer hold, or when dominant ideas of privacy, normality, gender, race, and even the human are forced into crisis. The course thus studies selfhood as an unfinished and contested process whose meaning changes across different historical worlds.

The course will move through a range of questions and constellations, including autobiography in Saint Augustine and Sei Shōnagon, self-refashioning in Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Gloria Gervitz, and Olga Gutiérrez, transgression in Toni Morrison and the Count of Lautréamont, postcolonial formations of the self in Ciro Guerra and Joseph Conrad, individualism in Ralph Waldo Emerson and Thomas Carlyle, gender and selfhood in Maggie Nelson and Clarice Lispector, and the posthuman in Julio Cortázar and Carlos Castaneda, among others.

As part of the University’s R&C requirement, this course will help students refine their critical reading and writing skills. This is a writing-intensive course with a focus on formulating theses, finding and evaluating textual evidence, and conducting and incorporating secondary research. All readings will be available in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

subject: COMLIT
title: Diaxplorando: Journeys of Belonging with Latin American Diasporas in the United States
description:
On July 4, 2025, Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny released a new installment in a growing series of music videos that accompany hits from his recent album “DtMF” (“DeBí TiRAR Más FOToS”). Previous videos in the series had geographically rooted themselves in Puerto Rico, featuring characteristic palm trees, a nostalgic grandfather figure who serves as keeper of the island’s memory, and even a dancing (and yoga-practicing) claymation version of the tiny coquí frogs endemic to Puerto Rico. The carefully-timed U.S. Independence Day video release, however, took audience members on a different kind of journey, somehow without entirely leaving the island—or Latin America—behind. “NuevaYol” ventured around 1,600 miles (2,575 km) away from Puerto Rico to New York City—a city that the video recognizes as home to some of the United States’ most cherished national icons like the Statue of Liberty but also home to the sounds of salsa, the rhythms of Spanglish, and the barrios where people with physical and cultural ties to Latin America have put down new ‘American’ roots. This is “NuevaYol,” the video tells us: a U.S. cultural capital remade with a Spanish accent and un toque latino. This is “NuevaYol”: a place where Puerto Ricans and Latin Americans—though often labeled ‘alien,’ ‘other,’ and unwelcome—continue to actively make themselves a home.

Taking as inspiration “NuevaYol”’s blending of languages, geographies, and national iconographies, this class will think through past and present-day forms of diasporic belonging explored and experienced by people of Latin American diasporas living in the United States. What are the possibilities and limitations of the now common term diaspora? How do Latin American people and communities in the U.S. use their bodies and tongues to practice and articulate forms of diasporic belonging? Together, we’ll explore questions like these in conversation with materials produced by Caribbean, Chicanx, Afro-indigenous, Nuyorican, Mexican, and Central American thinkers who position themselves both inside and outside the United States while testing the larger boundaries of nation-states and historically-defined languages. Our major writing assignments—including the final research project—will be composed in English, but readings will move across Spanish(es), English(es), and Spanglish(es), as will our class discussions, so a strong desire to read and dialogue in and across Spanish is a must for every member of the class community. Students who consider Spanish their ‘home,’ first, or heritage language are especially encouraged to join this course. 

Note: This course requires students to have significant Spanish-language skills in terms of reading, comprehension, and conversation. The course also fulfills the second semester of UC Berkeley’s undergraduate writing requirement.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: The Beauty and Joy of Computing
course.description: An introductory course for students with minimal prior exposure to computer science. Prepares students for future computer science courses and empowers them to utilize programming to solve problems in their field of study. Presents an overview of the history, great principles, and transformative applications of computer science, as well as a comprehensive introduction to programming. Topics include abstraction, recursion, algorithmic complexity, higher-order functions, concurrency, social implications of computing (privacy, education, algorithmic bias), and engaging research areas (data science, AI, HCI). Students will program in Snap! (a friendly graphical language) and Python, and will design and implement two projects of their choice.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Computer Architecture and Engineering
course.description: Instruction set architecture, microcoding, pipelining (simple and complex). Memory hierarchies and virtual memory. Processor parallelism: VLIW, vectors, multithreading. Multiprocessors.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: User Interface Design and Development
course.description: The design, implementation, and evaluation of user interfaces. User-centered design and task analysis. Conceptual models and interface metaphors. Usability inspection and evaluation methods. Analysis of user study data. Input methods (keyboard, pointing, touch, tangible) and input models. Visual design principles. Interface prototyping and implementation methodologies and tools. Students will develop a user interface for a specific task and target user group in teams.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B or COMPSCI 61BL.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Computer Security
course.description: Introduction to computer security. Cryptography, including encryption, authentication, hash functions, cryptographic protocols, and applications. Operating system security, access control. Network security, firewalls, viruses, and worms. Software security, defensive programming, and language-based security. Case studies from real-world systems.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B, COMPSCI 61C, and COMPSCI 70.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Operating Systems and System Programming
course.description: Basic concepts of operating systems and system programming. Utility programs, subsystems, multiple-program systems. Processes, interprocess communication, and synchronization. Memory allocation, segmentation, paging. Loading and linking, libraries. Resource allocation, scheduling, performance evaluation. File systems, storage devices, I/O systems. Protection, security, and privacy.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B, COMPSCI 61C, and COMPSCI 70.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Programming Languages and Compilers
course.description: Survey of programming languages. The design of modern programming languages. Principles and techniques of scanning, parsing, semantic analysis, and code generation. Implementation of compilers, interpreters, and assemblers. Overview of run-time organization and error handling.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B and COMPSCI 61C.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to the Internet: Architecture and Protocols
course.description: This course is an introduction to the Internet architecture. We will focus on the concepts and fundamental design principles that have contributed to the Internet's scalability and robustness and survey the various protocols and algorithms used within this architecture. Topics include layering, addressing, intradomain routing, interdomain routing, reliable delivery, congestion control, and the core protocols (e.g., TCP, UDP, IP, DNS, and HTTP) and network technologies (e.g., Ethernet, wireless).
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B; COMPSCI 61C is recommended.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Software Engineering
course.description: Ideas and techniques for designing, developing, and modifying large software systems. Service-oriented architecture, behavior-driven design with user stories, cloud computing, test-driven development, automated testing, cost and quality metrics for maintainability and effort estimation, practical performance and security in software operations, design patterns and refactoring, specification and documentation, agile project team organization and management.
course.requirements: COMPSCI C88C or DATA C88C or COMPSCI 61A or COMPSCI 47A; and COMPSCI 61B or COMPSCI 61BL or COMPSCI 47B.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Efficient Algorithms and Intractable Problems
course.description: Concept and basic techniques in the design and analysis of algorithms; models of computation; lower bounds; algorithms for optimum search trees, balanced trees and UNION-FIND algorithms; numerical and algebraic algorithms; combinatorial algorithms. Turing machines, how to count steps, deterministic and nondeterministic Turing machines, NP-completeness. Unsolvable and intractable problems.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B and COMPSCI 70.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Cryptography
course.description: Cryptography or cryptology is the science of designing algorithms and protocols for enabling parties to communicate and compute securely in an untrusted environment (e.g. secure communication, digital signature, etc.) Over the last four decades, cryptography has transformed from an ad hoc collection of mysterious tricks into a rigorous science based on firm complexity-theoretic foundations.  This modern complexity-theoretic approach to cryptography will be the focus. E.g., in the context of encryption we will begin by giving a precise mathematical definition for what it means to be a secure encryption scheme and then give a construction (realizing this security notion) assuming various computational hardness assumptions (e.g. factoring).
course.requirements: COMPSCI 70

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Computability and Complexity
course.description: Finite automata, Turing machines and RAMs. Undecidable, exponential, and polynomial-time problems. Polynomial-time equivalence of all reasonable models of computation. Nondeterministic Turing machines. Theory of NP-completeness: Cook's theorem, NP-completeness of basic problems. Selected topics in language theory, complexity and randomness.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 170

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Intro to Computer Vision and Computational Photography
course.description: This advanced undergraduate course introduces students to computing with visual data (images and video). We will cover acquisition, representation, and manipulation of visual information from digital photographs (image processing), image analysis and visual understanding (computer vision), and image synthesis (computational photography). Key algorithms will be presented, ranging from classical to contemporary, with an emphasis on using these techniques to build practical systems. The hands-on emphasis will be reflected in the programming assignments, where students will acquire their own images and develop, largely from scratch, image analysis and synthesis tools for real-world applications.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B; MATH 53; and MATH 54, MATH 56, MATH 110, or ELENG 66. COMPSCI C182 or COMPSCI 189 should be taken as a co-requisite.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Foundations of Computer Graphics
course.description: A broad introduction to the fundamentals of computer graphics. The main areas covered are modeling, rendering, animation and imaging. Topics include 2D and 3D transformations, drawing to raster displays, sampling, texturing, antialiasing, geometric modeling, ray tracing and global illumination, animation, cameras, image processing and computational imaging. There will be an emphasis on mathematical and geometric aspects of graphics, and the ability to write complete 3D graphics programs.
course.requirements:

Linear Algebra: Matrix and vector operations, dot/cross products, transformations, eigenvectors.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Database Systems
course.description: Access methods and file systems to facilitate data access. Hierarchical, network, relational, and object-oriented data models. Query languages for models. Embedding query languages in programming languages. Database services including protection, integrity control, and alternative views of data. High-level interfaces including application generators, browsers, and report writers. Introduction to transaction processing. Database system implementation to be done as term project.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61C or COMPSCI 47C. COMPSCI 47C may be taken as a co-requisite for transfer students.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
course.description: Ideas and techniques underlying the design of intelligent computer systems. Topics include search, game playing, knowledge representation, inference, planning, reasoning under uncertainty, machine learning, robotics, perception, and language understanding.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61A, COMPSCI 61B, and COMPSCI 70.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
course.description: Theoretical foundations, algorithms, methodologies, and applications for machine learning. Topics may include supervised methods for regression and classication (linear models, trees, neural networks, ensemble methods, instance-based methods); generative and discriminative probabilistic models; Bayesian parametric learning; density estimation and clustering; Bayesian networks; time series models; dimensionality reduction; programming projects covering a variety of real-world applications.
course.requirements: MATH 53 and MATH 54; and COMPSCI 70 or consent of instructor.

subject: COMPSCI
title: Functional Programming and AI-Assisted Application Development
description:
Course Description: 

An introduction to functional programming, algebraic type systems, web technologies, software application design, and AI-assisted application development.

Course Objectives:

This course directly follows the introduction to programming and computer science provided by Computer Science 61A and Data Science C88C and prepares students to build a full application using modern tools and technologies. The learning goals of this course include:
-Preparing students to learn how to use statically typed programming languages such as Java and Rust in future courses, such as CS 61B and CS 162.
-Preparing students to use World Wide Web technologies in application development in future courses, such as CS 160 and CS 169.
-Preparing students to extend their understanding of programming languages and programming tools in future courses, such as CS 164.
-Gain experience with AI-assisted programming.

subject: COMPSCI
title: STAR Assessments for Proficiency-Based Learning
description:
In this special topics course, small teams (2-3) of graduate and undergraduate students will use PrairieLearn to develop and rigorously evaluate rich, machine-gradable assessments that would address learning goals that might arise in typical EECS courses.

The assessments will promote mastery learning (aka proficiency learning) by following the acronym STAR: Specific to a particular competency, Tagged to specific learning outcomes, Autogradable, and Randomized so that many variants can be auto-generated on demand.

In addition to developing assessments, student teams will evaluate them by using the methods of HCI and education research to run either informal or formal pilot studies. We will encourage students to make any resulting artifacts available as open educational resources.

subject: COMPSCI
title: Single-cell immunology: from statistical machine learning to biomedical discovery
description:
Advances in single-cell technologies have transformed modern immunology, enabling major discoveries in cancer, autoimmunity, and other diseases. However, the scale and complexity of the resulting datasets necessitate specialized machine learning expertise to fully realize their potential. This course examines the computational challenges posed by emerging biotechnology platforms and how addressing them can advance molecular medicine, with a particular emphasis on cancer immunotherapies.

This is an experimental class designed to mirror the interdisciplinary and collaborative nature of modern biomedical research in industry and academia. Students are expected to have a prior exposure to EITHER the computational or the immunological aspects, but not necessarily both. From the computational side, we will cover statistical inference from atlas-scale omics data, drawing heavily on high-dimensional statistics and variational inference. From the immunology side, we will introduce some of the latest technological developments in single-cell genomics, including spatial transcriptomics and massively parallel pooled CRISPR screens, and survey their applications in molecular medicine. Our guiding focus will be the characterization of molecular states of immune cells in solid tumors (or: "why does the immune system fail to kill the tumor and what can we do to help it").

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Graduate Computer Architecture
course.description: Graduate survey of contemporary computer organizations covering: early systems, CPU design, instruction sets, control, processors, busses, ALU, memory, I/O interfaces, connection networks, virtual memory, pipelined computers, multiprocessors, and case studies. Term paper or project is required.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61C

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: User Interface Design and Development
course.description: The design, implementation, and evaluation of user interfaces. User-centered design and task analysis. Conceptual models and interface metaphors. Usability inspection and evaluation methods. Analysis of user study data. Input methods (keyboard, pointing, touch, tangible) and input models. Visual design principles. Interface prototyping and implementation methodologies and tools. Students will develop a user interface for a specific task and target user group in teams.
course.requirements: Computer Science 61B, 61BL, or consent of instructor.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Human-Computer Interaction Research
course.description: This course is a broad introduction to conducting research in Human-Computer Interaction. Students will become familiar with seminal and recent literature; learn to review and critique research papers; re-implement and evaluate important existing systems; and gain experience in conducting research. Topics include input devices, computer-supported cooperative work, crowdsourcing, design tools, evaluation methods, search and mobile interfaces, usable security, help and tutorial systems.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 160 recommended, or consent of instructor.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Advanced Topics in Computer Systems
course.description: Graduate survey of systems for managing computation and information, covering a breadth of topics: early systems; volatile memory management, including virtual memory and buffer management; persistent memory systems, including both file systems and transactional storage managers; storage metadata, physical vs. logical naming, schemas, process scheduling, threading and concurrency control; system support for networking, including remote procedure calls, transactional RPC, TCP, and active messages; security infrastructure; extensible systems and APIs; performance analysis and engineering of large software systems. Homework assignments, exam, and term paper or project required.
course.requirements: 162 and entrance exam.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Implementation of Programming Languages
course.description: Compiler construction. Lexical analysis, syntax analysis. Semantic analysis code generation and optimization. Storage management. Run-time organization.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 164; COMPSCI 263 recommended.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Combinatorial Algorithms and Data Structures
course.description: Design and analysis of efficient algorithms for combinatorial problems. Network flow theory, matching theory, matroid theory; augmenting-path algorithms; branch-and-bound algorithms; data structure techniques for efficient implementation of combinatorial algorithms; analysis of data structures; applications of data structure techniques to sorting, searching, and geometric problems.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 170

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Randomness and Computation
course.description: Computational applications of randomness and computational theories of randomness. Approximate counting and uniform generation of combinatorial objects, rapid convergence of random walks on expander graphs, explicit construction of expander graphs, randomized reductions, Kolmogorov complexity, pseudo-random number generation, semi-random sources.
course.requirements: 170 and at least one course numbered 270-279.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Foundations of Decisions, Learning, and Games
course.description:
This course introduces students to the mathematical foundation of learning in the presence of strategic and societal agency. This is a theory-oriented course that will draw from the statistical and computational foundations of machine learning, computer science, and economics. As a research-oriented course, a range of advanced topics will be explored to paint a comprehensive
picture of classical and modern approaches to learning for the purpose of decision making.These topics include foundations of learning, foundations of algorithmic game theory, cooperative and non-cooperative games, equilibria and dynamics, learning in games, information asymmetries, mechanism design, and learning with incentives.
course.requirements:
Graduate-level mathematical maturity, including proof-based graduate-level courses in at least two, but recommended three, of the following categories:

Statistics and Probability, e.g., STAT205A, STAT210B
Economics, e.g., ECON207A
Algorithms, e.g., CS270
Optimization, e.g., EE 227B
Control theory, e.g., EE 221A

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Machine-Based Complexity Theory
course.description: Properties of abstract complexity measures; Determinism vs. nondeterminism; time vs. space; complexity hierarchies; aspects of the P-NP question; relative power of various abstract machines.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Intro to Computer Vision and Computational Photography
course.description: This course introduces students to computing with visual data (images and video). We will cover acquisition, representation, and manipulation of visual information from digital photographs (image processing), image analysis and visual understanding (computer vision), and image synthesis (computational photography). Key algorithms will be presented, ranging from classical to contemporary, with an emphasis on using these techniques to build practical systems. The hands-on emphasis will be reflected in the programming assignments, where students will acquire their own images and develop, largely from  scratch, image analysis and synthesis tools for real-world applications.
course.requirements:
CS61B, enough programming experience to debug complicated programs without much help.
CS70
Math 53 (or another vector calculus course)
Math 54,
Math 110, or equivalent like ELENG 66
Strongly recommended: CS182

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Designing, Visualizing and Understanding Deep Neural Networks
course.description: Deep Networks have revolutionized computer vision, language technology, robotics and control. They have growing impact in many other areas of science and engineering. They do not however, follow a closed or compact set of theoretical principles. In Yann Lecun's words they require "an interplay between intuitive insights, theoretical modeling, practical implementations, empirical studies, and scientific analyses." This course attempts to cover that ground.
course.requirements: MATH 53 and MATH 54 or equivalent; COMPSCI 70 or STAT 134; COMPSCI 61B or equivalent; COMPSCI 189 or COMPSCI 289A (recommended)

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Foundations of Computer Graphics
course.description: A broad introduction to the fundamentals of computer graphics. The main areas covered are modeling, rendering, animation and imaging. Topics include 2D and 3D transformations, drawing to raster displays, sampling, texturing, antialiasing, geometric modeling, ray tracing and global illumination, animation, cameras, image processing and computational imaging. There will be an emphasis on mathematical and geometric aspects of graphics, and the ability to write complete 3D graphics programs.
course.requirements: Computer Science 61B or 61BL; programming skills in C, C++, or Java; linear algebra and calculus; or consent of instructor.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
course.description: This course provides an introduction to theoretical foundations, algorithms, and methodologies for machine learning, emphasizing the role of probability and optimization and exploring a variety of real-world applications. Students are expected to have a solid foundation in calculus and linear algebra as well as exposure to the basic tools of logic and probability, and should be familiar with at least one modern, high-level programming language.
course.requirements: Mathematics 53, 54; Computer Science 70; Computer Science 188 or consent of instructor.

subject: COMPSCI
title: STAR Assessments for Proficiency-Based Learning
description:
In this special topics course, small teams (2-3) of graduate and undergraduate students will use PrairieLearn to develop and rigorously evaluate rich, machine-gradable assessments that would address learning goals that might arise in typical EECS courses.

The assessments will promote mastery learning (aka proficiency learning) by following the acronym STAR: Specific to a particular competency, Tagged to specific learning outcomes, Autogradable, and Randomized so that many variants can be auto-generated on demand.

In addition to developing assessments, student teams will evaluate them by using the methods of HCI and education research to run either informal or formal pilot studies. We will encourage students to make any resulting artifacts available as open educational resources.

subject: COMPSCI
title: Physics-Inspired Deep Learning
description:
Machine learning in the context of scientific problems is an exciting emerging area of research, and often requires the development of new methods that can incorporate and exploit the inductive biases and structure needed for such problems. There are also now numerous examples of concepts in physics historically influencing machine learning methods development more broadly. This course will give an overview of different physics-inspired machine learning methods, and the connections between concepts in physics (numerical methods, dynamical systems, symmetries, conservation laws) and machine learning.

Topics include: overview of different types of physical constraints for neural networks, connections between dynamical systems and neural networks, implicit differentiation and differentiable physics, geometric deep learning including graph neural networks and incorporating symmetries into neural networks

subject: COMPSCI
title: Data-Centric Large Language Models
description:
Advances in large language models (LLMs) have been driven by the growing availability of large and diverse datasets. But where do these datasets come from? How are they being used? How can we leverage them in better, more creative ways? What challenges or issues do they present, and how might we address them? In this seminar, we will explore these questions as part of a broader effort to rethink how data is used in the development of LLMs: what data we use, how we use it, why it works, and what problems it brings.

The class is primarily designed for PhD students and is based on paper readings, discussions, and an open-ended project. Students are expected to independently understand assigned papers and have a background in ML, NLP (CS 288 or equivalent), and LLMs.

subject: COMPSCI
title: Single-cell immunology: from statistical machine learning to biomedical discovery
description:
Advances in single-cell technologies have transformed modern immunology, enabling major discoveries in cancer, autoimmunity, and other diseases. However, the scale and complexity of the resulting datasets necessitate specialized machine learning expertise to fully realize their potential. This course examines the computational challenges posed by emerging biotechnology platforms and how addressing them can advance molecular medicine, with a particular emphasis on cancer immunotherapies.

This is an experimental class designed to mirror the interdisciplinary and collaborative nature of modern biomedical research in industry and academia. Students are expected to have a prior exposure to EITHER the computational or the immunological aspects, but not necessarily both. From the computational side, we will cover statistical inference from atlas-scale omics data, drawing heavily on high-dimensional statistics and variational inference. From the immunology side, we will introduce some of the latest technological developments in single-cell genomics, including spatial transcriptomics and massively parallel pooled CRISPR screens, and survey their applications in molecular medicine. Our guiding focus will be the characterization of molecular states of immune cells in solid tumors (or: "why does the immune system fail to kill the tumor and what can we do to help it").

subject: COMPSCI
title: Forecasting: A Critical Retrospective
description: This class studies statistical algorithms that use counts and summaries of data to make predictions, take actions, and draw inferences without probabilistic models of data generation. We will cover stochastic algorithmic innovations in control, optimization, signal processing, and learning theory in purely deterministic frameworks, showing the surprising frequency with which the gaps between deterministic and probabilistic modeling are small. We will find examples where deterministic analysis coincides with average-case analysis and look for general algorithmic principles for nonstochastic statistics.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models and General-Purpose Robotic Learning
description: This course will cover general-purpose models for robotic learning, with a particular focus on vision-language-action models. course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: CS Scholars Seminar: The Educational Climate in CS & CS61A technical discussions
course.description: Computer Science 36 is a seminar for CS Scholars who are concurrently taking CS61A: The Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs. CS Scholars is a cohort-model program to provide support in exploring and potentially declaring a CS major for students with little to no computational background prior to coming to the university.   CS 36 provides an introduction to the CS curriculum at UC Berkeley, and the overall CS landscape in both industry and academia—through the lens of accessibility and its relevance to diversity. Additionally, CS36 provides technical instruction to review concepts in CS61A, in order to support CS Scholars’ individual learning and success in the CS61A course.
course.requirements: Prerequisite satisfied Concurrently: Participating in the CS Scholars program, and concurrently taking COMPSCI 61A.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Instructional Methods in Computer Science for Academic Interns
course.description: This is a course for aspiring Academic Interns (AIs). It provides pedagogical training and guidance to students by introducing them to the Big Ideas of Teaching and Learning, and how to put them into practice. The course covers what makes a safe learning environment, how students learn, how to guide students toward mastery, and psychosocial factors that can negatively affect even the best students and best teachers. Class covers both theoretical and practical pedagogical aspects of teaching STEM subjects—specifically Computer Science. An integral feature of the course lies in the weekly AI experience that students perform to practice their teaching skills.
course.requirements: Completion of any DS or CS lower-division course and concurrent participation in the Academic Intern experience in EECS at UC Berkeley.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Adaptive Instruction Methods in Computer Science
course.description: This is a course for aspiring teachers or those who want to instruct with expertise from evidence-based research and proven equity-oriented practices. It provides pedagogical training by introducing the big ideas of teaching and learning, and illustrating how to put them into practice. The course is divided into three sections—instructing the individual; a group; and psycho-social factors that affect learning at any level. These sections are designed to enhance any intern’s, tutor’s, or TA’s teaching skillset. Class is discussion based, and covers theoretical and practical pedagogical aspects to teaching in STEM. An integral feature of the course involves providing weekly tutoring sessions.
course.requirements: Prerequisite satisfied Concurrently: experience tutoring or as an academic intern; or concurrently serving as an academic intern while taking course.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Completion of Work in Computer Science 61A
course.description: Implementation of generic operations. Streams and iterators. Implementation techniques for supporting functional, object-oriented, and constraint-based programming in the Scheme programming language. Together with 9D, 47A constitutes an abbreviated, self-paced version of 61A for students who have already taken a course equivalent to 61B.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B, COMPSCI 9D, and consent of instructor.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Completion of Work in Computer Science 61B
course.description: Iterators. Hashing, applied to strings and multi-dimensional structures. Heaps. Storage management. Design and implementation of a program containing hundreds of lines of code. Students who have completed a portion of the subject matter of COMPSCI 61B may, with consent of instructor, complete COMPSCI 61B in this self-paced course.  Please note that students in the College of Engineering are required to receive additional permission from the College as well as the EECS department for the course to count in place of COMPSCI 61B.
course.requirements: A course in data structures, COMPSCI 9G, and consent of instructor.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Completion of Work in Computer Science 61C
course.description: MIPS instruction set simulation. The assembly and linking process. Caches and virtual memory. Pipelined computer organization. Students with sufficient partial credit in 61C may, with consent of instructor, complete the credit in this self-paced course.
course.requirements: Experience with assembly language including writing an interrupt handler, COMPSCI 9C, and consent of instructor.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: The Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
course.description: An introduction to programming and computer science focused on abstraction techniques as means to manage program complexity. Techniques include procedural abstraction; control abstraction using recursion, higher-order functions, generators, and streams; data abstraction using interfaces, objects, classes, and generic operators; and language abstraction using interpreters and macros. The course exposes students to programming paradigms, including functional, object-oriented, and declarative approaches. It includes an introduction to asymptotic analysis of algorithms. There are several significant programming projects.
course.requirements: MATH 1A (may be taken concurrently) or Math 10A or Math 16A. Programming experience equivalent to that gained from a score of 3 or above on the Advanced Placement Computer Science exam.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Data Structures
course.description: Fundamental dynamic data structures, including linear lists, queues, trees, and other linked structures; arrays strings, and hash tables. Storage management. Elementary principles of software engineering. Abstract data types. Algorithms for sorting and searching. Introduction to the Java programming language.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61A, COMPSCI 88, or ENGIN 7.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Great Ideas of Computer Architecture (Machine Structures)
course.description: The internal organization and operation of digital computers. Machine architecture, support for high-level languages (logic, arithmetic, instruction sequencing) and operating systems (I/O, interrupts, memory management, process switching). Elements of computer logic design. Tradeoffs involved in fundamental architectural design decisions.
course.requirements: 61A, along with either 61B or 61BL, or programming experience equivalent to that gained in 9C, 9F, or 9G.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Discrete Mathematics and Probability Theory
course.description: Logic, infinity, and induction; applications include undecidability and stable marriage problem. Modular arithmetic and GCDs; applications include primality testing and cryptography. Polynomials; examples include error correcting codes and interpolation. Probability including sample spaces, independence, random variables, law of large numbers; examples include load balancing, existence arguments, Bayesian inference.
course.requirements: Sophomore mathematical maturity, and programming experience equivalent to that gained in 3 or the Advanced Placement Computer Science A course.

course.subject: DATA
course.title: Principles & Techniques of Data Science
course.description: In this course, students will explore the data science lifecycle, including question formulation, data collection and cleaning, exploratory data analysis and visualization, statistical inference and prediction​, and decision-making.​ This class will focus on quantitative critical thinking​ and key principles and techniques needed to carry out this cycle. These include languages for transforming, querying and analyzing data; algorithms for machine learning methods including regression, classification and clustering; principles behind creating informative data visualizations; statistical concepts of measurement error and prediction; and techniques for scalable data processing.
course.requirements: DATA C8 or STAT 20 with a C- or better, or Pass; and COMPSCI 61A, COMPSCI/DATA C88C, or ENGIN 7 with a C- or better, or Pass; Corequisite: MATH 54, 56, 110, ELENG 66, PHYSICS 89 or equivalent linear algebra (C- or better, or Pass, required if completed prior to Data C100).

course.subject: DATA
course.title: Designing, Visualizing and Understanding Deep Neural Networks
course.description:
Deep Networks have revolutionized computer vision, language technology, robotics and control. They have growing impact in many other areas of science and engineering. They do not however, follow a closed or compact set of theoretical principles. In Yann Lecun's words they require "an interplay between intuitive insights, theoretical modeling, 
practical implementations, empirical studies, and scientific analyses." This course attempts to cover that ground.
course.requirements: MATH 53, MATH 54, and COMPSCI 61B; COMPSCI 70 or STAT 134; COMPSCI 189 is recommended.

course.subject: DATA
course.title: Data Engineering
course.description: This course will cover the principles and practices of managing data at scale, with a focus on use cases in data analysis and machine learning. We will cover the entire life cycle of data management and science, ranging from data preparation to exploration, visualization and analysis, to machine learning and collaboration, with a focus on ensuring reliable, scalable operationalization.
course.requirements: COMPSCI 61B, or INFO 206B, or equivalent courses in programming with a C- or better, or Pass; and COMPSCI C100 / DATA C100 / STAT C100, or COMPSCI 189, or INFO 251, or DATA 144, or equivalent upper-division course in data science with a C- or better, or Pass.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Principles and Techniques of Data Science
course.description: Explores the data science lifecycle: question formulation, data collection and cleaning, exploratory, analysis, visualization, statistical inference, prediction, and decision-making. Focuses on quantitative critical thinking and key principles and techniques: languages for transforming, querying and analyzing data; algorithms for machine learning methods: regression, classification and clustering; principles of informative visualization; measurement error and prediction; and techniques for scalable data processing. Research term project.
course.requirements: COMPSCI C8 / INFO C8 / STAT C8 or ENGIN 7; and either COMPSCI 61A or COMPSCI 88. Corequisites: MATH 54 or ELENG 66.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Introduction to Embedded Systems
course.description: This course introduces students to the basics of models, analysis tools, and control for embedded systems operating in real time. Students learn how to combine physical processes with computation. Topics include models of computation, control, analysis and verification, interfacing with the physical world, mapping to platforms, and distributed embedded systems. The course has a strong laboratory component, with emphasis on a semester-long sequence of projects.

course.subject: STAT
course.title: Statistical Learning Theory
course.description: Classification regression, clustering, dimensionality, reduction, and density estimation. Mixture models, hierarchical models, factorial models, hidden Markov, and state space models, Markov properties, and recursive algorithms for general probabilistic inference nonparametric methods including decision trees, kernal methods, neural networks, and wavelets. Ensemble methods.

course.subject: STAT
course.title: Foundations of Data Science
course.description: Foundations of data science from three perspectives: inferential thinking, computational thinking, and real-world relevance. Given data arising from some real-world phenomenon, how does one analyze that data so as to understand that phenomenon? The course teaches critical concepts and skills in computer programming and statistical inference, in conjunction with hands-on analysis of real-world datasets, including economic data, document collections, geographical data, and social networks. It delves into social and legal issues surrounding data analysis, including issues of privacy and data ownership.
course.requirements: This course may be taken on its own, but students are encouraged to take it concurrently with a data science connector course (numbered 88 in a range of departments).

course.subject: STAT
course.title: Foundations of Data Science
course.description: Foundations of data science from three perspectives: inferential thinking, computational thinking, and real-world relevance. Given data arising from some real-world phenomenon, how does one analyze that data so as to understand that phenomenon? The course teaches critical concepts and skills in computer programming and statistical inference, in conjunction with hands-on analysis of real-world datasets, including economic data, document collections, geographical data, and social networks. It delves into social and legal issues surrounding data analysis, including issues of privacy and data ownership.
course.requirements: This course may be taken on its own, but students are encouraged to take it concurrently with a data science connector course (numbered 88 in a range of departments).

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Computational Structures in Data Science
course.description: Development of Computer Science topics appearing in Foundations of Data Science (C8); expands computational concepts and techniques of abstraction. Understanding  the structures that underlie the programs, algorithms, and languages used in data science and elsewhere.   Mastery of a particular programming language while studying general techniques for managing program complexity, e.g., functional, object-oriented, and declarative programming. Provides practical experience with composing larger systems through several significant programming projects.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Honors Social Implications of Computer Technology
course.description: Topics include electronic community; the changing nature of work; technological risks; the information economy; intellectual property; privacy; artificial intelligence and the sense of self; pornography and censorship; professional ethics. Students may lead discussions on additional topics.

course.subject: COMPSCI
course.title: Senior Honors Thesis Research
course.description: Thesis work under the supervision of a faculty member. To obtain credit the student must, at the end of two semesters, submit a satisfactory thesis to the Electrical Engineering and Computer Science department archive. A total of four units must be taken. The units many be distributed between one or two semesters in any way. H196A-H196B count as graded technical elective units, but may not be used to satisfy the requirement for 27 upper division technical units in the College of Computing, Data Science, and Society with a major in Computer Science.
course.requirements: Open only to students in the computer science honors program.

course.subject: COMPSS
course.title: Computing I
course.description: Predictive models are a core tool for computational social scientists. This class aims to provide students with a practitioner’s level of understanding of different models and techniques: which methods exist, how they relate to each other, the shortcomings they may have, and their most relevant applications. The focus is on methods which are used in practice in industry, which tend to be off-the-shelf rather than cutting edge, and are often chosen for reliability and ease of use rather than performance.
course.requirements: COMPSS 201 or passing the computing waiver exam.

course.subject: COMPSS
course.title: Data Visualization
course.description: In this course, students will learn to create effective visualizations for both analysis of data and communication of findings.
course.requirements: Passing grade in COMPSS 201 (Introduction to Computing) and COMPSS 202 (Introduction to Applied Statistics), or waiver exams for those courses.

course.subject: COMPSS
course.title: Applied Statistics I
course.description: As social scientists we study human behavior and its consequences on others and the world around us - both physical (e.g. the environment) and non-physical (e.g. currency markets). In order to test hypotheses of interest, one needs to choose the right tool for the right problem in order to come up with a valid answer to the question(s) one is asking. The goal of this course is to get students to: identify a problem or research question of interest, formulate a testable hypothesis, characterize the data generating process, chose the correct statistic to test their hypothesis, carefully characterize the data to conduct their test, conduct their test using software, correctly interpret test results, and write up or present their findings.
course.requirements: COMPSS 201 and COMPSS 202

course.subject: COMPSS
course.title: Computational Social Science
course.description: This course introduces students to the tools and applications of computational social science in a variety of fields such aseducation, technology, and social impact. Students will learn how data science and statistical methods can be applied topressing challenges faced by society and organizations. These skills are translatable to many other topics and data science applications.
course.requirements:
Passing grade (C+ or better) on COMPSS 201 and COMPSS 202 or passing
grade on waiver exams for these courses.

course.subject: COMPSS
course.title: Career Development I
course.description: This course is designed to provide students with the tools to strategically plan their careers at the crossroads of data and social science. Through a blend of self-discovery, career exploration, and targeted skill enhancement, students will emerge with a clear, strategic plan for their professional future. This course will involve a blend of self-discovery, career exploration, and skill development. The course is structured to help students understand their interests, values, and skills, and how these align with various career paths.
course.requirements: COMPSS 201, COMPSS 202

course.subject: CPH
course.title: Computational Precision Health Cornerstone A
course.description: CPH students will develop skills and expertise in both the computational sciences and health sciences. In this three-part course series, students learn to integrate core foundations of computational precision health in small multidisciplinary teams using a Problem Based Learning pedagogical approach. Students will learn core computational foundations including in machine learning and causal inference and they will obtain deep exposure to multiple clinical areas including cancer and cardiology.

course.subject: CPH
course.title: Lab Rotation
course.description: For first-year CPH graduate students, this course will provide an introduction to experimental methods and research approaches in the different areas of Computational Precision Health. Ten week laboratory rotations spread out over the fall and spring semesters (summer will be on a needed basis). Research is conducted under the direction of an individual faculty member.

course.subject: CPH
course.title: Computational Precision Health Seminar
course.description: Computational precision health is a rapidly evolving field at the intersection of the computational (to include computer science, data science, and statistics) and the health sciences (clinical medicine, population health, clinical research). The seminar series will consist of a combination of journal club-style discussion of recent literature in Computational Precision Health, guest faculty speakers drawn from across the program’s faculty and beyond, presentations by second-year students on work completed during lab rotations, and presentations by third-year students on “work in progress” on active dissertation research. Each cohort of PhD and DE students will have their own breakout sections to build community within that year.

course.subject: CPH
course.title: Special Topics in Computational Precision Health
course.description: Computational precision health (CPH) is a rapidly evolving field at the intersection of the computational (to include computer science, data science, and statistics) and the health sciences (clinical medicine, population health, clinical research). The advent of generative AI models has significantly boosted the rapid progress of CPH research, with new major contributions occurring within very short spans of time. Because this field is rapidly evolving, some of the most exciting recent advancements could not be covered in traditional foundational courses and warrant a dedicated thematic lecture series. This course will involve a set of invited lectures by world-leading experts who made fundamental contributions in the fields of computation

course.subject: DATA
course.title: Foundations for Computational Precision Health
course.description: Students will build expertise in developing machine-learning tools to address challenges in health care. The course emphasizes both “how to formulate useful computational health problems”, and “how to develop computational solutions”. On the health side, we’ll get clinical guest lectures exploring challenges across diverse areas of healthcare (e.g., cardiology, cancer, primary care). On the computational side, the course will cover machine learning and deep learning foundations, state-of-the-art neural networks, and then advanced research topics. The course will emphasize rigorous evaluation, algorithmic bias, deployment, and auditing. The class will culminate in an open-ended final project, integrating skills learned in the course.
course.requirements: Data C100 and Data C140

course.subject: CRITTH
course.title: The Classical Frankfurt School: The First Generation of Critical Theory
course.description: This course will explore the founding texts of the Frankfurt School's first generation: Horkheimer, Adorno, Benjamin, Marcuse, Lowenthal, and their circle. It will follow the development of critical theory through its Weimar years, American exile, and return to postwar Germany.
course.requirements: Admission to the critical theory designated emphasis or consent of instructor.

course.subject: CRITTH
course.title: Contemporary Critique and Critical Theory
course.description: This course will explore various contemporary engagements with the foundations of critical theory in relation to other histories and locations. Topics will vary by instructor but may include: post-continental political theory, critique and the problem of political dissent and citizenship, gender and race in relation to critical practices, psychoanalysis, and literary and art theory and criticism.
