course.title: Special Topics in Technology Innovation and Entrepreneurship
course.description: This course will explore various topics around technology innovation and entrepreneurship. Topics will vary by semester.

subject: ENGIN
title: Advanced Product Management: Strategy, Scale, and AI
description:
In an era shaped by rapid innovation, platform disruption, and AI acceleration, Advanced Product Management prepares students to confidently step into senior product leadership roles across global corporations, high-growth startups, and mission-driven ventures. This immersive, case-based course explores the full complexity of modern product leadership, equipping students with the skills to design, scale, and lead resilient product organizations. Emphasizing the practical application of strategy, students will learn to translate vision into execution while navigating uncertainty and operating at the intersection of engineering, design, and business.


The curriculum explores how to scale high-performing product teams in both hypergrowth and enterprise contexts, design inclusive and globally relevant solutions for emerging markets such as Africa and LATAM, and apply differentiated product strategies across peacetime and wartime market conditions. Students will evaluate build vs. buy vs. partner decisions through both financial and technical lenses, and learn to embed AI and machine learning into product experiences and workflows. The course also emphasizes ethical product design, inclusive innovation, and governance frameworks for responsible AI. Finally, students will examine how to build strong product cultures and organizational rituals that support continuous experimentation, growth, and innovation at scale.

Through a combination of real-world case studies, leadership simulations, and executive guest lectures from top Product Leaders, students will begin to develop the necessary mindset and capabilities to lead the next generation of transformative products.

Students who will benefit the most from this course:
–non-STEM students exploring careers in tech
–STEM students seeking preparation for product-centric tech roles
–Students who have already taken a SCET Berkeley Challenge Lab (ENGIN 183C) or ENGIN 183D
–Have a general understanding of modern product management and product development approaches (e.g. waterfall, agile/scrum)

subject: ENGIN
title: Exploring Sustainable Food Production: A Berkeley Changemaker Course
description:
A mushroom walks into a bar and orders a beer.

The bartender says, “I don’t serve beer to mushroom!”

The mushroom replies, “I am not a mushroom, I am a fun-gi” 🙂

 

Jokes aside, fungi is finally having its moment as a versatile ingredient with functional, nutritional, and structural applications.  In this seminar class, we will explore adoption of fungi based foods.  From the use of mycelium that mimics meat, to the use of various types of medicine fungi use as  medicine (not psilocybin), and how the rise in adoption of functional foods fit squarely into fungi.

Students will learn about the increasing popularity of fungi-based foods, as well as the basics of mycology, the applications of mycelium, and approaches for transforming fungi into products that can succeed in the mainstream food market. The course will culminate in team projects in which students develop fungi-based food concepts with potential for large-scale adoption.

This class is a great introduction to technology entrepreneurship and innovation and is required for two tracks of the SCET Certificate in Entrepreneurship & Technology. All majors will feel welcome. It is also part of the Berkeley Changemaker suite of courses, which is designed to activate passions and sharpen your sense of where you want to go and how to make that happen, with particular focus on critical thinking, communication, and collaboration.

course.subject: ENGIN
course.title: A. Richard Newton Lecture Series
course.description: This lecture series serves as an entry point for undergraduate and graduate curriculum sequences in entrepreneurship and innovation.  The series, established in 2005 is named in honor of A. Richard Newton, a visionary technology industry leader and late dean of the University of California-Berkeley College of Engineering.   The course features a selection of high-level industry speakers who share their insights on industry developments, leadership and innovation based on their careers.

course.subject: ENGIN
course.title: Startup Catalyst
course.description: Designed for students currently building a startup, this course helps teams navigate the critical "what's next" of their innovation journey. Whether you are building on momentum from a Challenge Lab, scaling a BMoE Bootcamp idea, or refining a revenue-generating prototype, this course provides the tools to avoid common pitfalls that stall early-stage ventures. Working closely with an experienced lead instructor, teams will honestly address difficult challenges regarding their market opportunity and team dynamics. This hands-on, collaborative environment leverages peer feedback, expert mentorship, and real-world execution to help you seek the truth about your startup’s future and prepare for accelerators or major investment.

course.subject: ENGIN
course.title: Manufacturing and Design Communication
course.description: An introduction to manufacturing process technologies and the ways in which dimensional requirements for manufactured objects are precisely communicated, especially through graphical means. Fundamentals of cutting, casting, molding, additive manufacturing, and joining processes are introduced. Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T), tolerance analysis for fabrication, concepts of process variability, and metrology techniques are introduced and practiced. 3-D visualization skills for engineering design are developed via sketching and presentation of 3-D geometries with 2-D engineering drawings. Computer-aided design software is used. Teamwork and effective communication are emphasized through lab activities and a design project.
course.requirements: ENGIN 26 or equivalent experience in three-dimensional solid modeling (e.g. Solidworks, Fusion 360) is recommended.

course.title: Engineering Thermodynamics
course.description: Fundamental laws of thermodynamics for simple substances; application to flow processes and to nonreacting mixtures; statistical thermodynamics of ideal gases and crystalline solids; chemical and materials thermodynamics; multiphase and multicomponent equilibria in reacting systems; electrochemistry. Sponsoring Departments: Materials Science and Engineering and Nuclear Engineering.
course.requirements: PHYSICS 7B and MATH 54.  CHEM 1B recommended.

course.subject: ENGIN
course.title: Introduction to Computer Programming and Numerical Methods
course.description: Fundamentals of computer programming and numerical methods with emphasis on engineering applications. The first part of the course provides an accelerated introduction to programming in Python, suitable for novices and those with prior experience. Topics include control structures, functions, data types, data handling, and visualization. Some programming in MATLAB will also be introduced. The second part of the course introduces several numerical methods commonly used in engineering. These include solving nonlinear equations, numerically integrating and differentiating functions, solving systems of linear equations, and simulating dynamical systems using ordinary differential equations.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Hearing Enslaved Voices
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

We will begin this seminar by reading the canonical, self-authored works of African and African-descended formerly enslaved people and some scholarly criticism around these texts: Olaudah Equiano, Mary Prince, Frederick Douglass, and Harriet Jacobs.  In these and other primary texts, our study will include the wages of freedom and unfreedom, literacy and the act of writing, memory and representation, embodiment and performance, geography, resistance, and gender among other topics.  We will then turn our attention to representations of enslaved people in the broader archive of American and Caribbean slavery, discussing the methods scholars and writers use to recover these figures and their lives.  Throughout, we will turn to literary criticism to inspire and to teach us, to spur our imaginations, to challenge easy answers, and to deepen our experience as readers.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Atlantic Haunts, Black Possessions
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

An introduction to Black diasporic criticism, this seminar uses various angles of approach toward notions of the spirit, the haunt, and the possession to explore Black literature and Atlantic history. We will study fiction, memoir, artifacts from the visual and anthropological archive, and examples from popular culture--a range of genres that suggests something of the multi-modal techniques of Black literary study.

With its focus on shifting landscapes, spatial intimacies, scrambled temporalities, and hybridities of all kinds, Black diasporic criticism resonates richly with the metaphorical wanderings of the ghostly. By traversing the myriad crossings of the haunt and the possession, we focus our analytical view on certain disavowals within cultural traditions and on their powerful re-assertions. For if a ghostly haunt may speak to that which is denied, then a spirit acknowledged can function as a welcome guest—as in the myriad Black cultural practices that involve the embodiment of immaterial energies. By thinking about these religious and spiritual practices of spirit possession, we put colonial and postcolonial positionalities into dialogue, observing profound shifts in knowledge, power, and agency.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Canadian Songs 1960-1999
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

The latter half of the 20th c. was a remarkable period in Canadian songwriting. Of course, the so-called “folk revival” and coffeehouse scene made those years remarkable for songwriting in many cultures; but in Canada, they coincided with a transformative period of political and cultural self-definition, in which Canada restructured its colonial relationship with Great Britain, and various component parts renegotiated their relationships with Canada itself. While some songwriters in this period built careers that made them well known in the U.S., others, especially those drawn to depictions of Canadian regions, historical events and cultural traditions, remain less, or differently, known here. As a course in English literature, this course’s engagement with this material will necessarily be partial -- songs combine two arts, poetry and music, of which this course will focus on poetry; and Canada recognizes several official languages, of which this course will focus on English. Nonetheless, even this partial perspective on these songs should afford ample material for exploring a body of literature in its own right and in relation to its context, and students will be welcome to develop broader connections in their final papers. And of course, the course will also address the value for poetry of universal health care.

Requirements will include attendance, participation, three essays (4pp., 6pp. and 8pp.) and two in-class quizzes.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Shakespeare and Criticism
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

How on earth have Shakespeare's 400-year-old plays accumulated the status (or "cultural capital") they enjoy today? What does it mean to interpret these old texts in our terms, and is it right to do so? What makes us think we haven't by now exhausted everything there could be to say about these plays? We'll examine the development of Shakespeare criticism, which is the backbone of the history of literary criticism in English. We'll consider how key terms from that long history resonate with some crucial concepts of 21st-century cultural critique. We'll focus on five case studies, drawing on recent filmed productions as well as on written criticism: subjectivity and power in Hamlet; intertextuality and desire in A Midsummer Night's Dream; racecraft and commodity in Othello; performativity and gender in The Taming of the Shrew; theatricality and colonialism in Cymbeline. Students will write a shorter paper engaging some criticism of Hamlet, and then develop a more extensive intervention into another of our critical debates.

This class fulfills the English 100 requirement for the major; it can also fulfill either the Shakespeare or the pre-1800 requirement.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Austen
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

Why are we obsessed with Jane Austen? From Austen “action figures” to Bollywood adaptations, from memes to merchandise to musicals, Austen’s popularity remains remarkably high. This course will address a range of questions about Austen’s continued relevance in our culture today. How have writers and artists from a wide array of backgrounds taken her writing as a model for social commentary? Why does poet W.H. Auden praise her “shocking” exposure of the “economic basis of society” and writer Ta Nehisi-Coates deem her “Jane Awesome”? Most importantly, what enduring connections do we as readers feel to her stories, her characters, and her social insights? This course will place Austen’s writing in her historical and political context while also offering students an introduction to Austen scholarship and the practice of literary criticism. Our discussions and writing assignments will allow us to think about Austen’s artistic innovations and development as a writer, and also to understand her legacy and reception.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Phenomenology as Method
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

What is phenomenology and what can we learn from it for reading and thinking about literature? In the first years of the 20th century, Edmund Husserl began publishing on a topic that might seem paradoxical: how to turn subjective experience into a scientific method. The project raised a host of difficult questions. How do we redirect our attention from everyday concerns to the style in which the world appears to us? What might such practices of attending reveal about the structure of experience? How do we get from the seemingly solipsistic exercise of examining our subjectivity to the reality of the world outside of us? Indeed, to what extent is phenomenology an aesthetic practice, a method of learning to see the world as if it were a work of art?

We will read selections from Husserl’s The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology, and from Merleau-Ponty’s The Visible and the Invisible, among others. Assignments include weekly bCourses posts, a short exercise in phenomenology, an essay proposal, an essay, and a final exam.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Poetics of Prose
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

Everybody knows that poetry is an art-form, that it transforms words into music and dance, creates patterns like a hand-woven carpet, demands special close reading, and draws out emotions as well as ideas. But all too often prose is treated as mere communication or information, a neutral medium whose meaning is its content. Historians of the novel also assume, sometimes, that prose is modern while verse is historical, traditional or antique. The line-breaks and other formal features of poetry – including rhyme, meter and stanza – force us to read it as a deliberate work of art, but we often forget to read prose with the same aesthetic eye, looking for the rhythms, pauses, sound-patterns, repetitions, word-choices and images that generate emotional meaning. This seminar will explore ways to analyze prose as artefact ‒ as poetry in effect ‒ and to sample its deep history. We begin with Chapter 14 of Ulysses, where James Joyce evokes and imitates the “embryonic development” of English prose over two millennia. Then we go back in time.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Marx as Literature
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

Marx’s Capital is one of the great books of the nineteenth century. Marx’s intentions are scientific—to describe the nature of the capitalist mode of production and to indicate for the workers’ movement how it might be overcome. But Capital is also a literary work, a non-fiction epic, which descends into the hell of the workplace and the violent origins of capitalism using a gamut of literary devices to relay its key points. In this course, we will read Capital as literature, examining how it uses literary technique and, in this way, anticipates literary modernism. 

We will also examine how twentiith-century writers have made use of Marx. Finally, we will read some additional texts by Marx in order to fill out our understanding of Marxism and to understand how writers have made use of it.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Work of Ursula LeGuin
description:
**Please read Class Notes for information about enrollment**

“Science Fiction is often described, and even defined, as extrapolative. The science fiction writer is supposed to take a trend or phenomenon of the here-and-now, purify and intensify it for dramatic effect, and extend it into the future. “If this goes on, this is what will happen.” A prediction is made… The outcomes seem almost inevitably to be cancer. …Strictly extrapolative works of science fiction generally arrive about where the Club of Rome arrives: somewhere between human liberty and the total extinction of terrestrial life.” 

This course will serve as a deep dive into the fantasy/science fiction work of Berkeley native Ursula LeGuin. As the quote above conveys, LeGuin eschewed her peers and contemporaries’ extrapolative narratives and technological determinism. Her fantasies and science fiction dwelt on our imaginative capacity to make and undo the world through culture, custom, language, and technology. But foremost in her extensive oeuvre is the social. We will read a wide selection of LeGuin’s novels, short stories, essays. We will also address LeGuin’s critics and interlocutors in an attempt to trace the long arc of her influence on genre fiction, traditional narrative fiction, and futurist writings.

subject: ENGLISH
description:
This class satisfies the "Pre-1800" requirement for the English major.

Hwæt! This course introduces the earliest English literature, with focus on giving students the skills to read its vibrant corpus in the original language. Step by step, we will build our grasp of grammar and vocabulary; from there, we will read a wide-ranging selection of verse and prose, including medical recipes and schoolbooks, love-laments and travel narratives, riddles, heroic poetry, guides for decoding dreams and even advice on haircuts. Throughout, emphasis on close reading will help us solidify our grasp of grammar and syntax, and attend to the ways early English writers themselves approached and valued the discipline of words. You will also practice reading from medieval manuscripts, and learn to use scholarly tools (lexicographical, codicological, digital) for conducting research in Old English. By the end of the course, you will be able to read most Old English texts with the help of a dictionary, and be well prepared for further study in medieval languages and literature.

No pre-requisites, nor is prior knowledge of Old English or medieval literature expected.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: Introduction to Old English
course.description: Basic introduction to the vocabulary, grammar, and syntax of Old English designed to get students reading original texts immediately. Typical Old English texts include: riddles, charms, medical recipes, laws, chronicles, elegies, saints' lives, heroic poetry, and monster lore.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Abroad in the Middle Ages
description:
Contrary to modern expectations, medieval people did a lot of travelling—for business or pleasure, out of curiosity or hunting for knowledge, as tourists or explorers, alone or with others in armies, bands of pilgrims or in thrall to human traffickers—walking the highways and byways of the known world or sailing its high seas, from Britain to Jerusalem to Africa, India and China. As they went, these travellers carried with them their own “baggage”:  their cultural origins, assumptions and beliefs which shifted kaleidoscopically in relation to the world they encountered, a world transformed in turn by their visit, and brought home in stories, in books we, along with their contemporaries, can read.

Looking closely at medieval maps, manuscript illuminations, documents and personal letters (the “trash” of the Cairo Genizah, for instance), guidebooks for sightseers and, especially, travel narratives of Christians, Muslims and Jews among others (including the famous accounts of Marco Polo and John Mandeville), we will aim to see more clearly the medieval world as it was seen by those who passed through it—its landscapes, its customs, its communities, its peoples, including our guides themselves, forced to look in a foreign mirror—risking our own transformation by the vicarious trip abroad.

No prior knowledge is assumed or expected for this course, which fulfills the pre-1800 major requirement.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: Medieval Literature
course.description: Development of literary form and idiom throughout the Christian West from the first to the fifteenth century.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Middle English Writing for Religious Women Readers
description:
This course will focus on the texts contained in a unique little thirteenth-century manuscript now in the Bodleian Library in Oxford (Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 34): the vitae, or lives, of three female saints martyred for their refusal to relinquish their virginity to earthly lords; a treatise on the advantages of marrying Christ rather than an earthly husband; and an allegorical homily, or sermon, on the guardianship of the female soul or inner self, figured as a castle under siege. 

Through a close study of these texts, their sources and literary progeny, as well as the cultural contexts of their production and dissemination, we will not only learn how to read early Middle English and decode the medieval manuscripts which preserve it for us to read; we will also come to a subtler, less stereotyped understanding of the lives of medieval women and the “feminist” attractions of a celibate religious life, which trades the natural yearning for family and physical intimacy for emotional stability and the promise of eternal validation and respect as well as infinite beauty, desirability and prestige. At the center of our inquiry will be the status of the female body, its vulnerability and its fortitude, and the ways in which pain and the threat of pain become a catalyst for spiritual transformation.

No prior knowledge is assumed or expected for this course, which fulfills the pre-1800 major requirement.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: Middle English Literature

subject: ENGLISH
title: The English Baroque
description:
In a now-famous note added to the second edition of Paradise Lost in 1674, Milton characterized the poem as an example of “ancient liberty recover’d to heroic Poem from the troublesom and modern bondage of Rimeing.” Written in the aftermath of the radical social and political experiments of the 1640s and 1650s, the note appears to suggest that literary form is an impediment to freedom. But Paradise Lost isn’t written in free verse, and as the note explains, what is at stake in Milton’s claim is to distinguish rhyme, which he characterizes as “vexation, hindrance, and constraint” from the “true Ornament(s)” of verse. What, then, is a “true ornament,” and how is it different from an untrue one? When do forms constrain freedom, and when do they license creation? Does free speech have a form peculiar to it? 

These are some of the questions we’ll discuss in the context of works by Mary Sidney, William Shakespeare, John Donne, Ben Jonson, Aemilia Lanyer, George Herbert, Katherine Phillips, Robert Herrick, John Milton, Andrew Marvell, and others.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: The English Renaissance
course.description: Literature of the 17th century.

subject: ENGLISH
description: Shakespeare’s plays are relentlessly unsettling, sublimely beautiful, deeply moving, rigorously brilliant, and compulsively meaningful: they complicate everything; they simplify nothing. As we puzzle over the way Shakespeare represents compassion, desire, identity, republicanism, colonialism, racism, freedom and unfreedom, and work, we will keep two overarching questions percolating: how does Shakespeare conceive of theater (its uses, its value)?; and what makes Shakespeare SHAKESPEARE? That is, what makes Shakespeare distinctive and what makes him a strange colossus, a touchstone for literary artists from Milton to Goethe, from George Eliot to Proust, from Emily Dickinson to Sarah Kane, from Brecht to Toni Morrison and for philosophers and theorists such as Hegel, Marx. Freud, Derrida, Kristeva, Lacan, and Zizeck? We will read a few handfuls of sonnets and roughly a dozen plays, including The Merchant of Venice, Julius Caesar, Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Antony and Cleopatra, Coriolanus, and The Tempest. We will also devote some class time to watching scenes from films and filmed performances of the plays. Requirements: one or two short assignments, a final paper; and an in-person final exam.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The English Novel from Haywood to Austen
description:
The period from which our reading draws has been credited with the “rise of the novel”—the
emergence of the then new genre that we now call the “novel.” While critics have qualified and
revised that claim, the texts we’ll read do experiment with new forms of prose fiction and new ideas
about what is worth representing that continue to inform prose fiction in English. We shall
investigate these forms, exploring how they might have coaxed readers into caring about characters
that were not, after all, real people and how they might have shaped what made up a sense of the
“real.” We shall think about why this new form often moved between claims to be “true stories” and
reminders that they were not. This cagey relation to the truth was one element that made the new
form suspect, and as we read these works and track their innovations, we shall also be interested in
considering what it was that some found dangerous about them. Like surfing the internet, novel
reading wasn’t something you wanted the “impressionable”—in the eighteenth century, that included
the young and women—to do alone, or maybe at all. Might the perceived threat have had something
to do with early novels’ connection to romance and the erotic? Might it have to do with the fact that
in some of the most popular of these books, male authors feature female heroines who claim to
describe, in an innovative, frank prose style, how a woman really feels? Highly conscious of these
debates, eighteenth-century writers responded to them, aiming to legitimate their generic
experiments through rhetorical and thematic means. They appealed to (and sometimes transformed)
moral discourse, and created hybrids of new and classical forms, all offering complex new writing
and, some would argue, new models of consciousness.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: The English Novel
course.description: Defoe through Scott.

subject: ENGLISH
description:
The novel emerged as the principal literary genre in 19th-century Europe and has dominated the literary market in Europe and North America ever since.  What were the formal elements as well as social and psychological concerns of novelistic narrative during its rise to prominence? Focusing on a selection of novels from the German, English, French, and Russian traditions, this course examines the many guises the novel assumed as it became, over the course of the 19th century, the central genre for deliberating key social, political, ethical, and aesthetic issues of its time. 

All novels considered in this course are markedly experimental. Each showcases a different dimension of the novel genre: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) is a sentimental epistolary novel; Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818), an epistolary Gothic horror novel that also lays the groundwork for science fiction; Alexander Pushkin’s Eugene Onegin (1823-1831), an ironic and fragmentary novel in verse; Gustave Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1856), a novel famous for its precise, unsparing prose and psychological realism; and finally, Leo Tolstoy’s magisterial War and Peace (1865-1869), a text that can be loosely termed a historical novel while raising crucial questions about the very premises of what it means to be historical and novelistic.

This is a course for students who love reading, are eager to brave substantial novels, and want to think deeply about how they work.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The 20th-Century African Novel
description: This course is a survey of 20th-century African novel. When, where, and how does the novel first appear in Africa? We will examine the specific sociohistorical forces that gave rise to the form on the continent and to which the African novel responds. We will explore how these novels thematize the particular historical junctures out of which they emerge and in which they seek to intervene. We will tend to how in the 20th century the novel form emerges as a site in which to historicize, interrogate, and imagine anew the process of subject-formation, questions of political theory, process of modernity, gender and sexuality, the politics of language, (post)colonialism. As we read key works of the century, we will also interrogate questions of canonicity, authenticity, and the critical discourses that contributed to the institutionalization of African literature.

subject: ENGLISH
description: This survey of U.S. poetries will begin with 17th- and 18th-century poems by two women, Anne Bradstreet and Phillis Wheatley, move to another (19th-century) pairing in Walt Whitman and Emily Dickinson, and then touch down in expatriate and stateside modernisms, the Harlem Renaissance, the New York School, and Language Poetry, on our way to the contemporary. Rather than cover all major figures briefly, we'll spend extended time with the work of a few: poets considered will include Paul Dunbar, Gertrude Stein, T.S. Eliot, Claude McKay, Wallace Stevens, Jean Toomer, Frank O'Hara, John Ashbery, Amiri Baraka, Claudia Rankine, and Layli Longsoldier. Along the way we'll consider renovations and dissipations of conventional form and meter, the task and materials of the long poem, seriality, citationality, who and what counts as a poetic subject, and how U.S. poetries have imagined community over and against their actual Americas.

course.description: A historical survey of American poetry and its backgrounds.

subject: ENGLISH
description:
This course will introduce students to the study of creative writing—fiction and poetry. Students will learn to talk critically about these forms and begin to feel comfortable and confident writing within these genres. Students will write a variety of exercises and more formal pieces. Class will be a combination of lecture/discussion and small in-class workshops where student work will be edited and critiqued by other students in the class.

Please note that the fiction we will be reading and writing in this class should work within the genre of psychological realism. That is, stories that belong to the (long and honorable) traditions of science fiction, fantasy, experimental fiction, etc. will not be accepted. As well, the poetry you read and write for this class should reflect your own voice and time period, i.e.: it should sound contemporary (like something a person would say or write today), and contemporary poets very rarely use strict end rhyme, archaic language, etc. In other words, we will read what's being written TODAY and you will be writing as if you were publishing TODAY. Come write with us!

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: Modes of Writing (Exposition, Fiction, Verse, Etc.)
course.description: Lectures and discussion on the crafts and/or processes of writing in various genres including fiction, poetry, creative nonfiction, etc. Topics for reading and writing assignments vary semester to semester.
course.requirements: R1A-R1B or equivalent.

subject: ENGLISH
description:
The aim of this course is to explore the genre of short fiction—to discuss the elements that make up the short story, to talk critically about short stories, and to become comfortable and confident with the writing of them. Students will write two short stories, a number of shorter exercises, weekly critiques of their peers’ work, and a final writer's reflection. The course will be organized as a workshop and attendance is mandatory. All student stories will be edited and critiqued by the instructor and by other students in the class.

Writing Sample:
Writing samples should be 6-10 pages of fiction (a complete short story, a few short shorts, a section of a novel, etc.). Since this is a class that focuses on psychological realism, please avoid genre fiction for your sample (no sci fi, fantasy, fan fic, etc.). No need to strive for perfection here (this class focuses on learning the craft of fiction, so I expect you have much to learn!), but strong sentences, an understanding that fiction revolves around conflict, and three-dimensional characters are encouraged. Also, I’d love to know why you want to take this class. Just a few sentences would be great.

Each participant in the workshop will edit student-written stories and will write a formal critique of each manuscript. Students will also take part in discussions about fiction. Throughout the semester, we will read published stories from various sources and also essays by working writers about fiction and the writing life. The intent of the course is to have the students learn about and practise the techniques that enable writers to construct a convincing and engaging representation of reality on the page. Please note that students will only write fiction within the genre of psychological realism. We will not workshop science fiction or fantasy fiction.

This is a workshop for reading, writing, and revising short fiction. We will read published short stories and other literary works to see how writers craft effective stories. Over the course of the semester, you will write two short stories. To apply for admission to the course, please submit a fiction writing sample of no more than 12 pages.

subject: ENGLISH
description:
This fiction workshop explores the possibilities and challenges of writing a novel or novella. Through readings, discussion, craft exercises, and peer workshops, students will learn to think about fiction as novelists do: considering questions of narrative voice and point of view, the management of narrative time, approaches to research, and the creation of fictional worlds that can sustain long stories.

Because of the scale of the form, the class focuses on beginnings. Students will draft the opening chapters of an original novel while developing a sense of the larger work it might become – its characters, conflicts, and unfolding architecture. By the end of the semester, each student will have the start of a manuscript and an understanding of the artistic and practical decisions involved in continuing beyond the class.

Admission to this course is by application. Please submit an original fiction sample of up to 15 double-spaced pages. The sample doesn’t need to be an excerpt from a novel; any form of fiction is welcome. Choose work that you feel best represents your strengths as a writer.

The readings for this course will be provided on bCourses, and will include examples of the literary form from Joan Didion to Zadie Smith. We’ll explore a wide range of prose, including the personal essay, cultural criticism, and the lyric essay. In addition to in-class writing exercises, students will complete two essays of their own. 
   
During the course, students will be responsible for constructively discussing their classmates’ work, sharing their own work, and reading closely for class discussion. Admission to this course is by application only. To apply, please submit a writing sample of no more than 12 pages. Creative nonfiction is preferred over academic writing for the purposes of this course, but submit whatever writing sample you’re most excited about. Working drafts are fine.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Fictions of Artificial Intelligence
description:
All of sudden, it seems, generative AI is everywhere: in our smartphones and social media, transportation and shopping, healthcare and politics, and pretty much everywhere else. But AI has a long history, both a literal history and a literary history, in which creators have investigated the definition of intelligence and the difference between what it means to be an artificial being and a real human being. Can only humans be conscious or develop self-awareness, feel love or suffer, want to live or die? If machines can learn, does that mean they can think? As AI increasingly processes our world for us, how do we process the meaning of AI? 

In this course, we will consider these questions and others with respect to contemporary utopian and dystopian visions of generative AI; virtual reality and material embodiment; imaginary robots, androids, and cyborgs; the possibility of AI-generated art; and the ethics of generative AI in the classroom. 

We will begin by reading several nonfictional treatments of the personal and political stakes of generative AI, especially ML (Machine Learning) and LLMs (Large Language Models). But our main focus will be the portrayal of artificial intelligences in 20th- and 21st-century short stories, novels, television and movies. Our texts may include short stories by Isaac Asimov, Brian Aldiss, William Gibson, and Chen Qiufan; novels such as Richard Powers’ Galatea 2.2 (1995), Ted Chiang’s The Lifecycle of Software Objects (2010), and Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (2021); and screen media such as Blade Runner (1982/2007), Star Wars: The Next Generation (1987-94), Her (2013), and Ex Machina (2015). This reading and viewing list is not yet fixed, so please do not purchase any of these books or videos before the first day of class. 

In addition to the assigned reading and viewing, assignments for the course will include frequent bCourses discussion posts, two short essays, and a take-home final exam.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: Writing Technology
course.description: An introduction to different modes of technological, critical, and creative writing and the intersections among them and to the representation of technology and science in literature, film, and other media. This course is writing-intensive and aims to serve students from across campus.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Chekhov
description:
In this class we will be considering a range of texts – including prose and drama – written by Anton Chekhov.

Most of the works we will read are short – less than thirty pages.  (The exceptions are “The Steppe,” “The Duel,” and, probably,  “Three Years.”)  Ideally, students should read each short story twice
Students in the class will write three short papers none of which should be longer than six pages.  There will be at least eight short, unannounced reading quizzes at the start of class; these will count for a substantial part of the class participation grade.  Students will be required to have hard copies of all texts.  No devices permitted in class.  
This class is intended for students who, like Chekhov, appreciate originality of thought and expression. The use of Gemini, Chat GPT or any other AI assistance is prohibited.  Papers written in full or in part with the assistance of AI will not receive passing grades.  Students taking the course on a Pass/Fail basis must receive passing grades on each of the four principal assignments in order to pass the course.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The 20th-Century Novel
description: This course is a survey of the 20th-century novel. The novel is the quintessential form of expression of modernity and modern subjectivity. In this survey of key works of the century, we will explore the novel form as it is framed by these three thematics: history, modernism, and empire. Some questions we will address: how have the vicissitudes of modernity led to a re-direction of historical narration within the novel; how has modernist aesthetic experimentation re-shaped the very form of the novel; and, lastly, how has the phenomenon of imperialism, the asymmetrical relations of power between center and periphery, widened the scope and influence of fictive milieu? We will conclude at the cusp of the 21st century with a work of speculative fiction.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Race and Revision in Early America
description: In this course, we will read both historical and literary texts to explore how racial categories came into being in New World cultures and how these categories were tested, inhabited, and re-imagined by the human actors they sought to define.  Our study will be organized around four early American sites:  Landfall in the Atlantic, Pocahontas at Jamestown, Witchcraft at Salem, and Jefferson’s Virginia. In each of these places Native, European, and African ways of making meaning collided, and concepts of racial difference were formed. These sites will function as interpretive nodes.  For each, we will read a selection of primary documents and then explore how racial constructions forged at each site have been re-imagined and revised throughout American cultural history.

course.subject: ENGLISH
course.title: Special Topics in American Cultures
course.description: In this course, students investigate the way literature and other art forms have both represented the diversity of the United States and shaped conceptions of diversity. English 166AC provides students with an opportunity to deepen and complicate their appreciation of the way fictions make meaning, shape our understanding and experience of the world, and transform society. Topics vary from term to term and might focus on a form (e.g. "Race and Ethnicity in American Cinema"), a literary historical period (e.g. "Race and Revision in Early America"), or a concept (e.g. nationhood in "Literatures of the Asian Diaspora in America").

subject: ENGLISH
title: American Culture in the Age of Obama
description:
This course traces, across many forms of American culture, what might be called “the Obama effect.” Writer Ta-Nehisi Coates has suggested that the election of Obama prompted a renaissance of black writing, in part by stimulating “curiosity about the community he had so consciously made his home and all the old, fitfully slumbering questions he’d awakened about American identity.” 

We’ll examine how a range of imaginative writers, in a wide spectrum of genres, took on those questions and offered counternarratives to conventional myths of American innocence, achievement, and glory. We’ll also explore works of music, film, and theater that, like Obama’s autobiography, rewrote the romance of America—whether, say, by adding hip-hop accents to the story of the country’s founding (Hamilton), turning a story of interracial romance into a horror tale (Get Out), or creating an Afro-futurist, queer-inflected story of slave revolt (Janelle Monáe’s Metropolis saga). 

Along the way, we’ll consider two of the social movements that coalesced and gathered force during Obama’s presidency: Occupy and Black Lives Matter. We’ll investigate how these movements challenged the limits—political, economic, moral—of the “age of Obama” through art and political action, and looked to create new forms of community while protesting inequality and state violence.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Writing Combat: The Literature of War
description: War, the most destructive of human activities, long predates writing. Wounds still evident in a mesolithic African cemetery tell us that the organized practice of humans killing humans predates the institution of the state itself. Taking part in mass murder appears to be an intractable part of being human. As I write, more than forty-one thousand people have died in Gaza. My father, when he was a young man, fought in a conflict that killed 85 million. Nothing so gives the lie to the notion of human progress than the inexorable fact of war -- and the frank willingness of humans, embodied today in vast nuclear arsenals, to destroy the world itself rather than suffer defeat. As a reporter, I have covered war and political violence in Central America, Haiti, the Balkans, and Iraq. I have seen much death and written about it. But I have not come to understand it. In this course, we will read and discuss some of the most powerful words that have been written about war. Our inquiry will encompass epics, novels, memoirs and reportage and will stretch from the siege of Troy to the invasion of Gaza. Throughout we will focus on great writers' attempt to understand the incomprehensible: our irresistible attraction to mass murder and destruction.

subject: ENGLISH
description:
Homer’s Iliad was composed in the eighth century BCE. Both the story that it narrated (the conflict 
between the Greeks and the Trojans) and the particular form that the story took (the genre of the epic) 
would become foundational building blocks of the Western literary tradition. This course will follow 
these two threads from antiquity to the Renaissance. We will read the story of Troy and the Trojans as it 
was told and retold by the Greeks (Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey), the Romans (Virgil’s Aeneid), in the 
Middle Ages (Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde), and in Elizabethan England (Shakespeare’s Troilus and 
Cressida). At the same time, we will see what happens to the genre of epic over time, as historical 
circumstances change and cultural priorities shift. We will define what we mean by “epic,” as well as 
what Homer, Virgil, Chaucer, and Shakespeare meant when they invoked the genre. Each of these texts 
imagines a world of possibilities and limitations; we will compare those freedoms and unfreedoms, what 
is speakable and unspeakable in Homer’s world versus Virgil’s world versus Chaucer’s world versus 
Shakespeare’s world. We will ask ourselves how the epic as a genre contributes to shaping the 
limitations and possibilities imagined by these texts.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Black theory, Black aesthetics
description:
This course explores aesthetic experiments following on theories of Black life and subjectivity. It is organized around three major topics of theoretical intervention in Black literary and cultural studies: the archive; the sonic; and the human. We will read major works of criticism and theory on these topics and follow these readings with explorations of recent works of art influenced or inflected by them. Students will then have the opportunity to deepen their understanding of the relay between theory and aesthetic practice in Black culture through the development of a rigorous research paper. Final papers will be grounded in one of our required course texts paired with a companion text selected by students from a storehouse of possibilities offered by the instructor.

Readings on the archive will include works by Michel-Rolph Truillot, Saidiya Hartman, Diana Taylor, Dionne Brand, M. NourbeSe Philip, Marisa Fuentes, Jose Munoz, Tavia Nyong’o, and Stephen Best. Readings on the sonic will turn to works by Amiri Baraka, Hazel Carby, Gordon Rohlehr, Shane Vogel, Brent Hayes Edwards, Alexandra Vazquez, Shana Redmond, Tsitsi Ella Jaji, Paul Gilroy, and Daphne Brooks. And for interventions around the idea of the human we will look to Sylvia Wynter, Edouard Glissant, Kamau Brathwaite, Fred Moten, Hortense Spillers, and Zakkiyah Iman Jackson.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Poetics of Non-Place
description: The French anthropologist Marc Augé coined the term non-lieux or “nonplaces” to describe transient and anonymizing sites of supermodernity that negate the relationality and historical resonance that we come to expect from the anthropological space. Augé proposes that in the nonplace no sociality exists and no dwelling occurs. Instead, bodies are surveilled and disciplined while time is hastened. Here, we might here echoes of Foucault’s concept of heterotopia in Augé non-lieux as both are invested in discursive “other spaces” where time is experienced differently. But what happens when the uneven temporality, the injury against relationality, and the denial of recognition that define the nonplace are no longer temporary experiences but an indefinite condition that governs the rhythms of daily life? In this course, we will examine six sites—the border, the refugee camp, the clinic, the prison, the metropole, and the future—that help elucidate the politics and poetics of the non-place. Engaging with literature, film, and other works of art that take up the non-place, we will examine the forms political life, practices of future-making, and modes of insurgencies that have the potential to emerge in these spaces of exception and extremity. Moreover, we will examine how contested desires, illegible bodies, and racialized relations of power mediate our encounters with the nonplace, how they evince and become repositories for the spatiality of power.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Sensation Novel in/and Victorian Britain
description: Sensation novels constitute a vastly popular -- if somewhat controversial -- genre of fiction that made their mark in Victorian Britain.  The serial publication of these novels, which upended bourgeois probities of domesticity enthralled the reading public even as it provoked the ire of literary critics and reviewers. In this course, we will focus on a fairly limited number of sensation novels, but we will study these novels to ask a broad range of questions that will include (among other themes): the relation between literary aesthetics and the “market;” the gendering of authorship; the relation between seriality and novelization; the technomodernity of the sensation novel; the sensorial and cognitive aspects of novel reading; the relation between sensation novels and material culture; and the ideations of race, sexuality, and empire as forged through the genre of sensation.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Thomas Pynchon and the Postmodern
description: Though little discussed now, the postmodernism debate engaged by Fredric Jameson in the early 1980s raises important and unanswered questions about the relationship between literature and capitalism since the 1970s. This course will begin by staging an encounter between Jameson’s ideas about the cultural logic of late capitalism and the novels of Thomas Pynchon, in particular his magnum opus Gravity’s Rainbow. From this encounter, students will conceptualize, research, refine, draft, and revise a 20-page research essay on a topic of their choosing.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Ecopoetics: Tides, Seasons, Clocks
description:
What is the role of literature and, in particular, poetry in the notation of seasonal passage and recurrence? How can practices of patient “close reading” help us negotiate the gap between the slow time of environmental phenomena and the fast time of extraction and consumption?

In this class we will study the line of verse in relation to breath cycles, sleep cycles, clocks, tides, seasons, and other periodic cycles occurring at different scales—moment-to-moment, hourly, daily, monthly, yearly. Taking our cue from the alternation between the higher high and lower low tides of “spring” tides and the less differentiated highs and lows of “neap” tides, we will give particular attention to regular patterns of fluctuating intensity within these cycles. We will explore alternatives to telling the time by the “clock” –the abstract measurement of labor-time under capitalism--and to the logic of ever-presentness and ceaseless, perpetual availability that Jonathan Crary has called “24/7.”  We will read poems and essays addressing seasonal patterns at a moment in planetary history defined by global warming temperatures and seasonal dysregulation. 

Readings will include poetry by Etel Adnan, Matsuo Bashō, Louise Bogan, Lucille Clifton, Emily Dickinson, Camille Dungy, Lorine Niedecker, and non-fiction essays by Rachel Carson, Jonathan Crary, Gunter Klein, Robert Macfarlane, Nathaniel Mackey, E.P. Thompson, among others. 

To borrow from Mike Hoerger, founding director of Louisiana’s HealthPsych PhD program, I would like to make this class a “COVID Sanctuary” and create a compassionate, inclusive, equitable environment that follows evidence-based COVID precautions and respects the needs of the most vulnerable among us. It is my sincere wish and hope that we will agree to wear masks as a class; KN95s will be provided. One aim of the class will be to address the connections between chronic illness, literary study and practices of ecological attention.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Harlem Renaissance
description: The Harlem Renaissance was a cultural movement of Black artists and writers in the 1920s and 1930s. Centered in the Harlem neighborhood in New York City, the movement extended outward through international collaboration. We will be reading together extraordinary works by writers including Claude McKay, Langston Hughes, Alain Locke, Nella Larsen, and Zora Neale Hurston as well as manifestos on the nature and function of black art. Course themes include migration and metropolitan living, primitivism and the avant garde, diaspora and exile, passing and identity, sexuality and secrecy, and the relationship between modern art and vernacular tradition.

subject: ENGLISH
title: LA Stories: LA in Literature, Film and Performance
description:
Los Angeles has been described, variously, as a "circus without a tent" (Carey McWilliams), "seventy-two suburbs in search of a city" (Dorothy Parker), "the capital of the Third World" (David Rieff), and "the city of angels and constant danger" (Tupac Shakur). This class will investigate these and other ways that Los Angeles has been understood over the last century — as a city-in-a-garden, a dream factory, a noirish labyrinth, a homeowner's paradise, a zone of libidinal liberation, and a powder keg of ethnic and racial violence, to name but a few. 

We will trace the history of Los Angeles from its complicated and contested origins to its rise as the sprawling megacity that has often been taken as a prototype of postmodern urban development. And we will do so primarily by looking at the fiction, film, drama, and music that the city has produced in the postwar era. 

This course is also a senior research seminar, so students will be led through the process of generating their own research question, locating sources, developing their analysis, and writing an original essay, of approximately 15-17 pages, that draws on both primary and secondary sources.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Meter
description:
This course offers an introduction to meter from the perspective of theoretical linguistics. Fundamental to this approach is the assumption that any meter is shaped, sometimes consciously and sometimes not, not only by the meter’s own language(s), but also by the human mind’s capacity for language in general, particularly as it pertains to rhythm.
        We will begin with what is probably the most influential and thoroughly studied meter in modern English, the iambic pentameter of Shakespeare’s Sonnets, considering its constraints on syllables, stress, and phrasing, its range of variation, and its aesthetic possibilities. From there, depending on students’ interests, we will turn to some of its predecessors in French, Italian, Old English and Latin, and to some of its companions and successors in modern English.  Finally, if time permits, we will consider some aspects of how meter in poetry is like and unlike rhythmic forms in music.
        Throughout, the focus will be on helping students conceptualize and contextualize meter(s) of poet(s) they themselves are studying. A sequence of practical assignments designed to support that will be the principal requirement of the course, leading to a short final paper.
        No prior training in linguistics or metrics is required.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Moral Philosophy and the Novel
description:
This course will examine key texts from the history of moral philosophy (analytic primarily) and juxtapose them with novels and literary criticism that share overlapping concerns. Questions of discussion will include: why is the novel so identified with moral development? How have different metaethical theories—i.e., Platonism, social contract, sentimentalism, consequentialism, etc.—pressed on the history of the novel? In what ways do these different theories inhabit novelistic form, and vice versa? Are there necessary relations between moral value and aesthetic value and, if so, how does the genre of the novel construe them? 

Novelists will likely include Jane Austen, James Baldwin, J.M. Coetzee, George Eliot, Ford Madox Ford, Graham Greene, Han Kang, Iris Murdoch, Mary Shelley, and Richard Wright. Literary critics and theorists will likely include Ernst Bloch, Jennifer Fleissner, Catherine Gallagher, John Gardner, F.R. Leavis, Georg Lukács, Deidre Lynch, Marina MacKay, Andrew Miller, Ian Watt, Raymond Williams, and others. Philosophical writings will likely include those by G.E.M. Anscombe, Aristotle, Aquinas, Jonathan Dancy, Philippa Foote, Miranda Fricker, Thomas Hobbes, David Hume, John Stuart Mill, Charles Mills, G.E. Moore, Iris Murdoch, Friederich Nietzsche, Martha Nussbaum, Derek Parfit, Plato, John Rawls, Peter Singer, P.F. Strawson, Judith Jarvis Thomson, and Bernard Williams. There will also be discussion of films by Carol Reed and Andrei Tarkovsky.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Victorian Prose Style
description: In this course, we’ll look at the idea of prose style in a few different ways. First, we’ll read some key texts on the theory of style (de Quincey, Goethe, Spencer, Spitzer, Shklovsky, Adorno, Barthes, Pater, Schapiro, Panofsky, etc.) to develop a vocabulary with which to talk about prose style.  What makes a sentence distinctly itself? What makes one writer different from another? What does it mean to see a style as inherently good or bad? Second, we’ll look more particularly at British Victorian conceptions of prose style—in fiction, historical writing, art criticism, autobiography, and elsewhere. What ideas about personal or public style characterize the Victorian period? Is there an especially Victorian politics of style (not to mention a Victorian style of politics)? Is there such a thing as a conservative or a radical style? Should Victorian accounts of intellectual, political, and aesthetic history be understood also as histories of style? Finally, using these different accounts of style, we’ll work closely to analyze examples of Victorian prose at the level of the sentence (in Dickens, Carlyle, the Brontës, Eliot, Arnold, Newman, Carroll, etc.). Put simply, is there such a thing as a Victorian sentence, and, if there is, how does it work?

subject: ENGLISH
description:
For better or worse, most roads in literary history lead either to or from Milton. The goal of this course is to find a way through the massive corpus of Milton's writing, to see how Milton “produces himself” in his work. You should get an adequate knowledge of the major poems, or new angles if you are already familiar with them, but we will also give a central place to hitherto marginal texts: prose, minor poems, manuscript variants, foreign-language writings. Without prescribing a theme, my selections will foreground Milton’s materiality, in several senses: awareness of economic corruption; political activism in the “Puritan Revolution”; educational theory that includes physical exercise and hands-on experiment; the “wanton growth” of the natural environment, the ecosystem of Paradise and the Fall; monist cosmology; visceral fear of gender inversion; conflicted relation to the body, especially digestion and sexuality (and later blindness); music, dance and scenery in the Ludlow Mask (“Comus”); the physical production and correction of Milton’s manuscripts and printed books.

The class meets only once a week, all morning with a short break. However, it is not planned as a specialist research seminar. I welcome students in entirely different periods and language areas, as well as Early Modernists and future Miltonists. Individuals can choose the amount of secondary literature they wish, and may concentrate on close readings. If you are a Modernist, say, a Classicist, a poet, an Italian Renaissance specialist, a political historian, a theologian or an Anglo-Saxonist you can craft essays that bring your own expertise to bear. His dark materials continue to generate new expressions.

The secondary literature on Milton is overwhelmingly vast, and I am concerned that attention to ‘the literature’ will crowd out the literature. I have curated an idiosyncratic selection of articles and passages from books, which will be optional rather than required; you will get full credit for papers that focus entirely on keen-eyed readings in Milton’s own oeuvre. To provide a ‘locovore’ tasting menu most of these anthologized texts will be by current or former members of the Berkeley faculty or PhD students who developed papers generated for this very course, English 218. (For the specialist I provide much fuller bibliographical listings, customized to the individual project.) I will also suggest a few instances of creative, as well as scholarly, responses to Milton’s work, dark with excessive bright.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Once and Future Mind: The University in the Age of AI
description: Generative AI, as we use it today, is something new. The university—the idea of a university—is very old. We’re hearing a lot of discussion about this tension, some of it abstract, or angry, or unrelentingly optimistic, and you’ll hear it (and feel it) as students. This course makes that conversation practical. We’re inviting you to have the discussion with us. We will think together about what it means to be college students in the age of AI: should you use it? Should we? When and how; why or why not? What does “AI literacy” mean, who should be teaching it, and how do you know when you have it? Co-taught by professors from English, Linguistics, and Computer Science, and with guest appearances by other faculty experts at Berkeley, this course will help you navigate the wide range of policies on campus, the different expectations in different disciplines, the whispers you’re hearing about “job preparation” and “professionalization.” We’ll consider how we might think about writing, speaking, reading, research, class discussion, grading and test taking in the age of AI. And we’ll end by talking in broader terms about the idea of a university, the ethics of AI, and what we all hope for when we think about learning and thinking and curiosity in the future. More than anything, we’re designing this course so that you are part of the discussion and so that you—the learners, the once and future minds—can be heard.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Romanticism: History, ideology, form
description: "Romanticism" presents us with the strange case of an aesthetic ideology posing as a historical period. While the condition has distorted study of the field in powerful and lasting ways, it has also contributed to its continuing vibrancy, through ongoing debates over politics and canonicity. We will focus on two works, each critically acclaimed as revolutionary for its respective genre (lyric poetry; the novel): Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lyrical Ballads (1798/ 1800) and Scott’s Waverley (1814).  We’ll consider claims made for the works’ innovative impact through attention to their literary-historical contexts (the ballad revival, minstrelsy and “popular poetry”; the “greater Romantic lyric” and Romantic ode; national tales and historical novels), reception history, and the theories of lyric poetry, the novel, Romanticism and realism built upon them, including still dominant critical approaches.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The New Border
description: Gloria Anzaldúa’s description of the US-Mexico border as “una herida abierta [an open wound] where the Third World grates against the first and bleeds” stands as both the most influential contemporary theorization of the border and an object of critique on multiple axes. Perhaps the most salient aspect of Anzaldúa’s landmark book Borderlands / La Frontera, however, is that its 1987 publication predates sea changes in legal, economic, and social arrangements at the border, including increasingly militarized enforcement; the paradoxes of “free trade” under NAFTA; and the flows of Central American, Caribbean, and other migrants to the border in the twenty-first century. This course seeks to explore literature and theory that helps us understand the border after Anzaldúa. How have changed migratory patterns transformed border zones in both the United States and Mexico? How have writers imagined the border landscape in the face of climate change and increased infrastructure, including walls and fences? What resources do theorists such as Thomas Nail, Melissa W. Wright, Claire Fox, Jason De León, and Roberto Hernández offer for reimagining the border as a contact zone in the age of globalization?

subject: ENGLISH
description:
What is the English literary tradition? Where did it come from? What are its distinctive 
habits, questions, styles, obsessions? This course will answer these and other questions by 
focusing on five key writers from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance: the 
anonymous Beowulf poet; Geoffrey Chaucer; Christopher Marlowe; John Donne; and John 
Milton. We will start with the idea that the English literary tradition is a set of interrelated 
texts and problems that recur over the course of several centuries. Some of these 
relationships are formal; we will pay special attention to the genres, techniques, and styles 
that poets use to create their works. Some of these relationships are linguistic; students 
will learn to read Middle English (out loud, too!) and explore the significance of linguistic 
change as the Middle Ages becomes the Renaissance. Other relationships are historical; we 
will explore not only the pressure of contemporary events on literature, but also literature's 
role in creating both historical continuity and change over time. And some of these 
relationships are cultural, as poets reflect upon, seek to change, furiously criticize, or 
happily embrace a variety of human behaviors, from religious practices to love relationships 
to debates about gender to death and dying.

subject: ENGLISH
description: Historical survey of literature in English: The late-17th through the mid-19th century. This course is a survey of British and American literature from the late-seventeenth through the mid-nineteenth century.  We will look at how literary genres evolve alongside new forms of knowledge, understanding, and experience, with particular attention to the changing place of literature in the social lives of its readers.  We especially will consider literary responses to an “age of revolution” on both sides of the Atlantic.  Authors include Defoe, Pope, Franklin, Equiano, Jefferson, Austen, M. Shelley, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Melville, and Whitman.

subject: ENGLISH
description: This course examines a range of British and American texts from the period with an emphasis on literary history and its social and political contexts. We will focus on the emergence, development, and legacy of modernism as a set of formal innovations that help us see how literature operates as a means of cultural response in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. We will also consider modernism alongside other literary modes and styles that pursue different strategies for representing our experience of the world—and for finding a place for literature within it. Particular attention will be paid to close reading and questions of literary form even as we think about such larger issues as the relationship between reading and entertainment, the changing status of art in respect to new technologies of information and representation, and the challenges to traditional conceptions of the self that are posed by new languages of psychological, national, and racial identity.

course.description: Historical survey of literature in English: the mid-19th through the mid-20th century.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Coming of Age on the Margins
description:
This course will explore one of the central genres of the Western novel: the bildungsroman, or, the novel of formation. Traditionally, this genre follow a protagonist as they grow up, undergo an education, pass from innocence to experience, and reconcile their individual desires with their place in society. In the United States, the experience of coming of age is often accompanied by developing awareness of one’s racial or ethnic identity, including what that means to others. In this class we will read a selection of 20th and 21st century novels of formation, focusing on how ethnic writers writing from the margins of dominant culture negotiate, deploy, and remake the genre of the bildungsroman, whose traditional ending features the successful integration of the individual into their society. Our concerns in the class will include: subject formation, the relationship of the individual to both their own ethnic community and to dominant society, immigration, diaspora and assimilation, citizenship and belonging.

Possible texts include: James Weldon Johnson, Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man; Jessie Fauset, Plum Bun; D’arcy McNickle, The Surrounded; Ania Yezierska, Bread Givers; Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God; N. Scott Momaday, House Made of Dawn; Toni Morrison, The Bluest Eye; Maxine Hong Kingston, The Woman Warrior; Sandra Cisneros, The House on Mango Street; Junot Diaz, The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao; Faye Myenne Ng, Bone.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Narrative Time
description:
How does fiction represent time? How does a narrative move between past and present, memory and event, reflection and experience? And how do the formal choices a writer makes – about structure, perspective, pacing, and sequence – shape the meanings readers draw from a text?

This course introduces students to the practices of literary study through a sustained engagement with short stories and novels that approach time in strikingly different ways. Over the semester, we will read a small group of twentieth- and twenty-first-century works of fiction that experiment with narrative time: some unfold through retrospective narration, others through fragmented chronology or the shifting rhythms of interior consciousness.

Our central activity will be careful, attentive reading. In class discussions and written work, students will learn how to notice and analyze the details of language, structure, and perspective that shape a literary work’s effects. Assignments will guide students in developing interpretive claims, supporting them with precise engagement with the text, and refining those ideas through revision.

By the end of the semester, students will have practiced a range of approaches to reading fiction closely and thoughtfully. The course aims to build confidence in working with complex literary texts, developing arguments about how they operate, and articulating those ideas clearly in writing.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Of Nature
description: We might say that the essay, the literary and philosophical form of nonfiction writing characterized by playfulness and curiosity, wonder and digression, criticality and irony, and the *nature* essay have always been one and the same. The “relationship of nature and culture is [the essay’s] true theme,” writes a foremost theorist of the form, Theodor W. Adorno. Some of the earliest modern essayists were natural philosophers; some of our contemporary critics have suggested that the genre best suited for representing climate change and environmental devastation is the essay. This class will ask why. What is the relationship between nature and the essay? How does the essay encourage us, or allow us, to notice the planet? How does the essay track and shape our attention to the overlooked, the taken-for-granted, the world of microbes and bugs and porcupines and sea cucumbers? If nature writing falls into cliché, what does it risk obscuring? Henry David Thoreau saw the nature essay as a way to register what we stand to lose; Camille T. Dungy sees it as a way to enshrine what we value; the film essayists Chris Marker and John Akomfrah turn to the nature essay as a means to interrogate the complex and fraught connections between us. We will explore the global history of the nature essay, from classical Greece to 10th-century Japan, from 16th-century Tenochtitlan to 20th-century France, and from the 21st-century US to the outer rim of the solar system to form our own theories about how the nature essay works and what modes of attention, care, and action it might encourage. You will also practice writing nature essays in this seminar; you’ll cultivate the mode of attention the form demands, the sustained questioning it rewards.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Extending the Document: Asian American Lives
description: When the archive is fragmented, families are silent, and histories are withheld, how can a story be told? This seminar explores how Asian American writers confront erasure, displacement, and the instability of memory across genres including memoir, poetry, and fiction. Reading across literature, history, and theory, we will examine how narrative and lyric forms can challenge, reconstruct, and reimagine what has been lost or excluded from personal and institutional memory. Authors may include Maxine Hong Kingston, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Bhanu Kapil, and Viet Thanh Nguyen. The course combines critical inquiry with creative practice: students will write analytical essays alongside a creative personal  essay and respond to in-class writing prompts related to the readings.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Theology and the Sentimental Novel
description: Although often left unsaid, religion and theology pervaded England in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and directly influenced its literary production. This class will take the sentimental novel as a case study of one such site of influence, close reading texts of sympathy such as Clarissa and Pamela, as well as Tristram Shandy and works of Gothic horror. We will also find that the theological meaning behind sentimentality may persist into more recent novels--as such, one or two novels by Philip K. Dick will be selected as an accompaniment, where sympathy with God becomes a cosmological concern. Theological and Biblical texts will also be assigned in excerpts as needed.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Historical Fiction: The Many Lives of Ivanhoe
description: What is “historical fiction”? Why do we write and read it? What are its pleasures? What are the political and cultural functions of such fiction? Georg Lukács argued that the true historical novel emerged with Walter Scott’s work. We will use Scott’s fiction to explore these questions and others. Ivanhoe, published in 1819, was one of Scott’s most influential and widely read novels. Set in 12th-century England, the novel brought together the now familiar medieval tropes of Normans versus Saxons, Robin Hood and his outlaws, the longed-for return of Richard the Lionheart from Palestine, discrimination against Jews, tournaments, secretive Knights Templar, and a witch trial. Ivanhoe sparked an interest in the Middle Ages as a literary territory not only in Britain, but across Europe and beyond, inspiring works in different languages and countries that adapted aspects of the original story to their own local contexts. In fact, Ivanhoe has remained popular to this day—as proven by its many incarnations in film, TV, and opera—and the various elements of Scott’s imagined medieval England have become part of popular culture and real landscapes. There is an “Ivanhoe Road” in Oakland. In addition to the books below, we will also look at medievalist tropes in film.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Asian American Short Stories
description:
The short story form has been foundational to the historical development of Asian American literature. After the invention of "Asian American" as a category for political coalition in the late 1960s, editors, literary scholars, and publishers have retrospectively claimed a large archive of pre-1960s stories as key elements of the textual coalition now known as "Asian American literature."

The twenty-first century has also seen an explosion of authorial practice and readerly interest in the short story as a contemporary literary form. This course will focus on close readings of, and frequent writing about, selections from this vast archive.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Science Fiction of Ted Chiang
description:
Aliens and sentient robots, time loops and parallel universes—Ted Chiang’s fiction has all the out-of-this-world trappings of traditional science fiction. At the same time, each of his 18 short stories—a notably slim output for a writer who has been publishing for more than 34 years—is meticulously crafted, polished to the exquisite sheen of a well-wrought urn. His fiction elegantly combines the “hard science” of STEM fields with the social analysis and emotional impact of the “softer” sciences and humanities. It reveals the entanglement of such seemingly contradictory perspectives as physics and philosophy, free will and determinism, memory and speculation, and cognition and feeling. 

In this seminar, we will explore Chiang’s oeuvre—most of his stories, along with some of his essays and interviews—while practicing the art and craft of literary analysis. We will experiment with various modes of textual interpretation while developing our skills as readers of literature and writers of critical argument.
