subject: ENGLISH
title: Reading Dramatic Literature, or, Queer Method Acting
description:
Method acting conjures visions of actors whose embodied commitment to preparing for a role involves dissolving the boundary between art and life in their rigorous refusal to break out of character offstage. Taking up the conceit of “method acting” to stress the connection between interpretive labor and embodied practice, this introductory course will serve as a rehearsal to prepare prospective majors for advanced coursework in the English department by trying out various foundational methods of literary analysis (e.g. close listening, queer reading) and genres of creative-critical expression (e.g. class discussion, (auto)ethnographic reflection in response to live theatre) alongside honing skills of academic writing through revision and peer review. Students will exercise their critical intuitions by making connections and distinctions across a multi-genre archive spanning poetry, (short) novels, plays, films, sit-coms, and popular culture alongside excerpts of scholarly writing on the primary texts studied. 



Along the way, we will consider the questions posed by the “queer” spin placed on scenes of queer method acting (e.g. Thai BL actors’ performances of homoerotic intimacy onscreen and homosocial friendship offscreen for their female fans) and reading methods we will encounter and practice. If “queer” is irreducible to a stable concept of identity, what does it mean for an actor to inhabit a queer role or for a scholar to undertake a queer reading without necessarily identifying as queer in their lived identities? How do we think critically about the desire (whether perceived to be justified or uncritical) as expressed by fans for an actor’s professed sexual identity to be aligned with the role they play, and the desires that animate our own interpretive practices when engaging with texts that seem to correspond (or not) to our sense of self and the roles we play in everyday life? How does “queer” translate when we consider texts that do not explicitly identify as such or that critique its limitations when applied to non-Western contexts, and how might we recalibrate our interpretive lens in response?

subject: ENGLISH
description:
This course is an application based course - students who are interested in doing the Senior Honors Thesis for English must apply. For more information about the honors program - please visit our website: https://english.berkeley.edu/undergraduate/department-honors

H195 is a two-semester course that provides the groundwork for and guides you through the completion of a 40–60-page Honors thesis. This course offers you the opportunity to immerse yourself in a research topic over the course of an academic year. The course also provides an important opportunity for more meta-critical reflection about what it means to do humanistic research in a university setting. Beyond the important individual questions of "should I, or should I not, pursue an honors research thesis," lie more difficult, historical-structural questions: why (and when) did public universities begin to offer selective "honors"? What are the historical (colonial/imperial) legacies of such programs? What possible futures might such research programs have in a world in polycrisis, when universities and other educational-cultural institutions may soon look nothing like what they do now?

In the fall semester, to establish a common, if provisional, frame of reference across multiple periods and genres of research interest, we will read two shared primary texts drawn from the genres of dark academic and post-apocalyptic fantasy: R. F Kuang's _Babel_ and N. K. Jemisin's _The Broken Earth_. These texts will anchor our exploration of critical and theoretical approaches to literary study. We will also discuss research methods and the various stages involved in undertaking a thesis project. In keeping with timelines established in past honors seminars,* our fall semester discussions will help you choose a topic, formulate a thesis, use library resources, and structure a multi-part essay to sustain your argument. A research proposal and annotated bibliography are due at the end of the fall semester. During the spring semester, students will primarily meet with the instructor in individual conferences and also share preliminary drafts in working groups. Portions of the thesis will be submitted for feedback at regular intervals. A draft of the entire thesis will be due by spring break; the final version will be due in early May. No written work other than the Honors thesis is due in the spring.

Please contact the instructor at andrewleong@berkeley.edu if you have any questions. 

*I thank Profs. Eric Falci and Sukanya Banerjee for providing their course descriptions from the 2025-2026 academic year.

description: This course is the first of a two-semester sequence for English majors writing who are writing an honors thesis. We will read and discuss a range of texts that will provide grounding in contemporary critical methodologies, as well as various genres of literary and cultural analysis that inform the style(s) of academic prose in the humanities. subject: ENGLISH
title: Introduction to Shakespeare
description:
English R17 offers an introduction to the study of Shakespeare.  The premise of our class is that Shakespeare's texts are remarkably good to think with—remarkably pleasurable, remarkably productive. The class will give sustained attention to half a dozen major plays, using them to develop a rich set of themes and ideas as the semester unfolds: ideas about beauty and cruelty, performance and nature, citizenship and individuality, companionship and solitude, future and past.  WE will also think with Shakespeare about the nature of writing, reading, and performance.

English R17 is also an R1B Reading and Composition course. In addition to lecture meetings, you will meet for two hours per week in section. There are two main components to the sections and to your interactions with your section leader. First, sections are a forum for discussion of themes raised in lectures and for further exploration of the assigned readings. Participation in discussion is an essential aspect of the course; you’ll consider the relationship between reading and analysis, discussion and argument, research and writing. Your section leader will help you think about how to turn the insights that emerge in class discussion into sustained writing projects.  Second, sections serve as writing intensive classes and writing workshops. Students will receive intensive weekly instruction in research, development, writing, and revision. You’ll work in the classroom and in your assignments on everything from how to do research, and especially literary research, generate questions, form and sustain arguments, use literature as evidence, and refine your own writing style. The portion of the class will also consider how writing about literature is also training for writing in other disciplines and in your professional lives.

subject: ENGLISH
title: True Love
description:
Perhaps nothing is more human, more desired, and more poorly understood than love. What does it look like? What makes it "true"? How can we trust it? What are its boundaries or lack thereof? Who decides? Shakespeare tells it one way, Thích Nhất Hạnh another. Marvin Gaye and Lauryn Hill and all those pop stars spin more versions still. Any path you take will lead to poets and prophets, heartbreak and healing, justice and struggle, but each path starts and ends with you and what kind of love you have for yourself. For in the end, the fate of personal, public, and planetary health all rest upon a fundamental commitment to compassion as an energy of transformation.

Together in this course, we’ll think love, read love, write love, and unlearn love. We'll work through its expansive manifestations across poems, novels, parables, letters, songs, films, and spiritual guidance all over time and space. Moreover, as a writing-intensive course and Cal requirement, we’ll hone the analytical skills needed for critical thinking, patient attention, and nuanced, persuasive argumentation. Expect to read something new every day, and prepare to be consistently engaged with drafting, journaling, reflection, and revision. With consistent dedication, you’ll be stunned to see not only growth in clarity and confidence in style but lasting self-discovery.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Satires and Shandyisms
description:
Few literary modes make as many formal demands upon their crafters as satire; formal satires, of course, must be satiric, but they also must preserve enough of the mechanics of what they satirize lest their chosen object be lost entire. As such, successful formal satires are fundamentally critical, not (just) in tone, but also in their capacity to represent (generally) truthfully if also comically that which make their chosen objects tick. In this course, we’ll consider English satires and mock-forms, both on their own terms, but also as tools to discover how some of the played with-forms: essays, novels and epics, mechanically work themselves.
For the first of the course’s two major movements, we’ll concentrate on the era of English literature wherein satire perhaps was at its most flourishing; namely the Augustan era (~1700-1744), and we’ll orient ourselves largely around the mock-epics and treatises of Alexander Pope. Nevertheless, Jonathan Swift’s mock-essays and Henry Fielding’s parodic novellas will also make their appearances then. For the second portion of the course, however, we’ll push forward a few decades as we consider Laurence Sterne’s The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman (1759-1767), a work so idiosyncratic in form and technique that it’s oft called the first postmodernist novel. But in both portions of the course, we’ll focus on reading our mock-works primarily as tools to teach us, through and in their exaggerations, the compositional and formal requirements and yet most extreme possibilities of the forms with which they play.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Documentary Poetry from the Margins: From Evidentiary to Experiential
description:
In this course, we’ll dive into a current of contemporary poetry called “documentary poetry,” also known as docupoetry or docupoetics. To document is to gather the evidence and information to prove something happened—to furnish an awareness or understanding of a moment in time. Across the 20th and 21st centuries, minority poets writing in the margins of the Global North have created poetry collections that stage this work of documentation for their readers. These poets use historical records, found texts, and archival materials within their poetry to counter official histories, generate marginalized histories, and alter cultural memory. 

This is a class that works with poets and poetry. We’ll read poetry collections from Mai Der Vang, for example, who writes on the use of chemicals in Laos during the Cold War; Diana Khoi Nguyen, who works with family archives to reflect on the loss of her brother; Bhanu Kapil, who documents the diasporic experience of Indian women; Layli Long Soldier, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, M. NourbeSe Philip, Solmaz Sharif, Bhanu Kapil, and Vanessa Angélica Villarreal, among others. You can expect engage with various critical texts written by poets such as Muriel Rukeyser, Audre Lorde, Susan Briante, Mark Novak, and Carolyn Forché. You’ll produce documentations of your knowledge that you’ll develop with me and your classmates throughout the semester. There will be opportunities to write creatively if you choose.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Bartleby and His Others
description:
What kind of action, if any, is inaction? What kind of feeling, if any, is unfeeling? Is it possible for these negative states to be politically efficacious? How does inaction undermine imperatives of productivity? How does a person relate to their labor? This class takes Herman Melville’s short story “Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall Street” (1853) as the starting point for addressing such questions. Bartleby, a copyist who stops work, is perhaps best remembered for the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement’s adoption of his famous refrain: “I would prefer not to.” At stake in Melville’s political allegory is Bartleby’s refusal of his boss’s demand not only for speedy work but for sympathy (“fellow feeling”); therefore, the story serves as a rich heuristic through which to explore overlapping discourses of affect, labor, sexuality, and biopolitics in a range of other literary texts. We will read across nineteenth- and twentieth-century U.S. authors, situating them within the historical development of the “totally administered society.” In so doing, we will consider the Bartlebyan affects, aesthetics, and ideologies that institutions—eg. the family, the corporation, the state—produce and manage for subjects of power. Possible additional literary readings includes Melville’s “The Paradise of Bachelors and the Tartarus of Maids” (1855), Henry James's In the Cage (1898), selections from Charles Chestnutt’s The Conjure Woman (1899), Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s “The Yellow Wallpaper” (1899), Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Patricia Highsmith’s The Talented Mr. Ripley (1955), Billy Wilder’s film The Apartment (1960), and Helen DeWitt’s The Last Samurai (2000). Possible excerpted scholarship includes Sianne Ngai, Lauren Berlant, Herbert Marcuse, Michel Foucault, and Georg Lukács. 

The course’s themes will help us ask, what kind of work is the writing that we do as readers and critics, and why is it important? Students will sharpen their critical thinking skills in reading both primary work and secondary criticism, class discussion, and writing. This R1A focuses on revision, with an aim to help students become more precise and confident writers.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Of Foxes & Fables
description: From Reynard the Fox to Fantastic Mr. Fox, the animal kingdom has long inspired the imaginations of poets, fabulists, artists, composers, philosophers, filmmakers, and naturalists. This course asks what stories about animals have to say about human life: how animals, real and imagined, have been used to teach morals, delight readers, advise rulers, satirize current events, and inspire scientific study and wonder. With a special focus on medieval British writing, we will examine fables, epics, and story-cycles about talking animals across cultural contexts, literary genres, and media to think about what it means for human readers to identify (or fail to identify) with the varieties of animal life. In addition to reading fables from Ancient Greek, Latin, Sanskrit, Arabic, Middle English, and Middle Scots, we will also think about animals in music, film, animation, manuscript illumination, architecture, and tapestry. Modern English translations will be available for all texts.

title: Periodizing the 90s
description:
The first Gulf War, chat rooms, the “End of History.” What were the 1990s? What is the influence of this decade on geopolitics, culture, and literature today? Following Fredric Jameson’s injunction to re-examine the 1960s and its legacy in his 1984 essay “Periodizing the 60s,” this R1A will periodize, interrogate, and trace the final decade of the twentieth century: a span of years during which we must contend with the development of the internet, U.S. empire and imperialism preceding the “War on Terror,” and an increasingly globalized economy. Our study will also necessarily consider the status of infrastructure at the end of the twentieth century: from the space of the shopping mall or grocery store, to transformations in national security and surveillance, to the American highway and its metaphoric rejoinder in the form of the “information superhighway.” 

In this R1A, you will be tasked to examine problems of historical method, articulations of the relationship between the political and the aesthetic, and what we mean by formal experimentation—both in the works we study and within our own practices. This writing-centered course will provide regular, collaborative, and generative occasions for writing in and outside class. The course’s structure prioritizes opportunities for revision and how it is made available through media technologies developed at the end of the twentieth century. Our effort to periodize the 90s, in other words, will also require us to periodize our own writing and research practices.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Shock of the Old
description: In this course, we will practice our reading, writing, and thinking skills through a series of encounters with the past. These encounters will take many forms: from poetry to prose, visual artworks, material and cultural artifacts, contemporary criticism, even a few films. Our focus throughout will be the medieval period—though, as we shall see, the matter of historical periodization is rarely as straightforward as it seems. Our guiding question, one that we’ll return to again and again over the semester, is a deceptively simple one: what is the point of engaging with the past? Why should we care what people five hundred or a thousand years ago did, wrote, thought, knew, or believed? Significantly, the answer to this question isn’t set in stone. Rather, we choose how to react to the past, what it may or may not mean to us today, how to feel and what to think about it. The medieval world is an ideal laboratory for our experiment in historical meaning-making: it is extraordinarily capacious (lasting almost a thousand years and covering anywhere from a small portion of Western Europe to the entire globe, depending on the definition), separated by great temporal distance from our own society, and—perhaps most importantly—both weirder and more surprising than we tend to give it credit for.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The English Sonnet Tradition
description:
This course will familiarize students with the craft of critical, reflective, and persuasive writing by introducing students to the English sonnet tradition. In this R1A we will consider the use of the sonnet form to express impassioned feeling, and will learn about the tropes of Petrarchan verse in order to assess some of their implications. But we will also consider the ways in which the sonnet consistently opens up to other discourses—commercial and economic, political and imperial, theological, metaphysical, and devotional, theatrical, seasonal and ecological, agrarian and animal, scientific, medical, and astronomical etc. We will consider the sonnet as an introspective medium as well as a relational and social one.

This course will provide students with an opportunity to practice close reading in a compact form. We will move roughly chronologically from the origins of the sonnet form in England through the contemporary sonnet sequence. We will practice critical and creative response writing, aiming to develop as rigorous readers, thoughtful interpreters, and clear writers, and we will also exercise the note-taking practice of keeping a commonplace book. 

Many of the sonnets that we will encounter in this course self-consciously reflect on writing as a process or activity, and as a technology for introspection, self-preservation, or reproduction. We will attend to these provocations both by reflecting on the qualities of language and formal tensions produced in works which seek to be rhetorically efficacious while simultaneously understanding themselves to be unable to engender their intended effect, and by thinking together and with our sonneteers about what makes writing painful, and what makes it pleasurable.

subject: ENGLISH
title: How to Read
description:
What does it mean to say that one has read something? Is it possible to say that one has read a word or sentence without knowing how it sounds or understanding what it means? Answering these questions requires some sense of what the process of reading actually involves. In that sense, they can be answered only once we have learned how to read.

 

In this course, we will learn how to read. We will devote much of our time together to the careful study of a small set of poems, working to develop increasingly competent accounts of what we find there and how we came to find it. Our aim will not be to extract a summary or decode the “meaning” of a text, but to attend to the limits of such reductive approaches, reframing the practice of reading as itself a form of play. We will also engage selectively with a tradition of thought that explores the boundaries between “reading” and “interpretation,” reading accounts of reading both ancient (Aristotle, Origen) and modern (Spinoza, Freud, Wittgenstein, Richards) in order to test their methods and evaluate the results for ourselves.

 

Students will complete a sequence of scaffolded assignments that progresses from descriptive and expository prose to more sustained essayistic treatments of independently chosen objects, before culminating in an oral examination focused on articulating and defending interpretations in conversation, the revision of a previously submitted paper, and a narrative self-assessment of their own learning.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Thinking Everyday Poetics
description:
This course will survey various tendencies of modern and contemporary poetry, including poetic practices stemming from ideas of “experiment” as well as practices that assume more “expressive” poetic orientations such as those illuminated by theories of the lyric. As this course considers how these tendencies have been distinguished and entangled, you will be introduced to recent critical perspectives in black studies and feminist theory. We will balance readings of whole poetry collections with suites of individual poems as well as short critical writings regarding poetics. 

As we study (mostly chronologically through the twentieth and twenty-first centuries), this course will dramatize the significance of the everyday and investigate the political and aesthetic dimensions that permeate day to day scales of change. Ever focused on form, this course will study with and through poems, meaning that we will take seriously small but demanding ideas as we learn to appreciate how poems devise unique ways of paying attention, especially unruly approaches to questions of being—what is everyday being? and how to be?—both of which are philosophical questions. By practicing how to shape and revise questions with poetry, both at the level of the sentence and through the arc of an essay, you will refine your daily habits of critical inquiry and writing.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Death and Dying
description:
A body on the dining room floor supplies the catalyst for our most entertaining mysteries. Murderous outlaws fascinate, become legends or even celebrities. In so many texts, who lives and who dies, who succumbs and who rises from an illness, define and show us if the world is just or cruel. In this class, we will consider how artistic perspectives on death and dying have evolved across time and how these evolutions might reveal,  or shape, our own feelings and beliefs about war, sickness, environmental catastrophes, pandemics, violence, burial, and grief. Rather than treat these “harsh truths of life” as morbid, this class will focus on how we can speak and write meaningfully about how we view, and what we value in, our lives as well as the lives (and afterlives) of others. 

Students will hone their close reading and analytical writing skills by reflecting on the various forms of rhetoric and style involved in representations of death. With each theme, students will practice writing with intent. This process will focus on developing more explicit and detailed arguments through the process of consistent revision. Couse assignments will include short writing reflections, analytical essays, and a creative project. Our texts will most likely include fiction (by Edgar Allan Poe, Arthur Conan Doyle, N. Scott Momaday, and Shirley Jackson), poetry (by Emily Dickinson, WWI soldiers, and Thomas Hardy), film (Hayao Miyazaki, Terence Malick, and zombie cinema), as well as some philosophy, news articles, painting, and photography.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Gothic
description:
This R1A course will explore the emergence and evolution of the aesthetic of the gothic from the late eighteenth to the nineteenth century. We will ask what the “gothic” might mean in relation to anxieties surrounding race and gender, expanding empire and colonial contact, the Enlightenment, and political revolution. Throughout the course, we will engage both literary and theoretical texts in order to understand the gothic as a cultural mode that reflects broader historical tensions of the Romantic and post-Enlightenment periods. The gothic is one response to a rapidly changing world system, that tries to make sense of the persistence of the past and pre-enlightenment systems of knowledge into modernity. Topics will include the aesthetics of the sublime and terror, the legacies of colonialism and enslavement, the role of decaying aristocratic worlds, and the persistence of repressed desire, forbidden knowledge, and patriarchal violence.

Our course readings will range across geographical space and genre. We will read excerpts from Edmund Burke’s Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful and Sigmund Freud's The Uncanny. We will read the first gothic novel, The Castle of Otranto by Horace Walpole and the 1798 American gothic novel Weiland by Charles Brockden Brown. We will consider these texts in relation to how Olaudah Equiano takes up terror and sublimity in his slave autobiography, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano or Gustavo's Vassa, the African, Written by Himself. We will also dip into Romantic poetry by Percy Bysshe Shelley, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and John Keats, to consider how the gothic is taken up by Romanticism, and we will conclude with a screening of Rebecca (1940) to consider the 20th century legacies of the gothic. Through close reading, analytical writing, and sustained discussion, students will develop critical approaches to literary interpretation while refining the argumentative and compositional skills central to college-level reading and writing.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Encountering and Describing the Archive
description:
In 2001, philosophy and comparative literature scholar Rebecca Comay asked: “What isn’t an archive these days?” A quarter of a century later her exasperated yet crucial inquiry continues to be relevant when considering that our understanding of “the archive” as a concept has proliferated in meaning due to multidisciplinary criticism and engagement from scholars, activists, writers, and artists alike. In this course, we will engage with this “crisis” in/of archives by exploring: What exactly is an archive? The building itself? A counter-institutional space? A collection of documents? A discipline/profession? A form of scholarly research? A historiographic method? A direct encounter with the past? A bundle of occlusions and omissions? A metaphor or metonymy for memory/power/history/knowledge?

Throughout the semester, we will be reading provocative scholarship (such as Foucault, Derrida, and Benjamin, among others), non-academic writing, and creative texts that will acquaint us with (both directly and indirectly) the discourse surrounding the idea of archive(s). Some driving inquiries that we will consider include: Why are archives, and the process of archivization, important to society? How are they critical, creative, or problematic forms of expression and of knowing? What are the ethical considerations of archival praxes? What is their use in determining the past and present? Additionally, we will actually visit various archival spaces such as the special collections at the Bancroft Library and Ethnic Studies Library here at UC Berkeley as well as local and born-digital community archives in California and beyond. We will encounter and adopt sundry archival documents and artifacts that invite our sustained attention over the course of the semester. What will you choose (or better yet: what will choose you)? A Black Panther Party documentary in Oakland? A series of historical maps of SF before the 1906 Earthquake? BART construction proposals and blueprints? Internment camp photo albums of Japanese American families from the Bay Area? Textual ephemera from the Chicano Movement? A basket from the Pomo tribe of Northern California? These archival encounters will motivate the assignments for our course, and they will provide the opportunity to cultivate, discuss, and challenge college-level writing modes and skills. Furthermore, this course will introduce you to research spaces and resources here at Berkeley that will be helpful throughout your college career. Through it all, we will discuss the significance of writing in/through/between/against archives as a creative and critical form of engagement.

Again: What is an archive? Perhaps the words of the character Chazz Michael Michaels from the film Blades of Glory (2007) are most apt: “No one knows what it means, but it's provocative! . . . it gets the people going!”

subject: ENGLISH
title: The New Sincerity
description:
Ours is an era that values, perhaps above all, genuineness and authenticity. The premise of this course is that the construction of this ideal in American culture has a literary history, most notably in the late-twentieth and early-twenty-first century movement now known as the New Sincerity. One prominent theorist has called sincerity “a congruence between avowal and actual feeling”—or, in other words, a commitment to meaning what you say and saying what you mean. Sincerity can thus be contrasted with irony, the quality of saying things that one does not actually mean, and which, according to New Sincerity authors, was the most prominent trope of the postmodern current in literature against which they reacted.

 

 In this course, we’ll read a range of stories short and long by Donald Barthelme, Grace Paley, David Foster Wallace, Donald Antrim, Zadie Smith, and Susan Choi as we consider what fiction should be and do in an age when the “human” is increasingly under duress from social and ecological catastrophe on the one hand and the dullness of late-capitalist labor routines on the other. What aesthetic emerges from pursuing humanity in an inhuman world? Does the New Sincerity, by emphasizing human subjectivity, resist neoliberalism, or, by prioritizing individual choice and personal responsibility, reinforce it?

 


Beginning with these questions and others, students will subsequently learn how to develop and explore their own through writing. What knowledge about the world can be gleaned from fiction? What are you seeing in these stories that others perhaps aren’t? You will, in addition, be invited to consider how your own academic interests may intersect with course material. Assignments will consist of brief reading responses, two medium-length papers, and a longer final paper.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Detective Novels of Chester Himes
description: “It is not a very fragrant world, but it is the world you live in. . . .” So Raymond Chandler characterizes the world out of joint painted by “the realist in murder.” The tradition of hard-boiled detective fiction offers (arguably) some of the most significant attempts to grapple with the nature of violence (criminal, institutional, and everything in between) in American society, whether we agree with it or not. In this course we will read as much as we can of Chester Himes’s series of novels—compelling, sometimes hilarious, frequently disturbing—featuring detectives Grave Digger Jones and Coffin Ed Johnson. These are novels to enjoy; but we will also use this “lowbrow” genre to ask questions about the “literary”: What is the relationship between literary style and popular language? What do we do when we read for the plot; and what are the values and dangers of this kind of reading? How do specific forms of narrative (like the mystery novel) model social structures? There will be regular short writing assignments. The assigned reading will include the four novels collected in Chester Himes, The Essential Harlem Detectives (Everyman’s Library, 2024) as well more to be decided.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Queer Horror
description:
The formula of the slasher movie is a staple of modern horror: its (often virginal) “final girl” acts as heroine, sometimes a passive one, who watches her friends fall off one by one. Typically, death results as a punishment for acting on sexual desires or deviating from social norms. But questions of gender, sexuality, and taboo begin much earlier than than the slasher. Full of uncanny monsters, vampiric seductions, and hidden secret transgressions of social norms, the horror genre itself has been a place for authors to explore queer themes and characters from its outset.

Viewing and analyzing the horror genre through a lens of queer theory will aid us in accomplishing the main goal of this course: to develop stronger reading, writing, and research skills. Our assigned “texts” range from early medieval bestiaries to films made in the last few years. We will use these to see how the genre has evolved and changed (as well as stayed the same) in its explorations of the intersections of gender, sexuality, race, and marginalization. Along the way, we will develop research skills and present secondary sources to help our collective goal of better understanding and analyzing the major ideas of queer theory and how they relate to fiction.

Sometimes queerness will seem incidental to the stories we read. Most often, however, we will see authors using the queer to explore the horrific and using the horrific to explore the queer. We will sometimes encounter stories that reel in horror at queerness, and we will read queer perspectives on and contributions to the genre. We will confront that which is uncomfortable, strange, and humorous along the way, using our explorations to try to understand the links between queerness and horror in diverse literary and artistic traditions.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Writers of the Ordinary
description: This course will explore representations in literature of ordinary lives, everyday happenings, and unremarkable things. We will focus on writers that give us a glimpse into the world not as we imagine it but as it is, writers that throw into relief what usually receives our inattention. We will concern ourselves with works that cast light on what we are every day, the unextraordinary things that surround us, and the mundane matters with which we occupy ourselves. Rather than investigate murders, betrayals, thrills, crimes, explosions, or catastrophes, we will explore the importance of the completely unremarkable. Underneath the invisibility of the ordinary, we will learn to uncover tremendous moral weight, political charge, conceptual insight, and personal significance. Our texts, among others, will include poetry (William Wordsworth, Emily Dickinson, William Carlos Williams, Gwendolyn Brooks), fiction (Jane Austen, James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, Toni Morrison), drama (Henrik Ibsen, Samuel Beckett), and film (Kelly Reichardt, Chloé Zhao) in addition to excurses into other media and traditions that will aid us in grasping the historical and conceptual dimensions of our interest in the ordinary.

subject: ENGLISH
title: What Is Poetry For? The Case of Tomas Tranströmer
description:
What is poetry? How does it work, and how does it work on us? In this course, in search of answers to these and other questions, we’ll read a selection of poetry by one of the greatest poets of the twentieth-century, Tomas Tranströmer of Sweden, a social worker, a psychologist, and the winner of a Nobel Prize in literature. We’ll look at his works in English translation, comparing versions, reading as much of his oeuvre as we can, as well as interviews with Tranströmer and poetry and prose by other poets, contemporaries and historical heavyweights alike. Our aim is to understand what poetry can look can look like, and how it might function in the broader culture, now and in the past, maybe even as something that might help us live, and help us see our own lives a little bit better. 

The broader purpose of this course is to develop your critical reading and writing skills, whatever your major might be. Over the semester, you’ll write a series of short papers and revise three of them. We’ll study the summary and synthesis of materials we read, the construction of logical and persuasive arguments, the conveying of attitudes and information. You’ll learn by practicing these skills, by thinking about and talking about your own efforts and those of your fellow students, and by analyzing the work of other writers.

subject: ENGLISH
title: A Queer Eye: Mrs. Dalloway and the Twentieth Century
description:
In this course we’ll focus on one novel, reading and rereading it slowly over the semester. That novel is Virginia Woolf’s modernist classic, Mrs. Dalloway. We’ll also read various adjacent and critical texts to deepen our understanding of the work. We’ll talk about the ways in which this book responds to the history of the twentieth century, reflecting and challenging it. We’ll talk about form, syntax, poetry, and the development of a kind of writing meant to mimic the monologues of a character: the stream of consciousness. And we’ll explore and debate the ways in which the novel signals a new era of queer of literature.

The broader purpose of this course is to develop your critical reading and writing skills, whatever your major might be. Over the semester, you’ll write a series of short papers and revise three of them. We’ll study the summary and synthesis of materials we read, the construction of logical and persuasive arguments, the conveying of attitudes and information. You’ll learn by practicing these skills, by thinking about and talking about your own efforts and those of your fellow students, and by analyzing the work of other writers.

subject: ENGLISH
title: The Asian American Novel
description: This course will introduce students to classic debates and core concepts from Asian American studies through a reading of some contemporary novels. We will explore why and how Asian American writers have chosen to incorporate their (ethnic, racial, gender, sexual, class) identities into their writing. We will also consider how the histories of war, colonialism, migration, and racial exclusion have shaped Asian America as a political formation. By focusing on the contemporary novel, this course will investigate what it means to bring these histories to bear upon our present moment. As part of the Reading & Composition series, this course will help develop students’ skills in close reading, note-taking, and argumentative writing. Please note that class participation will be mandatory.

subject: ENGLISH
title: WRITING THE AMERICAN CITY
description:
The American city is a complex and dynamic organism—and the subject of a great body of literature (both fiction and non-fiction) and film. Focusing on New York City, Los Angeles, and the Bay Area, this course will trace and critically engage how American urban development has been depicted on the page and on screen from the early twentieth century to today. 

By studying how writers and filmmakers have addressed the dramatic changes that impact American urban spaces, this course asks students to write critically about race and urban development from 1930s redlining and white flight to the battles over “urban renewal” the impact of 1970s neoliberal policies, “war on drugs” and militarized “broken windows” policing of the 1980s, urban uprisings of the early 1990s, and today’s hyper-gentrification. Paying special attention to how different racial groups have engaged, avoided, or confronted each other within these urban spaces, we will study how these changing cityscapes have on the one hand reflected and on the other hand actively influenced seismic changes in racial formation in the United States. 

Building on the skills students have acquired in R1A, this course will continue to develop reading, writing, and research skills with the aim of practicing writing longer essays that are rhetorically aware and partake in relevant scholarly conversations. To this end, students will practice creating varied, rhetorically aware compositions; reflect on writing practices, processes and strategies; and incorporate feedback to globally revise drafts. To develop responsible positions, students fine-tune research skills, evaluating scholarly and non-scholarly sources and incorporating a variety of perspectives. Overall, students will write and revise two shorter papers and a final research essay.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Experiments in Description in the New World Avant-Garde
description: In this class, we’ll be thinking about the role that the history of science and its “epistemic virtues” have had on experimental or avant-garde literature in the 20th century. Do experiments in literature require writers to incorporate the same practices and principles as that of scientists? What does it mean to “make it new” in language? What makes writing “experimental?” What role does description play in experimental writing? These questions will guide our reading and research. Poets and writers we’ll be reading may include: Gertrude Stein, William Carlos Williams, Aimé Césaire, Marianne Moore, Sylvia Wynter, Robert Hooke, and Gilbert White, among others.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Two Detective Novels
description:
As the title indicates, we will read two detective novels—Arthur Conan Doyle’s A Study in Scarlet (1887) and Alain Robbe-Grillet’s The Erasers (1953)—in this Reading & Composition course. We will also read a play (Sophocles’ Oedipus Tyrannus (ca. 429 BC)), a handful of short stories (by Edgar Allan Poe, 1840s) and some literary theory and philosophy (by Gérard Genette, Sigmund Freud, Ernst Bloch, and Carlo Ginzburg, among others).

Detective novels are, unsurprisingly, lots of fun to read. But they are also valuable texts for thinking about broader problems of narration and interpretation. After all, the task of the detective—much like that of the literary critic—is both retrospective and hermeneutic: the detective must interpret clues and weave them together in order to reveal the missing narrative of the crime. Our goal together as literary critics, therefore, is not only to be entertained by the “what” and the “who” of murder (i.e., the content), but to pay attention to the twin “how”s of its resolution and representation (i.e., the form). How does the detective crack the case? How does the writer produce the mystery? How, in short, does the detective novel work, and what can its workings teach us about how we read, write, and think?

As the second semester of the Reading & Composition sequence, this course will culminate in an eight- to ten-page essay that draws on both primary and critical sources to make a single, complex argument. The meta-critical capacity of the detective novel to reveal the logic of interpretation means that it can pull double duty in helping you towards this end: the detective novel will serve both as a site for practicing the skills of reading, writing, and thinking, and as a model for considering what it means to read (clues/evidence), write (narratives/analyses), and think (about the relationship between the two).

subject: ENGLISH
title: PETRO-FICTION AND CLIMATE FICTION
description:
“[W]e are living on borrowed time—borrowed from the past and from the future,” Rob Nixon argues, noting that fossil fuels on the one hand represent “the stratified death compacted over millennia that technology has enabled us to resurrect as the force that drives our fleeting, internal combustion civilization” but also, on the other hand, “[convey] an aura of antiquatedness, of built-in obsolescence inadequate to future needs.” Other scholars, such as Masao Miyoshi, have pointed out that, in their lack of critical engagement with worsening climate chaos, literature—and the humanities at large—are at risk of becoming obsolete. This course engages the spirit of these critiques—and the urgency they demand. 

Our semester begins by heeding Amitav Ghosh’s observation, in 1992, that “[a] great deal has been invested in ensuring the muteness of the Oil Encounter.” Attempting to challenge this omerta and make oil’s imprint on our civilization visible, we analyze literary representations of fossil fuel extraction’s profound disruption from Southern California to Oklahoma and Saudi Arabia, focusing on “resource curses” and “sacrifice zones” in works by Upton Sinclair, Abdelrahman Munif, and Linda Hogan. The second half of the semester will heed Amitav Ghosh’s subsequent pronouncement, in 2016, that fossil fuel-driven climate breakdown “casts a much smaller shadow within the landscape of literary fiction than it does even in the public arena.” Confronting this silence, we will read fiction by John Steinbeck, Dave Eggers, and Barbara Kingsolver to better understand the emergence of what Naomi Klein has termed “climate barbarism” or “climate fascism”—a trend that we will also see explored in works of the emerging genre of climate-fiction by Octavia Butler, Paolo Bacigalupi, and others. 

Building on the skills students have acquired in R1A, this course will continue to develop reading, writing, and research skills with the aim of practicing writing longer essays that are rhetorically aware and partake in relevant scholarly conversations. To this end, students will practice creating varied, rhetorically aware compositions; reflect on writing practices, processes and strategies; and incorporate feedback to globally revise drafts. To develop responsible positions, students fine-tune research skills, evaluating scholarly and non-scholarly sources and incorporating a variety of perspectives. Overall, students will write and revise two shorter papers and a final research essay.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Writers of the Ordinary
description:
This course will explore representations in literature of ordinary lives, everyday happenings, and unremarkable things. We will focus on writers that give us a glimpse into the world not as we imagine it but as it is, writers that throw into relief what usually receives our inattention. We will concern ourselves with works that cast light on what we are every day, the unextraordinary things that surround us, and the mundane matters with which we occupy ourselves. Rather than investigate murders, betrayals, thrills, crimes, explosions, or catastrophes, we will explore the importance of the completely unremarkable. 

Underneath the invisibility of the ordinary, we will learn to uncover tremendous moral weight, political charge, conceptual insight, and personal significance. Our texts, among others, will include poetry (William Wordsworth, Emily Dickinson, William Carlos Williams, Gwendolyn Brooks), fiction (Jane Austen, James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, Toni Morrison), drama (Henrik Ibsen, Samuel Beckett), and film (Kelly Reichardt, Chloé Zhao) in addition to excurses into other media and traditions that will aid us in grasping the historical and conceptual dimensions of our interest in the ordinary.

subject: ENGLISH
title: Utopian and Dystopian Fictions
description:
What would it be like to live in a perfect world? What could be worse than the world we live in now?

This section of English R1B traces attempts to answer these questions in English writing from medieval visions of heaven and hell to twentieth-century speculative fiction. With the help of selected critical and historical essays, we will consider why these questions have interested so many writers over the years; how social identities including gender, class, race, and disability figure in imagined worlds; and how the worlds that writers imagine relate to the historical worlds in which they wrote. We will discuss the relationship between story-telling and argument in the stories and essays we read, and over the course of the term we will practice steps for developing compelling interpretive arguments of your own.

Writing is central to this course as a way of thinking and understanding as well as a means of communication. Reading, writing, re-reading, and re-writing will be required. In addition to shorter writing exercises, you will plan, draft, peer-edit, and revise two essays including a final research essay.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Introduction to Environmental Design
course.description: This course will teach anyone how to start to be a designer, not just of drawings and objects, but also buildings, landscapes, and urban spaces. And not just in isolation, but in the complex web of ecological and man-made systems which makes up our shifting environment. You will take from the course first-hand experience of drawing, measuring, and design  which form the basis of the professions of architecture, landscape architecture, and urban planning and which culminate in a final design project in the course. The course is open to all undergraduate students.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Climate Change and City Planning: Adaptation and Resilience
course.description: This course introduces students to major issues in urban resilience and adaptation planning, particularly in relation to anthropogenic climate change. By the end of the course, students will have: (1) a critical understanding of key concepts such as risk, vulnerability, adaptation, and resilience; (2) an understanding of the interaction between adaptation planning, policy, and urban operating systems such as infrastructures, finance, and land use governance; (3) a basic introduction to practical tools such as vulnerability mapping, urban carbon budgeting, and participatory vulnerability assessment. The course will primarily draw on case material from the United States and secondarily from selected international cases.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Design Frameworks
course.description: This course begins with an open-ended question (“What is design?”) and asks students to think critically about the central tenets, commonalities, and limits of design in an ever-changing complex world. A historical and theoretical overview of predominant schools of thought across all scales of design (i.e. industrialization, modernism, post-modernism, and beyond) will ground the discussions to follow. Topics related to environmental sustainability including industrial ecologies, ecological design principles, lifecycle, biomimicry, LEED and accreditation systems, and closed-loop cycles will be presented.
course.requirements: ENVDES 110.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Designing Sustainability
course.description: This class aims to help you engage with and navigate the resources of the CED, including a broad overview of sustainability in contemporary life. In discussions and guest lectures, we will frame contemporary conversations around sustainability with an emphasis on current dialogues. Guest speakers will share their perspectives about how the discussion of sustainability can and should be framed. You will be introduced to important campus resources and faculty who will assist you in designing your own path through the Sustainable Environmental Design program.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: The Community Design Process
course.description: The Community Design Process will give CED undergraduate students the opportunity to effect change in the Bay Area through direct engagement and mentorship of Bay Area teens. Through a unique partnership with FamFirst Family Foundation, undergraduates will support a new generation of innovative thinkers to create solutions for the future of Oakland and the world. This interdisciplinary course will engage undergraduates in activities that range from curriculum development to direct mentorship, teaching, project planning, project management, and direct engagement with FamFirst teens at the West Oakland Youth Center.
course.requirements: Please note that there is a formal application process for enrollment in this course.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Introduction to Methods and Thesis Preparation
course.description: The Senior Thesis in Environmental Design is an advanced research and writing project that presents an original and thorough analysis of a topic of individual interest in architecture, landscape architecture, or urban studies. This class provides an introducion to various methodologies relevant for a senior thesis including qualitative, quantitative, and descriptive research approaches.

course.description: Students taking this class will use it to complete the writing of their thesis under the supervision of a Senior Thesis Advisor. This class will operate as an independent study; faculty with more than one Senior Thesis student may choose to meet them in group sessions.
course.requirements: Environmental Design 195A.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Advanced Urban Design Studio
course.description: The advanced urban design studio builds on the conceptual and design skills taught in the introductory studio, adding more complex contexts, sites and programs. The studio will address realistic contemporary urban, suburban, or rural situations requiring innovative solutions. The studio projects will be either sponsored or led by professional firms. Students will undertake in-depth research, understand economic, political, social, and cultural dynamics, investigate challenging sites, and produce creative responses.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Thesis Research and Preparation
course.description: Seminar focuses on individual urban design interests, the design and research work that students are pursuing in other courses, and development of thesis or final design projects.
course.requirements: Students must be in the Master of Urban Design program or obtain consent of instructor.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Topics in Environmental Design
course.description: Course examines current topics and issues in the field of environmental design. Topics may vary from year to year and will be announced in preparation for each term.

course.subject: ENVDES
course.title: Supervised Teaching
course.description: Professional courses for prospective teachers.
course.requirements: Appointment as graduate student instructor.

course.subject: PUBPOL
course.title: Dismantling Racism in Planning, Design, and Public Policy Clinic
course.description: This Clinic seeks to develop students to advance an anti-racist future guided by the principles of love, healing, and justice.  Students are required to enroll in the companion theory course, EnvDes C231, Critical Race Theory in Planning, Design, and Public Policy.  This Clinic focuses on four areas of professional practice.  First, students are supervised by experienced professional practitioners.  Second, students will learn the framework of racial equity analysis through applied theoretical frameworks and case study pedagogy.  Third, students will apply the framework of racial equity analysis to real-world projects. Fourth, students will engage in reflection of their experiences through peer learning and regular journal entries.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Intermediate Microeconomics with Applications to Sustainability
course.description: Covers the basic microeconomic tools for further study of natural resource problems. Theory of consumption, production, theory of the firm, industrial organization, general equilibrium, public goods and externalities. Applications to agriculture and natural resources.
course.requirements: C1 or Economics 1 or C3; and Mathematics 16A and 16B or Math 1A and 1B; or consent of instructor

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Economics of Innovation and Intellectual Property
course.description: This course addresses the economics of research and incentives for innovation including intellectual property rights. Topics include the standard modern economics of invention; modern intellectual property rights; innovation examples from agriculture, energy, pharmaceuticals, software, and electronics; the roles of the public and private sectors; innovation and market structure; the needs of the poor; and global intellectual property negotiations.
course.requirements: ENVECON 100 or ECON 100A or ECON 101A with minimum grade of C+

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Health and Environmental Economic Policy
course.description: This course introduces students to key issues and findings in the field of health and environmental economics. The first half of the course focuses on the theoreticl and statistical frameworks used to analyze instances of market failure in the provision of health and environmental goods. The second half focuses on policy-relevant empirical findings in the field.
course.requirements: Intermediate microeconomics, 100, Economics 100 or 101A, and some statistics.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Energy and Environmental Economics Mentorship
course.description:
The course is designed to help students envision and prepare for a graduate program in energy and environmental economics by providing training, mentoring, and hands-on research experience. Students are assigned a mentor. Each mentor will have 2 - 3 students as mentees. Mentors are doctoral students who have an active research project within the energy and environmental economics field and have a desire to mentor undergraduate students interested in the field. The course includes weekly workshops for the class and weekly meetings for the mentors and mentees. The mentor meetings will be scheduled with the mentor. Mentees are
also expected to spend at least 6 hours per week on assignments given by the mentors and instructors.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Advanced Topics in Development and International Trade
course.description: This course discusses recent efforts to understand behavior and institutions in village economies, with particular attention paid to the importance of risk. Economic analysis of savings, consumption, insurance, production, trade, welfare distribution and institutions of villages in developing countries. Roughly equal parts of theory, evidence, and policy.
course.requirements: 100 or Economics 100A.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Population, Environment, and Development
course.description: This course takes a quantitative, hands-on approach to understanding the challenges of feeding the human population of the planet Earth. We’ll discuss topics of nutrition, subsistence food consumption, and consumer demand for food to develop our understanding of the current situation. We’ll then develop both theories and computer models of population dynamics taking into account people’s decisions about childbearing, changes in mortality, and changes in food supply in order to learn something about the future of food. Focus throughout the course will be on developing practical tools to work with real-world data.
course.requirements: ENVECON 100 or ECON 100A or ECON 101A, and STAT C8 or INFO C8 or COMPSCI C8, and MATH 54 RECOMMENDED

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Advanced Topics in Environmental and Resource Economics
course.description: The roots of environmental and resource economics. Theories of land and resource rent. Models of optimal use of renewable and nonrenewable resources with applications to energy and timber. Balancing environmental and extractive values. Resources, growth, and sustainability. Special topic: the problem of global climate change.
course.requirements: 100 or Economics 100A or Economics 101A; 101 recommended.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: The Production and Business of Beer, Wine, and Spirits
course.description:
Raw materials, process flow, production methodology and quality control will be introduced in the first half of the class
for the first half of the semester. Students will also be introduced to basic chemistry and microbiology of fermentation
and distilling. The second half of the semester will be an introduction to finance, cost accounting, sales and marketing for the alcoholic
beverage industry. The goal will be to enable the students to write a business plan by the end of the semester.

course.requirements: Upper division standing and consent of instructor.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Sponsored Projects for Undergraduate Research (SPUR)
course.description: The Sponsored Projects for Undergraduate Research (SPUR) program helps students get involved in research projects with world renowned faculty and staff researchers in the Rausser College of Natural Resource

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Freshman/Sophomore Seminar
course.description: Freshman and sophomore seminars offer lower division students the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member and a group of peers in a small-seminar setting. These seminars are offered in all campus departments; topics vary from department to department and from semester to semester.
course.requirements: Priority given to freshmen and sophomores.

course.subject: ECON
course.title: Introduction to Environmental Economics and Policy
course.description: Introduction to microeconomics with emphasis on resource, agricultural, and environmental issues.
course.requirements: Mathematics 32.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Environmental Economics
course.description: Theories of externalities and public goods applied to pollution and environmental policy. Trade-off between production and environmental amenities. Assessing nonmarket value of environmental amenities. Remediation and clean-up policies. Environment and development. Biodiversity management.
course.requirements: 100, Mathematics 16A-16B, or Economics 100A or 101A.

course.subject: IAS
course.title: Introductory Applied Econometrics
course.description: Formulation of a research hypothesis and definition of an empirical strategy. Regression analysis with cross-sectional and time-series data; econometric methods for the analysis of qualitative information; hypothesis testing. The techniques of statistical and econometric analysis are developed through applications to a set of case studies and real data in the fields of environmental, resource, and international development economics. Students learn the use of a statistical software for economic data analysis.
course.requirements: Statistics 2, 20, 21, or equivalent

course.subject: ECON
course.title: International Environmental Economics
course.description: This course studies the following question:How should policymakers and scholars design and analyze environmental policy in a globalized world where much economic activity and pollution crosses political borders? The course addresses issues including climate change, air and water pollution, deforestation, species extinction, and others. The course also analyzes a variety of ways that countries and regions interact, including trade, foreign direct investment, outsourcing, international agreements and treaties, and others. The course also teaches a range of tools used to analyze these issues, including life-cycle(also called environmental footprint) analysis, simple econometrics, environmental market design, non-market valuation, and the data.
course.requirements: ENVECON 100, ECON 101a, ECON 100a or  or equivalent

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Development Economics
course.description: This course covers theory and empirical evidence on the determinants of economic development and the global fight against poverty. The course aims to introduce students to modern empirical research methods that are being used to inform policy making in developing countries. Students also learn how to implement these tools themselves using real-world data sets and widely used statistical software for impact evaluation.
course.requirements: EnvEcon 100 or Econ 100A or 101A; Econ 140 or 141 or EnvEcon/IAS C118

course.subject: IAS
course.title: The Economics of Climate Change
course.description: The course will start with a brief introduction and evaluation of the scientific aspects behind climate change. Economic models will be developed to analyze the impacts of climate change and provide and critique existing and proposed policy tools. Specific topics studied are impacts on water resources and agriculture, economic evaluation of impacts, optimal control of greenhouse gases, benefit cost analysis, international treaty formation, discounting, uncertainty, irreversibility, and extreme events.
course.requirements: 106, 107, Economics 1, or equivalent.

course.subject: IAS
course.title: Climate Change Economics
course.description: This course is a self-contained introduction to the economics of climate change. Climate change is caused by a large variety of economic activities, and many of its impacts will have economic consequences. Economists have studied climate change for more than two decades, and economic arguments are often powerful in policy decisions. The course will familiarize students with these arguments and equip them with the tools to participate in discussions of climate change policy through an economic lens.

course.subject: ECON
course.title: International Trade
course.description: The theory of international trade and its applications to tariff protection. This course is equivalent to UGBA 118; students will not receive credit for both courses.
course.requirements: Economics100A-100B or Economics 101A-101B.

course.subject: ENVECON
course.title: Advanced Topics in International Economics
course.description: Globalization and its consequences have interested economists and the public since Adam Smith and David Ricardo. However, the nature of the global economy has changed dramatically over time. Paraphrasing Ricardo’s famous example, “it’s not wine for cloth anymore.” This course will introduce a modern view on international trade focusing on firms as vehicles of trade. We will study key theoretical models of New Trade Theory and apply them to understand the consequences of a range of trade policies from the recent past, such the NAFTA agreement and China’s entry to the WTO. We will combine theoretical models, empirical econometric tools, and data to understand the impacts of trade and offshoring on trade flows,aggregate welfare,and inequality
course.requirements:
•	Microeconomics (Envecon100, Econ100 or Econ101A): required
•	Econometrics (EnveconC118, Econ140 or Econ141): required but can be taken concurrently
•	International TradeEnvecon/EconC181): optional. This course is complementary to C181; a few extra readings will be provided to students who have not taken that class;
•	Students should have a basic knowledge of calculus (roughly at the level of Mathematics 16A and 16B) and be comfortable understanding mathematical arguments.

course.title: Honors Research
course.description: Supervised independent honors research specific to aspects of environmental economics and policy, followed by a oral presentation and a written report.
course.requirements: Upper division standing. Eligibility restrictions related to GPA and unit accumulation. Open only to Environmental Economics and Policy majors in the College of Natural Resources.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Minerals: Their Constitution and Origin
course.description: Introduction to structural, compositional, and physical properties of minerals, their analogs and related substances, their genesis in various geological and synthetic processes, and laboratory techniques to identify and investigate minerals. One field trip to selected mineral deposits and visits to laboratories.
course.requirements: Some background in chemistry and physics.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Field Geology and Digital Mapping
course.description: Geological mapping, field observation, and problem-solving in the Berkeley hills and environs leading to original interpretation of geological processes and history from stratigraphic, structural, and lithological investigations. Integration of the Berkeley hills geology into the Coast Ranges and California as a whole through field trips to key localities. Training in digital field mapping, global positioning systems, and laser surveying. Interdisciplinary focus encourages participation by nonmajors.
course.requirements: 50 or equivalent introductory course in Earth and Planetary Science.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: History and Evolution of Planet Earth
course.description: Formation and evolution of the earth. Nucleosynthesis; formation of the solar system; planetary accretion; dating the earth and solar system; formation of the core, mantle, oceans, and atmosphere; plate tectonics; heat transfer and internal dynamics; stratigraphic record of environment, and evolution; climate history and climate change.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Quantitative Approaches in Earth Systems
course.description: The course will focus largely on the concepts of scaling and estimation – how can we reasonablyestimate some parameter within the Earth system (e.g., the viscosity of the Earth’s mantle) withlimited information and simplified approaches. We will also expand to discuss topics at theintersection of Earth Science and Data Science, including analyses of time-series data of past ice-age cycles and how these may be linked to the presence of Jupiter and Saturn, and therelationship between earthquake magnitude and the frequency of events. Finally, we will discusstopics in vector calculus, examining ground water flow and the origin of shear in ocean gyres.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Geodynamics
course.description: Basic principles in studying the physical properties of earth materials and the dynamic processes of the earth. Examples are drawn from tectonics, mechanics of earthquakes, etc., to augment course material.
course.requirements: 60, Physics 7A, or Mathematics 53, 54.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Computer Simulations with Jupyter Notebooks
course.description: Introduction to modern computer simulation methods and their application to selected Earth and Planetary Science problems. In hands-on computer labs, students will learn about numerical algorithms, learn to program and modify provided programs, and display the solution graphically. This is an introductory course and no programming experience is required. Examples include fractals in geophysics, properties of materials at high pressure, celestial mechanics, and diffusion processes in the Earth. Topics range from ordinary and partial differential equations to molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations.
course.requirements: Math 1A or equivalent.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Stratigraphy and Earth History
course.description: Collecting, analyzing, and presenting stratigraphic data; dating and correlating sedimentary rocks; recognizing ancient environments and reconstructing Earth history; seismic and sequence stratigraphy; event stratigraphy and neocatastrophism; applications of stratigraphy to climate change, petroleum geology, and archaeology.
course.requirements: 50, 100A, 100B, or consent of instructor.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Structural Geology and Tectonics
course.description: Introduction to the geometry and mechanics of brittle and ductile geologic structures; their origins and genetic relation to stress fields and their use as kinematic indicators; case histories of selected regions to elucidate tectonic evolution in different plate tectonic settings. Laboratory exercises will focus on analysis of hand specimens and structural relations portrayed on geologic maps. Several trips to observe geologic structures in the field to supplement laboratory exercises.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Geomorphology
course.description: Quantitative examination of landforms, runoff generation, weathering, mechanics of soil erosion by water and wind, mass wasting, glacial and periglacial processes and hillslope evolution.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors
course.description: Gravity field, density distribution, and internal seismic structure of the Earth and planets. Constitution, composition, temperature distribution, and energetics of the Earth's interior. The geomagnetic field and the geodynamo, and concepts in seismic imaging and geophysical fluid dynamics. This course welcomes physics, computer science, engineering and applied maths majors.
course.requirements: Physics 7A-B, Mathematics 53-54, or equivalent.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: The Earth’s Energy and Mineral Resources: Geoscience Concepts and Challenges
course.description:
The Earth’s crust hosts invaluable resources such as fuels, geothermal energy and
critical minerals. This course will review these resources, introduce geoscience and
geoengineering concepts for locating and utilizing them, and summarize some of the
substantial and fascinating challenges for doing so effectively. This course provides
students from different disciplines a broad technical background and some practical
experience of multidisciplinary research for better use of the Earth’s resources.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Geochemistry
course.description: Chemical reactions in geological processes. Thermodynamic methods for predicting chemical equilibria in nature. Isotopic and chemical tracers of transport processes in the earth. Chemistry of the solid earth, oceans, and atmosphere.
course.requirements: 100A-100B, Chemistry 1A-1B.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Case Studies in Earth Systems
course.description: Analysis and discussion of three research problems on the interactions of solid earth, hydrologic, chemical, and atmospheric processes. Emphasis is on the synthesis and application of the student's disciplinary knowledge to a new integrative problem in the earth sciences.
course.requirements: 50, senior standing or consent of instructor.

course.subject: EPS
course.title: Geophysical Methods for Shallow Ground Investigations
course.description: This seminar explores case histories of geophysical methods for shallow ground investigations. Topics include using geophysics to characterize soil profiles, rockhead, slope/retaining wall stability, water leakage, and buried contaminants. The course covers selecting, instrumenting, and possible limitations of techniques like ground-penetrating radar, seismic wave spectral analysis, electrical imaging, microgravity, gamma spectroscopy, and infrared thermography.

course.title: Field Study
course.description: Written proposal signed by faculty sponsor and approved by major faculty advisor. Supervised experience relevant to specific aspects of students' EPS specialization in off-campus organization. Regular meetings with faculty sponsor and written report required.
course.requirements: Upper division standing and declared major in Earth and Planetary Science.
