Using economic and ecological concepts, students will solve practical problems in this field. The course covers relevant theories and frameworks for assessing natural resource management, ecosystems services, economic valuation, climate change and water, corporate carbon footprint, forestry management, and strategies to add value through corporate sustainability. The course emulates the assessment and decision making processes that are the norm in this field. Students will improve their decision making process related to natural resources and their understanding of how those decisions influence competitive advantage in business.

The course includes an assignment to a consultation team that works with a select nonprofit client to help them succeed in an entrepreneurial venture. A partnership with a professional management consulting firm, McKinsey & Company, the course includes experienced McKinsey consultants coaching each of the student teams.

course.description: This is an advanced case-based course intended to provide the background, tools, and themes of the venture capital industry. The course is organized in four modules of the private equity cycle: (1) fund raising -- examines how private equity funds are raised and structured, (2) investing -- considers the interactions between private equity investors and the entrepreneurs that they finance, (3) exiting -- examines the process through which private equity investors exit their investments; and (4) new frontiers -- reviews many of the key ideas developed in the course.

course.description: This course is intended to provide the core skills needed for the identification of opportunities that can lead to successful, entrepreneurial high technology ventures, regardless of the individual's "home" skill set, whether technical or managerial. We examine in depth the approaches most likely to succeed for entrepreneurial companies as a function of markets and technologies. Emphasis is placed on the special requirements for creating and executing strategy in a setting of rapid technological change and limited resources. This course is particularly suited for those who anticipate founding or operating technology companies.

The course examines businesses across industries and phases of a firm's growth. Critical entrepreneurial strategies are illuminated for new ventures or in building a new enterprise inside a corporation. The course provides students with the skills and knowledge to rapidly assess and shape business models to their advantage in constructing new enterprises.

subject: FILM
description: This course focuses on the earliest years of cinema, from its 19th century prehistory in optical technologies, such as the panorama and photography, to its cultural life at the end of the 1920s. We will consider how film technology, industry, and art took shape in the late 1890s and how cinematic narrative forms that are familiar to us now (like the serial and the feature film) became codified during the early years of the 20th century. The course will introduce students to influential national styles and movements, such as German Expressionism and Soviet Montage. Students will also learn about the transition from silent to sound cinema in the 1920s, culminating in the American film industry’s practice of self-regulation, the Motion Picture Production Code. Students will be introduced to the basic vocabulary of film form and how to develop a compelling and original analysis of film sequences using visual, as well as narrative, evidence.

course.subject: FILM

course.description: This course will focus on the development of film art, technology, and industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

subject: FILM
title: As Real as It Gets
description: This course surveys the history, theory, and form of the documentary film. It examines the major modes of documentary filmmaking, including cinema verité, direct cinema, investigative documentary, ethnographic film, autobiography, and the personal essay, as well as recent postmodern forms that question the relationship between fact and fiction, such as the docudrama, the archival film, cine-recreations, and "mockumentaries." By considering works from a diverse range of filmmakers across geographies and time, our analyses will focus on film form and the ways in which these works make meaning and create their own sense of what is real. Throughout, we will explore some of the theoretical questions that have surrounded this genre and practice. How do documentary films shape notions of truth, reality, and point of view? What are the ethics and politics of representation? Who speaks for whom? Does documentary mean objective? What does it mean?

course.subject: FILM
course.title: Documentary Forms
course.description: This course will focus on topics in documentary cinema, television, video, photography, and/or new media.

subject: FILM
title: Experimental, Alternative, and Radical Indigenous Media and Art
description: This course will explore both the limits and capaciousness of the terms “experimental” and “media” from a critical Indigenous media theory perspective. This will include interventions made by Indigenous media practitioners/theorists which often blur the boundaries between experimental, alternative, and radical media production. Attending closely to the sense of the collective and the communal in their works, what Fred Moten and Stefano Harney call an “ongoing experiment with the informal, carried out by and on the means of social reproduction,” we will put these in relation to a conception of the minor. This class will investigate how Indigenous media operates as a site of social and political experimentation against colonial, imperial, and other dominating and reductive forces. We will experience work by Indigenous media creators who push the boundaries of form, materiality, expression, technology, sociality, visuality, legibility, identity, and politics. A significant emphasis will be placed on collective and community-based work as well as radical and revolutionary media and media that contends with forces of destruction. We will also read and discuss theories of mediation and the sensorium. Media will be understood capaciously, with little distinction between “old” and “new” media, though we will discuss these discursive formations outside of developmental historicism and in relation to their social uses. This will range across archival documents, AI and martial technology, filmic and digital images, sound experimentation, etc.

description: This course examines the influence of digital technology on contemporary film and visual culture. Beginning in the year 2000 we look at how computational media have transformed the way we make, view, and understand filmmaking as a creative and cultural practice in the 21st century. From computer graphics to TikTok and artificial intelligence, we will explore new tools and develop new skills to help us understand and analyze digital cinema today.

subject: FILM
title: Film Genres of the Depression
description: The stock market crash of 1929 triggered the Great Depression, a decade-long period marked by record rates of poverty, unemployment, and economic stagnation, which would continue until the outbreak of WW2. At the same time, the period also saw the emergence of several defining genres of classical Hollywood cinema, so much so that it is often looked back upon as a “Golden Age.” Highlighting four such genres—the gangster film, social problem film, musical, and screwball comedy—this course asks how cinema mediated the economic, social, and political struggles of the 1930s. Over the course of the semester, we will approach the film genres of the depression as not only cathartic or escapist, but also as popular languages that gave shape to both the material realities of economic precarity and the abstractions of political economy, occasionally erupting into unabashed critique. Classics from the Hollywood canon by filmmakers such as Howard Hawks, William Wellman, and Busby Berkeley will be complemented by lesser-known American films as well as range of international productions, which offer distinct perspectives on a manifestly global economic crisis.

subject: FILM
title: Alfred Hitchcock
description: Popularly know as the “Master of Suspense,” Alfred Hitchcock was one of the most commercially successful filmmakers of the 20th century, while also exemplifying the possibility of the director as artist. This class will track the long span of Hitchcock’s career, from the silent era in the UK to New Hollywood in the 1970s, investigating the way in which his films explore a consistent set of themes while adapting to ever changing industrial and cultural contexts. At the same time, the course will look at the way in which Hitchcock’s films have served as a consistent point of engagement through which film studies has developed various theoretical positions, including auteur theory, feminist film theory, and queer theory.

subject: FILM
title: Beginning Screenwriting
description:
Students explore the art and craft of developing and writing a feature-length,
narrative screenplay.  Each writer pitches story ideas, develops a plot outline and
completes a portion of their screenplay.  All students workshop outlines and
scenes in class.  There are weekly writing assignments that guide the writer
forward with their own project and highlight the rewriting process.
 
Lecture topics include narrative feature concept development, analysis of a
variety of story structures, plot outlining, character development, openings, scene
structure, dialogue, screenplay form/style. 
 
Prerequisites: No screenwriting experience needed.  Consent of instructor
required.  The class is open to juniors and seniors, qualified seniors given
priority.  Preference is given to Film & Media majors.  A writing sample is

academic essay).

The focus is on rewriting, with regular presentations of outlines and scripts to fellow writers. The emphasis is on story structure, character development, and screenplay form.

subject: FILM
description:

writing serialized narrative scripts. In the first half of the course students simulate
the creative and collaborative process of a TV writers’ room by working together
to develop a spec script based on an existing series. In the second half of the
semester each writer creates a portion of their pilot script for an original series. 
All students will workshop pitches, outlines and scenes in class.

Lecture topics include episodic concept development, analysis of a variety of
story structures, “breaking” a story, creating engaging characters, plot blending,
and building arcs for characters, episodes and seasons.

subject: FILM
title:
Intermediate Moving Image Production (Focus on
the Narrative Short)
description:
This intermediate film production course explores the process of making
narrative shorts.  Students will write, pre-visualize, direct and edit three short
films, as well as act as cinematographer and assistant director for their
classmates’ projects.  Scripts and cuts are presented in a workshop setting.
 

Lecture topics include strategies for writing an engaging short script, pre-
visualization, directing actors, shot choice/composition, continuity and coverage,
sound design, lighting, editing aesthetics.  Narrative shorts from around the world
are screened to facilitate discussion of strategies for making an effective short

subject: FILM
title: Experimental Nonfiction
description:
This production course focuses on experimental nonfiction filmmaking. The course will explore experimental approaches and methods that are pushing the form in new directions. We will explore durational, conceptual, sensory, poetic and essayistic approaches of this vibrant and evolving filmmaking mode. The class will consider the ways in which aesthetics, ethics and politics shape the formal considerations of these films. Class meetings are organized around screening and analyzing clips, discussions, technical demos, in-class exercises, hands-on work and project critiques. Students will create two projects that utilize some of the alternative approaches that will be discussed in class. This class is dynamic and rigorous, with many of the assignments and much of the work done outside of the scheduled class hours.

description:
This course will introduce each student to the fundamentals of documentary filmmaking. Over the course of the semester students will complete several short exercises and will direct, shoot, and edit one final film in collaboration with a class partner. Students will acquire hands-on experience in cinematography, sound recording, and editing. Students will also perform various crew roles for other students as assigned. Critiques of creative work will emphasize the conceptual, aesthetic, and technical aspects of film production. The class will explore a variety of documentary techniques, such as the observational camera, the interview, voiceover use, and working with archival materials. We will address some of the major questions of the documentary form today, such as issues of representation, authorship, subjectivity and point of view. The class will also examine how these issues are addressed through formal approaches. course.description: This course focuses on practices and techniques of non-fiction film and media. The course examines important techniques of non-fiction media production, such as research and writing for non-fiction; the observational camera; filming in public; the interview; voiceover; working with archival images and other documents; as well as editing techniques. subject: FILM
title: Theory of Photography
description: This capstone seminar offers a deep dive into the theory of photography. Drawing on a range of texts from across the medium’s almost two centuries of history, it asks how photography—whether understood as a visual technology, documentary medium, or vehicle for artistic expression—has transformed the way we see, think about, and understand the world. The study of texts by major theorists such as Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes, and Ariella Azoulay will be complemented by the visits to local collections, where we will view and discuss photographic objects in person, as well as occasional hands-on workshops, where students will gain an embodied understanding of select historical processes. Over the course of the semester, students will develop a substantial research project which may take the form of a seminar paper or well-developed creative project.

subject: FILM
title: Public Criticism
description: This course is an exercise in practical theory: a semester-long conversation about the nature and aims of film criticism, complemented by a workshop approach to writing about film for a general audience. The main goal is to learn to write better — more beautifully, more intelligently — about moving images. We will experiment with form and tone: from the capsule review to the critical essay, from personal feeling to shared history. At the center of the course is a series of films drawn from across national cinemas and historical periods — works chosen, above all, to make you want to reach for a pen.

Students will read texts about film writing, texts about academic writing, and film scholarship and criticism that model the forms of analysis they are learning to practice.

subject: FILM
description:
This course introduces students to foundational theories and methods in the scholarly study of audiovisual and other forms of media, including print media, television, film, video, and digital media. We will explore how different media shape social formations and systems of communication, an influence cultural ideas in relation to their historical and political context.

One of the key focuses of this course will be on how media inform the very production of subjectivity—our sense of who we are and how we participate in society. This course will take you beyond everyday ways of thinking about media and into the complex territory of 20th and 21st-century intellectual history. Focusing on both form and meaning, we will consider the unique technological, material, formal, and aesthetic characteristics that define different media and their modes of representation

course.subject: FILM
course.title: Film and Media Theory
course.description: This course is intended to introduce undergraduates to the study of a range of media, including photography, film, television, video, and print and digital media. The course will focus on questions of medium "specificity" or the key technological/material, formal and aesthetic features of different media and modes of address and representation that define them. Also considered is the relationship of individual media to time and space, how individual media construct their audiences or spectators, and the kinds of looking or viewing they enable or encourage. The course will discuss the ideological effects of various media, particularly around questions of racial and sexual difference, national identity, capitalism, and power.

course.subject: FILM
course.title: Graduate Film Theory Seminar
course.description: This seminar will examine both traditional and recent critical approaches to a systematic and historical study of film. Although we will emphasize contemporary structuralist-semiotic, psychoanalytical, and socio-critical methods, we will also study the classical debates in film theory about representation, filmic vs. literary signification, sexual difference, and the social function of images in modernism and postmodernism. Illustrations will be taken from film history from 1910 to 1980.
course.requirements: Graduate standing or consent of instructor.

course.description: A seminar introducing Film Studies graduate students to the field, the profession, and the faculty practicing film studies. Envisioned as a way for new students to learn what is expected of them and for more advanced students to pass through the all-important last years of their training in an atmosphere of helpful camaraderie. Introduces students to the intellectual and physical resources of the Berkeley campus as well as the Bay Area. By the end of the semester students should gain an understanding of the expectations of their performance in graduate school, have identified the major goals on the way towards getting a Ph.D., and, depending on where they are in their studies, have begun to achieve those goals.

subject: FILM
title: Hermeneutics of Doubt: Media, Philosophy, Meaning
description: This graduate seminar considers doubt as historically varied modes of inquiry and understanding that unsettle a determinist worldview. We will trace a genealogy of doubt by placing the history of philosophy in conversation with the philosophy of technology. The course tracks the history of skepticism and hermeneutics but dwells on three significant moments: the turn of the twentieth century American Pragmatism; the postwar rise of hermeneutics; and the rise of poststructuralism which heralds a post-hermeneutic and posthuman turn but also opens up meaning through an aesthetics of doubt. We will consider these three particular moments because of their historical relationship with experimental science, their bearings on questions of medium, form, and meaning, and their close association with phenomenology but also philosophy of history and philosophy of knowledge. Readings include René Decartes, Immanuel Kant, Charles Peirce, Bernard Stiegler, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Paul Ricoeur, Jacques Derrida, Ian Hacking, Karen Barad, among others.

subject: FINNISH
description:
(Fall only. Finnish 1B will be offered in Spring)

This is a cross campus listed course and will be taught with the quarter schedule to accommodate students from other UC campuses. UC Berkeley students will meet with the instructor in the classroom on 8/26 but instruction begins formally on 9/24 when other UC campuses start their Fall Quarter. UCB students will participate in this class in the classroom, enrolled students from other campuses via Zoom, a conferencing / distance teaching platform.


COURSE OBJECTIVES:
Students will learn the basic structures of the Finnish language and will be able to use them in simple, everyday conversation. All four language skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing will be studied and practiced. In addition to the basics of Finnish language, this class introduces students to everyday life in modern Finland, Finnish customs and holidays, and more.

Workload: About five hours of work outside of class per week (includes online homework), 3 quizzes, and an oral and written final.

COURSE TEXTS:
Suomen mestari 1. Suomen kielen oppikirja aikuisille. (FinnLectura 2020) Sonja Gehring & Sanni Heinzmann, ISBN 978-951-1-33423-1

We will use the updated and fully revised edition. Students need the 2020 edition (or later )!

Additional materials will be provided.
If you are not a currently registered student, you may be able to enroll via Concurrent Enrollment, UC Berkeley Extension. Please note that the Concurrent Enrollment application must be approved by the department. Approval is based on availability of space in the class; enrolled UC students on a waitlist have priority. Elementary Finnish is open to all students without prior knowledge of Finnish. The course is not open to native, or near-native-speakers of Finnish. Course can be repeated only with consent from the language coordinator.

Prerequisites: None. All welcome / Tervetuloa!

The internship duties and the academic requirements must remain distinct, though they inform one another.

course.description: This seminar explores the emergence of notions of tradition and modernity and their reproduction in Eurocentric epistemologies and political formations. It uses work by such authors as Anderson, Butler, Chakrabarty, Clifford, Derrida, Foucault, Latour, Mignolo, Pateman, and Poovey to critically reread foundational works published between the 17th century and the present--along with philosophical texts with which they are in dialogue--in terms of how they are imbricated within and help produce traditionalities and modernities.

Students read a selection of works from different media and genres including short stories, poems, plays, letters, essays, paintings and films. subject: FRENCH
title: The Ideological Creation of the French Empire
description:
L’objectif de ce cours est l’analyse de la question coloniale en France, depuis la création de l’empire colonial, pendant le dix-neuvième siècle, jusqu’aux débats récents du vingt-et-unième siècle sur le post-colonialisme. Après un panorama historique, nous focaliserons nos analyse sur la question du Maghreb colonial. Au nombre des questions que nous discuterons, on peut noter: la propagande coloniale, l’engagement des écrivains et des philosophes dans la lutte contre le
colonialisme, l’utilisation systématique de la torture pendant la guerre d’Algérie, ainsi que le statut  de la femme dans l’univers colonial. Parmi les auteurs critiques de la colonization, que nous étudierons il faut noter: Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Memmi, et Frantz Fanon. Un “reader” sera disponible à “Copy Central”. Le cours est donné en français.

subject: FRENCH
title: Inventing Modern Comedy: Molière and His Time
description:
This class is taught in French.

Molière was France’s most prominent comic actor, playwright, and stage director during the Classical Age, and his plays remain central to the French imaginary to this day. This class provides an introduction to Molière’s works and times. We study a selection of his plays, ranging from his Italianate farces and the comédies-ballets (or musicals) he produced for the Court, to the high-flying social critiques he wrote and staged for his Parisian audiences. We also explore Molière’s role in the social and political institution of the theater at a time when playwriting and acting were first codified and legitimized. We give particular attention, in this respect, to Molière’s relationship to Louis XIV, and to the ways in which the King’s patronage impacted Molière’s theater. We also enquire into the history of early modern performance, studying both how Molière’s texts were pronounced and how they might have been staged in his time. Modern filmic reconstitutions, from Ariane Mnouchkine to Vincent Dumestre, serve as a point of departure for this investigation into the history of performance. Finally, we trace the canonization of Molière’s œuvre, most notably by studying a selection of modern and contemporary performances, ranging from recent Comédie-Française video productions to excerpts of historic performances available on INA’s website (Institut National de l’Audiovisuel).

All readings, lectures, class discussions and written work are in French. This class also focuses on developing your writing skills. Written exercises include a final paper to be outlined collectively in class and developed in stages over the second half of the term, with individualized support from the instructor.

subject: FRENCH
title: Why write?
description:
This class is taught in French.

These days, writing is no longer required. It’s beyond easy to outsource: to AI, Gemini, ChatGPT, lesser-paid ghost-writers, offshore “content producers.” So why bother writing at all? What do we give up, as individuals and as a society, if we give up writing? This course will be a group-think about what is at stake in the practice of linguistic composition. We’ll consider writing as a category broadly construed (inclusive of interior monologue, dictating, texting, typing, handwriting, creative writing, academic writing, and so forth), examining its enduring association with personal and political freedom, as well as its capacity to be transformative: of writers, of their societies, and of language itself. Discussions will be organized around reflections on writing by major thinkers of the 19th-21st centuries (Bui, Macé, Leiris, Hugo, Rimbaud, Mallarmé, Derrida, Benveniste, Condé); topics to be covered include language as a social fact and as a medium of personal expression; the relation of thought and language; writing as process / product; private language; linguistic diversity. Our aim will be a clear-eyed understanding of all “writing” is, and what is lost when one decides not to write—or stops writing—for one’s self.

subject: FRENCH
title: French for Professions: French for Science, Medicine, and Environment
description:
This class, conducted entirely in French, provides a solid introduction to French-speaking scientific matters, including medical and environmental ones. 

The course’s cultural objectives are coupled with 1) linguistic objectives to help you talk about scientific issues in French, and 2) intercultural objectives to prepare you for studying or working in francophone organizations, i.e. for an internships, especially if you follow the new professional certificate offered in the French Department (for more details, contact Nina Cohen, frendept@berkeley.edu, and look here: https://french.berkeley.edu/index.php/undergraduate/certificate-of-french-for-professional-purposes). 

This class will be an asset if you want to continue your studies in French-speaking countries, apply to med school in the US, or work in research, public health, environmental policies, or any medical-related field (like international NGOs in Western Africa). It is well suited for majors/minors in French and as a complement for majors in STEM and pre-med fields of study, Environmental Sciences, Global Studies, Psychology, among others.

After this class, you will be able to:
-	Do a clear oral presentation with slides in French; 
-	Draft and read research proposals, abstracts, and scientific papers in French;
-	Discuss the situation of scientific research in France, but also public health and environmental issues (including energy and water) in French;
-	Conduct a medical examination in French;
-	Apply for Master degrees in French or search for internships/jobs in French (CV, cover letter, interview).

The class will be organized around 5 chapters:
•	Introduction (Day 1): we will reflect on your professional project + why speaking French can help you build or achieve it. 
•	Chapter 1 (Epistemology of Science): we will first study the history and epistemology of science in a French-speaking context – spending time with important figures such as the pioneer woman Marie Curie, but also Pasteur, Buffon, Auguste Comte, Jean Piaget, Bruno Latour, among others. We will learn how to draft a research proposal and French scientific papers in French.
•	Chapter 2 (Research in France): We will then study the current organization of research and higher education in France (including engineer studies), their strengths and weaknesses.
•	Chapter 3 (Health issues in French): We will then focus on medicine, its organization in France and in the francophone world (NGO’s), and public health issues. You will learn how to discuss health issues and perform a medical examination in French.
•	Chapter 4 (Environmental Questions): We will finally move to environmental issues, including the impacts of climate change in France and Europe, environmental policies, while also exploring the questions of water and energy. 
•	Chapter 5 (Working and Studying in French): Last, we will how to prepare for the French-speaking higher education system and job market. You will prepare a CV and a cover letter in French and learn how to perform during recruitment interviews in French.

subject: FRENCH
title: The Crafting of the French Philosopher: from Montaigne to Foucault
description:
This class is taught in English.

Public intellectuals are a key feature of contemporary political culture. But how did such figures come to be? French society was one of the first Western societies in which men and women whose principal talents were reading, writing, and thinking managed to create a substantive audience for themselves, deriving from this effort a form of collective recognition unheard of since Antiquity. This survey course examines some of the ways in which these men and women outlined, both in their writings and in their way of life, specific understandings of what the public practice of philosophy should be. The focus is not on the study of philosophical doctrines or systems per se. Rather, the class asks why and how the public — and often specifically literary — practice of philosophy became, in France, a distinct social and political possibility. To this end, careful attention is paid to the social and institutional settings in which (and, in many cases, outside of which) these writers conducted their activities. We also examine how they created or mobilized a variety of literary genres to circulate their thoughts (essays, narratives, autobiographical writings, etc.). Discussions will also consider how these publications worked to transform and/or uphold the society in which they appeared, with the aim of shedding light on how key representations of public philosophical activity — such as enlightenment or engagement — were developed. Readings start with Foucault, Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir, moving backwards to Montaigne and Descartes, and from there Rousseau and Madame de Staël.

This class will introduce you to the cultural and intellectual history of France over four centuries. It will develop your capacity to engage with Continental philosophy as well as your ability to read, analyze, and comment upon French literary works in translation. This class also focuses on developing your writing skills. All readings, lectures, class discussions and written work are in English.

subject: FRENCH
title: What Is a Peasant? Being Political Aware in 1848
description:
This class is taught in English.

1848 in Europe was a year of revolution against authoritarian forms of rule. In France it saw the founding of the Second Republic. Yet within a few years, France had become an Empire again, and this new form of authoritarian rule would last roughly twenty years. What happened?  Central to the story people often tell of these years in France is the figure of the peasant. What kinds of politics to peasants have?  Why do they vote the way they do? How do they come by the political awareness they have? At the center of our study this semester will be one novel by Honoré de Balzac, The Peasants and two by George Sand, The Sins of Monsieur Antoine and The Master Pipers, all three of which are attempts to think about the place of the peasantry in mid-nineteenth-century French society and in larger political histories. Along with reading the three novels, we will read related texts by other nineteenth-century thinkers: Michelet, Proudhon, Marx as well as work by contemporary historians that take different approaches to understanding the figure of the peasant and the shape of nineteenth-century French (and European) cultural, political, and social history.  We’ll be interested in how novels both reflect, and reflect on the political trajectories of their moment, and, more generally, in how to think about what it means to be politically aware and engaged in the context of the mid-nineteenth century. Writing assignments and readings in English for nonmajors; writing assignments and French readings in French for French majors and minors.

subject: FRENCH
title: The Cultures of Franco-America
description:
In this course, we will consider a broad range of literary and cultural texts that emerge out of the long history of the French in North America and of Americans in France. Our readings will include novels, poetry, and short stories—including the earliest known work of African American fiction, written in French and published in Paris in 1837. Alongside these literary texts produced by French writers in America and American expatriates in France, we will consider travel narratives and missionary accounts describing interactions between European and Native American populations; historical, ethnographic, and political writings; foodways and other popular cultural forms such as music, comic strips, films, and television programs.

Throughout the semester, our discussions will focus on the politics of representation— we will work to understand the processes through which categories of “race” are shaped over time through the interplay between Anglo- and Franco-American cultures and ideologies, even as these categories are challenged from the perspectives of minority populations. As we trace these processes of racialization, we will be particularly attentive to intersections between “race” and class, gender, and sexuality; at the same time, we will consider the ways in which all of these categories of identity are inflected by language, by regional and national forms of belonging and exclusion, and by the presence of “mixed-race” communities.

Over the course of the semester, our readings will include selections from the following texts/authors: The Jesuit Relations, François René de Chateaubriand, Alexis de Tocqueville, Hippolyte Castra, Armand Lanusse, Victor Séjour, Kate Chopin, Louisiana Story (dir. Robert Flaherty), Jean Arceneaux, J’ai été au bal (dirs. Blank & Strachwitz), James Baldwin, Gwendolyn Bennett, Langston Hughes, Josephine Baker (cinematic performances), William Gardner Smith, M.F.K. Fisher, Samuel Chamberlain, Julia Child, Michael Pollan.

subject: FRENCH
description:
This class is taught in French.

Ce cours est destiné aux étudiant(e)s qui désirent se familiariser avec les bases de la linguistique française. Aucune expérience en linguistique n’est requise, mais une bonne connaissance du français parlé et écrit s’impose. Le cours abordera les domaines principaux de la linguistique : la phonétique et la phonologie, la morphologie, la syntaxe, la sémantique, et la pragmatique, ainsi qu’une brève introduction à la sociolinguistique. Le but sera de présenter des concepts et des outils essentiels qui permettront une exploration ultérieure plus approfondie. Nous commencerons par un bref survol historique pour encadrer la discussion de notions telles que « langue », « langage », 
« signe », « mot », « phrase » et « grammaire ».  Ensuite nous explorerons les sous-disciplines indiquées ci-dessus, avec des exercices pratiques pour concrétiser les principes présentés en classe et dans le manuel. Nous considérerons les différences (considérables !) entre le français parlé et le français écrit, nous étudierons la langue dans le contexte de son emploi dans la communication (y compris la communication en ligne), et nous finirons par appliquer des approches linguistiques à l’analyse du discours et de la conversation.

subject: FRENCH
title: Pronoun Wars
description:
Pronouns have become a hot-button political issue across the Western world in the past decade or so. These bitter and sometimes violent controversies have primarily revolved around the relationship between third-person pronouns and sexual identity, and in particular new gender-neutral pronouns (or new, gender-neutral usages of existing pronouns, like “they”). But they also touch on antisexist or inclusive language more broadly. This course proposes a genealogy of these “pronoun wars.” We will begin the semester by looking at the current state of the debate in the francophone public sphere with a focus on France. Then we will turn our attention to the deeper roots of this issue, which lie in the decisive encounter, in the period running from roughly 1940 to 1990, between (1) the feminist, queer, and trans liberation movements, (2) experimental literature, and (3) structuralism in the social and human sciences.

This is a course in intellectual and literary history. It is structured around Monique Wittig’s pronoun trilogy: the coming-of-age novel L’Opoponax (1964), the science-fiction utopia Les Guérillères (1968), and the collection of gothic-erotic prose-poems Le Corps lesbien (1973). We will read the first two books in their entirety, and excepts from the third. Also on the syllabus: primary sources from an array of academic disciplines (anthropology, linguistics, literary criticism, sociology); literary texts (including work by Roland Barthes and Hélène Cixous); and ephemera (activist pamphlets, newspaper articles); as well as historiography about linguistics, feminism, and literature.

subject: FRENCH
title: Scenes from the History of the Novel
description:
This seminar has both an introductory and a research dimension. On the one hand, it will present students with an overview of the early (pre-Realist) French novel, along with critical-theoretical milestones on the genre’s “rise.” But we will also have a more specific goal, which is conceptualizing changes in the use of scenes in fictional narratives over a span of 150 years.

The scene-summary distinction is among the oldest in narratology. Summary telescopes a temporally dilated series of important actions by excluding the proximate context and details of each. By contrast, scenic narration approaches the pace of recounted events by restoring detail, often plunging the reader into the sensory world of the characters. By some accounts, scenes start to push out summary in the nineteenth-century novel, leading to the critical orthodoxy expressed in the Jamesian injunction, “Show, don’t tell.” So the question for us will be: Is it possible to see the modern scene emerge in these earlier novels? Or are they organized around entirely different (and coherent) narrative principles?

subject: FRENCH
title: Le roman comme expérience: Littérature, savoirs, engagement
description:
Course discussions will take place in French.
In this seminar, we will study the influence of politics and science on literature. Our focus will be on three writers associated with the Nouveau Roman: Nathalie Sarraute, Alain Robbe-Grillet, and Roland Barthes. We will read their work in relationship to three contexts: (1) Jean-Paul Sartre’s call for political commitment (engagement); (2) the querelle de la nouvelle critique, the conflict over historicist and structuralist approaches to literary criticism; and (3) the rise of the social and human sciences (SHS; in particular, anthropology, linguistics, and psychoanalysis).

All three authors defended aesthetic experimentation in literature and produced a “double corpus” composed of novels/narratives and essays. As we read, we will ask: What is the relationship between formal innovation and the competing claims that politics laid on literature during this period? What is the relationship between these formal elements and the SHS’ claim to interpret the human? Did this combination help them articulate a rejection of political engagement, or to rearticulate it in a different form? Finally, how can we understand the relationship between a given writer’s narratives and essays?

Readings primarily from J.-P. Sartre, C. Lévi-Strauss, N. Sarraute, A. Robbe-Grillet, R. Barthes.

subject: FRENCH
title: French Culture and the History of Emotion
description: From "Crimes of Passion" to existentialist melancholy the French have defined, in large measure, the ways in which western culture has understood and reflected on the emotions.  In this course we will study the complex history of emotion--of passion, affect, and sensation. Through a study of literature philosophy, painting, and film we will examine the ways in which different emotions have been understood and "located" in the self, as well as the ways in which writing about the emotions has shaped cultural history.  Among the topics to be studied:  why are certain emotions "in vogue" at different historical moments?  How can we "read" emotions in the body?  When is an emotion not an emotion?  Among the writers and artists to be studied:  Montaigne, Racine, Moliere, Rousseau, Barthes, Colette, LeBrun, David, Delacroix, Romer, and Manet.

subject: FRENCH
title: Introduction to Translation Studies
description:
This course provides a general introduction to translation studies. Translation studies is a relatively new field which lies at the intersection of a range of disciplines from literature and linguistics, through gender and postcolonial studies, to cognitive and computer science. We will explore the history of the way that people have thought about translation from the ancient world and thinkers such as Cicero and Dao’an to the formal field of translation studies which emerged in the 1980s. We will also explore translation studies as a field today, discovering the many different theories and methods that can be used to understand what translation is as a linguistic, textual, and socio-cultural practice. This will involve looking not just writing about translation but also analyzing specific translations and the choices made by translators. One thread running throughout the course is the central role that translation plays in our multilingual world. We will discover that translation is everywhere but is often invisible so we will discover the role that it plays shaping not just literature but also the media, science, technology, politics, diplomacy, the law, and business. The course will also highlight the importance of translators themselves.

You will be asked to carry out some translation in this course but this does not mean that you need knowledge of French or any other language; students can opt to translate between different registers and varieties of English instead of using another language. ASL and other sign languages can also be used for translation exercises.

Fulfills Social & Behavioral Sciences, L&S Breadth requirements

By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1.	Chart the history of thinking about translation
2.	Map the current discipline of translation studies
3.	Situate, analyze, and compare different texts about translation
4.	Apply appropriate theories and models to specific translations and translation choices
5.	Use appropriate methods and tools to reveal the importance of translation in a range of different contexts

course.subject: FRENCH
course.title: English Composition in Connection with the Reading of Literature
course.description: This course is designed to fulfill the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement. The primary goal of this course is to develop students' reading and writing skills; a series of assignments will allow them to formulate observations made in class discussions into coherent argumentative essays. Emphasis will be placed on the refinement of effective sentence, paragraph, and thesis formation, keeping in mind the notion of writing as a process. Other goals in this course are a familiarization with French literature and the specific questions that are relevant to this field. In addition, students will be introduced to different methods of literary and linguistic analysis in their nonliterary readings.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Worldings: Regions, Peoples and States
course.description: Geography is a way of thinking deeply and expansively about our place in the world and this course is designed to transform how you think about America though understanding its place within a global context. Through concepts central to the field of geography such as space, nature, empire and globalization we will explore the issues of race, culture, ethnicity that pepper the pages of newspapers almost every day in stories of immigration, police violence, global warming, ethnic cleansing, and terrorism.  We explore these issues in a way that will change how you understand both America and the world.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: How Modernization and Colonialism Shaped Israel/Palestine
course.description: This course uses the paradigms of modernization and colonialism to examine the dramatic spatial transformation of Israel/Palestine since the end of the Ottoman Empire. It explores British and Ottoman perceptions, the rise of Zionist colonization, and the establishment of the State of Israel to understand their impact on modern urban and rural spaces. Topics include the contested lasting effect of the Biblical gaze, town planning and architecture as colonial tools, urban heritage and its decolonization, and the ongoing displacement of Palestinian and other communities. It is ideal for students in geography, sociology, political science, and design and those interested in Jewish, Israeli and Middle Eastern studies.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Writing the World
course.description: This course delves into written narratives that reflect and engage with diverse worldviews. Students will engage in close readings of texts from various cultures and regions, examining how writers navigate language, identity, and power. The course will use discussions, writing workshops, and collaborative projects, to refine critical thinking, research skills, and written expression. Topics in the course will include: • Cultural Perspectives in Literature: Analyzing how cultural backgrounds shape narrative styles, themes, and characters in literature from around the world. • Writing Across Borders: Exploring border narratives. • Translation: Examining the complexities of translating literary works across languages.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Geographic Film Production
course.description: What makes a film geographical? How can we explore humans’ relationships to their environment through sound and image? How might we make nonfiction films which foreground place and give it actual agency and voice? How can we use documentary film practices to depict place, culture, society, gesture, movement, rhythm and ﬂow in new and exciting ways? This is a production workshop where each student will conceptualize, shoot, and edit one short documentary film project that centralizes some aspect/s of geographic thought. This course is geared towards first time filmmakers. All film projects must fit the theme designated by the instructor, per term.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Global Environmental Politics
course.description: The course focuses on the political, economic, social, and cultural factors shaping the relationships between societies and the environment in different global contexts. Topics include land tenancy and land use change, resource extraction, agro-industrial development, environmental justice, water politics, militarism, and the politics of alternatives and solutions to environmental crises.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Physiography and Geomorphologic Extremes
course.description: In this course we review the physical landscapes and surface processes in extreme environments: hot arid regions, glacial and periglacial landscapes, and karst terrane. Using this knowledge, plus an understanding of tectonics and temperate watersheds (gained from prerequisite courses), we explore how unique combinations of geomorphic processes acting on tectonic and structural provinces have created the spectacular and diverse landscapes of North America. Regions to be explored include the Colorado Plateau, Sierra Nevada, North Cascades, Northern and Southern Rockies, Great Plains, Appalachian Highlands, and Mississippi Delta.
course.requirements: 140A (formerly 140), or Geology 117, or equivalent.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Global Climate Variability and Change
course.description: The course presents a conceptual basis for understanding of the workings of the global climate system, and how they conspire to bring about change. The goal is to give the student a climate dynamics basis for understanding global climate change.  Covered topics include observations of the climate system; the earth's energy balance; atmospheric radiative transfer; atmospheric circulation; the role of the ocean and the cryosphere; climate variability on various timescales; climate feedbacks and climate change.
course.requirements: Concepts in physics are used in the text, so knowledge at the level of first course in undergraduate physics is recommended; you should have at least taken physics at high school level.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Preparing for Community Engaged Research
course.description: The first of two related courses, this course introduces students to the idea of community engaged research in general and Community Geography specifically. We first do some conceptual groundwork. What is the public? What are counterpublics? What is community? Why would we want to engage with them, who are we to do so, and how can we do so as members of UC Berkeley, among other communities? Next, we look closely at community-engaged research projects, giving special attention to the methods employed and the forms of research produced. This section of the course is not comprehensive; it examines a few methods, approaches, and projects community-engaged researchers can pursue in the hopes of inspiring future student projects.

subject: GEOG
title: Capitalism and Climate
description: The relations between capitalism and climate are an urgent issue. Did climate play a role in the origins of capitalism? Could capitalism have arisen and spread without fossil fuels? How have coal, oil and gas shaped economic growth, labor, everyday life and the environment? We will review the effects of a warming climate on people and economies in various parts of the world, and we will ask whether climate change poses a threat to capitalism’s continued dominance. Who has suffered and who has benefited from extreme weather events such as hurricanes and floods? We will also explore the politics of climate change in the US since the 1980s: When did the scientific consensus about global warming emerge? When and why did it become a partisan issue in Washington? What role has the fossil fuel industry played in preventing policies and regulations to combat climate change? How has climate change skepticism emerged and evolved? Finally, we will survey proposals for mitigating climate change and adapting to it. Why do so many of these proposals rely on markets rather than legislation? Where can we find other ways to confront this enormous problem?

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Special Topics in Geography
course.description: This course is designed to provide a vehicle for instructors to address a topic with which they are especially concerned; usually more restricted than the subject matter of a regular lecture course. Topics will vary with instructor. See departmental announcements.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Ecological Marxisms
course.description: This course explores the writings of Karl Marx, some of his critics, and some contemporary thinkers influenced by his critical project, with the goal of understanding whether or not Marxism and ecology are compatible. After reading relevant parts of Marx’s writings, we turn to environmentalist thinkers who saw in Marx an inherent commitment to industrialization, which they understood to be necessarily antithetical to the natural world. Finally, we turn to contemporary eco-Marxists who return to Marx in light of climate change and other pressing environmental issues.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Racial Ecologies
course.description:
This course will introduce the ways race and racism are relevant to ecological processes and management through topics that broadly span both environmental and climate justice, while also exploring how we can understand non-dominant ways of knowing and relating to the environment, particularly focusing on Black and Indigenous ecologies and ecological relationships. In this course, students will learn the interconnections between ecological processes and the complexities that shape our social world. Students will learn how to apply a racial ecologies lens to the world around them. We will examine traditional and emerging directions in the fields of Political Ecology, Environmental and Climate Justice, Geographies of
race, and more.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Urban Field Study
course.description: In this course, we will critically “read" urban landscapes in the Bay Area. Walking tours, on-site lectures, individual wanderings, and archival research will explore built environments, spatial histories, and broader patterns of urbanism in Berkeley, San Francisco, Emeryville, Oakland, Pleasanton, and beyond. At every juncture, we will consider the dynamic interrelationships between built form and everyday life, becoming attuned to the power of landscape to both express and suppress identities and opportunities. We will travel by BART and on foot (~3 miles of walking per class!) to pursue ways to think critically about the spaces we inhabit, what remains to be explored, and the contours of our future.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Visual Geography
course.description:
This is a practice-based course in which students will shoot and edit photographic works that document and interpret the landscape and people along San Pablo Avenue from Oakland to Hercules, CA. Through the process of making photographs, analyzing them, editing them into a body of work, and critiquing them along the way, this course will
engage with questions of how photography can help us understand the people we encounter and the spaces we move through everyday.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Globalization
course.description: How do processes of production, exchange and consumption work in our contemporary era of volatility and fragility? This course takes a historical and geographical approach to understand how areas of the world have been incorporated into contemporary global processes differently.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Fundamentals of Geographic Thought and Research
course.description: This course is the first in a required three-course sequence for doctoral students in Geography. The course has three core aims. First, to help students see, think, and write geographically--that is, to interpret the making and meaning of physical and human landscapes. We will do so by exploring various concepts, theories, and methodologies in geography, focusing on nature-society relations. Second, to cultivate skills for conducting geographic research. We will do this through collaborative discussion of, and curiosity about, the range of approaches to geographic inquiry. Third, the course will foster cohort building through collective field trips and introducing students to the practices and expectations of scholarly work.
course.requirements: Required of all first year graduate students.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Traditions of Geographic Theory and Analysis
course.description: This course is the third in a required three-course sequence for doctoral students in Geography. The course has three core aims. First, to build a geographical perspective on canonical social theory. We will do this by reading texts that are often considered foundational with and through people who contested, undermined, and remade them. Second, to strengthen analytic and other scholarly skills, to be achieved by dedicating time to questions of method, argument, and interpretation in our discussion of texts. Third, through reading extensively and engaging with foundational texts, this course will also support the skill of reading endurance to equip students for their qualifying exams.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Nature and Culture: Social Theory, Social Practice, and the Environment
course.description: The relationship between societies and natural environments lies at the heart of geographical inquiry and has gained urgency as the rate and scale of human transformation of nature have grown, often outstripping our understanding of causes and effects. The physical side of environmental science has received most of the emphasis in university research, but the social basis of environmental change must be studied as well. Recent developments in social theory have much to offer environmental studies, while the latter has, in turn, exploded many formerly safe assumptions about how and what the social sciences and humanities ought to be preoccupied with. This seminar allows students to explore some classics in environmental thought as well as recent contributions that put the field on the forefront of social knowledge today.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Black Geographies
course.description:
This graduate seminar explores the inextricable connection between blackness and geography.
Considering Katherine McKittrick’s claim that Black geographies are “‘the terrain of political
struggle itself’ or where the imperative of a perspective of struggle takes place,” we will situate
the spatial relations of blackness by placing Black people at the core of spatial production and
examine the mechanisms by which this takes place. In this course we ask: what are the
limitations and possibilities of traditional geographies? How does Black geographic thought
produce wider material and conceptual space for geographic knowledge? How does Geography
account for and understand blackness as condition, experience, and imaginary?

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: The Art of the Pitch: Grant Writing, Research Proposals & Fellowships
course.description: This is a practical course with an emphasis on applying for grants and fellowships. Students will choose a fellowship program and complete application components during the course. We’ll also be conducting in person mock interviews. This class is most useful for those who plan to apply for a grant of fellowship such as the Foreign Language Area Studies grant (FLAS), a Fulbright Fellowship or similar funding opportunity that is based on a personal statement and research proposal.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Capital, Value, and Scale
course.description: This seminar focuses on major works in political economy and social theory concerning capitalism, human action, and space-time. We grapple with what "value" means in "Capital", paying particular attention to issues of historical specificity, abstract labor time, and the "value theory of labor." We spatialize the argument by a close reading of David Harvey, and we look at attempts to understand capital's relation to human action and other forms of value, in anthropology and the work of Pierre Bourdieu.  Finally, we take up the issue of scale in hope of formulating a coherent conceptual framework for integrating across scales, from the human-body (or even smaller scales) up to global, economic, cultural and ecological processes

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Freshman Seminar
course.description: The Freshman Seminar Program has been designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. Freshman seminars are offered in all campus departments, and topics vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to 15 freshmen.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Topics in Trace Gas Biogeochemistry
course.description: This graduate seminar will cover classic and modern research papers in trace gas biogeochemistry.  Specific topics will vary by semester and may include: greenhouse gases, ozone-depleting gases, biosphere-atmosphere exchange, tropical forest biogeochemistry, Arctic biogeochemistry, peatland/wetland biogeochemistry, atmospheric impacts of croplands, volatile organic compounds, field and lab methods, the evolution of Earth’s atmosphere, and air-sea gas exchange. Class sessions will involve the presentation, analysis and discussion of research papers in biogeochemistry. In addition, students will have the opportunity to present their own research, contextualized in the broader field of atmospheric biogeochemistry.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Geospatial Analysis for Biodiversity Research
course.description: This graduate seminar will provide an introduction to the theory and practice of geospatial analysis for biodiversity research. The course will consist of lectures on the nature of geographic data, representation of geographic information, sources of geospatial data, field sampling, and spatial analysis, modeling, inference, and uncertainty. Lectures will be complemented with reading discussions illustrating current research on biodiversity using geospatial data and analysis. The class will furthermore consist of field activities that will use geographic information science (GIS), remote sensing imagery, global positioning systems (GPS/GNSS), and field sampling to understand patterns of biodiversity across space and time.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Topics in Economic Geography
course.description: Research seminar on selected topics in economic geography.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Topics in Urban Geography
course.description: Research seminar on selected topics in urban geography.

subject: GEOG
title: Space, Visuality, and the Refusal of Catastrophe
description: John Berger argues that the work of art can offer an enduring resistant way of seeing, a form of “modern prophecy” that involves “a geographical rather than historical projection” because “it is space not time that hides consequences” of power, violence, or exploitation. And yet we live in a time of hyper-visibilization of certain forms of emplaced/ embodied violence. This course addresses this contradiction with tools from Marxist geography’s dialectical approach to space as produced, contested, and prone to crisis and restoration, in relation to changing regimes of visuality. Can the work of art still provide a point of critique? We approach these matters through a set of classic and contemporary works. Participants will work on a visual work or problem, to workshop a paper, receive comments and revise it during the course of the seminar.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Topics in Earth System Remote Sensing
course.description: Questions asked about a changing planet are strongly influenced by data collected across a variety of spatial and temporal scales. Remote sensing of globally distributed ecosystems and human landscapes enables the exploration of questions not possible without the extension of those dimensions. This course will focus on developing scalable Earth system research questions using a variety of tools including advanced remote sensing methods, image acquisition including UAV systems, data synthesis and analytical approaches, literature review, progress reporting, and student presentations.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Pedagogical Practices in Geography
course.description: This course centers the work of teaching as a foundational aspect of our practice as geographers. Undoubtedly, the interdisciplinary nature of geography provides multiple avenues from where we can address some of our most pressing social, environmental, economic and political dilemmas. But how do we bring theory to practice? And how do we do this in a classroom setting? To answer these questions, this course offers pedagogical frameworks and practical skills for how theory and practice connect for both instructors and students. We will begin with a review of pedagogical literature and an analysis of how foundational scholars like Paulo Freire and bell hooks approach teaching as an act of community-making and empowerment.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Introduction to Earth System Science
course.description: The goals of this introductory Earth System Science course are to achieve a scientific understanding of important problems in global environmental change and to learn how to analyze a complex system using scientific methods. Earth System Science is an interdisciplinary field that describes the cycling of energy and matter between the different spheres (atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, cryosphere, and lithosphere) of the earth system. Under the overarching themes of human-induced climate change, stratospheric ozone depletion, and biodiversity loss, we will explore key concepts of solar radiation, plate tectonics, atmospheric and oceanic circulation, and the history of life on Earth.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: California
course.description: California had been called "the great exception" and "America, only more so." Yet few of us pay attention to its distinctive traits and to its effects beyond our borders. California may be "a state of mind," but it is also the most dynamic place in the most powerful country in the world, and would be the 8th largest economy if it were a country. Its wealth has been built on mining, agriculture, industry, trade, and finance. Natural abundance and geographic advantage have played their parts, but the state's greatest resource has been its wealth and diversity of people, who have made it a center of technological and cultural innovation from Hollywood to Silicon Valley. Yet California has a dark side of exploitation and racialization.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: An Introduction to Geospatial Technologies: Mapping, Space and Power
course.description: This course offers an introduction to the increasingly diverse range of geospatial technologies and tools including but not limited to geographical information systems (GIS). Merging theoretical concepts with technical instruction, students will develop critical knowledge and skills in web-mapping, geographic information science and cartography, including how these tools take on and reinforce fundamental geographical concepts and shape our lives, our environments and, increasingly, our futures.

subject: GEOG
title: The World According to Moby-Dick
description: This Sophomore Seminar, “The World According to Moby-Dick” is an introduction to a geographer’s way of seeing the world, as we journey with a person who asks us to call him Ishmael, with a motley crew of sailors on a ship that leaves New England, across the Atlantic, with most of its journey across the Indian Ocean, and finally to the South Pacific. Through this journey on the Pequod, named for an enslaved and exterminated Native American tribe, we read Moby-Dick for its account of a world facing multiple crises. The only required reading is a physical copy of the 2018 Norton Critical Edition of Moby-Dick.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Sophomore Seminar
course.description: Sophomore seminars are small interactive courses offered by faculty members in departments all across the campus. Sophomore seminars offer opportunity for close, regular intellectual contact between faculty members and students in the crucial second year. The topics vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to 15 sophomores.
course.requirements: At discretion of instructor.

course.subject: CIVENG
course.title: Terrestrial Hydrology
course.description: A quantitative introduction to the hydrology of the terrestrial environment including lower atmosphere, watersheds, lakes, and streams. All aspects of the hydrologic cycle, including precipitation, infiltration, evapotranspiration, overland flow, streamflow, and groundwater flow. Chemistry and dating of groundwater and surface water. Development of quantitative insights through problem solving and use of simple models. This course requires one field experiment and several group computer lab assignments.
course.requirements: CHEM 1A, MATH 51, MATH 52, and PHYSICS 7A; or consent of instructor.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Atmosphere, Ocean, and Climate Dynamics
course.description: This course examines the processes that determine the structure and circulation of the Earth's atmosphere and ocean, and how they control regional and global climate. The approach is deductive rather than descriptive: to determine the properties and behavior of the atmosphere and ocean based on the laws of physics and fluid dynamics. Topics will include interaction between radiation and atmospheric composition; the role of water in the energy and radiation balance; governing equations for atmospheric and oceanic motion, mass conservation, and thermodynamic energy balance; geostrophic flow, quasigeostrophic motion, baroclinic instability, and dynamics of extratropical cyclones and wind-driven ocean gyres.
course.requirements: Mathematics 53, 54; Physics 7A-7B-7C.

course.subject: ESPM
course.title: Biogeography
course.description: The course will provide a historical background for the field of biogeography and the ecological foundations needed to understand the distribution and abundance of species and their changes over time. It will also discuss developing technologies (including genomic tools and environmental models) together with the availability of big data and increasingly sophisticated analytical tools to examine the relevance of the field to global change biology, conservation, and invasion biology, as well as sustainable food systems and ecosystem services.
course.requirements: BIO 1B

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: The American Landscape: Place, Power and Culture
course.description: What is America as a landscape and a place, and how do we know it when we see it? This course seeks to address such questions, to introduce ways of seeing and interpreting American histories and cultures, as revealed in everyday built surroundings—homes, highways, farms, factories, stores, recreation areas, small towns, city districts, and regions. It does so through the lens of cultural geography, an interdisciplinary practice that developed, in part, here at Berkeley. Our goal in this course is thus twofold: First, to develop literacy in the role of space and place in American culture, and second to develop a working knowledge of cultural geography as a practice.

course.subject: NWMEDIA
course.title: Cartographic Representation
course.description: This course introduces the art, science and politics of making maps in a mediated world. Much of the course focuses on key theories, concepts, principles in map design, visualization and communication, while building deeper theoretical, critical and experimental skills needed for the challenges of the future. This includes theories of new media, the history of cartography, the impact of the internet on critical, Indigenous and counter- approaches to mapping, contemporary media and cartographic arts including the experimental, expressive and artistic, and the technicalities of visualizing quantitative data through (carto)graphic design.

course.subject: LDARCH
course.title: Geographic Information Science
course.description: This course introduces the student to the rapidly expanding field of Geographic Information Systems (GIS). It addresses both theory and application and provides the student with a dynamic analytical framework within which temporal and spatial data and information is gathered, integrated, interpreted, and manipulated. It emphasizes a conceptual appreciation of GIS and offers an opportunity to apply some of those concepts to contemporary geographical and planning issues.
course.requirements: Some computer experience.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Introduction to Global Studies
course.description: This course is designed as an introduction to Global Studies. Using a social science approach, the course prepares students to think critically about issues of international development, conflict, and peace in a variety of societies around the world. As such, it provides students with a basic theoretical introduction to the impact of global interaction as well as an opportunity to explore such interaction in a variety of case studies.

course.subject: MELC

course.description: This course will introduce the student not only to ancient and modern Central Asia, but also to the role played by the region in the shaping of the history of neighboring regions and regimes. The course will outline the history, languages, ethnicities, religions, and archaeology of the region and will acquaint the student with the historical foundations of some of the political, social and economic challenges for contemporary post-Soviet Central Asian republics.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Writing Our Worlds
course.description: This course allows students to practice a variety of formats of writing leading toward exposition and argumentation. Students will develop fluency with sentence, paragraph, and thesis-development skills. This course delves into stories and narratives that reflect and engage with differing worldviews. Students will engage in close readings of texts from specific cultures and regions, examining how writers navigate language, identity, and power. The course will use discussions, writing workshops, and collaborative projects, to refine critical thinking, research skills, and written expression.

course.subject: GEOG
course.title: Storytelling in Place
course.description: As an R1B course, this class will include opportunities for students to express themselves and their ideas in writing, with an emphasis on writing, editing and rewriting. This course also aims to develop students' fluency in writing longer and more complex papers with specific attention to the development of research skills. Through reading and writing, this course will examine how places shape stories and how stories influence places. Drawing from the fields of geography, journalism, and creative writing, students will investigate the ways in which storytelling intersects with notions of place and identity. Through a combination of readings, films, and audio, students will also create their own place-based stories.

subject: GERMAN
title: Kafka and Modernism
description: Close readings of major works by Franz Kafka (1883-1924) will form the core of this course, especially of the novels Amerika and The Trial as well as a selection from The Complete Stories (all three volumes available in English translation as paperbacks from Schocken Books). The focus will be on narratives which complicate notions of linear and coherent identity through acts of performance – most prominently, the stories of the immigrant in America, of the ape addressing the academy, of the hunger artist in his cage, or of Josephine, the singing star of the mouse folk. Kafka’s riddled fiction is paradigmatic for the openness of modernist literature, and it has provoked a vast variety of interpretations, including biographical, psychoanalytical, theological, philosophical approaches. A reading of selected classic pieces of criticism, including Gilles Deleuze's and Felix Guattari’s Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature, as well as extracts from Kafka’s diaries and letters will raise fundamental questions of literary interpretation, focusing on questions of narrative voice and perspective and intertextual references. Our discussion of philosophical questions in Kafka’s texts will be expanded by historical contextualization, locating his writing in the multicultural force-field of Prague in the transition from Austrian rule to Czech nationalism and of the German speaking Jewish minority. The focus on laws and institutions of modern society in many of his texts will be central to our analysis. Kafka’s fascination with spectacles of popular entertainment such as cinema, circus and theatre performances has recently been documented as major inspirations for his literary production. These connections to other media and performance arts will open up a further dimension in our readings of these multivalent texts as sophisticated ‘minority acts’. We shall use some clips from films to complement our performance analysis.

course.subject: GERMAN
course.title: Kafka
course.description: One of the most significant and thought-provoking 20th century writers, Franz Kafka created works and fragments that continue to puzzle, inspire, deprogram, and transform their readers. We will explore Kafka’s writings in their literary qualities, their multifaceted cultural range, and their religious dimensions.

course.subject: GERMAN
course.title: Marx, Nietzsche, Freud
course.description: The aim of the course is to explore the central theoretical and philosophical premises of three of the most influential thinkers in the German-speaking world and to examine in detail several works in which problems of history, ideology, values, and methodology are considered. Lecture and readings in English.

course.subject: GERMAN
course.title: Politics and Culture in 20th-Century Germany: Fascism and Propaganda
course.description: This course will focus on the theory and practice of propaganda during the 12 years of the Third Reich. It takes a close look at the ideology the Nazis tried to transmit, the techniques, organization, and effectiveness of their propaganda. Challenging the idea of the total power of propaganda, it looks for the limits of persuasion and possible other reasons for which Germans might have decided to follow Hitler. Sources will include the press, radio, film, photography, political posters, and a few literary works of the time.

course.subject: GERMAN
course.title: Transnational Cinemas
course.description: This course will explore how experiences of migration, dislocation, or exile are visualized in cinema, and how processes of internationalization in film production and distribution intersect with the projection of a transnational global imagery. Some examples of transnational cinematic connections will be analyzed in historical perspective as well as contemporary examples of "migrant cinema." We will investigate how these films engage with debates about multiculturalism and assimilation/segregation of minorities, as scenarios of itinerancy and mobility are often intertwined with representations of ethnicity and gender.
