subject: HISTART
title: African Art at the de Young Museum: Nengi Omuku: The Gathering
description:
Nengi Omuku: The Gathering–opening at San Francisco’s de Young Museum in summer 2026–is the third exhibition curated by Natasha Becker that places the work of contemporary African artists in dialogue with the historical arts in the museum’s permanent collection. Omuku’s luminous, layered compositions–painted on a Nigerian fabric called sanyan–are ambiguous explorations of community and group identity. Her paintings imagine idealized scenes of assembly, community-building, and sanctuary, but they also reference practices of gathering inflected by real-world strife and inequality–particularly in Lagos, the Nigerian megacity where Omuku lives. This ambiguity resonates with the complex dynamics of the historical African artworks; the collection’s masks, sculptures, and textiles idealize forces that connect and unify, but they can also reinforce social, political, and ritual hierarchies. In this course, our rigorous engagement with this exhibition–including research on Omuku’s paintings and on the historical works–will serve as a springboard for our exploration of key themes in contemporary and historical African art.  

	R1B is the second installment in the university’s reading and composition sequence; this course is therefore designed to help students develop advanced critical reading, writing, and research skills. We will use the course materials to learn and practice methods of textual and visual analysis (involving close reading and looking). In writing assignments, which will increase in length and complexity over the course of the semester, students will practice crafting clear, concise, and insightful arguments about artworks. Students will learn how to find and engage with library resources, conducting research collaboratively for the midterm paper and independently for the final paper. For the final 10-12 page paper, students will develop their own research questions on objects related to the course topic and present original arguments based on visual analysis and scholarly research.

subject: HISTART
title: Image and/as Identity in pre-Colonial and Colonial Mexico
description:
This course explores how visual and material culture both reflect and construct Mexican identities over time by considering the role images play in the formation of a shared imagined community. By looking closely at select objects from the sixteenth century through the twentieth century, we will see how the colonized peoples of Mexico imagined their own histories through identity-making and how they were subject to the colonial power’s attempt to define their identities. Across five centuries of art history–beginning with sixteenth-century codices; then considering seventeenth-century “conquest” paintings, eighteenth-century casta paintings, and nineteenth-century landscape paintings; and concluding with twentieth-century performance art — we can discern identities being formed, reshaped, elided, reconstructed, and even corrupted. These formations subvert easy explanation; through case studies, we will explore the complex ways in which propaganda, mytho-histories, and mythologies shape national and other identities.

Over the course of the semester, you will be exposed to and practice increasingly complex methods of visual analysis, and you will learn how to conduct research that can productively inform your interpretations of Mexican and other artworks. During the second half of the semester, you will develop a research project culminating in a 10–12-page paper on a topic related to the course.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Global History
course.description: History 1 introduces students to core dynamics of global history. Traversing the experience of human societies from earliest origins to the complex, chaotic, and cacophonous twenty-first century, the course highlights recurrent themes including the origins and development of political order; the evolution of interstate (or international) relations; and the historical advance of globalization. From this vast panorama, students will acquire a broad, even foundational, perspective on the human past and new insight into transcendent problems in the human experience.

subject: HISTORY
description: The history of Africa is extraordinarily complex and rich in both tragedy and achievement. In this course, important issues in African history will be introduced including the following: how and why complex societies formed in Africa; the technological responses of different Africans to environmental changes; how various cultures, religions, and state ideologies helped to organize African social and political life; the effects of the trade in enslaved Africans on African social and political structures; the impact of European colonial rule on the continent; the political economy of post-colonial Africa; and some of the ways in which modern Africans have experienced the enormous transformations which have occurred in recent decades from globalization, pandemic disease and different episodes of violence. Our goal will be to achieve both an analytic sophistication in understanding the historical processes which have defined different parts of Africa over time, and an appreciation for the ways in which Africans have explained and understood their experiences in a variety of media.

subject: HISTORY
title: Sports and Gender in U.S. History
description:
This course welcomes all students to examine the social, cultural and political history of American sports, with a focus on sex roles, the body and public racial identities. From the colonial era through the long history of segregation to the growing empowerment of women, athletes have represented ideals of masculinity, femininity and nationalism. How have state, media, medical and corporate authorities framed winners and losers or placed limits on certain competitors? Readings, films, guest speakers and class discussion will emphasize the history of children's games, homophobia, coaching and fan behaviors, Olympic scandals and wartime teams (such as women's baseball leagues, and Little League ball in Japanese-American internment camps.) We'll consider gender, race and class in the history of strength training, recreation, mascots, sportswear, toys, body size and food. All cultural perspectives are welcome.

Instructor bio: Bonnie J. Morris is the author of 19 books and has taught women's sports history for twenty-five years, first at George Washington University and Georgetown, and recently on Semester at Sea, as well as at Cal. She is also a women's history consultant to Disney Animation, the Smithsonian and the State Department. Her new book, What's the Score, includes reflections from many students who enjoyed taking this course at Cal.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Special Topics in the History of the United States
course.description: Designed primarily to permit the instructors to deal with topics with which they are especially concerned, usually more restricted than the subject matter of a regular lecture course. A combination of informal lectures and discussions, term papers, and examinations, with all grading by the instructor. Instructors and subjects to vary.

subject: HISTORY
title: Fascism and Propaganda in the "Third Reich"
description: This course will focus on the theory and practice of propaganda during the 12 years of the Third Reich. It takes a close look at the ideology the Nazis tried to transmit, the techniques, organization, and effectiveness of their propaganda. Challenging the idea of the total power of propaganda, it looks for the limits of persuasion and possible other reasons for which Germans might have decided to follow Hitler. Sources will include the press, radio, film, photography, political posters, and a few literary works of the time.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Special Topics in European History
course.description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may also explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the complex political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors and subject will vary.

subject: HISTORY
title: Land of Three Religions: Spain in the Middle Ages
description: This course is devoted to the history of the Iberian Peninsula, home to modern Spain and Portugal, during the Middle Ages. The simultaneous presence of large communities of Christians, Jews and Muslims, and the influence they had on one another, distinguishes Iberia from (most of) the rest of medieval Europe. That phenomenon will be a major theme throughout the course. In chronological terms, it begins with the conquest of the peninsula by armies from North Africa in 711, establishing Muslim rule over the majority of the region. It then examines the era of Muslim ascendancy after 711, before turning to the small Christian kingdoms in the far north. In the eleventh century, political and cultural initiative shifted in their direction, and they achieved predominance on both counts by the dawn of the fourteenth century. The last part of the course takes us from 1300 until the defeat of Granada, the last Muslim realm, by the Kingdom of Castile in 1492. That same year, the Jewish population of Castile was expelled by royal command, bringing the religious diversity of medieval Spain to an end. There is no textbook for the course, though there are two shorter texts you will need to purchase or borrow. All other readings will be provided through bCourses.

subject: HISTORY
title: Carvings, Crosses, and Conversion: The History of Religion in Latin America
description: In this course, we will examine the history of religion in Latin America from the precolonial era to the present. Starting with indigenous religions prior to the arrival of Europeans, we'll cover the arrival of African, Middle Eastern, and European religious practices to the region and how they changed and developed over the last 500 years of the region's history. Topics will include: religious syncretism, Abrahamic religions in the New World, the continuation of indigenous religious practices, secularization, and the confluence between religious thinking and social practice. Along the way, we'll examine what religion is, how it works, and what it does in society. The course will be organized as an interactive lecture, with readings combining primary and secondary sources.

subject: HISTORY
title: Japanese Colonialism
description: This course explores the origins and effects of Japanese colonial rule in Asia and the Pacific Islands from 1869 to 1945. Spanning from the indigenous lands of Hokkaido and Okinawa to Taiwan, Korea, parts of China, the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia, the Japanese empire affected the lives of millions of people in the twentieth century and beyond. Why did Japan pursue imperial expansion? How did experiences of Japanese colonialism vary depending on a colonized person’s nationality, race, gender, age, and/or class? How was empire dismantled—or not—in a post-World War II period of U.S. hegemony in Asia? We will address such questions by focusing on selected locales and groups of people throughout the empire, with emphasis on settlers, migrants, laborers, and others on the move. Students will learn how to critically analyze an array of primary sources, including legislation, treaties, photographs, fiction, comics, maps, and songs, as well as how to assess historical narratives about colonialism that profoundly shape communities in the present day.

subject: HISTORY
title: Apartheid in African and World History: Concept, System, and Law
description:
This course examines the emergence, operation, collapse, and legacy of the South African apartheid regime. To do so, we will consider not only the formation of the South African legal apparatus around apartheid in this country, but its extension into greater Southwest Africa and place in continental African history in the twentieth century. This course examines the political landscape that produced and maintained this political-legal regime, its effects on diverse groups of people, and the ways it came to prominence in international law and debates about systems of governance based on racial exclusion. As such, we will situate apartheid in South Africa within broader global currents that shaped the political, legal, and cultural history of colonialism and decolonization in Africa and elsewhere. Through a comparative examination of contexts in South Africa, Kenya, Mozambique, the United States, and elsewhere, our aim will be to develop a nuanced understanding of how the institutionalization and policing of race have shaped the course of events in world history both during the 20th century and since.

Instructor bio: Dr. Christian Alvarado (Ph.D., History of Consciousness, UC Santa Cruz) is a historian of Africa with broad interests in the continent's culture, politics, and role in global life. His courses examine the intellectual and material networks that connect societies on the African continent with other parts of the world. Dr. Alvarado has particular expertise in the history of colonialism and decolonization during the 19th and 20th centuries.

subject: HISTORY
title: Marriage in the Middle East
description:
In this course we will explore the history of the multi-ethnic (i.e., Arabs, Armenians, Greeks, Palestinians, Persians, Turks) and multi-religious (i.e., Christians, Muslims, Jews) Middle East through the lens of marriage. We will ask how political, ethno-religious, ideological and economic factors in the wider Middle East transformed marriage practices, laws, cultural and political conceptions of marriage over the course of 500 years. We will examine how the institution of marriage and the cultural imaginations of marriage have been shaped by laws, norms of gender and sexuality, interethnic and interreligious relations, international relations, class relations and economic networks. We will examine how marriage has served as a tool of power for empires and for settler-colonialism.

The overarching goal of this course is to familiarize students with the history of the Middle East from the sixteenth to the twenty-first century, while getting them to think critically about the institution of marriage on a historical spectrum. The lens of marriage will allow students to grasp the multi-ethnic and multi-religious dynamics of the Middle East, while comparing marriage practices, laws, and traditions across different polities, religious and confessional communities.

Students do not need to have taken a prior course on the Middle East. Lectures in class will provide a historical background to the assigned readings. Students will be asked to read scholarly works from the disciplines of history, anthropology and literature, watch documentaries and films, and provide critical analysis of the textual and visual materials both in classroom discussions, writing assignments and in a podcast recording project, as well as undertake a writing assignment on marriage based on interviews that students will conduct with a family member.

subject: HISTORY
title: Decolonization: A History of the Global South since 1945
description: In the first few years after the Second World War, the structure of global order fundamentally changed. New international institutions like the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank were created as sites for debating and managing the dissolution of European empires and the rise of a system of postcolonial nation-states. Postcolonial governments meanwhile embarked on historic social and economic experiments of national development. Revolution, counter-revolution, military coups, and civil wars appeared across what came to be called the “Third World,” as some European powers attempted to maintain their hold on the natural resources and markets of former colonial territories, while new global powers, like the United States and the Soviet Union, asserted their interests in the international arena. Political and ideological conflicts between capitalism and communism—as well as other transnational movements like pan-Asianism, pan-Arabism, Third World socialism, and political Islam—remade national and global political cultures, forging geopolitical blocs for leveraging distinct visions of global solidarity. This class examines the maelstrom of the post-1945 world, centering the voices and ideas of postcolonial movements for national liberation, global revolution, and political economic restructuring as the core texts that defined the second half of the twentieth century. Students will engage with recent and classic historiography investigating the origins and trajectories of global decolonization, focusing on critical turning points, key figures, and foreclosed pathways. While the course will draw primarily from examples in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, attention will also be paid to how the age of decolonization impacted the politics and culture of the United States and Europe as well. No previous experience with these themes is required for enrolling in the course.

subject: HISTORY
title: Enslavement and the Economy in the Roman Empire
description: Enslavement—not least because of the horrendous statistics on global human trafficking—remains an enduring phenomenon and a topic of central interest to historians. The extent and nature of involuntary servitude today is difficult to measure, because since Mauretania abolished slavery in 1981 (but a law prosecuting slaveholders passed only in 2007 and has been sporadically enforced) it is no longer legal anywhere. In contrast, involuntary servitude, or slavery, was entirely legal in the Roman empire. Ancient sources, both in Latin and Greek, the principal languages of the Roman empire, tell us a great deal about enslaved persons, but nearly exclusively from the perspective of the masters and owners. Further, it is very difficult to quantify slavery, to gain a sense of the proportion of enslaved persons in the labor force, their origin, or their percentage at different points in time. In part, this is due to the vast expanse of the Roman empire, with many regional differences, which included different forms of agricultural and other labor, different levels of urbanization, and so on. The assessment and characterization of slavery and its role in the Roman empire depends, perhaps more than with any other topic, on a scholar’s methods and assumptions, specifically, what they think about the Roman economy. Therefore, in this course we will read mostly ancient sources (in translation) that describe various aspects of slavery, but also some contemporary scholarly debates about enslavement in Rome based on different economic theories.

subject: HISTORY
title: Crusading Things
description:
This proseminar explores the surviving material culture of the European movements known as "crusades" that originated in the late eleventh century and continued into the early modern era. Examining how scholars have reconstructed and interpreted the surviving material evidence of these movements as forms of pilgrimage, the seminar introduces students both to the study of material artifacts as historical sources and to the wider history of religious and intercultural contact c. 1000-1500 in the Mediterranean basin. Over their centuries-long development, crusades were transformed from campaigns to wrest Jerusalem from Muslim control into wars against all non-Christians, against eastern orthodox Christians, and against people within Latin Christian Europe deemed "heretics." Their history affected multiple religious traditions and many social groups in addition to producing cultural change and artifacts (literary, musical, and material). In sum, they provide a capacious topic for historical research to those with varied interests in the premodern past of the lands and peoples surrounding the Mediterranean.

The proseminar's focus will be on "things," material objects related to the crusading era and its cultural interactions, rather than the military battles and codes of martial honor that dominated popular perceptions of the crusades. The course is reading and writing intensive; it also requires each student to select an object as a focus of their research and to complete several in-class presentations and writing assignments on it.

subject: HISTORY
title: Human Person and Total State: First Person Accounts from Europe’s Twentieth Century
description:
For many historians, diaries, letters, memoirs and other first-person accounts offer the most reliable conduit into the past. But such accounts vary greatly in style and purpose, not to mention author and experience. In this course we use firsthand sources to look behind the facades of experiments with fascism, racial war, and Marxian socialism, "tried out" upon millions of human beings in twentieth century Europe, from Germany through Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. By way of searching first person reflections we explore fundamental questions of identity, solidarity, commitment, and belief that seem unavailable within conventional institutional history of societies where states do not test individuals on an everyday basis. How do people structure lives of freedom when a regime seeks to control not just their public acts but private thoughts?  What does freedom mean under those conditions?

Historians have developed crude categories like resistance, accommodation, collaboration to describe the responses human beings developed to would-be totalitarian rule. In fact, these and other dimensions of experience overlapped in single lives. Through perspectives of sensitive observers—poets, but also an architect, worker, student, schoolteacher, and several journalists—this course seeks to deepen students' appreciation of the nuances of everyday existence in a region renowned for its complexity, but also to awaken an appreciation for firsthand accounts as historical sources. What do we learn from such accounts that is otherwise unimaginable? What might memory tell about an event that was invisible to direct observation?  What do people forced to live under totalitarianism want to tell us in our day?

subject: HISTORY
title: Nuclear Berkeley
description: In his book Golden Dreams: California in an Age of Abundance, 1950–1963, the eminent historian of California, Kevin Starr, described the rise of the University of California to world prominence as a research institution as inextricably bound to the “arts and sciences of nuclear warfare.” This course will trace the history and historical validity of that claim, examining the myriad ways in which UC Berkeley (and the broader Berkeley and Bay Area) was involved in nuclear developments including weapons design and testing, strategy and policy, and innovations in science, engineering, medicine, and energy. We will approach these topics through a variety of perspectives and frameworks. Through a combination of lecture, discussion, and independent work, students will ultimately be expected to produce a major piece of research on a slice of the history of Nuclear Berkeley that can take the form of a substantial final paper, podcast, website, QR-driven walking-tour, archival report, or other creative project. For students working on World War II-related Nuclear Berkeley projects, a goal will be to get those projects linked to the website for the National Park Service’s Manhattan Project National Historic Park. Curiously, the three physical sites of that historic park—Los Alamos, NM,  Hanford, WA, and Oak Ridge, TN were all made possible by UC Berkeley scientists—Robert Oppenheimer, Glenn Seaborg, and Ernest Lawrence, the latter two of whom won Nobel Prizes—and yet somehow UC Berkeley is not even listed among the Manhattan Project’s “other places” mentioned in the website. We hope that some students in this class can help begin to correct that egregious omission in the historical record.

subject: HISTORY
title: Voting Rights: Battles for Suffrage and Representation in the U.S.
description:
Voting is a core privilege and responsibility for all U.S. citizens, but the long history of suffrage in this country shows us that this was not always the case. This course explores the gradual and hard-fought battles by which the United States amended the category of eligible voters since the nation’s founding through the modern day. Social categories such as race, class, and gender were central to the process of strictly delimiting the electorate. Grassroots social movements opposed this exclusionary system and successfully pushed for legislation that won voting rights for women, African Americans, young people, and more. Despite this expansion, tactics such as gerrymandering, racial discrimination, and voter intimidation hindered the full implementation of voting rights—challenges that continue to shape American electoral politics today.


Select Readings:
Alexander Keyssar, The Right to Vote: The Contested History of Democracy in the United States
Ellen Carol DuBois, Suffrage: Women’s Long Battle for the Vote
Martha Jones, Vanguard: How Black Women Broke Barriers, Won the Vote, and Insisted on Equality for All
Jon Grinspan, The Virgin Vote: How Young Americans Made Democracy Social, Politics Personal, and Voting Popular in the Nineteenth Century
Allan Lichtman, The Embattled Vote in America: From the Founding to the Present

subject: HISTORY
title: Conscience and Contraception—Religion, Law, and Health in the United States
description:
In 2014, the US Supreme Court handed down its 5-4 decision in the Hobby Lobby case. A divided court held that the Affordable Care Act’s mandate to cover contraception violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA). The majority opinion said that the contraceptive mandate substantially burdened the sincerely-held religious beliefs of Hobby Lobby’s evangelical Christian owners. Encoded in the policy and legal language of “contraceptive mandate,” “RFRA,” “substantial burdens,” and “sincerely-held beliefs” are decades of competing ideas about the intersecting, and sometimes conflicting, roles of religion, law, and health in the United States. Indeed, some legal scholars have identified “the Hobby Lobby moment” as a major turning point in religious liberty jurisprudence, an explosive social, “legal[,] and political blockbuster” that upended decades of consensus and augured a more polarized future. Was it? Is this a legal claim, a historical claim, or both?

This seminar takes the Hobby Lobby decision as a starting point for looking at the history of conflicts over religion and law in the United States. We’ll carefully read primary sources like court opinions, tracing the evolution of church-state legal doctrine by exploring decisions made, arguments constructed, briefs referenced, and cases cited by judges. We’ll also read secondary sources, including legal scholarship and legal histories, alongside histories of religion, contraception, and corporations, to build out a robust understanding of the collisions and conflicts animating tension over religion and law in the modern United States. Throughout we’ll consider the interpretive similarities and differences in the histories and analyses written by practitioners (lawyers and judges) and scholars of law and history.

Note: this discussion-based seminar meets in person, and students must be able to regularly attend

subject: HISTORY
title: The Sound of Women's History
description:
Is there a soundtrack to women’s history? How have historic efforts to suppress women’s voices (or disbelieve them) resulted in alternative means of sharing information and stories? This course introduces students to the women’s music movement in the United States, starting with a history of women’s social movements, sex roles and cultural production with a focus on the oral archives of speech, song, and broadcast propaganda. We’ll examine advocacy for the education and political inclusion of women, as well as differences among women—ethnicity, race, class, sexuality, religion, gender expression—which prevented broader unity at critical turning points. The main approach will be studying the arc of recorded music bearing witness to resistance, from Harlem Renaissance blueswomen to coal mining women and, eventually, the women’s music and production of the late 1960s through the 1990s and well into the 21st century. The readings also draw attention to the backlash against feminism and the social conditions which still define and divide women today. Films, recordings and guest artists will enhance thoughtful written work on issues of gender in the arts and oral traditions, preparing students for critical engagement with social and policy issues of gender, sex roles and the body, through the historical framework of sound legacies. Some course readings will be available online and through bCourses, others provided by the instructor. These include Jamie Anderson, An Army of Lovers, Ginny Berson, Olivia on the Record, Candie Carawan, Sing For Freedom, Angela Davis, Blues Legacies and Black Feminism, Caroline Mitchell, Women and Radio: Airing Differences, Lucy O’Brien, She-Bop: The Definitive History of Women in Popular Music, Linda Ronstadt, Simple Dreams, and Jennifer Lynn Stoever, The Sonic Color Line. The class will be conducted weekly, in-person, and includes one off-campus field trip into San Francisco and one performance event (TBA).

Instructor bio: Bonnie J. Morris is the author of 19 books and has taught women's history for twenty-five years, first at George Washington University and Georgetown, and recently on Semester at Sea, as well as at Cal. She is also a women's history consultant to Disney Animation, the Smithsonian and the State Department.

subject: HISTORY
title: Gender and the Body in United States History
description:
In this discussion-based seminar, we will consider how theories of gender and the body have shaped one another in the United States, and how links between gender and the body have been challenged or affirmed to support social, political, and economic desires. By engaging with critical work by gender thinkers including Dorothy Roberts, Mary Fissell, Brianna Theobald, Dorothy Ko, and Peter Boag, students will analyze how gendered and embodied experiences were mediated by race, religion, region, and historical era in United States history. How does gender shape our interactions as individuals, and our manifestations of mass politics? How have divergent experiences and performances of gender impacted our global exchanges? How is gender confirmed or denied by cultural creations in politics and the arts? The course will examine gender and the individual body, the body politic at home and abroad, and our shared cultural corpus of literature, theater, and television. The goal of this seminar is to identify how different beliefs about people's bodies helped stabilize theories of gender, gender roles, and gendered realms, and how using gender as an analytical lens can illuminate historical experiences that extended far beyond the body's physical form.

Instructor bio: Dr. Suzanne Winter received her Ph.D. in History with a Designated Emphasis in Women, Gender, and Sexuality from the University of California, Berkeley and received her B.A. in biology and comparative literature from Swarthmore College. She is a cultural historian of medicine and gender with special interests in public institutions, political philanthrophy, and activist women in the long nineteenth century American West. Dr. Winter works as a historical consultant in the performance arts, and her research contributed to a forthcoming musical about Dr. Elizabeth Blackwell and the upcoming season four of the tv show The Gilded Age.

subject: HISTORY
title:
KICKING THE HORNET'S NEST:
America in the Middle East from Truman to Trump
description:
From the recognition of Israel in 1948 to the wars in Iraq, the Arab Spring, the Abraham Accords, and the 2026 U.S.–Iran War, the Middle East has occupied a central place in American foreign policy. This seminar examines how successive U.S. presidents understood the region, the assumptions that shaped their decisions, and the consequences of those decisions for both the United States and the peoples of the Middle East.

Organized chronologically around presidential administrations, the seminar explores major crises, wars, diplomatic initiatives, and turning points that have defined American engagement in the region since World War II. Through the study of presidential decision-making, students will assess the interaction of ideas, interests, domestic politics, ideology, and international pressures in the formulation of U.S. foreign policy.

The primary texts for the seminar are Kicking the Hornet's Nest: U.S. Foreign Policy in the Middle East from Truman to Trump and Indecision Points: George W. Bush and the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict. Together these works provide a historical framework for understanding how successive administrations confronted recurring challenges involving Arab-Israeli diplomacy, oil and energy security, Cold War rivalry, terrorism, regime change, regional war, and great-power competition.

The seminar concludes by examining the Biden administration, the 2026 U.S.–Iran War, and the return of President Trump, asking what eight decades of American involvement reveal about the possibilities and limits of American power in the Middle East.

Instructor bio: Dr. Daniel E. Zoughbie is an entrepreneur, complex-systems scientist, diplomatic historian, and expert on presidential decision-making. He is Associate Project Scientist at UCSF/UCB Center for Global Health Delivery, Diplomacy, and Economics in the Division of Health Policy and Management at the School of Public Health.  Zoughbie is Principal Investigator of Berkeley's Middle East and North Africa Diplomacy, Development, and Defense Initiative, a faculty affiliate at Berkeley's Institute of International Studies, and a faculty affiliate at the New England Complex Systems Institute in Cambridge. 

Zoughbie is the author of Indecision Points: George W. Bush and the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict (MIT Press, 2014), and Kicking the Hornet's Nest: US Foreign Policy in the Middle East from Truman to Trump (Simon & Schuster, 2025).  His award-winning global public health research has been published in academic journals, including PLOS Medicine, PLOS Complex Systems, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, BMC Public Health, PLOS Medicine, Frontiers in Epidemiology, Preventative Medicine, PLOS One, JAIDS, and Social Science and Medicine.

Zoughbie has been awarded grants from the World Diabetes Foundation, the International Diabetes Federation, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Fulbright Commission and Department of Education. He was named a TED Fellow, a Rainer Arnhold Fellow, a PopTech Fellow, and a Moderator of the Robin Hambro Seminar in Moral Philosophy at Oxford. He graduated Phi Beta Kappa from UC Berkeley, studied at Oxford on a Marshall Scholarship and completed his doctorate, also at Oxford, as a Weidenfeld Scholar. He is the founder of Microclinic International and was previously appointed to the Board of Directors for the San Mateo County Community Colleges District Foundation and to the Governing Board for CASA at the University of Arizona.

subject: HISTORY
title: The History of Neoliberalism
description: Neoliberalism has become a catchword in academia and media. In History it is often used to describe the profound economic and social changes that took place in the 1980s after the election of Margareth Thatcher in the UK and Ronald Reagan in the US. However, the roots of neoliberal thinking promoted by economists such as Friedrich Hayek and Milton Friedman go back to the end of the Second World War. In this seminar we will explore how these ideas found their way into conservative and social democratic party programs in the 1980s and 90s. We will specifically discuss the role of think tanks in promoting neoliberal ideas and economic policies on both sides of the Atlantic. In a next step we will look at the impact of neoliberalism in countries in the Global North (UK and US) as well as in the Global South (Chile and South Africa). We will end the seminar by discussing the future of neoliberalism.

subject: HISTORY
title: Oral Histories
description:
Oral histories are sources that offer perspectives, life experiences, and ways of knowing that official written records can overlook or actively seek to erase from the historical record. This seminar will explore the methods, theories, practices, and controversies that have shaped oral history as an academic field, while paying close attention to the contributions and critiques from activist oral history practitioners. In weekly readings and discussions, students will gain an appreciation for this (at times fraught) history, while also gaining a foundation in current best practices for doing oral history.

Students will also have multiple opportunities for putting their oral history training into practice. The first half of the course will be focused on student engagement with oral history theory and scholarship alongside existing oral history collections (as primary sources) towards developing an understanding of the field and studying various models for doing oral history. In the second half of the course, as we continue this work, students will develop and execute an oral history project on a topic of their choosing that will involve: background research, research design, interviewing (with digital recording), transcription, and presentation of research findings in both oral and written formats. Over the semester, students will learn how to incorporate oral histories into their research, with particular attention to research ethics and questions of how knowledge is produced and why that matters in our study of the past. Students will practice oral history methods, engaging with oral sources to learn ways of interpreting and analyzing oral histories through topics that interest them.

Instructor bio: Dr. Lilly Havstad is a historian of modern Africa and the world and a dedicated teacher-scholar who enjoys working with students from across disciplines to gain the valuable knowledge and skills of the historian’s craft (critical thinking, close reading, argumentation and evaluation of evidence, and more). Her research in post-World War II Mozambique and Portugal explores the at times radical ideas that urban African women and men shared across transnational 20th century intellectual and activist networks for a more humane world than was possible under Portuguese colonial-capitalism. In the classroom, Dr. Havstad encourages students to pursue their historical curiosities through student-led projects while introducing them to critical debates on how knowledge is produced and whose knowledge matters in how we study the past. She works hard to foster collaborative and student-centered learning environments where learning can be fun, meaningful, and challenging. Prior to joining the History Department at UC Berkeley this fall, she taught at Harvard University, Northeastern University, and Boston University.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Comparative History
course.description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
course.requirements: Consent of instructor.

subject: HISTORY
description: How is history created? This course is designed to welcome students into the History major and prepare them to research and write a capstone/thesis in history (in either the History 102 or 101A/101B seminars). To that end its goals are (i) to introduce students to the methods and practices of history and historians; (ii) to explore a variety of approaches to the discipline and discuss them in lecture; and (iii) to provide opportunities in section to practice and hone historical methods and techniques. You will learn both how to think like historians and how to “do” history—by which we mean how to ask historical questions and go about answering them. More than other history courses you have taken at UC Berkeley, or will take, this course is focused on active learning and skill acquisition. The syllabus is structured according to the historian’s process, beginning with how to ask historical questions, moving through how to locate primary sources, how to analyze them, and how to write new histories for either public or academic audiences. Lectures and sections will familiarize you with different approaches and methods, and will give you the tools to construct your own historical research projects.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: The Craft of History
course.description: The principal aim of this course is to prepare students to write a capstone/thesis in history (in either the History 102 or 101A/101B seminars). To that end, its goals are (i) to introduce students to the methods and craft of history; (ii) to model approaches to the discipline of history and provide exposure to methods in lecture; and (iii) to provide ample opportunity in discussion sections to practice and hone these methods. The course is offered in fall and spring semesters, and is designed to precede the required 103 and 101/102 seminars.

subject: HISTORY
description: This course offers an introduction to the history of the Roman empire, from the advent of monarchy at Rome in the first century BCE to the breakdown of central state authority in the fifth and sixth centuries CE. Major themes include the overlapping networks of social power in the Roman empire (both institutional and personal); the unity and diversity of Roman imperial culture; the changing relationship between state and society; the political economy of the Roman empire; and the geography and ecology of the Mediterranean world. Lectures will provide an essential historical narrative and interpretations of central problems in Roman imperial history, and discussion sections will give students an opportunity to engage with key texts and artefacts from or about the Roman empire. There are no prerequisites for this course.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Ancient Rome: The Roman Empire
course.description: A history of Rome from Augustus to Constantine. The course surveys the struggles between the Roman emperors and the senatorial class, the relationship between civil and military government, the emergence of Christianity, and Roman literature as a reflection of social and intellectual life.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: United States Legal and Constitutional History since 1850
course.description: This course explores some of the major questions and problems of United States legal history since 1850. The course weaves together historical and legal approaches and materials. Themes include federalism and the evolving nature of constitutional authority; citizenship and rights; law and economic change; law and social movements; and popular understandings of ‘the law.’ We will look to the “high” sphere of constitutional jurisprudence and to other legal and extra-legal arenas where law was applied, argued over, and worked out. By the end of this course, you should be able to analyze different kinds of legal texts; understand key legal concepts and doctrines; and make evidence-based arguments about core themes in legal history.

subject: HISTORY
description: History 130 explores the historical development of US foreign policy. The course addresses the making and implementation of national strategy; the evolution of the international system; and the uses of history in the making of policy. Topics covered include the rise and nineteenth-century expansion of the United States; the redefinition of national security in the twentieth century; US involvement in the world wars and the Cold War; and the dilemmas of post-Cold War U.S. foreign policy.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: American Foreign Policy
course.description: This course will explore the history of American foreign policy since 1776, focusing on diplomatic and military interactions and the evolution of American strategic thought. Students will also traverse the broader history of international relations and will engage some of the basic vocabulary of IR theory. Topics will range from the territorial expansion of the United States to the making of Cold War strategy and beyond. Students will be asked to consider how historical knowledge and reasoning might inform the making of foreign policy.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Social History of the United States: Creating Modern American Society: From the End of the Civil War
course.description: This course examines the transformation of American society since the Civil War. The lectures and readings give special attention to the emergence of city culture and its possibilities for a pluralistic society; the experience and effect of immigration in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; the revolution in communications and industry; changes in family dynamics, the emergence of modern childhood, schooling, and youth culture; changes in gender relations and sexuality; the problematics of race and the changing nature of class relationships in a consumer society; the triumph of psychological and therapeutic concepts of the self.

subject: HISTORY
description: As longstanding symbols in American history and culture, “Wall Street” and “Main Street” typically refer to streets that intersect at right angles and places that represent the antithesis of each other.  In this rendering, Wall Street is home to nefarious big banks run by greedy financiers with deep pockets, while Main Street is home to unassuming “mom-and-pop” shops patronized by ordinary people of modest means who live in the surrounding wholesome small towns. What’s good for one is not good for the other. This course, which will be co-taught by a historian and corporate law professor, will examine critical junctures in the intersection of Wall Street and Main Street in American history and culture over the course of the twentieth century, how and why Wall Street and Main Street have been understood to point in opposite directions, the extent to which that understanding makes sense, and how and why the relationship between Wall Street and Main Street has evolved over time.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Wall Street / Main Street
course.description: As longstanding symbols in U.S. history and culture, “Wall Street” and “Main Street” refer to streets that intersect at right angles and places that represent the antithesis of each other: Wall Street is home to nefarious big banks run by greedy financiers, while Main Street is home to “mom-and-pop” shops patronized by people of modest means who live in the surrounding wholesome small towns. This course will examine critical junctures in the intersection of Wall Street and Main Street in the 20th century U.S., how and why the two streets have been understood to point in opposite directions, the extent to which that understanding makes sense, and how and why the relationship between Wall Street and Main Street has evolved over time.

subject: HISTORY
description: A brisk introduction to the nearly two millennia of recorded Japanese history. As a survey,  the course gives attention to broad themes and problems in Japan's political, social, religious, and cultural/intellectual history. Topics include the dialectic of national and local identities in shaping Japanese politics, Japan's interaction with the Asian continent and the Western world, and the relation of past to present in modern times.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Introduction to the History of Japan
course.description: A brisk introduction to the nearly two millennia of recorded Japanese history. As a survey, the course gives attention to broad themes and problems in Japan's political, social, and cultural/intellectual history. Topics include the dialectic of national and local identities in shaping Japanese politics, Japan's interaction with the Asian continent and the Western world, and the relation of past to present in modern times.

subject: HISTORY
title: The Great Transformations
description: This course looks at the massive economic and social changes that shaped the 20th century. As a compass that guides us through the century we will use the work of the Austro-Hungarian economic historian Karl Polanyi who in mid-century published the seminal book The Great Transformation. Therein Polanyi describes the pitfalls of an ultra-liberal capitalism that had emerged in the 19th century and predicted the more regulated from of capitalism that took shape after the Second World War. Polanyi did not foresee that the period of extraordinary growth and prosperity in the 1950s and 60s was followed by another major transition in the 1970s. The century’s second Great Transformation contained a return of a more (neo)liberal form of capitalism. The liberalization of markets and the cutting-back of the state was followed by a new wave of globalization and financialization and, ultimately, the 2008/9 financial crash.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: The International Economy of the 20th Century
course.description: Development and crises of the advanced economies, with particular emphasis on trade relations with third world countries. Economic impact of war, business cycles, and social movements. This course is equivalent to Economics 115; students will not receive credit for both courses.

subject: HISTORY
description: In the late fifteenth century, the world of traditional European Christianity began to collapse. The result were a series of religious and political revolutions that shaped the fate of both modern Christianity, and modern history more broadly. This course will guide students from the early years of this crisis to the age of eighteenth century revolutions. Along the way, we will meet religious reformers like Martin Luther and John Calvin, but also great Catholic thinkers of the age, like the founder of the Jesuits, Ignatius Loyola, and the Catholic mystic Teresa of Avila. We will also dig deep into the religious wars of the period, the many efforts to end them, and the uneasy rise of ideals like pluralism and toleration. The course readings will offer students the opportunity to engage major writers from the period in their own words, as well as important secondary texts. By the end of the class, students will have a firm grasp not just on the religious upheavals of the early modern era, but also of the religious politics that continue to shape our world today.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: The Reformation of European Christianity, 1500-1800
course.description: The European Reformations—when the old world of Latin Christendom collapsed—transformed not only Christianity, but also the political and cultural landscape of Europe. This course will explore the late medieval church, the birth of Protestantism, and the refashioning of the Catholic world, investigating the connection between these religious upheavals and the formation of modern political society. Battles between Catholics and Protestants, repression of religious heresy, witchcraft trials, the imposition of Christianity on New World peoples: these struggles helped create the political, legal, and religious orders of modern states. By understanding them, we'll seek to understand the religious and political complexities of our modern world.

subject: HISTORY
description:
This is an upper-division survey of French History from the Renaissance through the French Revolution (1500-1800). The course tracks the rise and fall of the French monarchy over the course of the early modern period. Out of the religious conflicts of the sixteenth century, France emerged as the most powerful nation in Europe under the rule of Louis XIV. But at the end of the eighteenth century “the old regime” was overthrown by revolution. We will examine the reasons behind this trajectory—why France became the home of absolutism, the Enlightenment, and democratic revolution. Along the way we will use France to understand broader developments of early modernity: the rise of the state; religious conflict; the little Ice Age; the transition to capitalism; overseas colonialism; and peasant and workers’ rebellions. Readings will include primary sources as well as classic works in social, cultural, and intellectual history. 

Instructor bio: Oliver Cussen is a historian of old regime France and its colonial empire. Originally from the UK, he studied at King’s College London and the University of Oxford before taking a PhD at the University of Chicago, where he taught for five years. In 2027 he will join Pomona College as Assistant Professor of Early Modern European History. His research has been published in the Journal of Modern History, Critical Historical Studies, and French History, and he writes occasionally for the London Review of Books. He is currently finishing a book about French colonialism in the eighteenth century.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Modern France: Renaissance to Revolution
course.description: This is an upper-division survey of French History from the Renaissance through the French Revolution (1500-1800). The course explores the economic, political and cultural factors that allowed France to emerge as the most powerful nation and global actor in Europe from the end of the middle ages to the reign of Louis XIV. We examine the extent of the kingdom's military, political and cultural influence and the realities of everyday life in 16th and 17th century France. We then turn to the key developments of the eighteenth century—capitalism, colonialism, global conflict and Enlightenment—that led to the collapse of French monarchy in 1789 and the unfolding of the first democratic revolution in the West.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Modern France
course.description: This course explores modern France and its place in the world.  We begin with the French Revolution, one of the truly earth-shaking events in history, and then we follow French history through a series of monarchical, authoritarian, and democratic regimes. In the process, we will also trace the emergence, expansion and decline of a great colonial empire. Issues of focus include French cultural and intellectual life; empire as a way of life not only for colonists but also for those living in mainland France; religion; immigration; battles over “who is French”; and dramatic changes in French economy and society during the past two centuries.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Renaissance and Baroque Italy 1350-1800
course.description: This course will focus on the history of Italy during a period when it was the leading center of European artistic and cultural production and the driving force in the revival of classical learning and literary ideals. At the same time, Italy was a political battleground through most of this period, both in the realm of ideas and theory but also in a literal sense. It was in Italy that "the art of war," as Machiavelli called it, took center stage as the peninsula became one of the major theaters of war between the great powers of the age, France and Spain. We'll study the artistic, intellectual, religious, and political history of Italy both as it developed internally and as it was related to the rest of Europe and the Mediterranean world.

subject: HISTORY
description: What makes an empire powerful? This course seeks answers in the history of Imperial Russia under Europe's last autocrats, the Romanovs. The two most consequential Romanovs, Peter the Great and—later—Catherine the Great, decided that command of the latest technologies was key, whether economic, military, or political. They also settled on size as a good measure. Consequently, both took Russia to war, using new technologies to transform Russia from a landlocked kingdom into a sprawling naval power, conquering territories from the Baltic states to Ukraine and Poland. Later rulers would further expand its boundaries into the Chinese Empire and Central Asia. By 1900, the Romanovs governed a multi-ethnic population of over 100 million people, speaking over 100 languages. They quickly discovered, however, that this diversity was a destabilizing factor. Resistance to expansion was often violent and grew pervasive with the spread of ethnic nationalism. Another definition of power emerged: one that measured strength by the capacity to discipline rebellious elements in the population, or, better yet, secure obedience by non-violent means. As leaders across the globe embrace and celebrate autocracy and territorial conquest, Imperial Russia is a good place to learn from past experience.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Autocracy and Society in Romanov Russia
course.description: The Romanovs ruled Russia from 1613 until 1917, when revolutions swept them from power. In three centuries, they transformed it from a landlocked country, inhabited largely by ethnic Russians, into a sprawling, western-oriented, multi-ethnic empire, governing well over 100 million people across some 8.6 million square miles. This course will focus on the techniques of rule that the Romanovs used to maintain and expand state power. It will inquire into the extent and limits of the reach of the administrative and military apparatus into subjects’ public and private lives. Nominally, Russia was an autocracy. How powerful were Russia’s Romanov autocrats in practice? What can the Russian experience teach us about the nature of the modern state?

subject: HISTORY
description: In this class, modern Jewish history means the period from the eighteenth to the twentieth centuries. It is the period in which Jewish culture became more diversified than ever before. Jews became more secular, more political, as well as more linguistically and religiously diversified than ever before. As ancient as Judaism is as a religious culture, the modern period gave birth to entirely new and now fully established forms of religious expression. During the period we’ll be studying, Hasidism, Reform, Conservative, and Modern Orthodox Judaism all emerged for the first time. From the standpoint of language, some Jews adopted vernacular languages for daily communication while others continued to speak Jewish languages. This happened among Ashkenazim as well as among Sephardim. Similarly, politics came to shape modern Jewish culture and with this development, the Jewish world split further in myriad ways. Among the topics we will examine are popular culture, religion, politics, language choice, urbanization, immigration, class stratification, religious experience, gender roles, war, the Holocaust, and the birth of Israel. Assigned readings will include a history of the Jews and many primary sources, which are first-person narratives written at the time events unfolded. Course requirements include one analysis of an object housed at the Magnes Collection of Jewish Culture in Berkeley (the class will visit the museum), two midterm exams, and a cumulative exam during finals week.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Jews in the Modern World
course.description: This course will examine the impact of modern intellectual, political, cultural, and social forces on the Jewish people since the eighteenth century. It is our aim to come to an understanding of how the Jews interpreted these forces and how and in what ways they adapted and utilized them to suit the Jewish experience.  In other words, we will trace the way Jews became modern.  Some of the topics to be covered include Emancipation, the Jewish Enlightenment, new Jewish religious movements, Jewish politics and culture, immigration, antisemitism, the Holocaust, and the state of Israel.

subject: HISTORY
description: Instructor bio: Yoni Furas is a scholar of modern Middle Eastern history, specializing in Palestinian history, the sociology of Arab knowledge, and the cultural dimensions of the Palestinian-Zionist conflict. His research focuses on the late Ottoman and British Mandate periods, with particular attention to intellectual life, education, and professional formation. His first book, Write down! We are a nation: Musa Kazim al-Husayni, a Political Biography (Tel Aviv University Press, 2017), examines the life and career of Musa Kazim al-Husayni, revealing him as the founding father of the Palestinian national movement. His second book, Educating Palestine: Teaching and Learning History under the Mandate (Oxford University Press, 2020), explores the development of historical consciousness through educational institutions, analyzing both Palestinian Arab and Hebrew pedagogical thought during the late Ottoman and Mandate periods. His most recent book, Palestinian Doctors: Medical Practice and the Transformation of Palestine, 1900–1948 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), co-authored with Liat Kozma, offers a social history of the Palestinian medical profession and examines how medical practice intersected with broader processes of social, cultural, and political change.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: History of Modern Israel: From the Emergence of Zionism to Our Time
course.description: The class explores the history of the Zionist movement and the State of Israel in all its complexity and contradictions. What is Zionism? What are its roots? Is it a liberation movement? A religious cause? A colonial ideology? A set of state policies? And what is the relationship between Zionism and the modern State of Israel? How do Zionism and Israel look different when considered from the standpoint of Jewish, Palestinian, European, or Middle Eastern history? Exploring Zionism and Israel from its roots in the nineteenth century to the present, this class offers in-depth knowledge and discussion on all of these topics and more.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Introduction to Science, Technology, and Society (Cal Teach)
course.description: This course is a parallel course to C182C, intended for students interested in teaching elementary or secondary school science and math. Students in the "T" course will attend the regular C182C lectures and a special section; this section will focus on techniques, skills, and perspectives necessary to apply the history of science in the juvenile and adolescent science classroom, including pedagogy, devising lesson plans for their classrooms, finding reliable historical information, and writing.

subject: HISTORY
description: The course deals with the beginnings of Christianity and its development into a legal religion in the Roman Empire. It traces the changes Christianity underwent as the Roman Empire changed into one of several powers in the Mediterranean alongside the Umayyad Caliphate and other post-Roman kingdoms. Focusing on the evolution of Christianity in the West, the course ends with the coronation of Charlemagne as emperor in Rome in 800 CE. Throughout, the beginnings of Christianity will be investigated in their historical context. That is, the emphasis will be on the societal givens that shaped Christianity. Those who made Christianity were part of those societies, and hence the development of the religion responded to the historical developments. The focus is therefore on the inhabitants of the Roman Empire and its successor states who became Christian. The course is based on primary sources and will include problems of historical method.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Christianity: The Beginnings
course.description: The course deals with the beginnings of Christianity and its development into a legal religion in the Roman Empire. It traces the changes Christianity underwent as the Roman Empire changed into one of several powers in the Mediterranean alongside the Umayyad Caliphate and other post-Roman kingdoms. Focusing on the evolution of Christianity in the West, the course ends with the coronation of Charlemagne as emperor in Rome in 800 CE. Throughout, the beginnings of Christianity will be investigated in the context of the societal givens that shaped it and to which the inhabitants of the Roman Empire and its successor states who became Christian responded. The course is based on primary sources and will include problems of historical method.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Eros: A History of Love from Ancient Greece to the Renaissance
course.description: What is love? An instinct, a thing of nature? Or an idea, a product of culture? European philosophers since Plato have sought answers to these questions, advancing in the process various theories about the relationship between nature, culture, and the human condition. This class considers these theories as a starting point of an historical exploration of love as represented in a variety of cultural artifacts from ancient Greece through the Middle Ages. Among them are the poetry of Sappho and Ovid; Greek and Roman sculpture; ancient, Byzantine, and medieval romances; marriage chests and wedding hymns; the letters of Abelard and Eloise; the New Testament and Augustine’s The City of God.

subject: HISTORY
description: Welcome to Berkeley Connect in the Department of History! This program aims to introduce you to History as a field of study and department, and to the wider community at Cal. You will work with two dedicated and experienced instructors/mentors to build a network of faculty, graduate students, alumni, and academic advisors. The core of this Berkeley Connect class is your attendance and participation in a variety of informative sessions and presentations organized by your mentors. Some sessions will be field trips to campus and/or local sites. Through these, you’ll learn more about History, research methods, and academic writing and resources to help you succeed in History and other social sciences and majors. All students with an interest in history are welcome to join. This class is open to all majors.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Berkeley Connect
course.description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

subject: HISTORY
title: Historiography of Modern Latin America
description: This seminar introduces students to historical scholarship on Latin America in the period since independence. Our discussions will focus on a selection of key themes prominent in the field. This semester’s themes will include: race and citizenship, environmental history, labor history, and global history. Over the course of the semester, we will read a selection of books in each of these subfields that illustrate the variety of methodological approaches that scholars interested in these areas have taken to understanding and writing about the past. In our discussions, we will consider the advantages of different approaches, and how trends in the scholarship have changed over time.

course.subject: HISTORY
course.title: Core Courses in the Literature of the Several Fields of History: Latin America
course.description: To provide a broad survey of the literature and historiographical problems of the different fields in history.

subject: HISTORY
title: The afterlife of Antiquity in the Greek, Latin and Arabic Middle Ages
description: The great majority of ancient literary works survive in manuscripts written more than a thousand years after the death of their authors. In spite of new discoveries in papyri since the late 19th century, the bulk of ancient literature that we know today is what medieval scribes and scholars chose to preserve because they saw in them qualities very different from the ones that interest Western modernity. The seminar will examine the motivation and mechanisms that enabled the transmission of ancient literary culture throughout the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. Reference will be made to the Greek, Latin, and Arabic Middle Ages. Problems in approaching the  visual culture will also be briefly mentioned.

subject: HISTORY
title: German Jewry
description: This seminar is designed to introduce students to an intensive examination of the major themes and issues concerning the history of the Jews in Germany from the eighteenth through the twentieth centuries.  Among the topics to be explored are the debates over Jewish emancipation, the German-Jewish struggle with Jewishness, Wissenschaft des Judentums, integration into and separation from the mainstream, German antisemitism and Jewish responses, economic and family life, and Jewish culture in the Kaiserreich and Weimar Republic.

subject: HISTORY
title: Imperial Russia, 1801–1917
description: This course offers an overview of scholarship on Imperial Russia. The first six weeks will survey standard readings on the nature of autocracy and its development in the nineteenth century, as well as the multilayered history of social "estates" and their transformation into social classes. In the second half of the semester, the syllabus will be tailored to student interests: ethnicity and religion; intellectual history; history of science, etc. Please contact me ahead of the semester so I can shape the syllabus to fit your needs!

subject: HISTORY
title: Interior Subjects: Public and Private Personhood in Early Modern England
description: Early modern England, once known to historians too grandiosely as the “first modern society,” was the site of precocious experiments to convert private subjectivity into public life, experiments we associate with the emergence of liberalism. In a wide range of contexts—religious interiority, republican theories of citizenship, life-writing, voting and majority rule, women’s roles in litigation, the rise of commercial credit, the bourgeois public sphere, and many others—interiority achieved a paradoxical new public significance, not only shaping people’s own experiences but shaping society. In this course, we will explore how early modern subjects created a familiar modern condition in which the more interiority matters, the more exposed it becomes. This focus will give students a chance to explore several canonical subjects in early modern British history and to think in novel ways about connections between them.

subject: HISTORY
title: Latinx/e Histories
description:
Latinx/e History is a critical and methodological intervention in North American History that challenges the broader field to reconceptualize the continent’s history from the ground up; center Indigenous, Black, and mixed-race communities; and decenter British America. Our reading seminar will examine the field’s origins in borderlands history and 1960s social movements and read several now classic texts like David Montejanos’ Anglos and Mexicans in the Making of Texas and Sarah Deutsch’s No Separate Refuge. We will also read more recent field changing texts like Camilla Townsend’s The Fifth Sun, Johanna Fernandez’s The Young Lords, Josefina Saldaña Portillo’s Indian Given, and Ada Ferrer’s Cuba. As we do, we will consider problems and difficulties in the field, collectively grappling with questions of race, gender, sexuality, indigeneity, and epistemic discrimination. 
 
The field of Latinx/e History is changing and expanding as new communities form and grow in the United States (often in step with ongoing U.S. imperial interventions in the greater hemisphere) and scholars interrogate some of the assumptions and categories of previous eras. Once a field centered on Puerto Rican and Chicano communities after U.S. annexation, it now encompasses many communities, geographies, and time periods. This presents an exciting challenge for the next generation of scholars and teachers on the frontlines of changing the narrative within and beyond the subfield, field, and discipline. 
 
This course is designed for history graduate students in the North American field, those who want to do North America as a second field or Latinx and/or borderland history as a thematic field, and those who want to deepen their understanding of racialization/racial construction, colonialism/empire, migration, and subaltern agency/survival. Students from other disciplines are welcome as well. For those who plan to teach U.S. history in the future, this course will give you a foundation for bringing Latinx/e history into your courses beyond 1848, 1898, and 1969.

subject: HISTORY
title: American Legal History
description: American Legal History (Law 267.4) is The Law & History Foundation Seminar for the Jurisprudence & Social Policy Graduate Program at Berkeley Law. It is a reading and discussion seminar taught under the auspices of the JSP Program, cross-listed with the Program in Critical Theory and with the History Department. The course is open to all JSP graduate students, Berkeley Law JD, LLM, and JSD students, graduate students from the History Department (History 280D) and the Critical Theory Program (Critical Theory 290), and graduate students from other campus programs and from other Bay Area institutions. As in previous years, Law 267.4 will explore the central themes of American legal development, while also investigating the way legal history has matured as a field of study or “discipline.” But we are living in interesting times, in which the varied exploitations of colonialism, racism, and capitalism have been made the subject of intense examination and argument. So this semester I want to give explicit attention to the question of how history – as theory, as philosophy, as method, or simply as narrative – can help us understand the role that law has played, and plays, in the construction of our times. The course will concentrate on the legal history of the United States, but it will begin and end with pointed glances at two other Anglophone common law jurisdictions – England and Australia. And, to set our discussion of theory and method in legal history off with a bang, we will begin with work by Louis Althusser, one of the most famous Marxist philosophers of the twentieth century, which poses the issue of how we should think about law as a phenomenon. In other words, what is law? Considered as a field of study, legal history is as much history as it is law, and history is primarily a discipline of the book. For this reason I have chosen to make Law 267.4 a course that focuses on books. Over the course of the semester our goal will be to develop a thorough grounding in American legal history’s formative literatures by reading a wide selection of the field’s best work, ranging from classics that have structured the field, stirred controversy, and inspired generations of scholars (like James Willard Hurst’s Law and the Conditions of Freedom and Morton Horwitz’s Transformation of American Law, 1780-1860), to the best work of the current generation of field leaders (like Laura Edwards’ The People and their Peace and Kunal Parker’s Legal Thought Before Modernism), to notable recent work by rising scholars (like Karen Tani’s States of Dependency and Ken Mack’s Representing the Race). We will accumulate considerable knowledge of the empirical substance of American legal history, but we will also give close critical attention to the very different ways in which scholars have chosen to write the history of American law (and the very different subjects about which they have considered it appropriate to write).

subject: HISTORY
title: Religion in the United States
description:
Religion is a “jack-in-the-box” that pops up and disappears in modern American history. Religion is “everywhere and nowhere” in histories of the United States. Religion is “hard for historians.” Religion has, in other words, presented a challenge to historians of the United States and, especially, historians of the post-Civil War United States. It is a topic of major interest to Americans who weave, recognize, or resist religion in their lives and a subfield connected to but sometimes set apart from many of the trending topics in American history. This reading seminar approaches religion in the United States as a vital area of scholarship with a tradition of its own and considers how it engages or resists dominant questions in current US historiography.

This seminar is designed for historians in the North American field, those who want to do North America as a second field, and those interested in religion as a thematic field. It will give students tools for thinking about how to incorporate religion into their own scholarship and future teaching. Graduate students from other disciplines in the humanities and social sciences are welcome.
